COMMODORE”S NOTES

With the AGM done and dusted I’m sure most of our thoughts are moving to the Festive Season, I know mine are.

There are a couple of points from the AGM and the subsequent Main Committee meeting. I was delighted to welcome David Thomas
to the Committee. He has announced his intention to represent the board sailors, something I see as a very positive move.

| was also very pleased to be able to co-opt Dave Williams to take over from John Salmon as Sailing Secretary. Dave is a very active
dinghy sailor and brings a lot of experience to the role. Kate, Dave’s wife and crew, tells me she will help to share the load of the
office, which is a recurring theme. Several of our Club Offices are now shared and it is working well.

One position that is not filled is that of Bar Manager. Maybe this duty could be shared between two or more members, there is
certainly no reason why this could not work. Please think hard and volunteer if you can. The bottom line is, no Bar Manager = No
Bar next season.

The AGM was less well attended this year than last, and the Committee agreed some minor changes to make the event more user
friendly. The venue will still be MASC Chelmsford, but the time will be 10.30 am. The Laying Up Supper will not be scheduled for
the previous evening,

This edition contains your Renewal Form for the year. Please make sure you fill in all the details including your insurance.

As I mentioned last month, this edition also contains the text of my Report to the AGM. It seems to have more relevance now than in
11 months time, when it is usually published. Useful bedtime reading if nothing else.

Have a good year.

Clive Shenton Blade Runner.

MSC AGM 1999 - Commodore’s Report

1.0 Introduction

I will now like to give the meeting my report on the Club for my first year as Commodore. It has been a year of steady
progress in many areas of the Club activity and I will attempt to summarise every aspect of the Club. I do intend to
mention names of members where they have been of particular service to the Club. Inevitably in a Club where at least a
quarter of the membership contribute to the running of the Club, I will not mention everyone and I apologise in advance
for any omissions.

I know that many of you have concerns about the MASC and how the take over by BAe will affect the future of the Club.

Most of you will know that Neil Pembleton is a Vice President of MASC and together with John Yorston, represents the
Sailing Club on that Committee.
Neil will make a statement on the future of the Club within the MASC, following this Report. This will form the first
item of Any Other Business. I ask you to save your questions on this subject until you have heard what Neil has to say.

2.0 Sailing

Sailing is the reason d’etre of the Club. I do not wish to preempt the Sailing Secretary’s Report, but I see all the signs of
robust good health in our Sailing Activities.

The Club enjoys extremely good sailing facilities with acres of boat storage space on land, excellent 24-hour access to
wide but still relatively sheltered sailing waters, and good back up facilities on land. Our members make good use of
these facilities in many divergent ways, which leads the Club to have a high usage, whatever the sailing conditions.

The Sailing Sub Committee under the chairmanship of the Rear Commodore Jenny Ball and the hard working Sailing
Secretary John Salmon controls sailing Activities. John is retiring this year after doing his three years and he leaves the
job well organised and in good condition for the next appointee.
Jenny and John, together with the fleet captains have arranged season long racing for all classes. This is no small
exercise, each race requires seven members to man the Race Box and run Rescue.

Another sub Committee Chaired by Lee Harrison, once again organised the East Coast Piers Race, which was another
resounding success with a new record amount of £5,300 being raised for Charity. The best cat sailors in Britain and
Europe continue to be attracted to the Race, and, despite a proliferation of such events, our Race continues to be unique
in its Charity concept.
The Club can feel justifiably proud of these endeavors.
Arrangements have already started for next years Race

Our Cruiser Section ranged far and wide, and this year has also seen a rebirth of Cruiser Racing with Frank Burgess,
Mike Tumer, Derek Gardner, Dave Payne and the Ball family much involved.

The Board Sailors continue to plough their esoteric wakes when the rest of us think the wind is only suitable to catch up
with the Gardening. We have successfully attracted a Board Sailor to seek nomination to the Main Committee. We look
forward to gaining an insight into the needs and aspirations of this section of the Club.

3.0 Safety

On stepping, down as Commodore Colin Kidner agreed to take on the unglamorous but essential role of Safety
Coordinator. The RYA has advised us that safety legislation applies to private Clubs as well as to business situations and
Colin has managed our response.

Fortunately the Club boasts a Health and Safety professional amongst its alumni, Malcolm Robertson. Malcolm has
worked throughout the year with dedication and skill. He has carried out Risk Assessments, Analysis and given advice
on operations. He has also helped in the formulation of Codes of Practice.
This year the launching and recovery of cruisers has been the subject of Malcolm and Colin’s attentions. I am sure they
would like me to recognise the practical efforts and enthusiasm of the Mooring Sub Committee in the detailed matters of
these operations, Murray Bates and Peter Clayton are the prime movers in that committee. Well done.

Certificated training in tractor driving has also taken place, again to bring our operations in line with industry standards.

We intend to eventually look at every aspect of the Cub’s activities both to comply with the law, but primarily to set up
systems to ensure that our fun is not spoiled by avoidable accidents.

4.0 Rescue

The Club continues to run three support boats, the Rib, Jack B and the Orkney.

This year the Main Committee agreed to improvements to the Orkney including a new engine and steering console, this
has greatly improved the effectiveness of this boat.

The Rib is nearing the end of its effective life, but continues to be the heart of our rescue strategy. Mick Richardson and
Rib Bosun Roy Hardwick have given much of their time to ensure that the Rib remains seaworthy, without excessive
expenditure.

The Jack B goes from strength to strength and is seemingly indestructible. This is an illusion, made possible by the
dedicated attentions of Geoff Josey, Gordon Preston, Ivor Pryke and Rob Davies. Jack B fulfills a duel role when it also
works with the Moorings and has proved its worth over the years.

The Sailing Secretary arranged a new and more efficient system of coordinating Rescue boat crews the year, and it is
working well. I sure his report will give more details. (Barry Hutt, Dennis Gilby and Tony Ferguson)

5.0 Cruisers

Cruisers make up almost half of the boats registered at the Club, Members who own cruisers enjoy good facilities at a
fraction of the fees charged by professional boatyards elsewhere on the East Coast. This pricing structure is only made
possible by the members themselves undertaking many jobs that are dirty, wet and physically hard. These self help
efforts alone would not be enough without the leadership of the Fleet Captain, Derek Kirby, and the work of the
Moorings Sub Committee under Peter Clayton and Murray Bates, which channels and manages the efforts of the
members to achieve the objective.

The Main Committee have authorised expenditure to power the winches and to purchase the travel hoist, which was
delivered in the late summer and has done good service during Laying up.

Tractors continue to be the most important single resource for handling boats on the shore. Our tractors are not new, but
the hard work of the Tractor Coordinator Roger Gibson and the mechanical skills of Roger Camp, have maintained the
tractors and even made modest improvements, at reasonable cost.

The moorings are layed and lifted each year by the members using the mooring barge. The investment made two or three
years ago in this barge continues to deliver efficient and low cost service to our members.

6.0 Cadets

For many years the Cadet Week at the Club has been an outstanding success, with many more applicants than available
places. This has been due to the efforts of Charles Anderson, Chris Davies, and the Cadet Committee and to yet another
team of dedicated helpers. This year was no exception, with over 70 cadets receiving instruction and a good holiday.
Two years ago the sailing and Cadet committees capitalised on this success by arranging Cadet Weekends at each Bank
Holiday, which have also proved popular. After many years Charles and Chris have stepped down. Peter Clayton, Steve
Monk and Kevin Dowley will take over the management of this winning team.

The medium and long-term future of any Club can be found in the enthusiasm of its Cadets. The future of Marconi
Sailing Club therefore must be assured.

Cadet Week constitutes but half of Camping Fortnight. I must thank Hilary Ashley for managing the applications once
again. This job requires the strength and judgement of Solomon to fit the supply to the over demand. Thanks Hilary.

7.0 Entertainments

The aftermath of last years AGM, produced several ideas and the volunteers to make them happen. Three such volunteers
were Claire Davies, Laura Gill and Hilary Ashley who asked to fill the vacant Entertainments Manager role.
The Committee arranged a Barn Dance in January, a Fitting Out Supper in April and a Quiz Night in September. All
events were well attended and enjoyable. They also served to bring Club members from various sections together in
social surroundings,
We look forward to Millennium Night at the Club on New Year’s Eve, and the Barn Dance at the end of January.

Steve and Debbie Glynn, arranged the Laying Up Supper last evening. Another very well attended, well organised and
most enjoyable event.

8.0 Membership

Our Membership has remained stable through the year at 413.
Within this figure many members are family members whose membership permits partners and children to use the Club
facilities which means around 1000 people make a call on the Club services.
I would like to thank Pat Black, Linda Chaplain and Steve Hill for their hard work in installing new software to handle
the tasks of membership.

9.0 The Site and Clubhouse

Three members have responsibilities for the Site. They are the Vice Commodore, Peter Bloomfield, the Bar Manager
Bob Goldbold and Clubhouse Secretary Mick Richardson. Steve Glynn Frank Bennett and Pat Black have also
contributed as has Mary Greygoose and her team of Ladies.
If the gate opened, the shower worked, the grass was cut, a pint was pulled or a bacon sandwich consumed it was due to
the organisation of one of these members.
Darren is the sole employee of the Club. He has operated a dedicated grass-mowing tractor during the year, and received
the necessary formal training. He has also undertaken regular cleaning duties
Tony and Wendy operated the Galley concession throughout the year, including the Winter Series. Judging from the
feedback I have received, they are delivering the service most people want.

Bob Godbold has been the Bar Manager for many years and has constantly worked to give the service most of us take for
granted. Bob is standing down this year to give another member the chance to shine in this role, We all thank Bob for his
work over the years.

Elsewhere on the site the cruiser park has been extended and a Cadet Cabin arrived free of charge courtesy of BP via
Steve and Debbie Glynn.

We must not forget Bob and Elsie Anderson, our gardeners, who have planted 20 kilos of bulbs donated by other
members, in addition to keeping the fewer beds tidy.

10.0 The Five Year Plan

The first, and most fundamental element of any Five-Year Plan must be that the Organisation should continue to exist at
the end of the period of the plan. Unsurprisingly the Main Committee embraced this ideal during 1998, and it continues
to be the prime objective.

In order to get early warning of outside influences that may affect the Club we have also adopted a policy of serving on
local Committees that deal with the future of the Blackwater. Ron Greygoose and I attended a one day Conference in
June that discussed the Blackwater Plan. Ron also attends the quarterly BACSPA meetings, and I join him whenever |
can. Derek Gardner and John Salmon also attend BJRC meetings. These Committees all serve to protect and enhance our
sport in the wider context of the River.

The Club spends most of its annual income on maintaining its present assets and on running expenses. However, every
year a small surplus is available to expend on capital purchases, and much of the time in Main Committee 1s taken up
with debate on where to allocate that money. In the past, the sections who have not been allocated expenditure have been
discontented. In order to rationalise this position in the future it was decided to plan our spending by the instigation of a
FIVE-YEAR PLAN.

The first step was to consult the members to ascertain where each member thought spending was desirable. The Plan was
announced in Navigans and a Consultation period was stipulated. By the end of that period I received replies from all sub
committees of the Club as well as about 70 direct communications from members. I have combined those replies onto
one list which has been circulated around Main Committee.

The next step is to arrive at a budget cost for each item on the list, which I often refer to by the shorthand of “Wish List’
I expect that such costings will be available by January, after which the Main Committee will discuss and prioritise the
items. I anticipate that we will be able to inform the wider membership of our deliberations at a meeting in April next
year.

I am expecting some lively Committee Meetings this winter.

11.0 The Secretariat

The Secretariat is made up of our Hon, Treasurer, Frank Bennett; our Hon, Secretary Pat Black and the Membership
Secretary Linda Chaplain. The Club cannot operate without the day to day attention to detail of these members, who
freely and willingly give up at least one day every week to their duties. Frank’s role is particularly time consuming, as
well as constantly giving good financial advice he is a familiar figure at Beehive Lane where he ensures the Club's
position is safeguarded.

Another important day to day task is that of Navigans Editor, and Kevin and Belinda Dowley have continued in the
traditions of Maureen Ball by producing an extremely readable and informative publication. They have recently achieved
savings by out sourcing the printing of the magazine, Tony Holbrooke distributes the publication every month.

Thank you all.

6

12.0 Unity

Over the last 12 months I have come to realise that one of the basic strengths of the Club is also one of its weaknesses
This strength is the number of sailing sections within the Club and the way that this enables us to fully utilise our
facilities. However the existence of sections gives rise to insularity and some friction between sections.

This friction sometimes manifests itself in a perception that too much spending has been allocated to one section. The
Five-year Plan is designed to overcome this problem. The Plan will make our spending intentions more transparent
which will led to greater understanding.

Another source of friction occurs on the rare occasions when our facilities become overloaded and members are
competing for the same space on the hard or on the water.

I, then, would like to end on a thought to take the Club into the next Century — Always try to see the other members point
of view, remember that he or she has a right to that view, and look for a middle way.

Let’s aim to unite the Club so we can meet the outside challenges of 2000 with one strong voice.

View from the Rear

And so ends another year! And looking back through the sailing programme for 1999. it has been a very full and successful year for
sailing at Marconi SC. The Commodore's report at the AGM really brought home the wide range of activities club members have
undertaken, both at home and away, in all kinds of boats and all this is borne purely out of enthusiasm and hard work!!

I should like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who has worked to support the sailing side of activities at the Club this year.
The members of the Sailing Sub Committee, (fleet captains, support boat co-ordinators, sailing and results secretaries), have all
worked very hard to co-ordinate sailing events and facilities throughout the year, allocating the clubs resources to the best possible
use. The Moorings Sub-Committee and the Club Bosuns have also worked very hard to maintain key items of club equipment eg
winches, tractors, support boats and to organise the complexities of mooring laying/lifting and cruiser launch/recovery, Finally, from
the sailing point of view, there have been a raft of volunteers to man the support boats and the race box each weekend and to assist
with Cadet events! I won’t try to thank everybody by name because | am bound to leave people out but I would like to mention John
Salmon, Peter Tovey, Geoff Josey and Roger Smith who have done sterling work for the club and have now elected to take a bit of a
rest! Welcome to new volunteers who have come forward to replace them and to carry on the good work.

Club Unity

Clive closed his Commodore’s Report for 1999 with a poignant reminder of the need for unity within the club. | would like to add
my own (somewhat obvious) comment that the real strength (or otherwise) of this club lies in the ability of all members to pul!
together to get things done. It was with some regret, therefore, that I noted the significant absence of certain sections of the club at
the AGM and the recent working parties (28th November / 5th December).

I know that the club makes many requests to you to give up your time and help out - from working parties, to committee meetings, to
race / OOD duties. 1 also know that we are all busy people with work, family and other interests to juggle outside of the sailing club.

However, putting in that couple of hours graft on a Sunday, (even if it is freezing cold!) or attending that meeting every month or
volunteering to maintain that piece of club equipment gives you many benefits in kind - namely, low membership fees, control over
how your club is run, a say in what your club facilities are used for and the ability to organise a full and varied sailing and social
programme for all members.

Do not be put off if you think you cannot commit enough time or help to be of sufficient use. Any help is beneficial and will take the
club forward - a few hours can make a real difference, If you've thought about it, call myself or any other committee member who
will be able to advise you on where your help will be needed. Please also try to support any other requests for assistance, such as
Working Parties, that may take place over the winter.

Here endeth the lecture.

Year 2000

The sailing programme for next year will be completed by the time this goes to press - 2000 promises to have a full sailing
programme as well as a number of social events, (it can’t always be hard work!). I am already looking forward to dusting off my
wetsuit and getting back on the water!

Wishing you a Happy New Year. Jenny Ball

AGROUND ON THE BAR?

Those who were present at the AGM will know that I have decided to take a rest from managing the club bar, and
probably noticed my surprise and pleasure at being presented with a beer tankard and gift token from our members who
have, I assume, enjoyed the results of my efforts over the years.

Firstly I would like to thank all those who contributed to this fine gesture and to assure them that the tankard is already
receiving regular exercise (after all I do have to keep in practice for the Friday evening sessions in the Dell Bar which
characterise the sailing season for some of us cruiser types). Also the gift token will be well applied, probably at the boat
show, for one of those luxuries that one never seems to get around to buying.

I particularly appreciated Pete's inclusion of the "king's shilling” in the tankard - he even managed to find a real shilling
(for the benefit of those born after nineteen-hundred-and-frozen-to-death; a shilling is an old 5p coin),

What was the kings shilling? As far as | remember the story:
In the days long gone, when service in the Royal Navy was a lot less than a career of choice, some under-handed tricks
were used to gain recruits. In particular you were considered to have volunteered if you accepted the "king's shilling”;
and to encourage sailors (and anyone else) to do so, gangs of recruiting officers were employed who frequented the
dockside pubs. There they would surreptitiously drop the shilling into the ale tankard of some unsuspecting drunkard.
Upon draining his tankard the shilling would touch his lips, which was conveniently assumed to constitute acceptance,
and he would probably awake from his hang-over on board ship and miles out at sea.

To avoid this trick tankards were made with a glass bottom (like the one which I received at the AGM) so that the
dreaded shilling could be spotted before it was touched.

And why the title of this piece "aground on the bar"? Well at present we still do not have a replacement to take on the bar
manager's job, so for the time being I continue to keep an eye on it. But be warmed that you also need glass-bottomed
tankards because I now have the shilling waiting to find a suitable home.

When we find a new manager I will, of course, be available to help whoever takes it on while they get into the swing of
things and to hand on information from our past operation.

Again, many thanks for your generous gifts which are greatly appreciated.

See you in the Dell Bar next season, or at New Year.

Bob Godbold.

WORKING PARTY SUNDAY 28TH NOVEMBER
This was the best turn out in recent years and a lot of work was carried out, as follows:-

Boundary Hedges. Good start on 'Cat field - a daunting task ably assisted by our high visibility Commodore!
Entrance Roadway Ditch. Good progress here on clearing this area.
Cruiser Park Hedges. More than half completed.
Cruiser Ditch Infill Space. A good start on clearance of this area has been made at the garage end. Sewage Plant/Calor Gas Compound. Cleared and tidied up in preparation for a new concrete base to accommodate a larger calor gas container, to enable us to obtain gas at a more favourable rate.
Broken drainpipe repaired This was near the water tap corner of the Clubhouse.
Winches Pete Sayer and helpers completed servicing and wintering all our active winches.
Tractors Roger Gibson hired equipment and steam cleaned all active tractors.
Boiler Room Door Rubbed down and painted by Pat Black.
Signposts. Seven holes dug and posts concreted in by enthusiastic gang
Dustbins. Emptied and rubbish cleared in cruiser park.
Hosepipe Stowage. Helpers led by Malcolm Yeoman dug holes and installed new steel posts, stop cocks and taps in Cruiser Park.
Jack B. This group led by Gordon Preston and Murray Bates positioned the travel hoist over the Jack B to provide a covered enclosure for work to be carried out during the winter period. This releases the normal Jack B tractor shed area for extensive re-furbishment to the four-wheel drive tractor.
Tractor Shed Extension. A gang led by Mike Smith commenced work constructing a ‘lean to' shelter on the rear of the tractor shed to house the red tractor and it's associated grass cutting and cleaning attachments, which hitherto have been laying out in the open all year round. The extension encroaches on to the windsurfers rigging area. This problem will be addressed by re-siting some of the winter-stored dinghies by the boundary hedge, thus making more space for the windsurfers.
Cold Showers. "Someone"!!! had recently turned off the club house gas supply hence no hot water. Gas now turned on and temperatures checked and re-set.

There was so much activity that you will have to forgive me if I have left anything out. Some of the work will be continuing over the winter and there will be another work party at the end of February, date to be confirmed in next edition of Navigans.

Footnote: Health, Family, Social and Work Commitments are all valid reasons for not being able to give up one Sunday to a working party but out ofall the members I have to say that there are many faces that are rarely or never seen. I would say to them come along and give it a go. You will be surprised at the satisfaction you can get from working along with others in a spirit of friendship and seeing a job well done

Peter Bloomfield
Vice Commodore

Thank you to all the volunteers who attended the work parties, just imagine what our annual membership fees would be if we had to hire contractors to complete all the tasks. Ed

cruiser park be kept clear of parked cars, especially unattended.

With regard to moorings Murray said there had been some problems early on, next year it is intended row "C" will be laid first
followed by rows "B" and "A". All moorings will be laid earlier next year, possibly being completed by the end of April.

Peter Bloomfield drew attention to the working party to be held on 28th November.

Election of Fleet Captain, Vice Captain and Race Co-ordinator was held and in the absence of any other contenders Derek Kirby,
Malcolm Yeoman and Frank Burgess were duly elected.

PAINT - Gordon Preston has undertaken to take on this onerous task. He has been on to suppliers who once again are prepared to
offer deals, providing there are enough orders, so please support this venture which benefits us all. Details are at the rear of this
issue.

MOORING CHAIN AND SHACKLES- Even though Don Holdworth has sold Milady D, he is still prepared to carry on the task of
obtaining chain and shackles at very advantageous prices. He can also supply both chain and boat anodes to those who need them.

PROPOSALS FOR 2000 SEASON - Everyone agreed the Shakedown Cruise to Burnham Yacht Harbour with an evening meal in
the Royal Corinthian Yacht Club be organised for late Spring Bank Holiday 27/28/29 May. Shotley would also be the venue for the
late Summer Bank Holiday 26/27/28 August with an evening meal on Sunday at the "Shipwreck Bar". It was also agreed that a
weekend visit to Brightlingsea be organised in May to host Peter Copeland (retiring Harbourmaster) and his wife to a meal at the
Colne Yacht Club. We will again be hosting members of the Royal Naval Sailing Association to a Barbeque at MSC on Saturday 9th
September, this has become an annual event enjoyed by RNSA and MSC members alike.

An enthusiastic vote of thanks was given to Bob Godbold for all his hard work in organising the Bar over the past years especially the
"Dell Bar" which has become a focal point of the Cruiser Fleets onshore activities.

Chris Davies outlined plans for a possible Cruiser Race in support of the Cirdan Trust, details have yet to be worked out with regard
to sponsorship etc. This is not intended to rival, but compliment the current ECPR, we await Chris Davies proposal with baited
breath. In the meantime members were thanked for their past support of the ECPR, long may it continue, it's for a good cause,

ANY OTHER BUSINESS - Winter meetings will take place at MASC on Thursdays 20 January, 17 February and 16 March.
Arrangements are being made with Ray Cruise to give a talk at the January meeting on the "Tall Ships" watch Navigans for further
details.

David Sandler, who is a new member indicated he would be willing to run an R.Y.A. Ocean Course, please watch Navigans for
further details.
Those of you who read Navigans (I sincerely hope you all do ED) will have noticed the Solo Fleet who, like us occasionally meet
socially off the water as well as on it, get together occasionally at Chelmsford for ten pin bowling. I therefore, approached them with
a suggestion that we get together for a match, they agreed and the date has been fixed for Saturday 19 February. Details will appear
in the next Navigans, anyone interested please contact me, I am sure it will be great fun.

Commodore's Notes

I wish all members good health and good sailing during 2000.

The New Year Festivities are now a memory, although I believe those members that celebrated at the Club have very rosy memories
of an excellent evening. I spent the holiday in the Alps and was rewarded with excellent snow and a terrific fireworks display.
Wherever you celebrated I hope you enjoyed it.

The racing sailors amongst us have cause to thank Derek Kirby for negotiating a relaxation of the recently extended 8 knot speed
limit in our sailing waters. While racing or training the limit will not apply to Club boats provided that a number of criteria are met.
These can be summarised as ‘boats must not be sailed in a dangerous or careless manner or in such a way to endanger or
inconvenience others’. We will continue to expect our sailors to observe the limit within our moorings and Club races will continue to
be set away from the area when speeds of 8 knots plus can be expected.
Please remember that concessions can be taken away as quickly as they are granted and act accordingly.

The BJRC is a long established group sailing the Blackwater and is supported by the majority of the sailing clubs on the river. It is
run by a general committee with each club having its own representative and has a separate handicapping committee to oversee
handicap fairplay.

It is well organised and efficiently run and gives the added opportunity to meet people from other clubs. The trophies have been
competed for since the mid thirties are rather fine and well worth winning for the year. As an added benefit the winners are generally
invited to the organising clubs Laying-up Dinner to receive their prizes!

For the Season 2000 there is to be a change from the regular Sunday only races. Most of the races will be organised around a social
event that will take place on the Saturday evening after the race, and there will, in most cases, be a Sunday race as well should you
wish to join in.

This new format is to try and encourage more boats to join the BJRC events. It is the intention to have shorter courses (duration of 3
to 4 hours) whilst still retaining the competitiveness that we have enjoyed in the past, although you do not need to be.an out and out
racer to compete.

A small joining fee (£12 pa) is payable to cover organisers expenses and postage. You do not need to pre register, as long as the race
organiser on the day knows who you are, he will inform the race committee. A Season 2000 Sailing Programme is attached so that
you can pencil the dates in your sailing diary.

We (Killara2) only compete in a few races per year, but we do thoroughly enjoy it. For Season 2000 it should be more fun with the
incorporation of the social events.

Muna’ Travels

PART ONE - LEAVING

By the time departure drew near, Muna's extensive refit had been going on for well over a year. She had been back in
the water for a couple of months during which time we had managed three or four trial sails back to Marconi to test our
various new systems. The last two or three weeks were predictably frantic, involving as they did final clearout of the
house prior to it being let and disposal of those things we just couldn't fit on the boat, cramming everything we were
taking on to the boat, stocking up of provisions, buying charts etc. etc., not to mention completing the fit out which in fact
went on to the very day of departure and beyond!

We finally set departure for Tuesday the third of August. We reasoned that however long we waited we would never be
completely ready and if we were going to get south this year we wanted if at all possible to be across the Bay of Biscay
by the end of August. High tide on the Tuesday was about five in the evening. As the day wore on, more and more
loose ends were finally tied. Bills were paid, the car was disposed of and last minute jobs completed. Word got around
that we really were leaving at long last and by the time the tide had made and we were ready to cast off an impromptu
farewell party had developed on the pontoon. Julian poured champagne over Muna's bows and presented us with a club
burgee. It was all a bit emotional, being seen off by many of the people who had been involved in Muna's refit and as we
finally maneuvered out of our berth | almost fell four of a marker buoy that the yard lads had put down right in our path!
We tied up for a few hours to one of the buoys just off the Nass Beacon. Then at one thirty the next morning we motored
out of the Blackwater in a flat calm and moonlight with the autohelm doing the steering (a new found luxury this - prior to
refit it had never worked properly). By dawn we were approaching the shivering sands fort where we attempted to sail
without success in light fluky winds. Resigned to motoring we plugged on in brilliant sunshine reaching Ramsgate by
about nine thirty. A light breeze encouraged us to sail, which we did as far as Dover. The wind died again but as it was
still early we decided to press on for Eastbourne. After a couple of hours the wind got up and we were soon sailing well
for the first time that day. By the time we reached Eastbourne just before dark we had a blustery force six on the nose.
Having found the entrance to Sovereign Harbour with some difficulty we locked in and were just tying up in a rather
oversized berth when the heavens opened and a 35 knot squall arrived. By the time we got below we were soaked
through.

We made the next day a lazy day and enjoyed the discreet charms of Eastbourne.

We made an early start the next morning locking out at five to be greeted with a beautiful morning and a slowly
developing north easterly, which allowed us a superb spinoa run to the Owers. | tried to get the monitor steering without
success but the autohelm handled the conditions well. By the time we had reached the Solent the wind had increased
appreciably and we got into a bit of a muddle getting the sails down before motoring into Portsmouth and picking up a
buoy for the night, just before dark and the rain started.

Another early start saw us motoring through a deserted Solent on the last day of Cowes week with the many craft that no
doubt could have caused us some embarrassment later in the day, still moored securely to their buoys. Out into Poole
Bay the wind got up from the South West and gave us an enjoyable beat, enjoyable that is until we realised that
subjected to extended immersion, the portholes on the starboard side in the saloon were leaking. What was particularly
galling was that they were never leaking prior to the refit but had been removed on the surveyor's advice for routine
examination.

On arrival in Poole we secured temporarily to a buoy and then managed to secure a berth in the Parkstone Yacht Haven.
A very comfortable, if expensive place to stay, we ended up staying for a week. When | reported the problem with the
portholes back to Tollesbury, Julian was very prompt in arranging for Steve, one of the people who had done a lot of
work on Muna, to come down while we were in Poole. We arrived in Poole on the Saturday. Steve arrived on Tuesday
and took the offending portholes out and rebedded them. We decided to go out the following morning for a trial sail to
see if we could get the portholes under and give them a proper test. This happed to be the 11th of August the day of the
Total Eclipse. | wasn't too happy about this initially, especially when we saw how many boats were leaving Poole
Harbour that morning. It was like the whole world had gone mad. The entrance channel was literally like a motorway
with yachts nose to tail and powerboats seemingly everywhere. Once clear of the entrance things calmed down
considerably as everyone made off for the area of total eclipse. There was enough wind for us to get Muna well heeled
)

over as we beat out towards Anvil Point. This trip happed to be Steve's first ever sail and I'm not sure that he found the
combination of heeling well over and being down below peering at the the portholes with a torch entirely to his taste.
However, when it came to the eclipse the clouds broke just sufficiently for us to get a good view and the rapid darkening
was quite awe-inspiring. The coastline was completely enveloped in darkness and all that could be seen were scores of
pinpricks of light as camera's flashed on the hills.

From Poole we had a lively sail to Weymouth with the races off St. Aldhelm's Head living up to their fearsome reputation.
Rafting up in Weymouth on a Saturday night in August was fairly hard work with little boats stuck on the inside of long
rafts of much bigger boats predictably wanting to get out. The next day we struck out across Lyme Bay. Like the last
time we were down this way | chickened out of taking the inshore passage round Portland Bill, when you pass seemingly
within inches of the cliffs, just inside the race and thus committed us to the long slog around the Shambles where for
several hours you seem as if you are getting nowhere. At one point | was sitting at the chart table plotting our extremely
slow progress against contrary tides (we had left early to get a fair tide across the bay and hopefully make landfall not too
long after dark) when | became aware of a persistent buzzing. Running through the various instruments that have
alarms, | failed to locate it until it dawned on me that it was the mobile phone. Picking it up | was amazed to find myself
talking to our youngest daughter Jenny, calling us from Australia, where she had been for the last ten months. It all
seemed rather surreal. In this day and age | suppose its nothing out of the ordinary, but when you're not expecting it, it
all seems rather strange.

Having picked up a favourable current in the bay we had a good beat across to Torquay creeping into the marina after
dark, as we had done on our last visit four years previously. We ended up staying in Torquay for five days while some
south westerlies blew through.

We set off early on the Friday in little wind and after managing a sail for a while were soon forced to resort to the engine.
Motoring through Plymouth Sound in a flat calm and brilliant sunshine we made for the Mayflower Marina in Devonport.
Our arrival in Plymouth coincided with strong north easterlies, which would have given us a fast if lively start to our
Biscay passage. We were in no rush as amongst other things we were experiencing problems with our brand new VHF
DSC. Right from the start it had not proved to be very user friendly and of all the new electronic equipment we had
bought, it was definitely the least satisfactory. Now it had started to develop addition faults such as changing channels
on its own accord and switching itself on and off. Tolley Marine where we had purchased it said that Sailor would send
us a new handset if we returned the old one first. | wasn't very happy with this as time was going by and | didn't want to
be delayed anymore than we had to.

Whilst in Plymouth the weather had deteriorated. By Wednesday 25th August the weather had eased slightly and we
had a pretty good sail in poorish visibility along the coast to Falmouth. Once there we carried on sailing right up the
Truro River to Malpas where we tied up on a visitor's pontoon, moored. In the morning we took the dinghy ashore and
did a pilgrimage to Muna's birthplace.

That night back on the pontoon we went through our options. We could go into Falmouth Marina and wait for favourable
winds. There was currently a high over the area giving little or no wind. However there were northerlies nearer to Spain.
The dilemma was whether to leave in little or no wind with the prospect of motoring at least in the early stages. We were
very conscious that time was pressing on. In the end we decided to make an early start downriver the next morning and
make a final decision when we got down to Falmouth.

PART TWO - BISCAY

Friday 27th August dawned bright and still. Starting the engine at seven thirty we motored downriver from Malpas in a
flat calm. After a bit of a wait we topped up our fuel tanks from the fuel barge moored off Falmouth. Then we motored
out to sea. On the way Helen phoned her brother-in-law Nick, who had been giving us long-range weather forecasts
from the Internet. His forecast confirmed that we were likely to have light winds initially with the prospect of stronger
favourable winds further north but nothing more that a five for at least the next few days. We decided to keep going.

As we had predicted the sea remained calm and the wind almost non-existent. We therefore kept on motoring knowing
full well that we had insufficient range to motor all the way even if we had wanted to. On the plus side the autohelm was
working with occasional lapses. We gradually got into our watch system, which at that stage consisted of three hours on
and three hours off. The night proved to be a pleasant one with a full moon. Early the next morning the wind made an
appearance. An early attempt at sailing petered out but as the morning went on a ten knot wind established itself from
10

the north and we managed to sail properly at last. The day was sunny and bright and the sailing was good. Up to this
point | hadn't managed to get the new monitor windvane self steering working. | now got out the manual and went
through the procedures in some detail. | then realised that | had mounted the windvane the wrong way round. The
difference when| tried it the right way round was miraculous!

That night just before dark we saw our first dolphins swimming right alongside the boat. We had some superb sailing
with the log reaching six knots in a calm sea and the monitor steering brilliantly. It was a pleasure to be on watch. We
had set a course well to the west and saw no ships at all that night. In the early hours the wind died again. By morning
we were struggling to keep up three knots. | reluctantly decided to start the engine again. Turned the key. Ignition light
came on. Pressed start button. Nothing.

After the initial sense of panic had subsided somewhat, | worked out that the problem was an electrical rather than
engine one. Decided that it was a question of by passing the solenoid in the control box. Avid reading of our electronic
troubleshooter failed to come up with the exact way of doing this. | didn't want to risk doing more permanent damage so
decided to leave things alone, at least for the time being. Meanwhile the day was spent trying to make to best of the little
available wind. More dolphins enlivened another warm sunny day. The light winds continued overnight and into Monday
morning with our speed rarely exceeding three and a half knots. | was beginning to get concerned about the state of the
batteries, which, in the absence of input from the engine had been relying on the solar panels. In my desire to preserve
power for the GPS | came very close to shutting down the sailing instruments.

At this stage the wind steadily increased from the northeast. By mid afternoon we were registering-a steady eighteen
knots true and our speed had increased to six and a half knots. In spite of it being a following wind the wind generator
began making a major contribution to the battery situation. That afternoon the Navtex started giving out gale warnings
for Galicia. At first we weren't exactly sure where Galicia was but then with some unease realised that La Coruna, where
we were heading, was right smack in the middle of Galicia. As the evening wore on the sea became increasingly lumpy.
We reefed the main and replaced the genoa with the yankee. Overnight the wind increased and we were registering
thirty-seven knots true. By morning we were down to staysail alone and still making between five and a half and six and
a half knots. The seas were coming at us from all directions. The state of the sea was a bit more comprehensible when
we realised that we were going rapidly from a depth of nearly five thousand metres to a rapidly approaching shore.

| went through a bad patch that morning feeling distinctly tired and unwell. Laura did sterling service for several hours
while | rested. As the day went on | recovered and took over. We sighted land somewhat mistily at about eleven that
morning. As we approached | managed to sail goosewinged for a while under reefed yankee and staysail. As we sailed
into the Ria the sun shone and we were grateful for the wind pushing us on past some treacherous looking rocks towards
La Corunda. Just before four in the afternoon we sailed around the breakwater and anchored off La Coruna.

No sooner had we anchored that a German came over and asked if we had engine problems. When | asked him how he
knew he replied "Because you sailed in".

A General Meeting of the Marconi Sailing Club will be held on the 6th March 2000 at the Marconi Athletic and Social Club, Beehive Lane, Chelmsford, commencing at 1930 hours

Commodore's Notes
January and February are traditionally quiet months for sailing, however we have been trying to run a Winter series when the forecast
is less than Force 7, but that has not been too often this year.

I was Race Officer at the end of January, and after deciding that racing was not possible, I went for a walk around our site. Although
there is not much happening on the water in the winter months there was plenty of activity in the cruiser park and especially in the
tractor shed, where repairs and maintenance to a tractor and the Jack B were underway. Our members truly are a dedicated and hardy
bunch of people.

The Barn Dance which was held on 29" January was a well attended and most enjoyable occasion. Barn dancing must be good
exercise too, judging from my poor aching body the next day. Thanks go to the Social Committee and Laura Gill in particular for
organising everything. Our President also ran a shove happenny game(but with 50p pieces) in the interval that enabled us to donate
£60 to the RNLI when he and I, Mary and Sue attended a recent Sherry Morning.

You will have noted in the last Navigans that we have called a General Meeting for 6" March at MASC Chelmsford. The purpose of
the meeting was stated in the Notice. but it has worried one or two members, who have contacted me. So, for clarity and peace of
mind I will summarise what it is all about. Some years ago Frank Bennett was able to negotiate with Customs and Excise to reduce the
tax burden on parts of our subscription income, and the saving was passed on to members. The VAT people have recently clarified
this exemption by saying that, in future, it will only be allowed to Clubs that declare themselves to be non profit making, that is where
no profit or surplus is distributed to members. In other words the exemption is only available to Clubs that are not run as a profit
making business. Furthermore this principle must be part of the Constitution of the Club. Hence the need to hold the General Meeting
to modify the Constitution.

I expect the Meeting to last less than 5 minutes, BUT, if we do not get a quorum of 30 members eligible to vote we cannot pass the
new Rule. So if you don't want to pay an additional 17 2% on your subs and get absolutely nothing for it, take the time to attend the
Meeting at 7.30 p.m.

Please don't leave it to others, come yourself.

By the time you read this the new season will be less than four weeks away. I for one am looking forward to it tremendously.
Clive Shenton

Part Three - The Spanish Rias

Within minutes of anchoring in La Coruna our new found German friend had shown me how to bypass the ignition system on the
engine and had the engine running, After he had done we reflection that we really had arrived in more ways than one. Looking round
the anchorage we realised we were among the cruising boats. Nearly every boat there had a wind generator and wind vane steering. It
was a lovely evening and I felt a very special feeling as the sun went down.

The next morning we inflated the Avon and Helen and I went ashore while Laura stayed on board and tidied ship. The helpful
Harbourmaster secured us to a marine berth and contacted a marine engineer. We were immediately impressed with La Coruna, a
bustling but untouristy sort of place. When we returned to the boat we discovered that the engineer had already been and sorted the
problem. Luckily it had been loose wiring that I hadn't detected rather than the solenoid itself.

We left La Coruna on Monday 6th September, visibility was marginal. We motored along the coast in flat calm, something of a
contrast to conditions when we arrived. As we closed the entrance to the next Ria we barely saw land as we entered. We anchored
and set about preparing supper. By nightfall we were surrounded by at least six other yachts, many of whom we were going to get to
know quite well over the next few weeks.

The next day still with little of no wind, we motored round the impressive Cape Finisterre, anchoring by the picturesque Puerto de
Finisterre. On rowing ashore we discovered that it was festival time.

The following day we managed to sail for a while towards the Ria de Muros. A particularly beautiful Ria. we managed to tour its
breadth and length in search of a suitable anchorage. We first ted a lovely secluded bay where having dropped the hook | decided
that some awesome looking rocks were far too close. From there we explored the little port of Muros where the harbour looked too
confined and the anchorage too exposed. We then enjoyed a pleasant sail across the Ria to Portasin where we anchored just outside
the Marina.

The next day as we made our way down the Ria visibility rapidly decreased until we were completely surrounded. The rest of the day
became something of a trial. By this time we were well on our way and decided that it would be as hard to go back as to go on. Most
of the time we had the auto pilot steering with Laura and Helen peering into the gloom while I stayed glued to the GPS and the radar
In this fashion we negotiated a quarter of a mile wide channel between an island and the mainland with a lit rock right in the middle of
the channel without seeing a thing. We had two near misses with fishing boats that came charging out of the fog, altered course round
our stern, gave us cheery waves and disappeared.

I was aiming for a bay by the little port of Porto Nova where I thought we could safely drop anchor as soon as it was shallow enough.
As we headed in Laura shouted from the foredeck that she could see land. I went on deck expecting to see the top of a mountain.
Instead I was greeted with the sight of a sunlit beach. As we were preparing to anchor the mist cleared further to reveal the harbour
entrance, Cautiously making our way we were greeted by the Harbourmaster in his launch who guided us to, then handed us a buoy.
Later on that evening when we were debating whether or not to inflate the dinghy to go ashore, the launch returned to offer us a lift
ashore. We had the same treatment the next day and when we left two days later the Harbourmaster came to see us off, but resisted all
my attempts to make any payment for all this service. The town itself appeared to be playing host to a motor bike convention. The
place was completely overrun. Day and night they could be seen and heard screaming up and down the waterfront, every wheclie and
backfire being greeted by cheers from the watching crowds.

From Porto Nave we had an enjoyable sail across to Bayona in the Ria de Vigo. On the way we passed some lovely beaches and
coves. As we negotiated the rocky entrance to Bayona we were greeted with leaping dolphins. Once at Bayona we found the marina
was full and had to anchor in the bay, Whilst in Porto Nova I broke a filling and had to visit the dentist. We found the dentist, I rang
the bell, explained the problem and within ten minutes I was sitting in the dentist chair. Problem soon corrected, no charge.

The next morning we were undecided whether or not to move down the coast into Portugal. our discussions as to the best course of
action became something of a marathon. Laura later described the conference as exceeding anything the United Nations could come up
with.

We left Porto Nova and had a pleasant sail to Vilano de Castello, 11 was a gentle spinoa run right up to the entrance.

10

Part Four - Portugal

Vilano de Castello gave us our first experience of Portugal and we found it to be an extremely positive one. It is a beautiful town with
a church set high on a hill above the town. So steep is this hill that an elevator runs up it.

When we moved to Leixoes our choice of weather wasn't quite so good. We found ourselves with strong head winds. deteriorating
visibility and a generally sort of yurgy sort of day. At one point a huge black cloud covered the whole sky behind us as a front moved
through. We had not idea what was about to hit us. In the event torrential rain with even further reduced visibility, As we made our
way to the harbour entrance a Cunard Liner leaving confronted us. Once inside the marina we decided that we would stay put for a
while. This was just as well, for the next two weeks were to give us some of our worst weather of the trip so far.

The day after we arrived at Leixoes several boats came in from Vilano. These were the last boats to come in for a while, because the
next day storm force south westerlies set in with a vengeance. On the Saturday gusts of 56 knots were recorded, in the marina. A
nasty swell came right into the marina and staff were hard pressed tying up finger pontoons that were trying to break away from the
main pontoons which themselves were bucking and twisting. That day we took a bus into Porto (Portugal's second city). It was a
fascinating place set on an incredibly steep riverbank. The back streets and shops that sell everything fascinated us.

We spent some time in the Internet cafe. One of the revelation's of the trip so far has been the wonder of E mail. Being a couple of
old luddites we were very wary of new fangled complications to life. Laura however. had discovered the convenience of E mail when
travelling in Australia and New Zealand. It took her a while in taking us through the various procedures. Once we tried it and started
getting messages back from people we were hooked. Communication on trips like this is always a problem. We came away with a
mobile phone, which whilst being incredibly convenient is also incredibly expensive. Internet cafes are a real saviour. Even boats
with Sat C and fax facilities on board, use the cafes whenever they can because it works out so much cheaper.

When we came out of the cafe the wind was howling and the rain was absolutely torrential. By the time we boarded the bus we were
soaked through. Back at the marina we found that there had been broken water pipes and all sorts of problems.

The next few days of enforced idleness proved to be a good opportunity for getting to know some of the many people who were
engaged in similar trips to our own. One thing we found very early on is that there is no standard formula. long distance cruising
people come in all shapes and sizes, age, background and sexual orientation etc. and sail in a wide variety of crew combinations. We
were surprised at how many young couples managed to get away comparatively early in their careers and fund quite longish trips.

Up to this point we had not used our SSB radio. Pat and Olivia on Aldeberran were on their way to Las Palmas to take part in the
ARC, as were several other boats we were getting to know along the way. When they had entered the ARC. they had been given a pre
ARC SSB frequency that could be used for ARC boats to make contact as they made theiir way to the Canaries. Like a lot of us Pat
had never previously used SSB. During August he had tuned into this ARC frequency at the allotted times and been very disappointed
not to hear anything. on about the third day of trying he had broken silence by saving "ARC net this is Aldebarran" and immediately
the airwaves had come alive with boats calling him up. Since then he had become the pivotal figure of the whole net. Everybody
seemed to wait for his voice every morning before they would come on air. Even though we weren't entered for the ARC, Pat
encouraged us to use the net as a means of keeping in touch once we had become separated, which we duly did. Ever since, halfway
across Biscay, we had come out of Radio 4 range, I had been having withdrawal symptoms for the Archers. Now suddenly I had a
replacement. The ARC net became a highlight of our day. The day to day gossip could be highly intriguing. We also built up a
whole dossier of information about possible ports of call, not to mention up to the minute weather reports from different places. Since
then we have come across other nets including an American one that gives out the most comprehensive weather information
imaginable. all emanating from one boat.

As the days wore on, people were getting increasingly restless. Eventually the winds decreased enough for several boats to make a
move, even though the wind direction was still very much north westerly. We decided to hang on in the hope of more favourable
winds. The Portuguese trades are supposed to predominate along this coast. blowing from the north east. For the whole of September
we only had approximately four days when this happened. In addition as you move further down the Portuguese coast there are less
harbours that are easy to get into. Many of the rivers have bars that can be treacherous. One of the boats with us in Leixoes had had a
narrow escape sailing into Porto when he had rolled in breaking waves on the bar and two crew members had been swept over the
side, Luckily they had been rescued by the local lifeboat.

We seriously considered heading directly for Madeira but only wanted to do that if we could be reasonably sure of some northerlies.
By Tuesday the 28th of September, we were fed up of waiting any longer and set off with just the faintest of northerlics. There wasn't

1]

enough wind to sail so we ended up motoring overnight, keeping well offshore to avoid the many lobster pots you get here and
arriving in Peniche just above Lisbon the next day. We had a lay day in Peniche and were very glad that we did. There was an
ancient fort there that up until the early seventies had been used as a political prison for the fascist regime that ruled at the time. It is
now a museum. I found going round it an extremely chilling experience.

We now had the option of pressing on still further down the coast or heading off for Madeira. We decided that if the promised
northerlies arrived we could head off.

In the morning we woke to find a fresh wind blowing us on rather than off the pontoons. The northerlies had finally arrived. on of my
self imposed deadlines had been to leave mainland Europe by the end of September. It was now Thursday the 20th of September.
Within an hour we had gone.

Part Five - Out to the Madeiras

We motored out of Peniche harbour, turned into the wind to put the sails up, pointed the boat in a south westerly direction, turned the
engine off and at last we were sailing again, the first time it seemed for weeks. With the wind generator and solar panels working well
it was to be more that two and a half days before we needed to run the engine again. That first day out we had fairly lively sailing
with winds of around twenty knots and a big sea running. With the main genoa set and the wind well aft, the monitor was steering but
with some difficulty. By pegging the tiller on one side Laura managed to help the monitor keep us on course.

By the next morning the wind had come even further aft, so we decided to give our, as yet untried, downwind rig a go. I should at
this point say something about this rig. When Muna had been built the first owner had had her equipped with twin booming out poles
which run in tracts on the mast, with the idea of at some stage buying twin downwind sails to be set flying. Along with this although
rigged as a cutter, Muna had been given a sloop genoa on roller reefing rather that a yankee. Although this genny had given Muna
much needed canvas in light air, it had never set that well to windward particularly when partially furled. I had always liked the idea
of having a yankee but didn't want to lose the extra area the genny gave us. I also wanted downwind sails but didn't want additional
sails taking up much needed stowage space down below. I was fascinated by twin headsail ngs as developed for round the world solo
events and people like Bernard Hayman. The more | thought about this concept, the more it made sense. The nig that finally evolved
consisted of the original forestay with roller furling genoa, just behind this an intermediate stay with a roller furling yankee and further
back still the original inner stay with hanked on staysail. For upwind work we now used the yankee and staysail and this combination
had already proved itself well. Downwind we could set the yankee and genny together. That's when the rig really came into it's own.

Now for the first time we were able to put the concept to the test. Back in Tollesbury David had painstakingly explained how to stay
the poles properly. In fact to be honest he'd explained it to Laura having given up on me! Following his instructions Laura and I now
set up the poles and unfurled the genny and then the yankee. The effect was both instant and miraculous. Muna steadied herself and
set off at a pace steering herself downwind before we even had chance to set the monitor. With the monitor set we found she would
steer thirty or forty degrees either side of downwind without any trouble at all. I have heard that some boats roll more with twin set.
We found quite the reverse. We were still rolling. but nothing like as badly as we had been with the main and genny goosewinged.
What is more there was none of that rhthymmic chatting that you generally get with a preventer rigged on the mainboom. In short we
were dead chuffed. On arrival in Porto Santo | quickly became a downwind rig bore in my attempts to convince people of the
amazing properties of the set up.

During Friday the wind eased to around 15 knots and the sea calmed considerably. The monitor who by this time had been christened
‘milk' steered us unerringly on. With the settled conditions we were enjoying a very pleasant routine, With no need to hand steer,
straightforward navigation and very little in the way of shipping, our nightwatches were very undemanding and we were doing four
hours on and eight hours off. which was something of a luxury. Helen was carrying on her tradition of preparing superb evening
meals at sea. In all life was good. I found myself spending a good part of my night watches, lying on my back looking up at the stars.
Studying the milky way I tried to remember when I had last seen it looking so clear. I finally remembered that it was on a cigarette
cards I had collected when I was a kid.

At one point that day we sighted a ship dead ahead on a reciprocal course. As it closed on us we altered course sufficiently for him to
pass down our portside. As he drew level I sat down at the chart table to record his passing in the log. As I did so the VHF crackled
into life "Muna, Muna this is ....... Having got over the shock of being called up by name in mid ocean, | set about responding. This
was a bit difficult, as by this time our main VHF set was refusing to transmit at all. I called him back on the handheld VHF. He
started off by complementing me on my fine vessel, Warming to him considerably we ended up having quite a lengthy chat.

12

On Saturday the wind gradually veered until it was too much on the beam for us to hold the downward ng. Reluctantly we dismantled
the poles and reset the main. Overnight conditions deteriorated. By Sunday morning the wind had increased to 25 to 30 knots, the
seas were decidedly lumpy and confused, the sky was overcast and it was raining. The monitor was having difficulty in steering. At
different times we all felt pretty awful. The conditions had given us a disturbed night and we were all feeling the effects,

As I had been charting our progress towards Porto Santo I had become concerned about the fact that we were sailing in depths of
several thousand metres, but right in our path was a tiny spot of just twenty metres. The more I| thought about it the more | disliked
the idea of sailing night over the top of a mountain, or as | preferred to think of it, an island that didn't quite make it. Every time |
plotted our position we seemed to be heading inexorably towards this spot. In an effort to avoid this spot completely | put in a course
change which only seemed to make our motion worse.

By nightfall the wind backed sufficiently for us to revert to the downwind rig. Peace descended once again and the seas moderated as
we settled once more into a pleasant round of night watches. The next day provided another pleasant sail, enlivened by the spectacle
of pilot whales and as the afternoon wore on our first sighting of the mountains of Porto Santo. We had known for some time that we
would be arriving at Porto Santo during the night, unless we made a particular effort to slow down and arnve the next day. Having
talked to Pat on the SSB, who had arrived there in Aldebarran the previous night, it seemed to be quite feasible to enter after dark. He
gave us some useful bearing lines for avoiding some unlit ship mooring buoys that lay near the harbour

We sailed on towards the island as darkness fell. Eventually as the wind dropped we started the engine but left the downwind ng up.
Somehow or other the monitor managed to keep steering us.

As we approached the anchorage just outside the harbour, Pat call us up on the VHF to say that he could see our lights. Calling him
back on the handheld VHF I realised that he was trying to guide us into the protected anchorage inside the harbour. Unsure whether
this was wide I called him back only to discover that our handheld VHF had chosen this moment to stop receiving. We now had a
farcical situation of a VHF that would only receive and a handheld that would only transmit. After our third circuit of the rather
crowded harbour we eventually anchored.

Malcolm and Helen Shaft......... log to be continued in next edition of Navigans.

Commodore's Notes

Many of our members have been busy through the last month.
The scheduled day for the Working Party tumed out fine, and about 40 members spent a full day maintaining the Club.
Our Vice Commodore, Peter Bloomfield, got us all well organised. The bramble cutting exercise was completed, thus
releasing areas of the site that we had forgotten existed.
Meanwhile the ladies cleaned the Clubhouse and work continued on the new tractor shed. The windsurfers, without the
benefit of wind, concreted some bases, a skill which they have honed by constant practice.

The General Meeting was held, and the motion was passed unanimously, so we will not have the spectre of VAT on our
subscriptions hanging over us. My thanks to the 30 odd members, in addition to the Main Committee, who tumed out to
ensure we had a quorum.

Elsewhere other winter tasks have been progressed. Tractors have been serviced, repaired and painted, the Rib has had its
seams stuck together by a professional and a new launcher is being made. There has been a lot of work done on the
mechanical side of Jack B, which is ready to launch, but the paintwork will require some action later in the season. As
usual the Moorings Committee have been busy with their black arts involving chain and shackles, sinkers, winches and
barges. Peter Clayton's brow has its usual pre-season furrows, but he says everything is under control and moorings will
be laid to schedule.

Hilary Ashley has again agreed to take on the role of Camping Week Co-ordinator's, a job that needs the judgement of
Solomon. We expect to publish the application forms for Camping Fortnight in the next issue of Navigans.

As you read this, the Racing season should be underway. I would like to call the attention of our Racing members to the
year long Bank Holiday series of races. These are all-in races run on the Sunday and Monday of each Bank Holiday
weekend. I am thinking of putting up a trophy for this series, so 1 would like to see a good entry.

Enjoy your sailing.
Clive Shenton.

At last, the winter is over (well, nearly) and the sailing season will be upon us by the time you are reading this edition of

Sailing Matters:

I have just spent a day on the water with a team of Sailboarders in the Club's Orkney which will, (among its many other
uses), be a support facility for the sailboarders when they are out during in the winter or during the week when other
members or an OOD are not around. Arrangements have been made so that specific members of the sailboard fleet have
access to appropriate keys and will be able to launch the Orkney in the case of an emergency. We spent a very useful day
going through the launching / recovery process and practising boat handling, man overboard skills and how to tow
windsurfing kit in the safest manner. I am delighted that we are able to maximise the use of the club’s property in this
way to enhance the safety of more of our members when they are sailing.

On the subject of safety, | have been in discussions with Stone Sailing Club about the positioning of our race marks. As
many of you may be aware, the Stone No.2 mark was very close to our F mark last year - and there were a number of
close shaves when the two fleets happened to be rounding the marks at the same time. As F mark is a Fisheries buoy, we
are not able to change its location and Stone have therefore kindly agreed to lay their No.2 mark further east this year. In
return, I have agreed to review the position of our B mark which is quite close to another Stone race mark. Hopefully,
with this co-operation, we should have safer race courses and be able to avoid some of the near-miss situations we had last
year,

Dinghy / Cat Park Matters:

Some of you may be aware that I have spent some time reviewing both the Cat and Dinghy Parks this winter - mainly in
an attempt to identify those boats / equipment whose owners are no longer fee-paying members and asking their owners to
have it removed. One important thing | noticed was that hardly any of the boats (both dinghies and catamarans) are
marked with their owner’s name or contact details. This has rendered my intent of clearing unwanted kit virtually
impossible. Could I take this opportunity to remind you that all boats stored at Marconi Sailing Club must be clearly
identified for the following reasons:

e Your boat may be damaged eg. by storms or another boat and another club member needs to let you know.
e Your boat may need to be moved from its current location and a club official would need to advise you of this.
e It identifies that your boat has not been “abandoned” at the club.

None of us would want to come to the club and find that our boat had been moved or damaged and no-one had bothered to
let us know. However, there are a large number of boats where we would not be able to contact the owner because there
is no form of identification. I have put a note to this effect on those boats that do not appear to have their owners’ details
displayed. I would be very grateful if you could mark up your boats accordingly. If you have any queries regarding this,
please do not hesitate to discuss it with myself or your fleet captain.

Thanks!

Finally, a big thank you to those sailors who turned up to the Working Party on 20th February. With the help of delightful
weather, a substantial amount of work was completed - including the much needed clearing of ditches, building of
concrete steps, work on the club support boats etc. Thank you!

Those of you with good memories will recall the RYA advice that Sailing Clubs like ours need to address the issue of
safety. If you read Navigans you will have seen that the Safety Committee reports at each Main Committee meeting. In a
nut shell Malcolm Robertson, a qualified marine safety engineer, has been assessing the hazards in activities associated
with cruiser launch and recovery and moorings laying and recovery. Following these assessments the Safety Committee
discuss his observations and use the information to draw up Codes of Practice for the different operations.
I will be monitoring practices at the club during the coming season to see if we are doing what we say we should be
doing!

particularly on a Sunday when dinghy racing is taking place, and I would like to remind all club members of the agreed
practice for this activity. I have extracted the relevant section from the ‘Dinghy Code of Practice and would ask all
members to read this extract carefully and bear it in mind when using the hard when dinghy racing and cruiser launching

or recovery is taking place.

I hope you agree that this code of practice allows all club members to use the hard safely for their preferred activity.
If you have any observations or suggestions which you think will improve safety during these operations please pass them

Agreed Code of Practice for Beach master during Launch / Recovery of Cruisers which all
Club Members should understand and accept.

Beach master role as defined in the Dinghy Code of Practice 1999 MSC P0102

2.1 Access to the hard through the gap in the sea wall and a 3.6 metre (12 ft) strip from this gap to the low water mark
should be kept free of parked dinghies and launching trolleys at all times. Dinghies can be launched or landed on any part of
the hard except during launching and recovery of cruisers.

2.2 When cruisers. are being launched or recovered on a Sunday or at any time when club dinghy racing is scheduled in the

with the Beach master’s instructions at all times. The cast side of the hard MUST NOT be used by sailing dinghies when
cruisers are being launched or recovered.

2.3 It is important to be particularly aware of cruisers being launched or recovered when approaching the hard to land
because of.

2.3.1. the risk of a serious accident should the cruiser be lowered onto a boat and crew

2.3.2. the risk of striking a partially submerged cruiser trailer and resultant injury to crew or damage to sailing
dinghy. The support frames of the cruiser trailer will be visible above the surface of the water to provide warning of the
trailer being partially submerged

2.3.3 the risk from steel wire ropes when winches or tractors are in use, Personnel who are not directly involved with
the launching or recovery of cruisers should stay well clear of the operation.

2.4 During lunch breaks between races when the hard becomes a large dinghy parking lot, safe parking of dinghies is
available at some states of tide on the east side of the scrubbing posts towards the club race box. At times when, due to high
tide, space is restricted early finishers of races should take their craft into the dinghy/cat parks.

It was agreed, at the last Safety Committee Meeting. that the practice of launching/ recovery of cruisers should not take place when

dinghies or cats were launching or returning from racing. Where a launch / recovery operation was in progress and this clashed with

the departure or return of dinghies or cats then the launch or recovery of the cruiser should be halted where this was practical and safe

to do so. Where an operation was in progress and could not be stopped then dinghy or cat owners should be warned and be asked to

keep clear. This warning and request should be given by the Beach Master.
