MARCONI SAILING CLUB

Code of Practice for Dinghy Owners. Revised 15th February 2000

1, General

1.1 This code of conduct has been produced to provide club members who sail dinghies with guidance. A similar document
has been produced for Cruiser sailors. By following the advice given all club members will find the club will operate
smoothly and provide a better environment for us all to gain benefits from the club facilities. "Dinghy" is used in this
document to encompass Dinghies, Catamarans, and Sailboards unless otherwise specified.

2. Use of Hard

2.1 Access to the hard through the gap in the sea wall and a 3.6 metre (12 ft) strip from this gap to the low water mark should
be kept free of parked dinghies and launching trolleys at all times. Dinghies can be launched or landed on any part of the hard
except during launching and recovery of cruisers.

2.2 When cruisers are being launched or recovered on a Sunday or at any time when club dinghy racing is scheduled in the
year book, a member of the cruiser fleet will act as Beach master and oversee activities on the hard. Members must comply
with the Beach master’s instructions at all times. The east side of the hard MUST NOT be used by sailing dinghies when
cruisers are being launched or recovered.

2.3 It is important to be particularly aware of cruisers being launched or recovered when approaching the hard to land
because of:

2.3.1. the risk of a serious accident should the cruiser be lowered onto a boat and crew.

2.3.2. the risk of striking a partially submerged cruiser trailer and resultant injury to crew or damage to sailing dinghy
The support frames of the cruiser trailer will be visible above the surface of the water to provide warning of the trailer
being partially submerged

2.3.3 the risk from steel wire ropes when winches or tractors are in use. Personnel who are not directly involved with the
launching or recovery of cruisers should stay well clear of the operation.

2.4 During lunch breaks between races when the hard becomes a large dinghy parking lot. safe parking of dinghies is
available at some states of tide on the east side of the scrubbing posts towards the club race box. At times when, due to high
tide, space is restricted early finishers of races should take their craft into the dinghy/cat parks.

3, Storage of Dinghies and Catamarans.

3,1 No boats may be brought to the club before registration and payment of the appropriate fees. unless specific permission is
granted by the Club Secretary. All trailers and launching trolleys must be clearly marked with owners name, boat
number, and telephone number. Boats should also carry some means of identification, eg. boat number.

3.2 Boats which are not clearly marked and show signs of neglect and could cause damage to other members boats will be
moved by representatives of the club to an areca away from other members boats.

3.3 Dinghy Park (Monohulls)

3.3.1 The Dinghy Park is available for occupation as soon as it is marked out pre-season and allocation sheets are shown on
the notice board. This is normally in early March. If in doubt call the Dinghy Park officer. At end of season the boats must be
removed when requested in Navigans.

3.3.2 Particular positions are taken up on a first-come, first-served basis, although dedicated areas are reserved for recognised
fleets and larger boats. These segregations should be adhered to.

3.3.3 Members shall park their boats in an appropriate area and write their name and boat details on the allocation sheets on
the Club Notice Board.

3.3.4 Members shall keep their allocated boat parking space tidy and the grass cut. Motor vehicles must not be brought into
the boat parking area. Road trailers must be stored in the trailer parking area, fitted with a locking device to prevent theft, and
marked in accordance with 3.1,

3.3.5 All dinghies WILL be securely tied down with no projections above ground level. Fixings shall be able to with stand
all possible wind conditions to prevent the dinghy from falling onto other boats. It is the club members own responsibility to
ensure the anchor attachments are adequate. Experience has shown that anchors 500 mm (18 inches) long formed from 50
mm x 50 mm (2"x2") angle iron is the minimum suitable. The whole of the anchor must be below ground level to allow for
grass cutting and to avoid injury to bare feet. The anchor should be shared between adjacent boats. It is also necessary to
ensure that the front of trolleys are secured if raised.

3.3.6 Dinghies, trolleys, and sails should not be left between parking lines obstructing access to the dinghy park for other
members,

3.3.7 All dinghies left at Stansgate during the winter months must move from their summer position to a winter position
along the hedge at the end of the season as announced in Navigans. (See 3.3.1) Winter storage can be paid in advance at the
renewal of annual subscription. In addition to the standards set out in 3.3.5 all dinghies must have their masts lowered before
being left for the winter.

3.3.8 A check will be made before the 1 December to ensure that owners of boats remaining in the Dinghy Park have paid a
winter storage fee.

3.3.9 Late payment of the winter storage fee will involve payment of a late fee determined by the Committee.

3.4 Catamaran Park

3.4.1 Each catamaran will be allocated a spot by the cat fleet captain. Members shall keep their allocated boat parking space
tidy and grass cut. Motor vehicles must not be brought into the boat parking area. Road trailers must be stored in the trailer
parking area and fitted with a locking device to reduce the risk of theft, and marked in accordance with 3.1.

3.4.2 All catamarans WILL be securely tied down. Fixings shall be able to withstand all possible wind conditions to prevent
the catamaran from falling onto other boats. It is the club members own responsibility to ensure the anchor attachments are
adequate.

Experience from the 1987 hurricane has shown that anchors and tie-downs must be able to withstand forces estimated at
1Ton. Boats not secured with suitable high standard anchors and tie-downs may be stripped of mast and trampoline by
representatives of the club to reduce the risk of damage to other club member's boats. IT IS RECOMMENDED THAT
DUCKBILLED GROUND ANCHORS ARE USED TO SECURE CATAMARANS. THESE ARE AVAILABLE
FROM THE CLUB THROUGH THE FLEET CAPTAIN.

3.4.3 All catamarans left at Stansgate during the winter, unless sailed regularly, must have their trampolines removed and
masts lowered before being left at the end of the season as announced in Navigans. Winter storage can be paid in advance at
the renewal of annual subscription.

3.4.4 A check will be made before the 1 December to ensure that owners of boats remaining in the Cat Park have paid a
winter storage fee.

3.4.5. A late fee determined by the committee is payable.

3.5 Wind surfers.

3.5.1 Sailboards should be rigged in the area in the dinghy park to the south of the Tractor Shed. Members should park their
cars in the Sail board car park after driving through the dinghy car park. The Sail board car park may be accessed via the hard
road in front of the clubhouse between 30 November and the first dinghy racing Sunday in March. Access to the water is
directly over the sea wall.

3.5.2 It recommended by the Coast Guard that wind surfers carry an orange distress flag when sailing. This flag should be
used when individuals require assistance. If the inshore rescue boat is called this flag will help the crew rapidly locate
individual(s) needing assistance.

3.5.3 The Coast Guard recommend that they are contacted (Ring 999) if a rescue is instigated by Club members so
that they are prepared to help if necessary. INFORM COAST GUARD OF THE OUTCOME. If personnel are
10

rescued but equipment is NOT RECOVERED then the Coast Guard MUST be informed so that fruitless searches for
personnel are not made.

3.5.4 If you are wind surfing on a day when racing is not taking place, it 1s strongly recommended that Windsurfers sail in a
group comprising at least three people. Should one person need help it will require at least two people to launch a support
boat to provide assistance.

3.5.5 In order to provide a level of support for Windsurfers on days when the Club dinghy racing programme is not taking
place, the following arrangements have been made'- Keys to access the Orkney (Garage No.5) and the Fuel Store have been
placed in a security box at the back of the Clubhouse lounge. A number of regular Windsurfing Members have access to these
keys, and have undergone a familiarisation session with the Orkney,

3.5.6 Before sailing - identify who you will need to approach if the Orkney needs to be launched during the day. Do not wait
until there is an emergency to do this - it will only delay you and waste valuable time. This will either be the OOD (on
Saturdays or Sundays) or one of the Windsurfers with access to the security box - (list of names posted on the Clubhouse
notice boards).

3.5.7 If you are sailing during the winter. check the availability of the Orkney as the boat or engine may require a service
during this time. Ring the Rear Commodore.

3.5.8 If the Orkney is used, then full details must be entered in the Log Book which is kept in garage No.5 with the Orkney

4, Personal Safety

4.1 Members, their families and guests are responsible for their own personal safety and the MSC, Committee and the MASC
cannot be held responsible for the actions of an individual. Advice given by any official of the Club is of an advisory nature
only, ’

4.2 Parents and guardians are warned that the Club is only able to provide support facilities for Club racing. Parents and
guardians have sole responsibility for their children and wards and must appreciate that the Club cannot be expected to
exercise supervision or control.

4.3 Club support boats have a prime responsibility to assist in protection of human life. The Duty Coxswain is in charge of
each rescue operation and dinghy crews are asked to assist the Rescue Services by following their instructions completely
Members boats will only be recovered if the operation will not place human life at risk.

4.4 All dinghies used from the Club shall be fitted with buoyancy to Class rules, or as the Committee may require.

4.5 It is recommended that members and their guests shall wear personal buoyancy when sailing. A wetsuit is not
considered to be adequate personal buoyancy. The wearing of this buoyancy shall be the personal decision of the
individual. Members and their guests are advised to wear Wet/Dry suits between the end of October and end of May
(Winter and Spring) whilst sailing.

4.6 It is strongly recommended that all sailors should carry a sailing knife which has a sharp blade and a shackle key

If you are sailing alone it is recommended that hand held flares are carried. These are available at the club and can be
purchased from the Officer of the Day or the Rear Commodore.

4.7 Under 18 year olds using Club dinghies shall wear personal buoyancy at all times, and between the end of October and
end of May (Winter and Spring) shall wear Wet/Dry suit whilst sailing.

4.8 Flag N flown from the Club house mast-head will provide the following information to members.

4.8.1. Flag N (Blue and White check) : All club racing abandoned. We advise NO SAILING AT ALL.

5. Speed Limit

5.1 An 8 knot speed limit exists along the full length of the southern shore of the river. Members are reminded to be
particularly cautious when leaving or approaching, the hard where swimmers are liable to be in the water and to exercise
caution when in the yicinity of moored boats. This warning applies particularly to catamarans. Any racing
dinghy/catamaran exceeding this limit may be protested and could be disqualified.

5.2 Any boat/dinghy/catamaran sailing within the cruiser moorings should exercise extreme caution, particularly with regard
to laden tenders manoeuvring around such boats.

6. Collisions

6.1 Any collision between boats sailing from the club must be reported to the owner of the vessel within 7 days of the
incident and reported to the OOD so that a record can be made in the OOD log. If a collision takes place when there 1s no
OOD on duty the helms person must contact an officer of the club and provide the name or sail number of any boat with
which they collide and brief details of damage. The only exception will be when all the vessels involved are racing from the
club and the appropriate penalty is complied with. There is an up to date membership list in the upstairs bar where members
should find addresses and telephone numbers to assist when making contact. In case of difficulty please contact the
Membership Secretary for help.

6.2 While racing, any dinghy/catamaran in collision with a moored cruiser shall retire. In the event of a helm not voluntarily
retiring and being subject to a protest, he/she will be disqualified. In this case the DSQ becomes a DND

Commodore's Notes

After good weather in February and early March, the sailing season starts and what do we get? Snow! There's a message
there somewhere.

I am pleased to be able to tell you that we have had a volunteer for the vacant Bar Manager role. His name - Neil
Pembleton. We are seeking to arrange for bar supplies to be delivered to the Club, so that will lighten the load. Also Neil
has announced his intention to manage, not do all the work himself and to this end the Main Committee believes that each
fleet should provide one person to join the bar committee to share the load of running the bar. This does not mean that
they will become glorified bartenders, far from it, the bar will continue to be staffed by the OOD and other designated
members. The members of the Bar Committee will each contribute to the smooth running of this facility.
If you think you would like to join the bar committee please contact me or Neil, we need your help.

Those of you who have been at the Club in the last few weeks could not help but notice that we have a new tractor. Well
its not new but the old 4 wheel drive tractor that has been the subject of major refurbishment. Thanks go to
Jack Goody, Gerry Champion, Harold Griffiths and Russell Hadley, not forgetting the ever present Murray Bates for a
hard winter's work.
Well done gentlemen.

I now wish to talk about the Five Year Plan.
You will recall that we carried out a major consultation with the members last year, which | have sifted, interpreted and
categorised. The raw list of suggestions would fill four Navigans but my summary of your suggestions is given elsewhere
in this edition of Navigans. If you don't recognise your suggestion its probably because I have included it under a slightly
different description, but its there some where I assure you.

A word of caution, every suggestion on the list has been made by a fellow member, in writing. Plainly it was important
enough for that member to take the time to do so. If the suggestions do not accord with your vision for the Club, please
respect the members right to hold a different view.

From this long list the Main Committee first arrived at accurate budget figures, and then began a winter of discussion and
analysis,
We have reached consensus within Main Committee and it is now time to open the debate to a wider audience.

It is my intention to publish the summary of the Main Committee's deliberations in the next Navigans. This will be
prioritised, costed and have a program for its delivery. In the next edition I will set a date in mid June for an open meeting
to which all members will be invited to give their views on the Plan. We may well need more than one such meeting, but
our intention is to reach consensus within the whole Club, before putting the proposals to a vote of the entire membership.

Have a good spring of sailing,

Clive Shenton

would like to dedicate all of my contribution this month to the Five Year Plan.

Firstly, | refer you to last month's Navigans when we printed the complete list of suggestions from members that constituted the Wish
List that was considered by the Main Committee.

We took that list and struck off the items that we thought were desirable but would always be beyond our ability to afford. So out went
the marina, the total rebuild of the Clubhouse and the first floor extension above the toilet block.

After some debate we decided not to proceed with the ‘wet bar at ground floor’ proposal, as when I floated it in Navigans last year,
there was a large ‘anti’ reaction.

There were several suggestions concerning our Hard, varying from the minor to the major. I think we all realise that without the hard
the Club would cease to exist. What is not so widely known is that I produced a report on the hard about five years ago. The report
was comprehensive, but the main conclusion was that the hard should not be rebuilt but be continually maintained and improved as a
facilities maintenance matter. You will see that all the Plans include the sum of £750 per year to achieve this maintenance.

Several items were combined under one heading, such as refurbishment of the Upper Saloon, to help simplify our thought processes.
Then each Committee member gave their first and second preference from the Wish List and these were rated on a simple points
system by myself.

There was a surprise number one choice - a veranda with river views to the west of the clubhouse. We tested this in discussion and
agreed that this was indeed the Main Committee's first choice. This, and all other choices are shown on the following pages headed
Plan A, Plan B and Plan C. Each Plan starts with the assumption that the sum of £5000 will be available each year as surplus income
after all other expenses including depreciation have been accounted for, but there are big differences between the Plans.

Plan A

Plan A shows what we believe we can achieve at the current subscription rates.

Plan B

Plan B shows what we believe we can achieve with a subscription rate increase of £50 per year.

Plan C

Plan C shows what we believe we can achieve with a subscription rate rise of £100 per year.

Each Plan is shown at current rates. The assumption being that inflation in the costs of the Plans will be offset by inflationary rises in
the subscription rates.

HEALTH WARNING

These Plans represent the best projections and priorities that the Main Committee can reach based on current information, but this is
an uncertain world. It is possible that unforeseen circumstances may develop that demand a radical change in direction. It is also
possible that our membership numbers may decrease thus reducing the money available which would slow the implementation of the
Plan.
In these extraordinary circumstances, we would need freedom to act in he best interests of the Club.

View from the Rear
We have had a busy start to our sailing season - which, although it has not been without problems, has been very successful so far - here are some of
the highlights!

Dart 15 Open
It may as well have been April Ist for the disasters we encountered at the start of the Dart 15 open. [| arrived at the club to find 1t was blowing a
bitterly cold, strong north-easterly wind complete with rain, which no doubt contributed to the reduced number of visitors this year. Brian Spencer
told me that he had had to tow the catering team's car to the club as it had taken an aversion to the rain and broke down en route. Mick Richardson
and Clive Shenton had spent a considerable amount of time and effort trying to ensure that the RIB trolley would be back and the RIB re-assembled
in time for the Saturday racing. Due to their efforts the RIB was ready for launch on the Saturday morning and the engine promptly conked out! - (it
is still not running as I write). Fortunately, the Glynn family had kindly come to our aid and provided additional support cover with their RIB over
the weekend - and we are very grateful to them for helping out.

However, despite the chaos, everyone pulled together to make the event a success and we achieved the following:
* Catering and bar facilities all weekend including an evening meal on the Saturday - (and yes, some of us were mad enough to camp down!!)
* Four excellent races (with support cover) in a whole range of conditions - (as is usual in Bntain, Sunday dawned in complete contrast - sunny
with light airs!)
* Four out of the top five prizes being awarded to Marconi sailors.

] apologise if | am duplicating coverage of this event with other write-ups which may appear in Navigans - but I wanted to take the opportunity to
thank the many club members who supported this event and overcame all the problems. The names are too numerous to mention but | would like to
thank the Race Officer and his team, all the support crews and the shore based team who ran the reception, sorted out trolleys etc. etc. The Dart 15
Fleet is very grateful!!

Bank Holiday Series

As usual the weathermen got it completely wrong for both Easter and the first May Bank Holiday! The Easter weekend provided beautiful weather,
if not much wind on the Sunday and Monday - but it was good to be sailing in the sunshine again! On the Saturday of the May Bank Holiday - we
allowed the unthinkable to happen. Several thousand Cadets - (OK slight exaggeration) - were let loose with green paint and brushes and set upon
the Cadet cabin to transform its appearance - a truly terrifying prospect. Not surpnsingly , most of the Cadets ended up the same colour as the cabin
(although they managed to avoid painting any unsuspecting catermeran or passer-by) - but the end was result is very good and a considerable
improvement on its previous colour scheme. A lot of electrics and other work was earned out to improve the cabin facilities and my thanks to Kevin
Dowley, the Monks family and John Bird for organising this work

Support Boats

As J mentioned above, we are still having a few problems with the RIB engine as I write, which we hope will be resolved shortly. I would like to
thank Clive Shenton, Mick Richardson and Roy Hardwicke for their continued efforts on the RIB - they have given up a lot of their time and effort
and it is very frustrating that we have encountered these additional problems. I would ask for your continued patience if you have been allocated as
a RIB Helm or Crew and that you support the races by taking the Orkney out instead. The Orkney is proving to be a very capable support boat and it
is important (sometimes essential) that we have two support boats out.

Request for help - Support Boat Duties

Which brings me to my next point - I always seem to be nagging about the need for help (1 apologise!) - but there have been a number of occasions
when support boat crews have not turned up to do their duty or have not arranged a swap. | know that there are usually good reasons for this - but it
would be very unfair on the sailors if we have to cancel racing due to lack of support boats, particularly when most of them have carried out their
own duties.

Muna's Meanderings Continued

Part Six - Meandering Around the Madeiras

The first thing | noticed when | looked through the porthole in the morning was that we were anchored night next to a mountain. More
accurately perhaps we were very near the top of a mountain, with just the peak towering above our heads. The Madeiras consists of
Madeira itself, Porto Santo where we now were and several uninhabited islands. We had made for Porto Santo as it has the best
harbour.

Later in the morning we launched the dinghy and set about completing formalities. This was a lengthy process involving Immigration.
Customs, Maritime Police and the Harbour Authorities. Each of these needed to see passports and all the ships papers. While we
were in the middle of this a dashing fellow, who turned out to be Miguel the Harbourmaster, stopped his landrover and asked Helen if
we were looking for a marina berth. When she said that we were he told us that there might be room later that day. When he
discovered that our length was only 10.5 metres he said he could fit us in right away which he duly did.

Porto Santo is a fascinating island. Largely arid, very little is now grown there. Rows of terraces on the steep hillsides give evidence
of how an earlier generation of islanders eked out a meagre existence form the land. A feature that made our stay there particularly
pleasant was the three mile long sandy beach that started just the other side of the harbour wall. A swim in the warm, crystal clear
water followed by a shower, then breakfast back on the boat made a very pleasant start to the day.

We had great fun exploring the island in a variety of ways. Laura and Katie from Fanai, another boat that we kept meeting us with,
seemed determined to explore every inch of the island by foot. Helen and | did manage to clamber up the steep hillside nearest to the
harbour. We had started by following a rough track which rapidly faded away to nothing leaving us to scramble as best we could over
the remains of old terraces and craggy frock faces. We did eventually reach the top, where the view over the island made the effort
worthwhile.. We also did the tourists bit and allowed ourselves to be persuaded to join in a mini bus tour of the island. It proved to be
a very good way of seeing the island. Some of the view, were spectacular, although I will admit to having my eyes shut on the way
down some of the mountain passes.

A couple of days after we had arrived in Porto Santo Pat and Chris decided to organise another mass dinner along the lines of the one
we had had in Leixoes. I decided that this would be and ideal opportunity to get my own back on Pat. On the way across to Porto
Santo Helen had one night heard strange noises coming from on deck. She tracked this down to Laura who was passing her night
watch by making up new words to 'All Things Bright and Beautiful’. It went on the lines of:-
All boats bright and beautiful
All ARC yachts great and small
All crews weird and wonderful
Pat Murphy knows them all.

I decided that this was a perfect vehicle. All that was needed was to write some verses which | duly did. After the meal which was a
great success with over fifty people taking over one of the local restaurants, I told the story or our arrival in Porto Santo and Pat's
commentary. I handed out photocopies of the song and encouraged wholehearted support to cover my own inadequacies in the vocal
department. I needn't have worried. | thought that we would at least need a practice. After the first chorus and verse | just said carry
on. It was a superb performance.

After a few days in this wonderful place we began to contemplate our next moves. Helen was keen to visit Madeira itself. The main
drawback to going there was the fact that Funchal its only harbour, had very little space for visiting yachts and the anchorage
immediately outside the harbour was not reputed to be particularly good one. A popular option was to leave the boat at Porto Santo
and visit Madeira by ferry. Several crews were oscillating between these options. In addition I was still trying to sort out the problems
with our VHF radio. Back in Leixoes when it had already stopped transmitting | had contacted Tolley Marine again. This time they
said that Sailor had agreed to send a new handset out to us, as long as I agreed to return the old one, once I had the new one. The only
thing that was needed was a forwarding address. I never like being too definite about future ports of call. There are just too many
imponderables. However on this occasion I had little choice if I wanted a new radio and had selected Porto Santo. I had at the same
time ordered a new back up GPS to replace our existing back up, an ageing Garmin that had gone down in the rollover in August.
(I had incidentally got Gamin going again after contacting the manufacturer's who explained the procedure).

When we arrived at Porto Santo there was no sign of the expected parcel. I phoned Tolley Marine but could get no answer. My
parents who live near Tolley Marine in Poole went round there only to find that they had gone bust. Enquiries to Visa produced the

15

SE — —E ———

disturbing news that my account had been debited. I made further investigations to try and discover just what was going on.
Eventually while all this was going on the parcel arrived. Unfortunately when | fitted the new handset it still didn't work.

Part Seven - Canary Bound

We left Porto Santo on Monday 18th October. There was very little wind and for once Laura wasn't keen to leave, but for some
reason both Helen and I felt that we should go. Once clear of the harbour we raised sail and with a westerly just aft of the beam made
reasonable progress. Aldebaran had left harbour about an hour after us and as the afternoon wore on were gradually gaining on us.
By early evening, just before Aldebaran caught up with us, we changed to our downward rig. Eventually Pat started his engine and
motored away, We persevered for two or three more hours, then as our speed dropped to two knots or less we too started our engine.
At this time we could just see Aldebaran's stern light in the distance. We carried on motorsailing all night with the monitor once again
proving it could handle the situation.

In the morning we could just made out Aldebaran's mast through the binoculars. It was then time for the ARC net. Pat did his usual
faultless performance as morning DJ. A little later Helen drew my attention to a yacht abeam of us that we hadn't previously seen. It
was a while before we realised that it was Aldebaran. Pat's story that we later heard was that at the start of the ARC net the autopilot
was steering. While he was conducting the net the autopilot took exception the amount of power the SSB was taking and did a 180
degree turn. Both Pat and Olivia who was sitting in the cockpit reading at the time were completely unaware of this. When Pat had
finished the net he came back on deck and staring over the stern asked Olivia what had happened to Muna. Turning round he then saw
a boat passing in the other direction on the port side. Sensing something familiar about it he looked through the binoculars and
realised that it was us. When we discussed this incident at the next opportunity on the SSB I promised not to tell anybody about it.
Trust me Pat, trust me!!

We then reverted to sail as Aldebaran steamed off in the right direction ahead. Progress was slow all day. Later that afternoon the
wind died away completely. Once again we resorted to the engine. This seemed to encourage the attention of dolphins who swam
alongside us for some considerable time. A little later we also saw a turtle swimming placidly by. Before dark the wind had returned
sufficiently for us to rely on sail again. From then on we had light but steady north westerly winds all the way to Lanzarote which we
sighted at dawn on the Thursday morning having slowed down the previous night to ensure a daylight arrival. This is yet one more
advantage of our much vaunted downwind ng. When you want to slow down all you have to do is roll it up a bit.

All in all it had been a superb passage. Slowish but sunny calm and steady. We had all slept well. even Helen who is notoriously bad
at sleeping at sea and were all fresh enough to appreciate the breathtaking landfall. Having never visited the Canaries before, I had a
rather jaundiced preconception based on lager louts and fish and chips. That first sighting of Lanzarote's craggy skyline rising
majestically from the morning mist did a lot to wash away that preconception.

We sailed straight into the channel between Lanzarote and Graciousa, a small island just to its north. Motoring the last couple of
miles to Sociedad the small harbour on the island of Graciosa, we initially thought that there was no room on the only pontoon and left
the harbour intending to anchor. Pat had then called up on our VHF which for a very short time had decided to function, to tell us that
a boat was just leaving and that there would be room on the pontoon. Returning to the harbour we manoeuvred successfully into an
awkward berth thanks to the combined efforts of this little pontoon community.

Once safely ensconced, we quickly fell in love with Graciosa. I decided that it was a safe bet that this would be one of the places that
we would look back on with particular affection. I was therefore determined it wasn't going to be a place that we would leave too
soon,

Part Eight - Isla Graciosa

We spent two weeks on Graciosa. An idyllic spot, it provided us with a perfect combination of restfulness and interest. There are no
roads on the island, only sandy tracks. The streets in the small town are sand. The single pontoon for yachts in the harbour had no
electricity or water but no charges either. so nobody was complaining. The transient community on the pontoon was an extremely
close knit and friendly one and it was great fun catching up with what by now felt like old friends and making new ones. Before we
came away we'd never realised what a sociable life it would prove to be. One young couple sailing a Halcyon 27 couldn't get over it.
"When we walk down the pontoon everyone we see talks to us. Back home in Lymington we could walk right through the marina and
nobody would say a word".

16

Laura and Katie did some more energetic exploring, until Fanai moved on to Lanzarote. During the time we were there Helen and
managed to get round most of the island. Although largely arid it was a surprisingly interesting place. We found a wide variety 0
volcanic rock. The beaches closest to the harbour weren't particularly good for swimming, but further afield we found some superb
secluded, sandy beaches. The water was even warmer than it had been at Porto Santo. We tried to time our walks, not always
successfully, to coincide with the cooler parts of the day.

The single pontoon in the harbour brought with it certain problems. Unlike commercially operated set ups there were no handy star
lines ready to be picked up. Instead there were simply concrete blocks with eyes let into them lying on the harbour bed. Securin;
stern lines involved diving with your line down to one of these blocks. While we were there three lads on a French boat ‘Jonathon
liked nothing better than having an excuse to go diving. Another complication was that whatever the wind was doing elsewhere 01
the island, it always seemed to be blowing half a gale in the harbour. For the first few days that we were there the wind was blowing;
our bows on to the pontoon. The trick was in getting the stern lines tight enough to keep our bows off the pontoon but not so tight a:
to make boarding impossible. To help with boarding | rigged up a system with our wooden boarding ladder hung over the stemhea
and our plank strung between the ladder and the pontoon. This worked reasonably well until, while we were away, the bows rode uj
over the pontoon trapping and damaging the ladder. The next day I experimented with a mark two version, using our plastic folding;
ladder. It just happened that Pat was out and about videoing the harbour. I was balanced between the pontoon and the boat, kneeling;
on the plank, attempting to secure it to the plastic ladder on which is was resting, when the end slipped off the ladder. 1 emerged
splattering from the water to be greeted by the sight of Pat pointing his video camera in my direction with his commentary on th
incident already in full swing. A crowd soon gathered. most of whom were too amused to be of much help. It was left to one of the
French lads to actually attempt to get me out of the water.

The next day we thought is was about time we tried out Little Mu, our Seahopper folding dinghy that I had built from a kit the
previous winter. More accurately Katie supported by Laura decided that we should try it out. It was the first time we'd sailed it o:
even had it out of its bag since Tollesbury. By the time we started rigging it, Maffick decided that they would have to get the rig up o1
their dinghy. It was a particularly windy day and we ended up having a mini regatta, with the dinghies charging across the harbour
with a different crew on every outing. We had a few teething problems, which resulted in me losing the mast and rudder on my firs
time out. Running repairs on the pontoon soon had us up an away again. Little Mu did very well, especially with Katie on board.
got rather anxious when one of the French lads insisted on standing up every time he tacked, but everyone got back safely and a good
time was had by all.

Garciosa is blessed with five volcanic mountains of modest size, but very steep sided, that rise abruptly from the sandy landscape. Fo:
the time we were on the island, Helen was determined to climb at least one. I was less keen, deciding that some challenges were bes
left unconquered. Helen persisted however and eventually we arrived at the base of the highest of these hills. The going was quit
hard and I decided that I needed to lie down in the heat that was already building up. When | finally got up Helen was some way ut
the steep incline, investigating possible routes. As | walked towards her, she shouted down that it didn't look very promising
Accordingly I went a bit further round and started climbing. It was hard going, but the higher | got the less | felt like coming down
way I'd gone up. So I went on, thinking that it must get better soon and that there must be an easier way to come down, as I did so. _
found myself at the highest point of the island, but more alone than I had intended to be. After waiting some time for Helen to arrive
I started looking for easier routes back down. This wasn't as easy as I thought it might be and I eventually scrambled down a rathe
precarious route that half way down led me through a deep crevice. At one point during this descent I was extremely relieved to catch
a glimpse of Helen at the foot of the hill.

When I reached the bottom, Helen having made several unsuccessful attempts to find a route to the top, was less than pleased the’
after all my complaints and protests I had made it.

One afternoon we were having a drink on board with an Australian couple. who had sailed their 27 footer from Australia to Norway)
via South Africa and were now slowly heading home, when we were haled from the pontoon. Looking up we were amazed to see Phi
from Tollesbury standing there, It turned out that he had been crewing for another ecastcoaster who had recently bought a boat in
Spain and was in the process of sailing her to Brazil.

The next day we decided that we really should be moving on. We had to pick up yet another VHF radio in Puerto Calero on
Lanzarote. In addition we were having problems with the single lever control on the engine. It had started playing up as we had left
our marina berth in Porto Santo. Reversing out of the berth I had gone from astern to forward only to discover that as the lever passed
neutral, the engine slipped out of gear. I only managed to engage forward gear with great difficulty and in the nick of time.

We knew that leaving our berth in Graciosa was going to be interesting to say the least. Everyone turned out in force to help us on our
way. In spite of all this assistance Muna swung the wrong way desperately close to the shallows and the countless moorings and lines

17

that surround the pontoon. As we had swung away from the berth I was on my hands and knees in the cockpit attempting to engage
reverse. As I did so I realised that we were now facing the wrong way, so carried on attempting to steer Muna in reverse. For one of
the few times in living memory she responded beautifully and we wove our way through the closely packed moorings until there was
sufficient space for us to round up and leave the harbour in grand style, to the accompaniment of applause and klaxons from the
pontoon. As we left the harbour I was visibly shaking.

Part Nine - Puerto Calero

Leaving the harbour of La Sociodad on Graciosa we motored over a heavy swell into the strong north easterly. Once clear of the
headland we were able to shape course down the east side of Lanzarote and bring the wind aft of the beam. We had a superb sail
making between six and a half and seven and a half knots.

Our arrival in Puerto Calero was almost as interesting as our departure from Graciosa had been. I took Muna as slowly as I could
down the long pontoon towards our allocated berth. As we reached it I gave her a quick burst forward to turn her into the berth, Then
I collapsed onto the cockpit sole desperately trying to engage reverse gear before we rammed the pontoon. Unable to see what was
going on I carried on steering blind expecting at any moement cries of anguish from the foredeck. in their absence | engaged reverse
then reverted to neutral. As I straightened up I found that we were neatly alongside the finger pontoon. Helen and Laura were already
tying up unaware that I hadn't been able to see anything as we had come in. Perhaps | ought to do it like that more often.

We had barely tied up before an extremely helpful French mechanic had arrived to start sorting out our gear change problems. Having
dismantled the single lever control, it was found to be beyond repair. A new one was duly ordered. When this arrived a few days later
and had been fitted with some difficulty (it had been impossible to get a morse control and the volvo control necessitated a bit of
surgery in the cockpit), we discovered that the gearbox had also suffered some damage. We were therefore committed to a longer stay
here than we had originally intended.

We made use of this time by sorting out some of the other problems that had developed along the way. A new company in the marine
M.A.S.T. run by an Englishman Brian and his Irish secretary Marie, proved to be extremely effective in finally locating our
replacment radio, which seemed to have been flying around Lanzarote for at least two weeks without actually finding its way to Puerto
Calero. Brian managed to get the VHF working, although out of a total of three handsets that we now had in our possession, he could
only get one to work! He also sorted out some connection problems we had experienced with the autohelm.

While all of this was going on we hired a car for three days and had a good time seeing the sights. It proved to be a fascinating island
much less spoilt by tourism than we had anticipated. Only one place had really suffered with an over abundance of fish and chips and
English pubs. We were intrigued by the fire mountains that steam continuously and can cause spontancous combustion and the large
areas of volcanic deposits.

The only problem with Puerto Calero is that without a car you could feel rather cut off there. An entirely recent, totally artificial
harbour it had a very opulent but rather contrived feel about it. Spotlessly clean, with brass bollards and palm trees, we were never
quite sure whether the uniformed and armed security guards were there to protect us and our yachts or to keep an eye on us. In fact
the marina was so difficult to leave on foot that it sometimes felt as if the guards were there to keep us in. Either way we did find their
presence somewhat intimidating. One night I was having one of my customary wanders up the pontoon before turning in for the night,
when I realised that I was coming under rather close scrutiny. As I climbed back on board Muna, this guard approached and asked if
this was my boat. Helen and Laura both thought the incident was hilarious. Helen said it was my fault for looking suspicious. It was
just as well that the guard didn't ask them if they knew me as they probably would have denied all knowledge of me.

While we were there we realised that the bilges were getting a bit smelly and needed a good clean. Pumping out bilges here was
strictly taboo along with hanging out washing and various other activities. The only answer was to secrete buckets of dirty water
ashore. The first time I did this | thought I had been very clever tipping the bucketful down a drain the car park. As I walked back
down the gangway I was a bit disconcerted to see my dirty bilge water pouring out of a pipe right next to me and pouring straight into
the marina. Subsequent trips took me further and further afield with my buckets of water, while Laura had the bright idea of watering
the palm trees which didn't seem to suffer unduly.

All in all we managed to get a fair bit of general cleaning, sorting out and maintenance done during our stay. We also managed to
catch up with yet more people we had met along the way as well as making new friends. One thing that surprised us was that having
felt rather dwarfed by a lot of English boats we were meeting up with, we were now finding that a lot of American boats were our size
or smaller. Up to now [| had thought of things American as tending to be rather big and brash, but this is certainly not the case with
their boats which also tend to be traditional in concept with long keels and generous displacement.

18

As I write this we are still in Puerto Calero awaiting the parts for our gearbox, but | am sure with a bit of luck and good behavior, it
won't be too long before we are able to leave and continue our voyaging. Up to now we have in fact been extremely lucky having a
great deal of good sailing. It has not been an easy season weather wise and a lot of people leaving both mainland Europe and Porto
Santo, just after us, had difficult and unpleasant conditions to deal with. Our problems have been comparatively minor ones and have
done little to mar the trip so far. A preoccupation at this time of year, in this part of the world has been the Atlantic crossing. | found
it quite unsettling when all the ARC yachts set off. Every day more boats leave.

I keep telling myself that it is very early to be going, while hurricanes are still blowing in the Caribbean and before the Trades have
had a chance to settle down properly. In fact when we finally leave here, we would still like to see some more of the islands. This
should be a bit easier now, because a major problem of cruising the Canaries during October and November is simply one of
overcrowding. Nonetheless, however much logic tells you that you are doing the right thing, as day by day boats move on, it is still
undecidedly unsettling.

Commodore's Notes

After a long discourse on the Five Year Plan last month, its nice to be able to get back to the more mundane things such as weather
and sailing.

A truly awful Bank Holiday weekend was appreciated by our newest members, the family of ducks swimming in the ponds in the cat
field, but not by anyone else. This was made up for, in part, by the following weekend which was reasonably warm and dry and with
good sailing breezes. It was good to see many members emerging from their overlong winter hibernation and taking to the water. The
imaginative course in the morning caught a few of us out (thanks Howard) but the afternoon race up to Maldon and back more than
made up for it.

We are now in that part of the season when all the planning over long winter evenings begin to bear fruit. Texel and the More Race are
imminent and the best race of all, our own East Coast Piers, will soon be upon us.
Lee Harrison and Charles Anderson are heading for a record amount this year, with both Ernst & Young and 3Com equal main
sponsors. BUT we can't run the race without adequate safety precautions and Charles still needs more mother boats. So all cruiser
sailors, please volunteer if you can. You might think that the discomfort of mooring at mile intervals along the course goes unnoticed,
I assure you it does not. As a regular competitor, and one who needed to trouble our rescue services last year, I assure you that mother
boats are much appreciated.

We have hit an unlucky patch with the Rib. No sooner do we fix one problem than another comes along, so that’s why you have not
seen it on duty recently. Fortunately the Orkney, much improved after the modifications last year, has been able to stand in. Roy
Hardwick, the Rib bosun is on the case and we won't be slow to engage professional help if necessary.

It has been a particular pleasure to welcome Ian Caruth back to the Club with his Robber. Mick Richardson and Mike Onyans have
also made the conversion from cat to cruiser racing and have already disturbed the established order by getting a first and a second in
their first two BJRC Races. Come on everyone, try harder, they are impossible to live with at the moment.

Good luck and good sailing to all members, cruising or racing. Particular luck to our Solo fleet whose Open meeting is imminent.
I hope the winds are fair but not weak.
Clive Shenton

I hope by the time this goes to print that our delightful British weather has finally sorted itself out. I have clearly been too vocal in my

around for Saturday and Sunday watching the wind and rain abandon all sailing. However, we managed to fit in three races on the

Solo - Sailing Downwind

Having been asked by numerous people what the secret to my speed was last year, I thought it about time I let you all into a few
secrets. Downwind speed is the big difference between the top ten and the rest of the fleet and if you can hang on up the beat you will
find that the majority of place changes occur on the reaches and particularly the runs. The key to speed on the sea is surfing and the
guy who catches the most waves will almost certainly be the fastest no matter what equipment he uses.

Now, I know you are all saying that you've heard it all before but there is far more to surfing than just bearing away down the wave.
The most important skill is to try and keep your average speed up. The faster you are going the easier it will be to catch the next
wave, which means wallowing in between waves will simply not do. When you feel the boat falling off the back of the wave steer up
to increase your speed and go looking for the next wave instead of letting it come to you!

Another important skill is being able to pick a path through the wave front. This requires you to look ahead for any gaps which you
can plane through and therefore jump the wave. In slower boats like Solos this is sometimes the only way that you can overtake a
wave as the boat is not fast enough to plane over the back of it. In these conditions most boats are only separated by one wave and the
people on the move are just better at finding the gaps.

OK, so you are still finding it difficult to catch those waves. Well that's probably because you're not pumping enough. "“Arrr he
mentioned the p word". Now I am sorry to bring up the forbidden subject but in fact is that one pump per wave is legal, so make full
use of it. Just as you feel the transom being lifted by the wave give the mainsheet a pump and throw your weight out and back in the
boat. This will increase your boat speed enough to catch those tricky little waves in intermediate conditions.

Right, now something for all you hot shots out there. In Looe the problem downwind was that the waves were small and close
together; this meant that as soon as you caught the waye you planed straight into the one in front. | managed to cope with this by Zig
Zagging. This is a technique of getting on the wave and bearing away hard so that you slide across the wave rather than down it. On
the runs this means that you will sail by the lee in one direction until you feel yourself falling off the wave, then head up sharply so
that you broad reach back which can increase your speed so much that it puts you back on the wave that you have just come off. To do
this you will need to let your kicker right off so that the top of your sail twists out in front of the boom. One warning though, it
really is tippy!.

* * *

I have only recently started sailing Solo's but I found this tip very useful indeed - especially at my club (Black Swan) where the winds
can be a bit fickle between the islands.

When sailing downwind in light winds, sit right forward of the centreboard case. Although this pushes the bow down, it has the effect
of lifting the rear of the bar clear of the water. It can have quite a dramatic effect - even of the extent of gaining a place or two!
Beware that gybing can become a bit tricky. Make sure you get back behind the thwart before gybing. This is for 2 reasons: (a) I
found the boat turns too slowly with the bow down and (b) you can get in a real mess as the boom swings across - remember you are
sitting right were the kicker comes across plus your arm holding the tiller is in the way of the main sheet!

As long as you remember to get behind the thwart before gybing, this technique can help you gain a place or two.

Additional Note

This technique does not work for all Solos. With our fleet at Lock Venachar, we have found that moving your weight too far forward
slows the boat down by allowing the bow to dig in. We have found that in certain boats, Boon and Jolly are good examples, that best
results are obtained by keeping your weight on the thwart. It certainly works for Steve Boon - he never goes forward of the thwart.

Any other thoughts?
Steve Ash - Solo Fleet Captain

Commodore's Notes

I have heard that you all enjoyed the Summer Solstice party at the Club when several members were unrecognisable wearing long
haired wigs to simulate the decade of ‘big hair’, the 60's.
I don't know what the weather was like in England because I was in Holland, meeting my ‘date with destiny’ at Texel. You know, the
biggest cat race in the world that I was unable to start last year due to breaking my rudders in the surf before the start.
This year Race Day dawned cloudy, windy and cold as forecast. We put on our woolly bears and dry suits in the hotel and were not
sorry to have done so.
After rigging in the rain, together with the other 700 entrants, we attended the briefing which was late and only said, in three
languages, that the weather was pretty awful and come back in an hour. About an hour and a half later, with several TV cameras
running, including one on Alex and I (perhaps we look Dutch?) the Race Officer began a long speech. Starting in Dutch he spoke for
ages and at the end there was a deep exclamation from most of the crowd.
When we heard the English version, we found out why. The wind was already blowing 6, but was expected to rise to 7 in the squalls
and
‘while acknowledging that many sailors had the ability to complete the 60 nautical mile course in those conditions, many were not’
Yes you've guessed it, the Race was cancelled.
Of course we were disappointed, and some people were angry, but, by the time we had got the boat back on the trailer, the surf was
coming in like the North Shore at Wakiki and it required a firm footing to stand in the wind. They definitely made the right decision,
but to be thwarted two years running, this time by the weather, was galling.
Alex has renewed determination to conquer the course, but I have resolved not to make any decisions until April next year, when I can
assess whether the time, money and effort is worth it.

The other thing last month was the Five-Year Plan Meeting. I must confess that I was a little disappointed with the turn out, however I
would like to thank the 28 members who attended on the hottest day of the year and Father's Day to boot. I started by making a
presentation of the Plan and after considerable discussion, we took a non-binding straw poll of those at the meeting. The majority
opinion was that Plan B was the best, with strong minority support for Plan A.
I have decided to hold another Meeting to discuss the Plan on:-
Tuesday 8" August at the Sailing Club starting at 7.30 p.m.
I am very keen to get as many of your opinions as possible, and hope you can make the meeting, which, of course, is on the second
Tuesday of Camping Fortnight. If you cannot make the meeting but would still like to express an opinion please give me your views in
writing.
My email is [redacted]. My home address is:-
82, [redacted], Leigh on Sea, Essex [redacted].
Fax is not possible at the moment, sorry.

Lastly, this edition should hit your doormat just before the Piers Race. This may not be the biggest cat race in the world, but it is
definitely the best and held at the best Club in the country - Ours. What is more, we continue to be the only Club in Europe to channel
all the profit from our major event into a Charity.
Every member, whether entering or helping with the running, can be rightly proud of this Event, none more so than Lee Harrison,
Charles Anderson and their hard working Committee. Now that Steve Monks, Bob Godbold and Mike Smith have fixed up a cellar
cooler we can confidently expect a good flow of cold beer as well!

I look forward to a good entry of Club boats. Don't forget that you can do the Colne Point Race if you think that Walton is a bit far.

Every entry is welcome.

See you on the start line.

Clive Shenton

the limelight and let the Memory overtake again. So Nick won followed closely by Dave, with Colin in

The “Doctor” Race

The Doctor Race sailed on the 2"4 July was aptly named, as most of the competitors wished that.a tonic had been prescribe for more wind. Ten hardy souls lined up for a race to no 10 bouy (off Herring Point Maldon and back to the club .
The start proved interesting, being on the flood tide with no wind, and it was noted that " Killara" and "Out of Focus " were fully crewed and keen to do well. How wrong they were going to be, " Bluster “ as usual showed the fleet how it should be done , dropping his anchor above the line and waiting . At the start with most of the boats now drifting the wrong side of the start line he "upped " anchor and showed the fleet a clean pair of heels. " Bluster along with " Sea Gem " and " Honey " were the only ones to get a clean start, while the rest of the fleet had to struggle back to cross the line and restart.
The race started as beat, but off Osea the wind both freed off and died ,with most of the yachts now flying kites on what proved to be somewhere between a reach and a rub . Buoy No 10 was “ Killara’s “ undoing as she touched the mark, but being a true gentleman he confessed and completed his 720. The race back proved better with the wind picking up and a long fast beat was had by all .Two boats retired “ Four Two “ and “ Shamall “. Is retired the right wording we know how old Chris is getting but Jez ? he looks old but surely not ? it must be his hectic life style.
The eventual winner was John Easton in “Sea Gem” beating “Bluster” on this occasion with “Honey” a close third, and we were pleased to see Ian Caruth racing his Robber.Dave Payne.

Hi folks, its nice to be back having spent the best part of June sailing along the French, Belgium coast to Holland on board "Happy
Medium", in company with Malcolm and Margaret Yeoman on "Suruca". We met up at Ramsgate before going on the Dover,
Dunkirk, and Ostend then into Holland via Flushing. For once the weather was generally fine and we had a grand time. Our visit to
Dunkirk on the outward leg of our journey coincided with the 60th Anniversary of the "Little Ship" rally and we were there to see
them arrive, a truly moving experience.

Well that’s enough of my holiday ramblings, what's been going on back at MSC? The trip to Brightlingsea, organised to bid a fond
farewell to Harbour Master Peter Copeland was attended by 15 boats plus one crew coming round by road due to the fact that they

Muna's Travels Continued
Part Ten - Tour of the Canaries

Eventually the gearbox was pronounced fit, various smaller jobs had been completed and after four and a half weeks we were able to
leave Puerto Calero. We left on the sixth of December with grateful thanks to Jean Michel the mechanic and Brian and Marie at
MAST who had sorted out a number of electrical problems and been tremendously helpful in getting things sent to the island We
drifted down to Papagaya, a superbly picturesque anchorage in the south of Lanzarotte where we celebrated our freedom from marinas
by swimming off the boat in crystal clear waters.

The next day we had a beam reach across to and down the coast of Fuerteventura to Puerto Castillo. From offshore the most
significant features of the island were the wide sandy beaches stretching for miles and the generally volcanic landscape. Puerto
Castillo proved to be a pleasant little marina reached by rounding a rather fearsome looking reef and crossing right over some only too
visible rocks literally inches below the keel. Around the marina was a modern holiday complex that seemed to stretch forever and
completely dominated the immediate area. We hired a car for a couple of days and discovered that much of the island was largely
unspoiled.

From Fuerteventura we sailed overnight to Puerto Rico in the south of Gran Canaria. We had intended to sail straight onto Tenerife.
As we sailed past Gran Canaria the wind having been weak and variable appeared to settle and increase giving us the prospect of a
dead run to Tenerife. Laura and I set up the downwind rig only to have the wind fade and die completely within ten minutes.
Thoroughly disheartened we started the engine and motored into Puerto Rico. At great expense we were given a berth in a dirty,
smelly and noisy part of the harbour. We had a lazy day there and were determined to walk out of the touristy over developed bay.
Puerto Rico is surrounded on three sides by high and steep mountainous ridges, we eventually found a way up the steep sides to the
bay. We had a wonderful if rather hot walk into the interior with impressive views across this very mountainous island. It was rather
depressing however seeing the way the island is being developed. As we walked up a dirt track into the mountains, we were
overtaken by a succession of lorries negotiating the steep incline to reach the top and deposit their loads into the deep valley in an
attempt to level it off and provide more space for tourist developments. One of these developments already in existence and right next
to this dusty track was emblazoned with the name 'TOURISTICA EXPLOITICA'

We had an enjoyable beat to Los Cristianos in Tenerife, leaving Puerto Rico before dawn. Anchoring in the harbour we never actually
got round to landing on Tenerife but spent a fascinating afternoon watching a succession of weird and wonderful events taking place
on the shore close by, with mime artists, bundles of rags that turned into people that then walked away, a series of altercations and
much more,

In the morning we motored across to La Gomera in a flat calm and were treated to the sight of a large number of pilot whales making
slow and stately progress across our track, in marked contrast to the schools of dolphins that we had seen that took great delight in
swimming along with us. As far as the pilot whales were concerned, we put the engine into neutral and had a ringside view as they
swam past.

It was a pleasure to be in La Gomera from the moment we arrived there, it quickly established itself as our favourite Canary Island.
Arriving on December 15th we stayed for nine days dividing our time between making final preparations for the Atlantic crossing and
exploring the island.

Helen and Laura took most of the responsibility for our last minute provisioning, I became obsessed with our water supplies which
are not excessive by any standards and seeing how many five litre containers I could squeeze into various comers of the boat. While
these preparations were going on we were all trying to get used to the idea of a voyage of nearly three thousand miles. I became
convinced that it was inevitable that we would be becalmed for several days at a time.

Christmas was fast approaching and we had a festive time meeting up with other yachties and attending a couple of really enjoyable
concerts at the very church that Christopher Columbus and his crew prayed at just prior to one of his Atlantic crossings.

We set our departure date for the day before Christmas Eve, the allotted day dawned windless so we decided to give ourselves a day
off.

Christmas Eve morning Helen and Laura did some last minute provisioning at the Christmas market. I checked out with the harbour
authorities, topped up the water tanks and we were ready to go. At twenty past two we started the engine and with a number of people
helping us out of our berth, made our way to the harbour entrance to the accompaniment of klaxons and cheers.

13

Part Eleven - The Atlantic Crossing.

There is always a slight sense of anxiety as you cast off your ties with the shore and head out of harbour. As we left San Sebastion on
Christmas Eve 1999, a very real anxiety was mixed with an even stronger sense of relief that we had actually made a start.

That morning a young German on a neighbouring boat had showed Laura how to contact a German website at the local internet café,
that gave a comprehensive forecast for the area. This showed that we would expect fairly strong winds out of the north for the several
days, and while I was convinced that we would suffer calms at some stage of the passage, my nightmare scenario was to be becalmed
whilst still in sight of the Canaries. Incidentally, getting forecasts locally and been quite a problem and our Navtex had refused to
cooperate whilst in Gomera, due to presumably the fact that we were enclosed on three sides by high cliffs.

Within ten minutes of leaving the harbour the engine was off and we were sailing well under just the genny with the wind almost dead
astern. I was a bit concerned about committing ourselves too early to the downwind rig whilst we were still coasting along La
Gomera, however after an hour or so of sailing under the genny alone, the wind appeared to be fairly settled. Laura and set up our by
now infamous downwind rig with the furling genny poled out on what we thought would be the predominately windward side and the
furling Yankee poled out to leeward. Once set up we connected the Monitor self-steering and with seventeen or so knots of wind
blowing from astern we were well and truly off.

That night we watched the lights of La Gomera receding astern and the wind gradually increased. By Christmas morning it was
blowing at about twenty-five knots and we were rattling along at between six and a half and seven and a half knots. During the day
the wind increased to the low thirties and Muna was having spurts of eight of nine knots. The seas were building all the time. In spite
of the conditions and the fact that Laura and I hadn't quite managed to find our sea legs yet, Helen produced a superb Christmas
Dinner, although in the end she decided to reserve the Christmas pudding for a later date. By the evening we were surfing down
waves and were jointed for a while by a school of dolphins swimming alongside and leaping out of the saves.

Early Boxing Day morning, Helen recorded in the log ‘Another wild night, up to 35 knots of wind, running under reduced sail. Muna
going well. We are getting tired but managing OK. L and M have been sick but have both slept a bit so hopefully will recover’,

I recorded in the log -
‘We are beginning to settle down to shipboard life. It was quite difficult with the strong winds early on but at least it gave us a good
start in terms of progress. It is surprising how long it takes to get into a passage like this. At first all you seem to be doing is feeling
tired on watch and then trying desperately to sleep the rest of the time. You gradually unwind and relax and begin to enjoy yourself.
Its beginning to happen now. Long may it continue’,

It was at this time that I finally managed to get through to Herb on the SSB. Herb is a weather guru who runs a net out of Canada,
covering the whole of the Atlantic. Yachts make an initial call giving their position. Herb then groups yachts according to their
location in various parts of the Atlantic. He then deals s with each area separately giving every yacht an individual forecast. Not
surprisingly this daily procedure can take anything up to three hours, depending on the number of participating vessels. We had been
unable to hear Herb at all when we were in La Gomera. Since our departure we had managed to hear him but had not made contact
ourselves. Now at last we got through. Up to now we had been heading in a generally southwesterly direction. The perceived
wisdom for the crossing is that you should head well south to be more likely to pick up and retain the trades. We had already heard
horror stories from this year alone of yachts being becalmed for many days at a time. The other advantage of going well south is that
in so doing you pass fairly close to the Cape Verdes and therefore have the option of breaking your journey there should it be
necessary. We had decided from the outset that we could call in there if progress was slow.

Herb's initial advice was that we should continue heading well south, not so much in search of the trades, which he confirmed we had
well and truly found and were likely to retain in abundance, but more to avoid the worst excesses of weather that were about. He was
advising yachts still in the Canaries to delay their departure for the time being because of the generally unsettled conditions there.

By day six Laura had revived sufficiently to record in the log - "Yes I am still alive. Something was definitely wrong as I had no
appetite and even had to force myself to drink water! Mum had achieved great feats in the galley, producing meals to tempt even the
most jaded of appetites. Yesterday was a lot calmer while the wind kept up a good speed, so the motion became much steadier and I
eventually began to settle in. This evening we have been surrounded by dolphins. They stayed for hours, swimming alongside and
mjmping across our bows. Last night was definitely my best night watch so far. We were sailing extremely well at around seven
knots with a relatively calm sea. I hardly wanted to go off watch. This morning blew away the cobwebs with a full salt water wash in
the cockpit. Very invigorating’.

14

On day seven, December 30th, just as Laura got into her stride Helen began to wilt after her heroic efforts over the first few days. In
the small hours of the morning she recorded in the log - ‘Feeling miserable. Have been trying to sit in the chart area. The only place
vaguely comfortable with the awful motion. Can't feel human anywhere, The wind is not that strong. It did get up to 33 knots earlier,
but the seas are lumpy’. @

By the next afternoon however she was recording that she had had a good sleep, been treated to breakfast in bed and was feeling
human again. Laura continued to be in fine form and spent sometime working out how to use the hand held water-maker we had
bought in the Canaries. As it entailed handing the filter over the side of the boat we eventually decided that it was an operation that
should be tackled when conditions were calmer, especially as there was no immediate panic over water. Having said that, Helen and
Laura both maintain that I had a fixation about water usage all the way across, the extent that they would be aware of me giving them
the evil eye if they dared to pump water from the tap.

By Friday 31st of December we had been at sea for exactly one week and had covered one thousand and fifty three miles giving an
average days run of 150 miles plus, much better progress than we had dared hope for.

After a slightly quieter day the wind got up again the evening. Our plans for a Millennium party became increasingly curtailed as the
evening wore on the winds got stronger. It was a strange feeling moving in to the year two thousand as we surged and plunged into
the blackness.

than building a veranda. By now you should have received my letter about our Opinion Poll on the Five Year Plan, together with a
Recording Paper and a stamped addressed envelope. If you have not already recorded your opinion and returned it, please do so now.

race was run. There was once again a very good entry, and Xylonite made a great starting line boat, very evocative of Essex and the
Blackwater. The Race was won by an Australian sailing an American cat (a Hobie Fox) registered in Holland. It seems to show what a

View from the Rear

I can’t believe that we are in September already - (probably October by the time you are reading this) - and the sailing season is nearly
over. Looking back though - we have had some superb sailing events this summer and at least the weather in August and September
has been considerably better than May, June and July. I believe the main sailing events may be covered separately elsewhere in this
magazine - but I just want to touch on the highlights.

ECPR

I think it was only a week or two before the Piers Race that I helped my Dad motor AmyJack back from Tollesbury - it was so cold,
wet and windy that we were in full winter gear and it could not have been further from the kind of weather you would want in July. I
remember fretting about how the Piers Race would turn out if this weather continued. Fortunately, the weather finally began to turn in
time for the Piers Race and, although it wasn’t the hottest weekend we have had, it did bring an excellent sailing breeze. With a turn
out of around 60 boats, the Piers Race proved it could still attract the key European cat sailors, (and one Australian who eventually
won the event), and a superb weekend was had by all. I extend my thanks to the ECPR Committee and the army of helpers and
volunteers who made all the arrangements - it takes a lot of hard work to bring off such an event.

Cadet Week

Words cannot express what Cadet Week means - and it goes from strength to strength. A staggering 85 cadets were catered for this
year plus 20 adult cadets - these numbers only outstripped by the numbers of helpers on shore and on water who ensured that everyone
could have a full week of sailing activities. Peter Clayton, Steve Monks and Kevin Dowley somehow managed to keep everything co-
ordinated and under control (!) throughout the whole week and it never ceases to amaze me how many people will give up a week’s
vacation to be run ragged by 85 children!! On a serious note, although Cadet week is hard work and puts a tremendous strain on club
facilities - the sheer activity and enthusiasm from those involved really shows the club at its best and is a credit to us all - long may it
continue - (although I am busy training up the older cadets to take over running things so the rest of us can retire!). If you ever
wonder about the future of our sailing club - come along to a Cadet Week prize giving and you will be very much re-assured.

Summer Points

The Summer Points series is now over and a vast improvement in turnout for all fleets compared to the Spring Points series. Although
dinghy/cat racing is only one part of what the club does - it is good to see such strong turnouts and I hope this continues into the
Autumn points - hopefully the weather will hold good through September and October. Thanks again to those people who have been
manning the support boats and race box so that we can continue to get out on the water every Sunday.

And Finally - Club Members Property

It seems a shame to have to include a “moan” in all the good news above - but there is one matter of importance that I would like to
bring to club members’ attention. Could I remind all members that if you need to move another members’ property on the club site -
you must ensure that you contact the owner and ask their permission first. Apart from the fact that none of us would like to arrive at
the site and find our belongings missing or moved - it also makes things very difficult for all concerned if anything is found to be
missing or broken from the property that has been moved. If you need to move an item and cannot identify the owner - please gather
as much information as you can about it and contact your Fleet Captain who will help you to track down who the owner might be. I
would greatly appreciate your co-operation in this matter.

1 look forward to seeing you all on the water for rest of the season!

Jenny Ball

This was held over the late summer bank holiday weekend and attended by eight visitors and one local (myself).

For those with long memories of the days of our Whitsun regattas will recall Kestrels sailing as a class amongst the multitude of racing dinghies. In those days the Kestrels were mainly from Maylandsea Bay Yacht Club, arriving by water. Since the demise of the Marconi regatta the club has kindly agreed to incorporate a Kestrel Open Meeting in the August bank holiday series. The venue has been very popular with travelling Kestrels from all parts of the country. A regular visitor coming from North Yorkshire.

This year the weather was warm and gave good but variable sailing conditions. The afternoon ebbing tides together with a sometimes-light west wind tested the competitors to the full. Simon Fay/Paul Jarvey using their superior upwind performance, which also gave them the recent title of national champions, won both the two races on Sunday. The Monday morning race was sailed in much stronger winds and won by Steve Worf/Lynn Worf with Simon/Paul in second place. With the meeting already won Simon and Paul swapped the roles of helm and crew in the 4th race and finished well ahead of the rest of the fleet.

Overall Results:
1st - Simon Fay/Paul Jarvey - 1548 - Deben Yacht Club
2nd - Steve Worf/Lynn Worf - 909 - Calshot Sailing Club
3rd - Dave Hearsum/Kate Hearsum - 1555 - Horning Sailing Club
4th - Liam Pike/Rachael Brown-Lee - 668 - Lakeside Sailing Club (Peterborough)

The Kestrel Association wishes to thank Marconi Sailing Club for holding the event and especially to the race officers and rescue crews over the weekend.

TOM PATTERSON- a friend and colleague remembered.

Tom died in hospital on 5th August as he approached his 91st birthday.

Few of present day members will remember Tom in his sailing days at Stansgate. Some, however, may have noticed in recent times a
small figure sitting on a chair on the top of the sea wall, sometimes alone and sometimes accompanied by his daughter Jean and his
grandchildren. He still drove his car to Stansgate at the age of 90 years, just to look out over the river and soak up the beauty of the
estuary and to watch the boating activities of the club and other river users.

I first met Tom when I transferred from Marconi New Street to the new Aerodynamic Manufacturing unit at Basildon in 1955. We
soon became friends and shared a common interest in sailing, particularly the aerodynamics and hydrodynamics of multihull design.
We became avid members of the Amateur Yacht Research Society, which did much to further catamaran and trimaran development.

Tom purchased a small 2-man catamaran, not unlike the early Hobies in that it had seating for the helm and crew, together with a rigid
floor between the hulls. It was great off wind but hopeless to windward and tacking usually entailed going into reverse! There was
only one other catamaran in the club at the time, a Prout built Swift. Jack Bigden was Commodore, George Underdown was the
Steward, ‘Petes Palace’ and the old clubhouse were the order of the day.

At the age of 90 Tom was still toying with the idea of buying a cat and getting afloat again! His love of Stansgate and sailing is an
example to us all.

Ron Greygoose.
