Adult Cadets 2000

During this year's cadet week, an Adult Cadet section was run. There were 22 cadets in this section all from a variety of backgrounds,
cat sailing, cruiser sailing, limited dinghy helming and crewing and some with no sailing experience at all.

The course was run in a relaxed and not-too structured way trying to provide for the cadets varied needs. However, every cadet
carried out the capsize drill on the Monday after seeing a demonstration on land. Using a spinnaker was covered on Tuesday and
general sailing on Tuesday afternoon. Wednesday was a general sailing day with some cadets putting into practice the capsize drill
learnt on Monday. Thursday was meant to be a sail to Mill Beach in Heybridge followed by a picnic, but a severe thunderstorm
knocked this on the head. When the storm cleared a good afternoons sailing resulted. Friday was an excellent sailing day with all
cadets being on the water at the same time in Enterprises, Mirror 16, Wayfarer, 420, laser 2, Pico and some cats. After a quick sail
around the marks by the club all of the cadets in the week sailed to Osea Island for a picnic on the beach. During the picnic a number
of Adults borrowed the Toppers and Picos and had some fun sailing off the beach. The week culminated with a sail around the Island.
During the week a number of club sailors stepped in to offer boats and instruction, this was greatly appreciated.

The prize giving was held on Saturday with all Adult cadets receiving a certificate, also best Adult Cadet was awarded to Jane Maggs
for her enthusiasm and improvement shown during the course. A special bravery award was also made to Iris Knights who suffered a
bad capsize during the week and spent a morning on Osea beach sitting out a thunderstorm but a no point did she moan or complain
but kept smiling.

Steve Ash

Muna's Travels Continued

New Year's morning we saw what was only our second ship since leaving the Canaries. | was going to call him up. Then when it
became clear that he was going to pass well astern of us, 1 decided not to bother. As he steamed off I went down below to write it up
in the log. When I went back on the deck I could hardly believe it when I saw another ship steaming straight for us. I called him. He
wished us season's greetings and confirmed that he had seen us and that he would pass safely across our bows without us altering
course. We spoke to a couple of French Yachts - both crews were very lively saying that they were drinking wine to celebrate the new
millennium. As we were English they assumed that we were celebrating by drinking cups of tea!

The Captain of the ship that was approaching us came on air to wish us his own greetings. He asked where we were from and was
very interested in our trip. He then asked if there was anyone we would like to send an e mail to.

All in all it proved to be a more sociable New Year's Day than we had anticipated. January 2nd brought with it a succession of
stronger squalls many of which were accompanied by heavy downpours. These were eagerly awaited opportunities for one or other of
us to have a freshwater shower in the cockpit. This activity seemed rather strange at first when we were rattling along in gale force
winds with huge seas rolling up behind us, many of them breaking. That night Laura recorded - 'Had a great night watch. Spent a lot
of time lying on the foredeck being at one with nature! Still gusty. During one were logging nine knots. Wind now steady 25 to 30
knots. Lots of flying fish, listening to world service’

After nine days at sea we were all experiencing highs and lows. At one point I went up into the cockpit to find Helen staring gloomily
over the stern at the rolling waves that were racing after us. She made the following comment in the log book’ I spy with my little eye
something beginning with 'S'.

Conditions carried on much the same with only minor variations., although the weather was getting steadily warmer.

Day 19 brought more squalls of 40 knots plus. Laura recorded - 'Our intended destination has officially been changed from Barbados
to St. Lucia. Only 300 miles to go. Opened another fruit juice to celebrate and Dad even ' broke out' another container of fresh water!’

Day 21, January 13th dawned to reveal the distant outline of St. Lucia. After nearly three weeks out of sight of land it was a very
special sight. At last confirmation that you have actually been getting somewhere.

As we sailed round the north of St. Lucia Laura suddenly remarked that it was the time of the ARC net. This was a daily chat session
that had started before the ARC crossing itself, when boats had been converging on the Canaries from various parts of Europe. The
intention had been to carry on this daily chat net after the ARC itself. I switched on the SSB to be greeted by the unmistakable lilt of
Pat from Aldebaran, chatting to another ARC boat. | was all set to call him up as soon as they had finished talking, when we heard
him asking if they had an news of 'Muna'. We very quickly made contact and when he had established where we were he invited us to
his son's wedding in St. Lucia two days later.

As we sailed round the island it was time to take in the downwind rig twenty days and three thousand miles after we had put it up. I
have long had something of a reputation for not doing any more sail changes than was absolutely necessary, but one sail change after
three thousand miles was rather taking things to extremes even by my standards.

Sailing under Yankee alone, closer to the wind than we had been all the way across we were suddenly aware just how strong the wind
was. This was reinforced by seeing large yachts exposing their keels as they plunged from wave to wave. Suddenly everything
seemed to happen incredibly quickly. As Helen put it after days at sea we were suddenly sailing into a picture postcard as we rounded
Pigeon Island and sailed into Rodney Bay. We started the engine and motored into the Marine in the lagoon, arriving twenty days and
two hours after leaving La Gomera. In that time we had logged three thousand and forty seven miles. The Monitor had steered nearly
all the way, and the downwind rig had really proved its worth. it overriding quality had been that we could reef it to whatever size
suited the conditions. The other piece of gear that had been superb was the wind generator. Together with the solar panels it had kept
the batteries up all the way to the extent that we had only had to min the engine for two hours out of gear for the entire trip when the
batteries had lookeda little low.

Having tied up in the marina we were suddenly inundated with locals offering to do our washing and clean our hull. We just looked at
each other slightly bemused. We had arrived.
Part Twelve - St. Lucia.

Having arrived in St. Lucia it took us quite a long time to accept that we had actually arrived. Although crossing the Atlantic was
something I had fantasised about for most of my life, as the actual event had drawn ever nearer I had found it increasingly difficult to
imagine being at sea for that length of time. Even during the crossing, it was difficult to have a concept of sailing three thousand

12

miles. For that reason the halfway stage was particularly significant as by then you knew what sailing fifteen hundred miles was like
and you only had the same distance to go. In the closing stages when we were within five hundred miles of making a landfall we
could relate this to previous trips.

We were much fresher when we arrived than we had expected to be. That first evening we caught up with the crews of several boats
that we had last seen over two months earlier, before they had set off with the ARC. The ARC had once again suffered from, or been
blessed with, mainly light variable winds with longest periods of flat calms. It was fascinating comparing our very different
experiences, Back on the boat it was a strange experience lying in our bunks without being thrown around.

We stayed in the marina at Rodney Bay for nearly two and a half weeks, far longer than we had initially anticipated. During that time
however, the trades continued to blow extremely strongly and it was pleasant to be able to relax and sort things out on the boat,
without having to worry about the safety of the boat. |We were also able to explore that part of St. Lucia at our leisure. Of particular
interest was the remains of the British Garrison on Pigeon Island, now a national park.

Just two days after our arrival we went to the wedding of Pat and Olivia's son. We had first met Pat and Olivia in Spain and had been
bumping into them ever since. The wedding turned out to be a double one with friends of Pat and Olivia's son making up the second
couple. The wedding was a superb day, quite a change from being at sea.

We were relieved to discover on phoning my parents in Poole, that Jenny had arrived safely in England on Christmas Day and was
intending to get a flight to join us for a few weeks.

As we were in no particular hurry, we decided to stay on in St. Lucia for the time being in the hope that Jenny would be able to join us
there before too long, In the meantime Pat and Olivia persuaded us to sail down the St. Lucian coast. This provided the push we (or
I) needed to get out of the marina. We sailed down the coast to Marigot, a tiny enclosed bay where Admiral Rodney (a contemporary
of Nelson) is reputed to have hidden his fleet disguised as palm trees while the French sailed by. From Marigot we moved onto
Souffriere an area of incredible scenery protected as a National Park. The anchorage nestles against a palm tree lined beach between
two amazing peaks known as Pitons. Their name has been taken over by the local beer, which is also very good. The authority
running the Marine Park have laid buoys along the shore in an attempt to protect the coral. The system is that you pick up one of these
buoys and tie your stern to a convenient palm tree. There are an abundance of boat boys competing for the chance of helping you
complete this operation. It is big business with boats meeting you a couple of miles offshore to secure your custom. Once secured, or
even before. other boat boys will appear attempting to sell you wares of all shapes and sizes.

We stayed for the best part of the week in this Marine Park, taking the opportunity to explore further inland. One of the most
energetic trips was a visit to the rain forests at the centre of the island) The recommended way of doing this was to take a tour,
whereby a taxi would take you high into the hills from where you walked through the forest trail. We decided to do it the hard way,
by local bus. A trip on the bus is always a fascinating experience. There is generally a ‘background! of very loud music, either
country or reggae. The drivers are very trusting, never expecting to be paid until the end of the journey. The walk around the
rainforest was an incredible experience, just seeing the variety and scale of the plant life. We spent several hours following the
various paths that had been cut out.

During our stay in St. Lucia we met some fascinating people. Helen was particularly taken by a boat/fruit vendor called Love who
always seemed to give her a good deal, putting in extra fruit after the deal had been struck. Another local who made a good
impression was Vision a charismatic character with perfect white teeth who kept wanting to take Laura and Helen to visit the banana
plantations and sunsets over Marigot bay where he lived.

The waterfront at Souffeire had been devastated by the recent Hurricane Lenny which had swept the island just two months earlier and
had hit particularly hard by virtue of the fact that unlike other hurricanes it had tracked from west to east, attacking the soft western
underbelly of the islands. Over the next few weeks we were to see more evidence of Hurricane Lenny on other islands. In Souffriere
we saw many people still living in houses that had all but been demolished by the wave that had swept the shore. What struck us most
forcibly was how happy and friendly they were in spite of the suffering they had been through. We were told by locals that although
they had very little they were well fed due to the abundance of fresh fruit readily available.

Eventually Jenny flew out to join us and we were reunited as a family for the first time in two years. Having given Jenny a brief taste
of St. Lucia we set off North for the French Island of Martinique.

Martinique
Coming out from behind the shelter of St.Lucia we faced a stiff north easterly of 25 knots or so and some fairly heavy seas between
the islands as we beat across to Martinique. Muna revelled in the conditions while Jenny enthusiastically settled back into sailing.
Only I, I'm ashamed to admit, felt decidedly queasy and had to lie down for a while. We sailed into the shelter of Martinique in great
style and anchored off Marin to check in at customs. Having landed we discovered that customs wouldn't be open until the morning.

13

We also immediately noted the contrast with St. Lucia. No boat boys, no locals clamoring to do jobs for you. The locals we came in
contact with were generally very reserved. Prior to crossing over | had been almost totally ignorant as to the status of the various
islands, apart from the fact that some had in the past been British colonies. It was only now that I discovered that Martinique was in
fact a full department of France with the same status as any other department such as Brittany. Anyone living on the island was able
to travel to France if they so wished and take advantage of any provision such as education and health care available to other French
citizens. The marina at Martin was teeming with French charter boats.

In the morning Helen and I went ashore in the dinghy to check in at customs. Meanwhile, unbeknown to us a large customs launch
anchored just upwind of Muna. The crew then disappeared below decks. The launch then proceeded to draw down on Muna. In spite
of the combined efforts of Jenny shouting from the foredeck and Laura calling them on the VHF, it was some considerable time before
they managed to elicit any response. When the crew finally did emerge, just as the two boats made contact, they tried to make out that
it was Muna that had dragged, upwind!

Once Helen and I were back on board we made our way over to St. Annes where we anchored off the beach just as Pat and Olivia
arrived from St. Lucia in Aldebaran. As soon as we had anchored we were all swimming off the boat. It was our 25th wedding
anniversary and Laura and Jenny prepared us a special Anniversary lunch. We had a very pleasant time sitting in the cockpit opening
cards and presents from home that Jenny had brought out with her. After lunch we went ashore where we met up with Pat and Olivia.
We all walked along the bay as far as the Club Med set on a peninsula where we sat on the beach as the sun went down and drank a
bottle of champagne that Jenny had bought us on the flight over. A very special moment.

When we went back into St. Annes we tried to get a table at a restaurant we had liked the look of earlier, only to find that it was now
fully booked. We eventually found somewhere else to eat that looked O.K. So far on our trip when we had eaten out we had been
very lucky and had some lovely meals, On this day of all days things went badly wrong. Having ordered before a quarter to eight, it
was nearly ten o'clock before we were served our first course, In the meantime I had made visits to the kitchen only to be told that we
would be served very soon. When the food finally arrived it was almost uneatable. It all became something of a farce. Olivia
complained that her vegetables were almost uncooked and cold. Her vegetables were taken away only to reappear two minutes later
on my plate. In the end we cut our losses and brought the meal to a close. Not the anniversary meal we would have liked but we all
managed to laugh about it. As Helen said, we'd had an unconventional wedding so it was only appropriate that we should have an
unconventional anniversary.

The next day was Pat and Olivia's anniversary so we had a barbeque on board Aldebaran as a joint celebration.

We moved onto Anse l'Anne opposite the capital Fort de France. We crossed over to Fort de France where Helen and I had the
memorable experience of watching a mass baptism off the local beach. From Anse I'Anne we made our way up the coast to St. Pierrre
a town that had been almost totally destroyed by a volcanic eruption in 1902. Almost thirty thousand people were killed and fifty two
ships sunk at anchor in the bay. There had been only two survivors, one of whom was being held on a charge of murder in the town
goal. He had been saved by the thickness of the cell walls and door. After the event he hae been given his freedom and been
exhibited in Barnham's Circus. We climbed the volcano, an expedition that became something of an epic as the local bus stopped
some way short (about four miles) of the start of the climb itself. By the time that Jenny, Helen and I reached the café at the start of
the climb we were already exhausted in the heat. Pat and Olivia had caught the bus before us and we later discovered that they had
managed to hitch a lift up to the café. It turned out to be a very exciting walk/climb. Pat and I reached the summit with me some
twenty minutes behind. As I got there the mist descended obliterating the view.

Setting off from St. Pierre we had fickle winds until we came out of the lee of the island. Between the islands the winds steadied as
they normally did and we had a good sail across to Dominica, another island that had once been a British colony.

Part Fourteen - Dominica

Dominica made another impressive landfall as we sailed in past Scotts Head and anchored off the Anchorage Hotel near Roseau, using
the anchor off stern to a palm tree technique. We were helped in this manoeuvre by a couple of boat boys. As another ex British
colony Dominica had a culture similar in some ways to that of St. Lucia but with it's own individual characteristics. The boat boys
were again in evidence but not to the same degree as in St. Lucia.

We had an interesting walk around Roseau in spite of the fact that it was dominated on the day we were there by the presence of an
enormous cruise liner tied to the tiny town quay. We got rather tired of being mistaken for passengers off it. A shop where I enquired
about having some films developed justified the highly inflated prices, by asking how much we were paying to travel on that ship.

From Roseau we motored up the coast of Dominica in an almost flat calm. It was still a novelty to be able to stay in deep water just a
little way offshore and have a really good view of the various settlements and changing scene as you went by. When we arrived at the
large sheltered anchorage off Portsmouth at the north west tip of the island, we were besieged by boat boys before we had even

14

anchored. Harassment of visiting yachts has proved to be counter productive to the local economy in the past and in Portsmouth they
have tried to address the problem by forming an association of official guides. We enlisted the services of one of these, Oscar, who
early the next morning rowed us up the Indian River deep into the heavily wooded interior. We had an invigorating swim in cool
fresh stream water.

Later Oscar took Pat and I across the bay to the custom dock. For this trip he used the full power of his Yamaha outboard. The
combination of traditional wooden long slim chined hull and modern powerful outboard (generally Yamaha) proved to be very
common in the islands particularly St. Lucia and Dominica. On this occasion we traveled faster than I can remember going before on
water.

In the evening Oscar persuaded us to go with him to his home for a meal. He assured us that the fact that Laura was a vegan would
not present a problem. In the event he was right because we all had a totally vegan meal, something that Pat was not to let Laura
forget some time. It was a fascinating evening however and a rare opportunity to have a glimpse of the local lifestyle. All the houses
we Saw were very simple affairs with corrugated iron roofs.

On the second of March we set off for Iles des Saintes just twenty miles to the north.

Part Fifteen - Guadeloupe
The Iles des Saintes are a group of small islands that are politically part of Guadeloupe, another French Island with the same status as
Martinique. We had a brisk sail from Dominica weaving our way between the off lying rocks and islets. Our first anchorage was in a
sheltered bay called Anse Fiedelling on Terre D'en Bas, a small extremely quite island. The houses we saw there were notable for
their solidity and comfort compared with the flimsy structures we had seen on Dominica. We had an enjoyable if rather hot walk the
length and breadth of the island.

Moving over to the main island in the group, Terre D'en Haut, we anchored off the main town of Bourge de Saintes. Ashore we saw
several really large iguanas that had been taken over a tree right on the shore. We had a very pleasant walk across the island to Baie
de Pointpierre, a lovely beach where after snorkeling we rested on the heavily shaded beach and Olivia was molested by several local
goats,

From Iles des Saintes we had another lively sail across to Basse Terre in the south of Guadeloupe. We had hoped to stop there to see
something of the carnival that was due to start in the next couple of days. However, we didn't like the look of the anchorage so carried
on up the coast to an anchorage near another Pigeon Island, where we were reunited with the crew of Johathon a French yacht we had
last seen in Graciosa in the Canaries.

We then stopped in the large sheltered anchorage of Deshaics on the north west corner of Guadeloupe. We stayed there for three
nights, enjoying superb walks through the forest, one of which involved following a mountain stream and where we were able to have
a wonderful swim in a natural freshwater pool. On the last day that we were there, Laura went off on one of her epic explorations, that
involved getting lifts from various people and touring practically the length and breadth of the island. Her return well after dark
unfortunately coincided with the arrival of a heavy swell which turned the previously idyllic anchorage into something of a
nightmare. Having looked for Laura ashore earlier to no avail, I was reluctant to leave the boat again as we pitched and tossed
dangerously close to other boats. A lack of wind meant that boats were swinging in all directions. Eventually Laura appeared from
the blackness in a high powered rib accompanied by two husky Americans.

The next morning we sailed the forty-five miles to Antigua in the company of Aldebaran and Vitamin Sea, another boat that we had
been meeting up with since Portugal. Sailing into English Harbour was like sailing into a page out of a history book, with its restored
Nelson's Dockyard. The landscape around the entirely natural harbour was sufficiently rugged to have staved off too much obvious
signs of development.

Part Sixteen - Antigua and Barbuda
Antigua gained its independence from Britain in the early eighties, together with Barbuda, a sparsely populated reef fringed island
lying some thirty miles to the north east of Antigua. Apparently the inhabitants of Barbuda were largely against independence and
resent being lumped together with Antigua.

1 really enjoyed our time anchored in English Harbour with its combination of natural beauty and historic interest. However we found
the locals working in and around the dockyard to be some of the surliest of anyone we had encountered on the trip so far. Helen put
this down to the fact that they were coming into daily contact with crews, owners and charter guests of some of the biggest yachts in
the world. In Falmouth Harbour, just next door to English Harbour we saw an amazing array of super yachts, both power and sail.
These exotic craft dripping with opulence and ostentation seemed to dominate and take over the area in the same way that colonial
powers like Britain had dominated the islands, in a heavy handed fashion, in years gone by. There were many occasions during our

15

time in these islands, especially when seeing evidence of the slave trade, when it was difficult not to feel a deep sense of shame at our
countries involvement in many aspects of these islands’ history.

We enjoyed some vigorous walks up to and around the headlands surrounding these bays, including an energetic climb up to Shirley
Heights, the site of one of many British Forts, where, entertained by a steel bank, we watched the sun setting over the hills and saw
Muna's anchor light burning in the bay far below.

From English Harbour we sailed round the reefs to a marina at Jolly Harbour, where amongst other things we caught up with a number
of jobs that needed doing on the boat. It was noteworthy that the locals we came across here were far friendlier than those we had
come across near English Harbour.

We had for sometime been keen to visit Monserrat, which had, suffered severe volcanic eruptions in 1995 and 1997. There had been
predictions of further volcanic action for the last few weeks. Under the circumstances, a sensible alternative to sailing across was to
visit by ferry. Pat and Olivia our Irish friends off Aldebaran had decided to do this on March 17th St. Patrick's Day. I hadn't realised
previously that Monserrat had strong Irish connections dating from a time when Irish settlers had fled there after facing persecution in
the neighbouring islands. To this day St. Patrick's Day is a national holiday on the island and is marked by festivities. As St. Patrick's
Day is also my birthday it seemed like too good an opportunity to miss and we decided that we would all go over as well. In the end
John and Margaret from Vitamin Sea and Michael from Edain also came across so we made up quite a party.

Having hurtled over from St. John's Antigua, on the early morning high speed ferry to Little Bay in the north west corner of Monserrat
we struck a deal with a taxi driver to give us a tour of the island. In marked contrast to other sightseeing trips we had done when |
would spend half the time with my eyes shut as we hurtled round yet another impossible corner with a sheer drop on one side, this tour
rarely exceeded walking pace. It is a beautiful island with a largely mountainous terrain in the north and a flat plain in the south in the
shadow of the volcano. prior to the eruptions that started in 1995, the vast majority of the island's twelve thousand inhabitants lived in
Plymouth on this southern plain. Now Plymouth is completely deserted. As we stood on the outskirts looking down into the town
everything looked intact but simply covered in this thick layer of ash. Absolutely everything was grey. There were many larger
houses on the hills overlooking the town that had been owned by Americans and Canadians. One of these had a carport with a jeep
still parked in it. The ash was halfway up the jeep's radiator.

Further from the town we passed the golf course that now lay under a thick layer of ash. We stopped at a hotel that overlooked this
golf course and the bay that had previously been a good anchorage. The hotel had been repeatedly cleaned in the hope that it could
eventually reopen. The whole visit was a sobering experience. Knowing the population had been reduced to just three thousand at its
lowest ebb, it now stands at four thousand, you wonder how the island economy can recover. However the people we met were all
incredibly friendly, positive and enthusiastic with wonderful senses of humour. Around the devastated town of Plymouth grass was
beginning to grow on top of the ash.

After the tour we arrived at the St. Patrick's Day Celebrations at the local school. It was an amazingly festive occasion. Pat had
dressed himself in patriotic attire and many of the locals were similarly attired. Pat revels in getting to know the locals wherever he
goes. We had a feast of local food. Preparations were underway for a pageant depicting a slave uprising on St. Patrick's Day during
the eighteenth century, but unfortunately we had to leave before it took place, to catch the ferry home.

Three days after our visit, a much anticipated dome collapse took place, covering the entire island with ash. One yacht anchored in
Little Bay reported seeing an incredible pyrotechnic display at night followed by ash covered decks the following morning. By this
time we had sailed from Antigua the thirty or so miles to Barbuda. This island has something of an awesome reputation surrounded as
it is almost totally by extensive reefs that are home to at least two hundred known shipwrecks.

Still sailing with Aldebaran we temporarily parted company when Pat headed for a tiny anchorage almost totally enclosed by reefs.
We opted for a slightly more straightforward anchorage where we met up with Vitamin Sea and Duchess, We walked along the beach
in front of a very exclusive beach hotel, reputed to cost in the region of a thousand dollars a night. Visiting yachtsmen were not
welcome apparently because they had no mechanism for charging for anything. As we walked along the beach a burly guard ambled
over and politely informed us that he couldn't stop us using the beach but he would be grateful if we didn't try and walk through the
premises.

By the morning the previously calm anchorage had developed a rather unpleasant swell. Vitamin Sea and Duchess both decided to
curtail their visit and head back to Antigua. The SSB was alive with Pat telling everybody about the wonderful anchorage he had
discovered, deep among the reefs, where from a flat calm he could watch the masts of boats anchored off Cocoa Point, swaying about.
That is of course where we were. While we were debating our options he called us up on the VHF suggesting we join them round the
corner. We decided that that was our best option and motored cautiously through the off lying reefs to a point off the anchorage where
Pat was waiting in his dinghy to guide us in. Once inside we anchored with barely six inches under our keel but with no motion at all.

16

Later I sounded out the anchorage with the dinghy and leadline and discovered that we were in a pool unmarked on the chart but
alongside a deeper pool acknowledged in the pilot book and on the chart. In honour of this discovery I named the pool, ‘Murphy's
Hole’, reached by means of ‘Paddy's Passage' and duly entered these details on my chart. That night we all had a barbecue on the
beach together with Ted and Muriel from Acedia, a Freedom 38 that had followed Aldebaran into the anchorage the night before.

After a couple of days in this idyllic spot we all set off on a rare overnight passage to sail the eighty-eight miles to St. Martin. In spite
of a noticeable lack of wind, with little time constraints, we managed to sail nearly the whole way. It was a lovely sail on a clear
moonlit night. Sailing by St. Barts in the dark the island stood out quite clearly. At one point | was dozing (all right sleeping) down
below when Laura who was on watch at the time, suddenly shouted out. Leaping up on deck, or as near leaping up as I can manage
these days I saw the shape of a fishing boat just off our bows. As we sailed by just in front of him we saw a very faint red light in the
rigging. Apart from that there was absolutely no sign on life. I called out several times but there was no response. We still wonder
whether we should have done more to check that everything was all right, but to be honest at the time the shock of a near miss was
uppermost in our minds.

In the morning the wind got up, but very unusually for the Caribbean, from the southwest. After a lively sail along the coast of St.
Martin we arrived at the normally sheltered anchorage of Simpson's Bay to find it an absolute maelstrom. Fortunately the bridge was
due to open and we were soon in the shelter of the inter lagoon.

Part Seventeen - St. Martin.
St. Martin is a rarity among Caribbean Islands in that it is part French and part Dutch. The French part is St. Martin whilst the Dutch
part is Sint. Maarten. Simpson's lagoon is part French and part Dutch. Anchored as we were in the Dutch part we could have day
trips to France in the dinghy. The lagoon has long had a name as a hurricane hole, but in recent years, hurricanes have tend to hit it
rather hard, thereby rather denting it's reputation. St. Martin is a duty free island. Not surprisingly it boasted several large chandlers.
Its amazing how wandering round large well stocked chandlers makes your realise how many things you need.

Whilst anchored in English Harbour, Antigua, our Avon dinghy with outboard attached had flipped. Five minutes later the Avon
dinghy and outboard of Acedia anchored just ahead suffered the same fate. No amount of tender loving care revived our aging
Yamaha and we now decided to replace it with a Yamaha 3. Putting this engine on the Avon caused me considerable anxiety, so we
started looking at various rigid transom inflatables on offer. In the end after much deliberation we opted for a heavily built large tube
Caribe, which in spite of being only 2.5 metres long proved to be an effective load carrier and surprisingly fast with just 3 hp on the
back.

After this spending spree we had to recuperate in the Soggy Dollar Bar where we met up with several more boats that we had got to
know along the way. Helen celebrated her birthday during our stay in the lagoon. We had a memorable evening during which Helen
insisted on having a T shirt as worn by the waitress in the restaurant. When she looked at it in the morning, she decided that her taste
the night before might have been slightly suspect.

After nearly a week in the lagoon and some pretty hefty restocking it was time to move on. On the 30th March we motored out of the
lagoon during the 5.30pm bridge opening in company with Aldebaran and Acedia bound like us for the British Virgin Islands and
Puffin bound for the USVI's. Motoring northwestwards we witnessed the green flash as the sun set. Another night passage started
with little wind. Just before seven we turned off the engine to have our supper in peace. in five knots of wind we were barely moving
but it was such a pleasant night we were loathed to restart the engine, so drifted slowly on. The wind gradually increased overnight.
By the morning it was blowing quite strongly and we sailed right into the BVI's arriving off Tortolla about half past one in the
afternoon. Our progress had slowed again and we were enjoying a quiet sail in when Laura discovered in the pilot book that you have
to pay the Customs overtime after three thirty. It was time to start the engine and motor in.

And so we reach the end of another sailing season and winter is upon us again. I know this to be the case, not only because the
weather has turned, but also because we have already begun the process of planning next year's sailing season!!

1 would therefore like to take this opportunity to remind you of some key usual events that will take place over the winter and to
encourage you to give them your full support:

Dinghy Park Clearance
Please could all owners of boats in the Dinghy Park (in front of the clubhouse) ensure that their boats are moved along the western
hedge by 25th November 2000. The masts should be lowered and the boats should be staked down. Please park the boats close
together to conserve space and do not leave your boat in the area designated for Windsurfer Rigging - (the area between the marked
barrier and the tractor shed). If you are going to have any difficulty in this, please advice the Handicap Fleet Captain, David Ball on
[redacted].

Any boat that is not moved from the Dinghy Park is liable to being removed by the sailing sub committee.

Fleet AGM's
Each Fleet Captain will organise an AGM for their fleet over the winter months. This gives you the opportunity to discuss matters,
which are important to your particular type of fleet, and to stand for fleet captain if you so wish! Please keep an eye out in Navigans
for your particular fleet's details.

Sailing Club AGM
Most of us dislike meetings - (very reminiscent of being at work for a start!) - but the AGM is one meeting that you should really
try to attend. No matter how much or how little use you make of the club, everyone has an opinion about how they would or would
not like it to be run. The best way for you to make that opinion heard is to come to the AGM. Full details of agenda and proposed
resolutions / nominations for Club positions are included in this edition of Navigans (See Pages 19-25) please take time to read
them and then come along and make your opinion known. (This year’s AGM will take place at the MASC, Beehive Lane,
Chelmsford on 12th November at lpm).

Working Parties
As you will be aware, we pride ourselves on being a self-help club and one of the ways we are able to keep membership fees to a
reasonable level is due to the voluntary hard work and commitment of members. One of the ways this is achieved is through the
work Party events during the winter where the principle of 'many hands make light work' is applied to get some valuable site
maintenance and other work done. I would again urge you to support these events in whatever way possible. Certain fleets were
conspicuous by their absence last year and as a result, we were not able to get all the tasks done that we wanted to. If you are not
able to participate at a Working Party but can contribute in another way - please do not hesitate to contact myself or another
member of the committee. The autumn working party has been scheduled for Sunday 26th November. (See Page 5)

Laying Up Supper
And finally - just to prove that it is not all work over the winter - the premier social event of the year, the Laying Up Supper will
again take place at the Three Rivers in Cold Norton on Saturday 18th November. (See Page 2) This is always a hugely successful
event and thoroughly enjoyed by everyone. Tickets are available from Committee Members, Fleet Captains and the Glynn family. I
look forward to seeing you there!

Finally, | would like to thank the Sailing Sub-Committee, all Support Boat Crews, Race Officers and Assistants and the many
people who have contributed to making this year's Sailing Programme so busy and so successful.
Jenny Ball

CRUISER RACING NEWS

Overcast skies and brisk Northerly winds greeted the competitors for the Knoll Trophy Race. The Bench Head course was selected and the fleet reached away, led by a new comer to club cruiser racing David Onyon’s in his Sonata ‘Quiet Airs.’ Ian Wood single-handed in his Contest 25 ‘Jan’ showed tremendous speed holding second place until caught at Bradwell by a reluctant ‘Ocean Slipper’. Mark and Neil Burgess in the Eygthene 24 ‘Chicane,’ another newcomer to club racing, held off Dave Payne’s “Live Wire’.
At the Bench Head ‘Quiet Airs’ led followed by’ Ocean Slipper’ and ‘Jan’ chased by ‘Chicane’ then ‘Live Wire’, ‘Bluster’ and ‘Four Two’. The return leg was a beat and a tussle developed between ‘Jan’ and Chicane’ all the way to the line with ‘Jan’ prevailing. However the tail end of the fleet was only 25 minutes behind, and once again Colin Leveridge’s persistence won through with Ian Wood a creditable second.

Helm of the Year Final Series 2000

The Series this year was once again sailed in Picos kindly loaned by Club Members for the occasion. It was sailed on Saturday 7th October, and as usual Navigans sent along it's roving reporter to marvel in this highlight of the MSC sailing season. Here is his report: -

The Helm of the Year title has for years been competed for by the Champions of each major fleet and this year they comprised - Colin Leveridge (Cruiser); Tim Wallace (Fast Cat); Peter Tovey (Medium Cat); Jenny Ball (Dart 15); David Ball (Handicap); Steve Monks (Solo); and Anthony Monks (Cadet).

A cool and rainy day was not ideal for the Final, but at least the SAW force 2 to 3 wind which slowly freshened to a 4 through the day, enabled the 5 race series to be completed without difficulty, and the enthusiastic spectators who turned up for the event were treated to a well sailed and exciting series.

The boats were rotated between competitors after each race, and one discard was allowed, so that the competition was as fair as possible. The decommissioning of Jack B during the week before the event due to a malfunction, meant that race box starts had to be used and hence course setting was more limited than usual, but all courses still contained a reasonable windward leg and provided a true test for the challengers.

In Race 1 Jenny established an early lead with Colin moving smoothly through the fleet to challenge her on the reach to the finish line. Jenny held on, and Anthony eased through to third place at the final windward mark, which was overstood by half the fleet. Peter held off Steve for fourth.

Race 2 saw Steve and Anthony at the front racing side by side down the first leg of the course, but on the run Anthony generated enough speed to take him clear of the others, a lead which he was able to extend through to the finish. Behind him Tim relegated himself to the rear of the fleet with a spectacular dismount on the run, while Colin again showed good speed to work his way through to second, in front of Steve.

Race 3 again saw Steve and Anthony side by side leading the first leg, with Anthony just in front at the start of the first beat, but his luck ran out soon afterwards when a capsize put him to the back, leaving Steve to win comfortably from David and Jenny.

Race 4 saw David and Jenny lead the fleet away, Balls instead of Monks, and these two passed and repast each other around the course until David finally was able to establish a lead up the final beat which he maintained to the finish. A good beat by Steve lifted him up to second just in front of Jenny

The final race was a classic with Steve, Jenny, and David all in with a chance of the title and all leading at some time during the race, and all three within feet of each other as they approached the end of the final beat with David just covering the other two. In a last desperate effort for victory Steve tacked early at the windward mark, diving under David's transom to lead away onto the final reach, but in doing so he just touched David's boat incurring a penalty which let David through for the win just in front of Jenny. This result enabled David to claim the overall title, a thrilling end to a great series, which provided 4 different winners in 5 races.

All competitors performed with credit, especially Anthony who at 11 years old showed a formidable talent, which will make him a hard man to beat in years to come.

Weekend 23/24 September proved to be a busy one with twelve boats taking part in the "Watercress Run" at Heybridge
Basin whilst the racing fraternity were busy competing in the "Medusa Race", which is the last of this year's cruiser races.

Twelve cruisers comprising Amyjack, Cornish Gold, Fantasea, Happy Medium, Icarus, Peace, Reflection, Rubicon,
Suruca, Trumpeter, West Marie and Winkler, made the early morning start to Heybridge Basin locking in about 0900. At
mid-day twelve dinghies and crews started the trip up the canal past Tesco's to Beeleigh Abbey in search of the now
elusive watercress. The weather was great the only ones who did not seem amused were the anglers on the canal bank
having coped with twelve dinghies first going up the canal then returning some two hours later. The day was rounded off
with everyone enjoying an evening meal in the "Ship" pub where Murray, Mike, Joan, Derek and Margaret joined us. The
return journey on Sunday morning was also very civilised - thank you to Sophie and Thomas for suggesting it.

Timber - should be placed on the old mooring trailer at the eastern end of the cat field.

Commodore's Report 2000
1.0 Introduction

I will now like to give the meeting my report on the Club for my second year as Commodore. It has been a year of steady progress
in many areas of the Club activity and I will attempt to summarize every aspect of the Club. I do intend to mention names of
members where they have been of particular service to the Club. Inevitably in a Club where at least a quarter of the membership
contribute to the running of the Club, I will not mention everyone and I apologize in advance for any omissions.

2.0 Sailing a

Sailing is the reason d’etre of the Club. I do not wish to pre-empt the Sailing Secretary’s Report, but I see all the signs of robust
good health in our Sailing Activities.

The Club enjoys extremely good sailing facilities with acres of boat storage space on land, excellent 24-hour access to.wide but still
relatively sheltered sailing waters, and good back up facilities. Our members make good use of these facilities in many divergent
ways, which leads the Club to have a high usage, whatever the sailing conditions.

The Sailing Sub Committee under the chairmanship of the Rear Commodore Jenny Ball and the hard working Sailing Secretary
Dave Williams control sailing. Jenny and Dave, together with the fleet captains have arranged season long racing for all classes.
This is no small exercise, each race requires seven members to man the Race Box and run Rescue.

Our Cruiser Section ranged far and wide, and this year has also seen a rebirth of Cruiser Racing with Frank Burgess, Mike Turner,
Derek Gardner, Dave Payne and the Ball family much involved. Two new kids on the block upset the natural order of things when
Mick Richardson and Ian Caruth won some races with the Robbers they have just brought to the Club,

The Board Sailors continue to use the Club when the rest of us are thinking of catching up with the gardening, ensuring full use of
our facilities.

3.0 Safety

It has been a year of consolidation and progress for Colin Kidner in his capacity as Safety Co-ordinator. I am sure he would wish
me to thank our safety advisor, Malcolm Robertson, for continuing to give his time and professional expertise to the Club.

The Safety Committee have continued to look at our systems for launching and recovery of cruisers. Peter Clayton & Murray Bates
have been much to the fore in the development of safe working practices. Thanks Gentlemen.
While the objective of this work is obviously to operate the Club in Safety, it has another important function. The Health and Safety
Executive quite simply do not believe an organisation has Safe Systems of Operations unless the Procedures are fully documented.
The work of the Safety Committee greatly reduces the chance of the HSE prosecuting the Club or Club Officer in the event of an
accident.

_ Eventually we intend to look at every aspect of the Club’s activities both to comply with the law, but primarily to set up systems to
ensure that our fun is not spoiled by avoidable accidents,

4.0 Rescue

The Club continues to run three support boats, the Rib, Jack B and the Orkney.

The Rib is our most effective rescue boat. However it has seen a lot of service and has needed heavy maintenance during the year.
The launching trolley was remade professionally, and the trailer was extensively rebuilt by Mick Richardson. The RIB is currently
at the Main Dealers having the engine serviced and repaired. The Committee will keep a close watch on such expenditure, and
judge the time for replacement. Thanks also go to the Bosun Roy Hardwick for his week by week maintenance that has kept this
valuable asset viable.

The Jack B has served the Club well over many years and has many more years service left in her. Geoff Josey has serviced the
engine and kept it sweet and I am sure I remember seeing Murray Bates one cold and windy winter Sunday changing the main shaft
bearing. We were not able to do much work to the hull this season and the new Bosun, Eric Cockerton will have a busy year.
Thanks for volunteering Eric.

The Orkney has performed reliably and well throughout the year and is especially useful during Cadet training sessions when its
controllability make it possible to give close quarters support. Tim Sweet & Barry Glynn have looked after the Orkney this season.

The system of rostering and notifying Support Boat crews was brought in last year and has been successfully managed this year by
Tony Ferguson, Barry Hutt and Dennis Gilby. However we do need more drivers, particularly for the Jack B. I am sure the Sailing
Secretary will say more.

5.0 Cruisers

Cruisers make up almost half of the boats registered at the Club. Members who own cruisers enjoy good facilities at a fraction of
the fees charged by professional boatyards elsewhere on the East Coast. This pricing structure is only made possible by the
members themselves undertaking many jobs that are dirty, wet and physically hard. These self help efforts alone would not be
enough without the leadership of the Fleet Captain, Derek Kirby, and the work of the Moorings Sub Committee under Peter
Clayton and Murray Bates, which channels and manages the efforts of the members to achieve the objective.

Tractors continue to be the most important single resource for handling boats on the shore. Our tractors are not new, but the hard
work of the Tractor Coordinator Roger Gibson and the mechanical skills of Roger Camp, have maintained the tractors and even
made modest improvements, at reasonable cost.
Another tractor was added to the fleet during the year. This machine is some years old but in a well maintained condition. Although
it was obtained by the Club at a bargain basement cost we are confident it will give many years good service.

The travel hoist has been in service for about a year and is proving its worth.

The moorings are laid and lifted each year by the members using the mooring barge. The investment made three or four years ago
in this barge continues to deliver efficient and low cost service to our members.

6.0 The East Coast Piers Race

Last Saturday I was privileged to present a BIG cheque to Nick Back of the Cirdan Trust in the sum of £8,000. Race Chairman Lee
Harrison, together with Race Committee members Chris Davis, Charles Anderson, Marcus Wallace and Debbie Yorston attended.
The event took place on the Cirdan Trust barge the Lady Galadriel at Maldon and was photographed for posterity by Geoff Baker.

Compared with the other attendees I did little more than enter the Race and fill in when Charles ‘The Voice of the Piers Race’
Anderson needed a break from talking at the Prize Giving. Nevertheless I was proud to represent the whole of the Club at this
ceremony, because the event can only be run with the full involvement of every section of the Club. Our Race continues to be the
only Race of its type in the UK that is run in aid of Charity and all the membership can feel justifiably proud oftheir involvement.

One section of the Club deserves special mention, the cruiser sailors who provide the mother and matriarch boats. This is an
unpleasant job with little of the glory. Crews get up and leave the Club hours before the competitors are awake, and rarely arrive
back at the Club until after the Prizes have been awarded. But we cannot run the Race without the safety and assurance that these
‘boats give.
That is why I was particularly pleased that Frank Burgess joined us at the cheque presentation. He was there to represent the 18
cruiser sailors and their boats who all gave freely of their time for the good of the cause.

Mike Turner again did his usual excellent job as Race Officer

After three highly successful years, Lee Harrison has stepped down from the Race Chairman’s position but has agreed to stay on
the Race Committee next year.
Thanks for a job well done Lee.

Chris Davies has already taken over as Chairman and arrangements for next year’s Race are underway.

The provisional date for next year’s race is Sunday is July, so put it in your diaries.

7.0 Cadets

When telling you of the presentation for the Piers Race, I spoke of being privileged to represent the Club, well I felt similarly
privileged to present the prizes for Cadet Week. You will recall that a new committee of Peter Clayton, Steve Monks and Kevin
Dowley took on the organization this year. They were aided and abetted by Steve and Debbie Glynn who never seem far away from
the centre of Club events.

Over 75 Cadets were given tuition during Cadet Week. It is probably not an exaggeration to say that twice that number would
attend if we were not restricted by safety and hygiene considerations.

The Prize Giving was a sea of young keen happy faces who had obviously enjoyed a great week. The prizes were almost endless
and I was glad ofthe help of my wife Sue in presenting them.

The medium and long-term future of any Club can be found in the enthusiasm of its Cadets. The future of Marconi Sailing Club
therefore must be assured.

Cadet Week constitutes but half of Camping Fortnight. I must thank Hilary Ashley for managing the applications once again. This
job requires the strength and judgment of Solomon to fit the supply to the over demand. Thanks Hilary.

8.0 Entertainments

The Social sub Committee comprising Laura Gill, Claire Davies, Chris Hutt, Fenella Thomas, Sally Ferguson and Hilary Ashley,
organized events throughout the year.
January saw the Barn Dance, April the Fitting Out Supper and September Quiz Night. In addition the new Century was seen in at
the Clubhouse and the Summer Solstice was celebrated in style. All events most enjoyable and were well supported, even if the
support did not materialize itself until the last minute. Thanks for all the ideas and hard work ladies.
Laura is standing down from the Social Manager role after two years and I am pleased to welcome Fenella Thomas who has agreed
to be co-opted onto the Main Committee to replace Laura. Thanks Laura and good luck Fenella.

Steve and Debbie Glynn, have again arranged the Laying Up Supper this year.
I look forward to the opportunity of seeing members next week clad in something other than sailing attire. Many thanks Steve and
Debbie.

Muna's Travels /continued

Part Eighteen - The British Virgin Islands
Most of what we had read and heard about the BVI's failed to prepare us properly for them. We had got the distinct impression that
they weren't really worth a visit. Consequently as we sailed through the protective ring of outer islands we were literally stunned at
how beautiful they were and from a distance at least, how relatively unspoiled they were. The vegetation is so lush that many of
the smaller islands are virtually unmarked roads. Small resorts have been established round individual bays with little intrusion on
the rest of the island. Having said that there are large numbers of charter boats, but there is such a wealth of protected anchorages
that it is never difficult to find somewhere to anchor.

11

Our arrival on Tortolla was slightly marred by an immigration officer, who, after comparing my experience with that of others,
appears to delight in making life difficult for visiting yachtsmen. When confronted with a windowless door with a large sign
saying knock and enter, most people do just that. If however on opening the door you discover someone already there then you are
shouted at for coming in when she is dealing with someone. When I was there my customs clearance that I had brought with me
from upstairs, completely disappeared while | was filling out forms for all the crew. Other people had come in whilst I was doing
these forms and most of them had been shouted at as well. When I realised that the form was missing, she just kept telling me that
it was my problem not hers and treated me like an extremely irksome and naughty schoolboy. When I eventually gave up and went
back to the customs upstairs, they were extremely helpful and after contacting the lady in immigration decided that someone must
have picked up my form by mistake and gave me a photocopy. To be fair, most of the customs and immigration officials that we
have come into contact with, have been friendly and helpful, particularly considering that some of the rules they have to enforce are
bizarre to say the least. Checking in and out is always an experience and sometimes a very lengthy one.

The anchorage at Road Town where you check in is a very exposed rather lumpy one, so once back on board we upped anchor and
moved across to Great Harbour on Peter Island which belying its name, was in fact a picturesque and sheltered little bay. We were
able to snorkel straight from the boat. The great thing about the BVI's is the ease with which you can move from one anchorage to
another.

The next day we attempted to explore the heavily wooded island. There was very little development apart from a very exclusive
resort in the next bay. In the afternoon we met up with Ian and Anne on Miss Chips, another boat that we had been meeting up
with at various times on our travels. It had become something of a joke that they would first know that we were around by
bumping into Laura in some obscure location. They were on their way to join in with a five day Virgin Island Rally that the Ocean
Cruising Club were organising. Ian showed me some of the OCC cruising information he had been given and I was most
impressed. He kindly offered to propose us as members and we decided to move over to Trellis Bay, the next day, for the start of
the rally.

On arrival, we were made extremely welcome by Mike Pocock, Commodore of OCC, on board Blackjack, the boat in which he and
his wife Pat circumnavigated about ten years ago and are now doing an Atlantic Circuit. This circuit was forming thee basis of a
whole series of OCC meetings and rallies. Some OCC boats were doing the whole circuit with Blackjack, others were just meeting
up for particular rallies. On board Blackjack when we visited, was Mary Barton wife of the late Humphrey Baron. Helen was quite
overawed when Mike having readily agreed to second my membership proposal, Mary insisted on seconding Helen's.

At Trellis Bay we met up with John and Anders from Fanai that we had last seen in the Canaries. The next morning we sailed
around the top of Tortolla, in company with Fanai, Astolata and Aldebaran, through some narrow reef lined passes down to Cane
Garden Bay, an anchorage sheltered by an off lying reef with just one narrow pass through it. While the others managed to anchor
in close proximity in the sheltered but crowded part of the bay, I incurred the wrath of the crew by doing my usual thing of circling
the anchorage three times, then opting to anchor in the more exposed part of the bay where we had plenty of swinging room. On
going ashore we all got involved in the rescue of a twenty-six footer that had come up on the beach. A combination of applied
technology and gang ho got it refloated. The owners a Canadian couple who had lived on the island for about twenty years invited
us all up to their house which had incredible views across the islands as far as St. Thomas in the USVI's.

The next day we made our way to an isolated by on Little Jost Van Dyke. We had the place virtually to ourselves with just
Aldebaran for company. We had a fascinating time sitting on the shore watching the pelicans diving for fish. The whole time that
we were watching them, we never saw one fruitless, or fishless, dive. In the morning the anchorage soon filled up as Ocean
Cruising Club boats arrived for a beach party. It turned out to be an extremely sociable day and a good opportunity for learning
from other peoples experiences.

From Little Jost Van Dyke we carried on our circumnavigation of Tortolla passing through a narrow pass at its southern tip and
sailing up the Francis Drake Channel to Cooper Island where we anchored outside the buoys in at least seventeen metres. Some of
the bays are almost totally filled by these mooring buoys, which you are free to pick up for the princely sum of twenty dollars. By
the time darkness fell most of the buoys would generally have been taken.

We had one of our best sails for a while close hauled up the coast of Virgin Gorda then motoring through a gap in the reef to the
large expanse of enclosed water that is Virgin Gorda Sound. Anchoring off the Bitter End Yacht Club we were again in company
with a number of OCC yachts for the last event of the rally, a dinner ashore for eighty-six.

Commodore's Report 2000

9.0 Membership

Our Membership has remained stable through the year at around the 400 mark.
Within this figure many members are family members whose membership permits partners and children to use the Club facilities
which means at least 1000 people make a call on the Club services.

The Main Committee feel that the Club has much to offer prospective members and believe the Club would benefit from a modest
increase in membership.
The added income would help the Club’s finances and new members often bring new ideas and enthusiasm. To this end the
Executive has invited Margaret Yeoman to draw up a plan for increasing recruitment to the Club, She has already got together a
sub committee to help her with the tasks, and you will see her name on the list of nominees to the Main Committee where she will
be able to keep us in touch with her progress.

10.0 The Site and Clubhouse

Two members have responsibilities for the Site. They are the Vice Commodore, Peter Bloomfield, and Clubhouse Secretary Mick
Richardson. Steve Glynn, Frank Bennett and Pat Black have also contributed their time and expertise in many ways.

If the gate opened, the shower worked, the grass was cut, a pint was pulled or a bacon sandwich consumed it was due to the
organisation of one of these members.

Darren is the sole employee of the Club. He has operated the dedicated grass-mowing tractor during the year. He has also
undertaken regular cleaning duties.

Tony and Wendy operated the Galley concession throughout the year, including the Winter Series. Judging from the feedback |
have received, they are delivering the service most people want.

In the Spring of this year Neil Pembleton took over the vacant position of Bar Manager. He reorganised the system of deliveries
and thus reduced the work load of the Bar Manager. Also a new cellar chilling system was installed by Neil, Steve Monks and other
members, this led to a full flow of cool drinks even at the busiest times.
Neil made it clear that he would only undertake the role on a temporary basis, and the position of Bar Manager is again vacant. We
need a volunteer, no Bar experience is necessary as Nei] will train the new recruit. The stark reality is, no Bar Manager, no bar, so
if you think you could help please see me after this meeting. TM

11.0 The Five Year Plan

The first, and most fundamental element of any Five-Year Plan must be that the Organisation should continue to exist at the end of
the period of the plan. The Executive has closely monitored the health of our parent MASC, especially with regard to the future
after the lease of Beehive Lane expires in October 2001. To this end the Executive has met with the MASC Committee on three
occasions during the year.

Some of the assurances we were seeking were not forthcoming and the Executive thought it prudent to set up a sub committee to
prepare a plan that would ensure that the Club could survive should the parent expire.
The sub committee has prepared a Business Plan which is ready to be put into action if necessary. | am extremely grateful to Chris
Davies, David Thomas and John Bird who joined Frank Bennett, Pat Black and myself in many long and productive meetings
during the year.

Several members joined me at the MASC AGM a week or so ago.
Les Murray, the President of that Committee, relayed verbal assurances that he had received from the Head of Property Services in
BAe, Dr. Malcolm Green.
It seems that BAe have decided to grant MASCa further lease of five years on Beehive Lane ‘on condition that the Club remains
solvent’. So it seems the threat may be receding. You may be sure the Executive will continue to monitor the position and will be
ready to act quickly if necessary. I will keep the membership fully informed.

In order to get early warning of outside influences that may affect the Club we have continued our
policy of serving on local Committees that deal with the future of the Blackwater. Ron Greygoose and |
have attended the quarterly BACSPA meetings. BACSPA is a local Committee of the RYA and is
dedicated to protect our right to sail on the Blackwater. | believe that by attending such meetings we
will be able to influence opinion and policy on matters which are of direct concern to the Club's future.

During the year the Main Committee have spent much time discussing, pricing and prioritising the future spending plans of the
Club over the next five years. I kept the membership informed via Navigans as each step was concluded.
Two consultative meetings were held with the membership during the summer.
The process of consultation culminated in an Opinion Poll wherein every member was given the opportunity to choose from three
proposed Plans for expenditure. The majority of members returned their Ballot papers and a clear pattern emerged. Members did
not wish the subscription rate to be substantially increased to finance expansion and improvement of Club facilities. Accordingly
the subscription rise you will be asked to approve later is for inflation only, and work at the Club will be implemented in
accordance with Plan A.

12.0 The Secretariat

The Secretariat is made up of our Hon. Treasurer, Frank Bennett; our Hon. Secretary Pat Black and the Membership Secretary
Linda Chaplain. The Club cannot operate without the day to day attention to detail of these members, who freely and willingly give
up at least one day every week to their duties. Frank’s role is particularly time consuming, as well as constantly giving good
financial advice he is a familiar figure at Beehive Lane where he ensures the Club’s position is safeguarded.

Another important day to day task is that of Navigans Editor, and Kevin and Belinda Dowley have produced an extremely readable
and informative publication which has grown in size as the enthusiasm of our members grows. To the members who tell me they
don’t read it, I can only say ‘You don’t know what you are missing’
In response to my request at the let AGM Mike & Maggie Boreham have taken over the distribution of the magazine.

Navigans is a vital organ of the Club, building enthusiasm and informing members, and I thank Belinda, Kevin, Maggie and Mike
for their dedication.

13.0 Main Committee

I would like to end my Report by thanking those members who have served on the Main Committee during the year. | will not list
them all by name as over twenty members serve on that Committee. The meetings have been well attended despite the fact they
regularly last two and a half hours. The wide range of opinions expressed were most helpful to the Executive and to the running of
the Club.
Some Main Committee members stood down this year. I thank Rob Davies, Jon Yorston, Eric Cockerton, and Mike Smith for their
contributions over the year or in many cases years. After this AGM I look forward to welcoming Margaret Yeoman, Steve Monks
and Chris Davies, and look forward to working with you.

The Executive have also met every month and have often sat late into the evening while discussing the Club’s business and future.
The Rear Commodore Jenny Ball has kept the main business of the Club running most efficiently, aided and abetted by the Sailing
Sub Committee. It is not widely known, but the Rear Commodore has a greater load of regular meetings than even the Commodore.
Three a month. Jenny’s involvement with Cadets and Cadet Week pushes that number higher. It is a lot to fit in with a full time job
and still get out sailing from time to time.
Our two ‘Honoraries’ have given much time and no little skill in the conduct of Club affairs. You will recall that the term Honorary
means ‘Unpaid’ which is very good for the Club as, if we were to employ professionals to do these jobs, we would need to double
the subscriptions. No praise is too high for the dedication of Pat Black and Frank Bennett.

One of the Executive comes to the end of his tenure at this AGM. He is Peter Bloomfield our Vice Commodore, Peter has worked
hard for three years to keep all of the Club’s on-shore facilities in working order. It is a mark of Peter’s quiet but determined
application that he did not wish to stand down. The Committee will not lose his expertise as he has indicated his willingness to
serve as Vice President. Thanks Peter.

I could not finish this section on the Committee without mentioning our President of many years, Ron Greygoose. He has continued
to promote the best interests of the Club throughout the year and in many ways. He suffered a spell of poor health during the year,
but we are all very pleased to see him back at Committee meetings where his counsel is highly valued.

14.0 Closing Statements

We have a difficult year ahead, but I am certain that, not only will the Club survive but it will come through stronger than ever.

I wish you Good Sailing in 2001.
