Muna's Travels /continued

We spent a couple of days taking it easy in Drakes’s anchorage behind the reef. While we were there | studied the charts and
decided that Anegada a reef strewn island 4 miles to the north of Virgin Gorda would be well worth a visit. When Aldebaran
joined us it turned out that they had been thinking much the same thing. We had by this time been cruising with Aldebaran for
nearly two months. There had been very little forward planning to our cruising itinerary. It had simply evolved as we had gone
along. Both boats would move on as they felt like it. Without any great arrangements, our plans just seemed to coincide. It had
added to the fun and been an added ingredient in our cruising.

The sail up to Anegada was another fast one and the arrival at the anchorage fairly uneventful with the entry through the extensive
reefs being well buoyed. The most alarming bit was when the depths in the entrance suddenly shoaled. Thinking we were going to
run aground at any second I chickened out and headed for one of the mooring buoys that had been laid there. In the afternoon we
attempted to explore some of the interior of the island. We found a large lagoon, home to pink flamingos, that we managed to get
fairly close to. Our attempts to penetrate further were thwarted by some extremely thick undergrowth that seemed to cover the
island. An extremely low lying island the highest point was reputed to be twenty eight feet above sea level. The next day we had
an exciting trip in an open truck that was called a taxi, across the island to a beach on the north side where the snorkelling was
particularly good.

While we were in Anegade we heard someone just off Tortola asking for help because the steering on his charter boat had jammed.
No one seemed able or prepared to help him and there must have been several boats in the area at the time. Tortola radio told him
to call the US Coastguard, who failed to reply. After repeated calls for help on 16, someone came on telling him to switch to a
working channel and not block 16 and then proceeded to book dinner for that night at one of the many shoreside restaurants!

The next day we had another fast sail back to Virgin Gorda and an area known as the baths. Free short stay buoys are provided for
where you dinghy into a bay. If, as on the day we went, there is a big swell running, you can tie your dinghy to a line between two
buoys and swim or snorkel ashore. We were rather concerned as to whether we would manage to get ashore at all. When we
finally got there we still weren’t entirely sure that we had come to the right place. I was therefore relieved to see a large kiosk with
the word INFORMATION emblasooned above it. Approaching the rather bored looking individual who was positioned underneath
this sign, listening to the radio, | asked whether this was in fact the place known as the Baths. Tearing himself away from his radio
with great reluctance, he looked at me soulfully and with considerable effort replied ‘Yeah’. I failed to elicit any further response
from him at all. We found our way into the Baths which turned out to be a whole series of partially flooded underground caverns,
formed by virtue of a large number of enormous boulders resting on one another. It took about twenty minutes to scramble from
one end of these walkways to the other through a variety of routes. The effect as the sea surged into these caveners with light
streaming in through gaps in the ceiling of rocks above was electrifying. At one point | clambered over a rock to see MUNA
perfectly framed in a gap between the boulders. Seeing me looking an American couple coming up behind me stopped to look as
well. ‘Don’t you just wish the view from home was as good as that?’ the man said. I was able to reply with some pride ‘that is my
home’.

Our next port of call was a return visit to Road Town with its very exposed anchorage. We needed to do some provisioning but the
main reason for our visit was that Jenny need to book a flight back to England. She was committed to returning b the middle of
May. All in all, this time as a reunited family had worked remarkably well. Clearly there were always going to be times when four
adults living on a ten metre boat for an extended period, was going to be a bit of a squash. That things went as well as they did
must be put down to a combination of the weather, which meant that there were very few times when we were all battened down
below decks and the tolerance and understanding of the skipper. That last bit will probably be edited out by my censors. The main
difficulty on board was not having a second sleeping cabin. This was not so much a problem at night when the girls were generally
quite happy sleeping the comparatively airy saloon, but more so during the day when in the general business of living we would on
occasions simply run out of space. We had always known that there was going to be limited space when there were more of us on
board. MUNA had in all fairness been designed for two people to live on. It was only at anchor that lack of space became a
problem. At sea there were few complaints. On balance there would have been times when we all got on each others nerves even
in a bigger boat. All in all it had been a good time for all of us and I think we were all genuinely surprised and pleased that it had
all worked out as well as it had.

Jenny got a flight booked from Puerto Rico for May the fifth. We had decided that it would be worth pressing on through the
USVI’s and the Spanish VI’s, before beginning our journey south for the hurricane season. We had left home without obtaining
US visas so we now had to take a day ferry trip the USVI’s which would give us a three month visa waiver in our passports. In the
event we had quite an enjoyable high speed ferry trip from Sophers Hole in the south of Tortola to St. Thomas in the USVI’s,
weaving our way through tiny rock strewn passes without any reduction in speed. We got the necessary stamps in our passports
and the prized green cards and were now in a position to embark on an epic hour and a half long voyage in MUNA to the states.

Part Nineteen — The U.S. Virgin Islands

Muna’s introduction to the USVI’s was a little bit fraught. Sailing downwind from Soper’s Hole in Tortola we had a pleasant
genoa run between a number of islets including the negotiation of an extremely narrow reef lined pass. I am a notoriously bad
delegator in situations such as this, so 1 was quite proud of the fact that I let Jenny steer us through and managed somehow or other
to keep my hands off the tiller. I did however succumb to a severe bout of nervous behaviours. We very quickly arrived at Cruz
Bay on St. John’s where we needed to check in. On taking the sails down and motoring in we discovered it to be a very small and
extreemnly busy port. As we ventured in towards the custom dock, fast ferries seemed to be charging in and out at an alarming
rate. Two buoys reserved for boats clearing customs were occupied. As we passed them in the narrow channel we could see the
customs dock ahead. In the pilot it said that boats could tie up alongside for short period. With Helen telling me that it was too
narrow and busy and that we should turn round and anchor outside the harbour, 1 headed for the customs dock and promptly ran
hard aground.

No amount of gunning the engine in reverse had any effect. Neither did the appearance of a customs officer who indicated where
we should tie up alongside the dock. Eventually a couple went by in an inflatable. They valiantly attempted to push our bows back
into deeper water with no success. While they were doing this an American in a powerful R.I.B. came over to us. “Got a problem’
he asked in a thick Texan drawl. Applying full power to our bows he was only successful in completely soaking himself. He then
attempted to push our stern out as I put the engine hard astern, again without success. He then came up with the idea of pushing
our bows onto the sandbank while I again went hard astern. It sounded crazy to me but this time I was willing to try anything.
With both our engine and his roaring at full power and spray flying everywhere, we moved. We were off. Helen went below to get
10

our rescuer a cold beer. With a loud ‘Yahoo’ he spun the R.1.B. around at full revs gave us a wave and disappeared as quickly as
he had come, in a cloud of spray.

Helen appeared in the companionway clutching the beer ‘Where is he?’ Then after a pause watching the cloud of spray disappear
into the distance, she said ‘Who was that?’ ‘That’ I said, narrowing my eyes for dramatic effect, “That was the Lone Ranger’.

Making our way gingerly back through the outer harbour we passed Aldebaran anchored sensibly near the entrance. Our recent
escapades had been hidden from their view by a steep promontory and they now assumed that we had successfully checked in. We
decided to anchor as a couple of other boats had done, right outside the harbour. As we were about to do this, one of the boats that
had been on a customs buoy, left the harbour indicating that the buoy was free. Heading back in we secured to the buoy with less
that six inches under our keel] and made our way at long last to customs.

After our experiences in the British Virgin Islands, the whole process of checking in was a revelation. The officials were
professional but polite and friendly. On of the stranger stipulations was that while we were in the USVI’s under no circumstances
were we to take any garbage ashore, even if we had bought the original product there, as by being on the boat it would have
become contaminated. When we asked what we should do with our rubbish, they asked where we were gong next. We replied that
eventually we expected to move on to Puerto Rico. ‘Take it there then’ they replied.

Our brief tour of the town was rewarded with happy smiling friendly faces, in marked contrast to the BVI’s. We could only stay
for a limited time on the customs buoy so we returned to the boat and motored around to the next bay, Cancel Bay, was unlike Cruz
Harbour there was plenty of space and an abundance of mooring buoys laid off a white sandy beach. A large part of the island was
given to the National Park by the Rockefeller family. Recent bequests have allowed the National Park Authority to fulfil its aim of
setting up mooring buoys in each of the bays overseen by the authority. The main aim of these buoys is to give people access to the
Park at the same time as limiting the damage being done to coral by anchoring. For the time being these buoys were free which
made another pleasant change after the BVI’s.

In spite of the wonderful surroundings the stress of the earlier part of the day had got to both Helen and myself so Pat’s idea of
going back into Curz by taxi to visit an Irish Pub ha had discovered earlier, turned out to be the light relief we needed, involving a
lively meeting with a group of Puerto Ricans and an impromptu game of darts.

We spent the next the days or so, circumnavigating St. John’ very slowly and loved all we saw of it. The National Park Authority
have made such a difference by ensuring that any development is restricted and effectively controlled. In the Cinnamon Bay our
second stop, a large campsite run by the Authority is masked by trees and completely invisible from the bay. This campsite proved
to be very welcoming and gave us the unaccustomed luxury of plentiful freshwater showers.

From Cinnamon Bay we tackled a fairly ambitious trek across the island to Reef Bay. The rough path cut deep through the dense
forest and was mercifully shaded from the intense glare of the sun on the way out. On the way out we saw ancient rock carvings
made by early Arowak settlers. By Reef Bay we explored the ruins of an old sugar mill factory with an intact stationary steam
engine manufactured in England. The island is now so densely forested that it is hard to believe that a hundred years ago it was
almost entirely cultivated.

We swam in the surprisingly warm water of Reef Bay, then made our way back up the steep track, now much more exposed to the
burning afternoon sun. During our time so far in the Caribbean we had acclimatised better than we had expected to. This was in no
small part due to the fact that the early months of the year had been somewhat wetter and cooler than usual. Now as summer
approached we were finding the heat increasingly hard to take, particularly on land. On the plus side the heat was proving very
beneficial to aching bones.

Back in Cinnamon Bay we attended a free open-air play illustrating the history of the island. From Cinnamon Bay we went to
Waterlemon Bay where we snorkelled and explored the remains of another sugar mill factory. Part of these ruins was a stoutly
built cell where reca Icitrant slave’s had been ensconced.

Further round the island we anchored in Hurricane Hole, as its name implies, an extremely sheltered spot behind the Mangroves.
From there we had to brave the exposed point of Ram Head, which came as something of a shock after the sheltered water we had
just left behind. Keeping well into the rocky headland to avoid an off lying shoal, we bashed under engine into the head winds and
seas. It was a great relief when we had rounded the headland sufficiently to bear away and bring the wind abeam. Its at times like
that when you realise how dependant you are on the engine. It’s a situation that makes me distinctly uneasy and gives me intense
respect for those brave souls who sail engineless, particularly in waters like these.

Heading into the sheltered Great Lameshur Bay, it was a special pleasure to be once again greeted by a plentiful supply of free
mooring buoys. As we secured to a buoy and began to take in our idyllic surroundings, I noticed a Maxi 1000 on another buoy. I
was just debating with myself whether it could be Maximum that we had me in Graciosa and had last seen in Puerto Calero, when I

1]

saw Jack and Jeanette climbing onto their dinghy and coming over to see us. It was yet another of those chance encounters. They
had been on the point of leaving when we came in. It was great fun sharing experiences and finding yet another potentially much
faster boat, that by tackling the Atlantic crossing over a month before us, had taken considerably longer.

This bay proved to be a superb snorkelling and simply enjoying the location,. We once again appreciated the existence of the
National Park which was responsible for preserving this tranquillity by preventing the kind of untidy development that would
undoubtedly have taken place. Ashore we were made extremely welcome at the environmental centre that functions as both
research centre and education camp for, mainly American, students. It was fascinating to see more evidence of the natural
reforestation of the island after years of cultivation.

This was a place we could happily have stayed on a lot longer. However we had a deadline with Jenny’s flight on the 12" of May
from Puerto Rico. It was now the 26" of April so we moved slowly down the coast following Aldebaran onto Rendezvous Bay, an
anchorage that initially I wasn’t too keen on, as it felt rather exposed and windy. Helen and I explored the nearby beach while Pat,
Olivia and Jenny went ashore at another more developed beach as they wanted to go back into Cruz Bay to use e-mail etc. On their
return it transpired that they had been given a lift into town by an American couple staying in one of the holiday villas and that we
had all been invited to have a barbeque with them that evening.

The barbeque turned out to be a lavish meal. We all had a thoroughly enjoyable evening while we marvelled at the unaccustomed
luxury of deep armchairs, sunken swimming pools and space.

Early the next morning we said our farewells to Pat and Olivia and settled down for a lively and enjoyable genoa run to Charlotte
Amalie on St. Thomas. As we approached we still had the VHF on 77 dual watch, the channel we had been using for inter boat
chat. Now we realised it was being used rather more formally by a cruise ship monitoring the activities of it’s boats, transporting
the passengers ashore. St. Thomas although part of the U.S., has been declared a duty free zone. It has therefore become a very
popular stop with American tourists. As we approached the harbour it slowly dawned on us that the ship that we had been listening
to was none other than the QE2. She made an impressive sight anchored just of the rocky harbour entrance.

Once inside the harbour we anchored a little way off the Cruise Ship Dock. Once ashore we had access to the biggest supermarkets
we had seen in a long time and as in St. Johns a remarkably cheap phone service. The next morning we visited customs to discover
that to move on to the Spanish Virgin Islands it was necessary to notify customs but not Immigration as we would be passing from
one U.S. state to another. The Spanish Virgins Islands are part of Puerto Rico which is officially party of a U.S. Commonwealth.
A 1993 referendum voted by a narrow majority to remain a Commonwealth, defeating those who wished the island to become a full
USE. state.

After leaving customs we made our way to the fuel dock where we topped up on diesel, petrol for the outboard and water. By the
time that we had done all this, time was pressing, so rather than head off for the island of Culebra, as we had originally intended,
we stopped off at Water Island, just off the entrance to Charlotte Amalie Harbour. After investigating one or two possible
stopovers we anchored in Flamingo Harbour. After investigating one or two possible stopovers we anchored in Flamingo Bay next
to two or three ‘ being worked on’ type of boats. It turned out to be a fascinating island. Just inside our anchorage was a narrow
cut to a shallow inner lagoon where some rickety pontoons served a collection on tatty but serviceable and powerful runabouts. By
the lagoon a collection of rusty old cars minus things like bonnets and doors, gave the place the look of a scrap yard. While we
were there, another powerful runabout roared in through the narrow pass. An affluent looking family unloaded their shopping,
climbed into one of the doorless and rusty cars and calmly drove off. On walking around the island we found it to be a strange
mixture of affluent properties and deserted ruins, some with optimistic for sale notices.

Minutes - November Meeting of Main Committee

Executive Meeting. Ai their meeting on the 25'" October 2000 the Executive discussed the following: Urinal replacement, RIB replacement, MASC AGM, MSC AGM, membership.

MASC AGM. The MSC was represented by C Shenton, MR & Mrs D Kirby, P Black, F Bennett, N Pembleton, Ron & Mary Greygoose. The revised MASC constitution is on hold. The Club Manager appealed for members to join the MASC Committee, during most meetings there are not sufficient members to form a quorum. The President, Mr L Murray said that there was a possible 5-year extension to the MASC Yease but this was not yet in writing and depended on the MASC remaining solvent. The Club Manager said that plans were being prepared to upgrade the Club and these were available for viewing.

Safety. White lining on hold for better weather. RIB accident, Ms J Ball said that additional training is being scheduled on boat handling and VHF radio operating procedures. East Coast Piers Race. Mr C Davis arranged for a presentation of the proceeds of the race to the Cirden Trust, £8000 was donated.

Clubhouse and Site. Work commenced on urinals. Sewage plant, we have received a letter from the Environment Agency, the system was re-inspected on the 3'9 October, no real result.

Clubhouse Window, progress contractor.

Mr F Bennett said that the skip had to be in an accessible position for the collecting vehicle and also where
the vehicle, which is large, would not cause any damage.
Social. Mrs L Gill has retired from the position of Social Manager; the committee thanked her for her contribution during the year. The new Social Manager is Fenella
Thomas.

Moorings Sub Committee. Mr P Clayton said that a large triple hydraulic pump, (Acquired and refurbished by M Bates at no cost to the club) has been trialed and the results were
good. Estimated costs, Valve £60; Tank £150; Filter £265; Interconnecting Hoses £20.00
All ex VAT. These costs could be offset against the purchase of a new snatch block £253.00, the existing block being condemned. Mr F Bennett asked if the winch proposal was a departure from the five year plan, a general discussion
ensued.

Muna's Travels /continued

Part Twenty - Puerto Rico and the Spanish Virgin Islands

We made an early start the next morning, leaving Water Island for Culebra. Once again we just had our genoa set and made good
progress past the well named Sail Rock, standing well out on it’s own and visible for miles around. Having negotiated the
extensive reefs surrounding Culebra we motored through the narrow reef lined entrance to Ensanada Honda, a lagoon that
stretches deep onto the island. Having made our way to the far end of the lagoon we anchored just off the town of Dewey. Jenny
and I went ashore to clear in at customs. I

To clear customs you had to go to the Airport, although airstrip might be a more accurate description. The customs official
clearly had little to do because he seemed quite genuinely pleased to see us.

We weren’t initially taken with the anchorage off Dewey, so in the morning after sitting out a torrential rain shower, we made our
way out of the tye lagoon towards the little island of Culebrita. The wind was blowing in the mid twenties and kicking up a nasty
chop in the channel. We were relieved to get in the lee of the island. We headed for an anchorage near to a path that led to the
top of the island. One yacht was already anchored there and as we circled behind him we discovered that the anchorage was
smaller than we expected and we slid across the top of a rock. Making our way further round the island we could see the bay that
is the best anchorage on the island. However to get to it we would have to negotiate a narrow pass through a reef. In the current
conditions the pass looked less than inviting. In addition being Sunday, the bay was full to overflowing with Puerto Ricon Navy,
large fast white powerboats with enough elevated structures above to keep a stainless steel worker in business for years.

We decided to anchor off the tip of the island in the shelter of the reef, from where we were able to dinghy ashore. The beach we
landed on was a superb example of the best of Caribbean beaches. White sand lapped by turquoise water and no one else to be
seen. The only drawback was that there were no paths allowing for us to explore the rest of the island, but we settled for a
deserted beach. Later on that afternoon we made our way back in Muna to Culebra where we picked up a mooring buoy just
behind the reef at the entrance to the lagoon. It was a wonderful spot. We were exposed to the full force of the wind, but
sheltered behind the reef the water was flat calm. As in St. Johns the buoys were again free, in this case provided by the
Government.

I learned that the buoys were free after talking to John on a 29 foot S and S design on a neighboring buoy. Although he based hi s
boat there, he was from Nantucket where he kept another boat. He divided his time between the two boats. This boat was now
engineless and he sailed singlehanded, with just Lucy his dog for crew. Lucy was an obedient and loyal a crew as you could
hope to find. John took great delight in restoring old dinghies and rigging them very simply for sail. While we were there he
gave us a great deal of interesting local information. He told us that Water Island off St. Thomas was occupied by eccentric
millionaires, many of whom had businesses on St. Thomas and who used Water Island as a recluse.

When John need some extra cash he would go ashore with Lucy and put a sandwich board around his neck advertising day
charters, apparently he never had trouble attracting custom. I was amazed that he could operate engineless from this lagoon, the
narrow entrance was dead into the prevailing winds.

Making the most of the quiet solitude of these islands, before we had to cope with what we felt would be the bustle of Puerto
Rico, we went the short distance to the little island of Cayode Luis Pena, just to the west of Culebra. The bay we headed for had
just two mooring buoys, one of which was occupied. The other boat turned out to be on a diving expedition and left shortly after
we arrived. We then had the place all to ourselves. We rowed ashore to the secluded little beach from where we were able to
walk across to a bay the other side of the headland. There we saw evidence of what looked like wartime military structures.

We sailed off the buoy early the next morning and had another fast downwind sail. After studying the charts and pilot books we
had concluded that the East Coast of Puerto Rico had very few sheltered anchorages and that we had little option but to make one
of our increasingly rare visits to a marina. Heading into the coast towards Puerto Del Rey we were conscious of the number of
reefs and rocky islets we were passing. It was akin to running merrily into the lion’s jaw.

Puerto Del Rey Marina was something of a culture shock. An enormous complex consisting of a long wide concrete dock,
complete with a three storey facility block halfway along its length and numerous smaller solid docks running off it. The normal
mode of transport around the docks were golf buggies. The marina was absolutely full with row upon row of mainly white,
powerboats. My introduction to this alien world consisted of being directed into an empty berth in a long line of smaller
powerboats and then being whisked off in a golf buggy to the main office. After the peace and tranquility of the smaller islands it
took a bit of getting used to.

We decided to hire a car for a couple of days to facilitate getting Jenny to the airport and also to see something of at least the
eastern end of the island. We also needed to refill a couple of our gas cylinders and get a few supplies in. Most of these services
seemed to be a fair distance away. We were definitely in a land of the car. My introduction to this aspect of the culture was a
little fraught. Having been assigned a large immaculate vehicle I had a bit of trouble dealing with the automatic gearbox, having
never used one before. The family hardly dared speak while I maneuvered with difficulty out of the marina car park and on to the
highway proper. We then experienced difficulties in translating the scale of directions we had been given at the marina office
into reality. Just a little way on your left turned out to be several miles. Consequently we turned off far too soon and instead of
arriving at the propane gas works, that had been our intended first port of call, found ourselves instead arriving at the Roosevelt
Roads Naval Base in the middle of a security clampdown, in response to anti American protests that were taking place at
the time.

Having successfully found the propane gas we needed wejoined the main highway to San Juan. This four and at times five lane
route proved to be an even more severe test of my already shredded nerves. Whatever speed I was doing didn’t seem to be fast
enough for the police behind me and whichever lane I happened to be in seemed to be the wrong one. After a brief beach stop
where a row of near identical bars seemed to stretch for a least half a mile, we turned off the highway and escaped up a side road
into the peace of the rain forest.

Reputed to be the only tropical rainforest on United States Territory it proved to be a magical experience. Parking the car high
up the mountain we walked through the lush and damp vegetation, realizing that for the first time for a very long time we were
actually cool. We eventually arrived at an impressive waterfall cascading into a pool that were able to swim in.

The next day we had to negotiate the main San Juan highway at morning rush hour. I was still finding great difficulty in coping
with the speed and sheer volume of traffic. The situation wasn’t helped by the fact that the turn offs are only marked once, some
distance prior to the turn off itself. The actual turnoff if simply marked Salida. It took me a while to realize that this meant exit.
I initially wondered why so many places had the same name. Eventually after only two wrong turnings we arrived at the airport
and saw Jenny safely on her way.

After leaving the airport we attempted to make our way into San Juan itself. The roads were even busier and we ended up getting
lost and heading of in totally the wrong direction. When we eventually got to the town we discovered that we had arrived in the
middle of another Vieques demonstration. San Juan proved to be a beautiful and fascinating port. The heat however seemed to
be gaining in intensity by the day and we were all rather wilted.

Heading back to Culebra meant bashing straight into twenty-five knots of wind, an adverse current and a short sharp chop that the
area is notorious for. We tried sailing but progress was painfully slow and our tacks took us worryingly near the many rocks and
outlying reefs that enclose the area. Eventually bruised and battered we headed into the little island of Cayo Luis Pena that we
had left the week earlier. Once again we had the bay to ourselves. It was a great relief to be able to swim straight from the boat
again and have a totally relaxing afternoon wallowing in the solitude. As we picked up the buoy I had noticed a patch of yellow
on the seabed, I took this to be sand among the coral. On diving in with her mask Laura made the alarming discovery that it was
in fact a sunken yacht lying just a few feet below our keel.

Heading back to Culebra we made contact with Pat and Olivia on Aldebaran . They had been in Culebra a few days having
picked up friends in St. Thomas. The previous night they had taken part in a turtle watch and had put our names down with the
warden as being interested. Having rendezvoused behind the reef we had a pleasant time meeting their friends Jim and Rita and
catching up with each other’s experiences. The next day I met the warden Hobino. We arranged to accompany him that night but
unfortunately heavy rainfall made the path down to the beach untenable and the expedition had to be cancelled.

The following night we went ashore and met up with Hobino. We were luck in that that night Sam, an American professor who
had studied turtles in general and leatherback turtles in particular was coming on the watch. He was a world authority on the
subject. He was also the owner of a Hang Christian 43 with a strong desire to sail off into the wide blue yonder and was very
interested in our activities. We were also joined by a group of high school students from Puerto Rico whose teacher was also
very interested in our activities as his parents were liveaboards in the states.

The group having assembled we made our way in Hobino’s four wheel drive accompanied by the school mini bus along a
succession of narrow rutted tracks until we could go no further. We then walked down a rocky path to one end of the Brava
beach. Sam told us that this beach had been a nesting ground for leatherback turtles since dinosaurs roamed the earth. They have
few predators, their worst enemy being man, originally for his desire to hunt them but more recently for his tendency to develop
resorts on their traditional nesting sites. Once this happens the turtles stop coming and are left to wander the oceans looking for
alternative sites. The New York Institute that Sam represented had been in discussions with the owner of this beach for some
years to persuade him not to develop the beach. So far they had been successful but they did not know how long this state of
affairs would last.

When we got to the beach we walked in single file along the shoreline so as to cause minimal disruption to the sand. Too much
disturbance and the turtle’s might be put off landing. Halfway along the beach we headed up to the vegetation and made camp.
The plan was that two groups of two would walk in opposite directions the length of the beach. They would wait ten minutes and
then return. If they spotted fresh turtle tracks they would flash a torch three times so that the rest of the group could join them.
Laura went off with Sam as one of the first pairs. Time seemed to pass very slowly; we tried to make ourselves comfortable.
Much to our surprise some of the students managed to go straight off to sleep. Suddenly we saw three flashes. Making our way
as quietly as we could we met Sam who told us that as he and Laura came back along the beach a turtle had just come up. When
we got there it was still digging an enormous hole with its flippers. These turtles are staggering large. With a shell over six feet
long they make tracks up the beach over eight feet wide, their flippers are incredibly powerful. When they start digging sand is
moved at a remarkable rate. Once the hole has been dug they start laying. At this stage the turtle goes into a trance and you can
approach to watch proceedings and even touch them without disturbing them.

Laura counted eggs as they were being laid. There were approximately eighty fertile eggs and twenty-four smaller infertile ones.
All the eggs in one batch were the same sex. If the turtle laid in the cooler sand near the top of the beach they would be female.
If they were laid in the cooler sand near the sea they would be male. Make of that what you will. It was an amazing experience
watching this huge creature laying eggs, oblivious of the people crowded around it, holding its rear flippers apart so that the eggs
could be counted. Once the laying was over the turtle reversed it previous action with its flipper filling in the hole until not a
trace remained. It then turned itself around and made its way laboriously to the sea. The whole process had taken about forty-five
minutes.

When we got back to camp someone started pointing just beyond the surf line, a dark shape could be clearly seen in the
moonlight
just approaching the shore. A turtle reached the beach and lumbered up the sand straight towards us. Hardly daring to
move we kept as still as we could until it finally stopped just a few feet away from just and started digging its nest. We had a
ringside view of the whole fascinating process.

Helen and I did one more patrol the length of the beach. It was then time to go. When we got back to our dinghy it was just
getting light and we made our way back across the lagoon to Muna.

We were now beginning to think seriously about heading back down south for the hurricane season. As we had visited a great
many of the islands on the way up, I like the idea of heading straight back down. The problem was that to make a southeasterly
course was to more or less head into the prevailing winds. The easiest thing would have been to head south to Venezuela or the
Dutch ABC islands. However we had not ventured below St. Lucia and were now keen to visit the Grenadines and Grenada. We
therefore decided to head for Bequia in the Grenadines.

We now had to tear ourselves away from Culebra. Having been initially unimpressed with the little town of Dewey we had now
become very fond of it and felt very comfortable and relaxed there.

In spite of the dry but painfully cold weather that lived up to its forecast, there was still a good number of hardy spectators present
to watch the event - many sensible ones crowding into the nearby pubs and Maldon Little Ship Club to escape the cold. Several
did brave the outdoors and either waited on the quay or took the walk along the river bank to keep the hard-working rowers in
sight. The West Mersea Inshore Lifeboat visited the event to remind everyone of the good use that will be made of the funds
raised.

Over 40 boats took part in the race and the event's record total income is expected to top £10,000. The Basin Oars ladies won
their usual prize for the most sponsorship attracted by one boat - over £4,000; and another boat wona prize for its single occupant
whose sponsorship amounted to over £2,000 - over half the event's income coming from just two boats. Grateful thanks were
expressed by the organisers at the prize-giving ceremony to all those who had contributed either through donations on the day or
Sponsorship of a boat.

Marconi Sailing Club made its presence felt again this year in the blue rowing boat kindly lent by Charles Anderson - thank you,
Charles. Their fancy dress theme was Thunderbirds, with David Ball as Brains (‘making a spectacle of himself’ according to
Malcolm Stuart); Lucy Boreham as Lady Penelope (Parker, having been given the day off, didn't appear); and Jenny Ball and
Claire Davies as two of the International Rescue pilots. The Marconi entry won the prize for fancy dress and also for being the
first to finish out of the mixed crew entrants.

There were a couple of collecting buckets to receive donations for the Thunderbirds boat, and Sarah Davies collected most of the
£51.70 that Club Members and other shivering spectators contributed - our thanks go to all of them. This money is in addition to
sponsorship of over £75 raised by the Thunderbirds crew from Club Members, families, friends and work colleagues.

Next year's event will apparently 'skip a year' and take place on New Year's Day in 2002 - you may want to mark your diaries
now!

Thank you to everyone concerned for your support of the Marconi boat.

Muna's Travels /continued

Part Twenty-One - Heading South for the Grenadines.

Setting off early on Monday the fifteenth of May we cleared the outlying reefs and in a fresh easterly made good progress,
holding a course to clear the eastern tip of Vieques and make for St. Croix. We had decided to make St. Croix an option as it is in
the USVI'S. If we had cleared out of Culebra it would have meant surrendering our temporary green cards something | was not
happy about doing with all the naval activity in the area. As it happened we reached St. Croix after dark. The main anchorage is
heavily reefed so the decision was made for us and we kept going.

After an uneventful night, the wind slowly dropped off the next day. We gradually settled into a slow but comfortable passage.
Well clear of the main island chain this Part of the Caribbean is very quiet. We saw no ships or yachts for the whole of our
passage. As we progressed southwards I became preoccupied with a small rocky islet that lay due south of us. The chart showed
it as having a light but I had heard that it was now reputed to be unlit. As the wind shifted our course was taking us first one side
of it, then the other. We eventually passed well to the east without ever seeing it. This rock is apparently part of Venezuela and I
was- later to hear a fascinating story about it. A few years ago a group of scientists had set off from Venezuela to study the rock.
This was before the advent of GPS and they took a little while to find it. When they eventually got there they landed and were
astonished to be greeted by three yachtsmen who had been wrecked on the rock three weeks earlier.

We had once again timed our passage to coincide with a full moon, which makes all the difference for night sailing. After a long
rest the monitor self steering was put back into action and once again did everything that was asked of it. Our watch system of
four hours on eight hours off once again ensured that we had plenty of rest. In the conditions our daily averages of between
eighty and ninety miles weren't too bad, although at times progress felt painfully slow compared with some of our earlier
passages. What little wind there was, was hard on the nose and as we had anticipate our problem was making enough easting. We
became obsessive about our course competing with each other as to who could make the most easting and who lost precious
easting when a wind shift went against them.

The lack of wind made the heat even more noticeable. On one occasion the afternoon was enlivened by the sighting of an
impressive looking Portugese Man of War swimming right by the boat. On the fifth night the wind dropped right away. |
realised that the way we were going we would eventually miss the whole island chain completely. We started the engine and
managed to motorsail and set a course directly for Bequia. During the night the wind increased until it was blowing between
fifteen and eighteen knots. It seemed al] wrong to be motorsailing with a good wind blowing so I turned the engine off.

Inevitably over the next few hours although we made good Progress our course sagged off. As the wind increased I realised that
it was going to be a real struggle to reach Bequia. A few calculations quickly showed that Union Island would be an easier bet.
Laura read up the Pilot and discovered that Chatkam on the Western side of the island was completely open to the west and
would be easy to enter. Just what we needed. A little way Out from Union Island we started the engine and motorsailed under
Autohelm straight into the bay. We anchored off the beach in the company of just two other boats five days and four hundred and
fifty miles from Culebra.

Part Twenty Two - Union Island and Carriacou.

The Grenadines are a very popular and busy part of the Caribbean. It was therefore particularly pleasant to be in a large bay with
just a couple of other yachts for company. We should have by rights checked in straightaway at a port of entry but we couldn't
resist staying in this lovely, peaceful bay for at least a couple of days. I say peaceful, but there was in fact a wind effect that
caused strong gusts to rush down between the hills. It was a beautiful bay for swimming and we enjoyed a fairly strenuous
scramble up one of the surrounding hills giving us glorious view over the rest of Union and surrounding islands. From that height
the reefs were particularly clear and showed up in glorious technicolour.

Two days after arriving in Union, we attempted to move round the island to Clifton to check in. Having missed Bequia we had
decided that after checking in we would make our way to the Tobago Cays, a spectacular reef lined anchorage. Motoring along
the coast of Union, the trades had returned with a vengeance and we found ourselves bashing into it head on. Negotiating the
narrow reef lined entrance to Clifton we, were suddenly in a crowded anchorage with boat boys coming alongside trying to gain
our custom. After the solitude of the last few days it was all a bit much and having failed to find a sufficiently large space to
anchor I turned Muna round and headed back out of the harbour. We headed through the reefs to Palm Island but the anchorage
there was decidedly rally. We did consider going over to Tobago Cays without checking in but at this stage my desire for a
simple life held sway and we unfurled the jenny and set course south for Hillsborough in Carriacou. Carriacou is officially part
of Grenada so once checked in we would be cleared for Grenada as a whole. We had a lovely sail inside the Jack A Dan a small
off lyin islet and anchored in hillsborough just in time to clear customs before overtime rates came into play. I had a bit of a
tustle with customs because I had failed to clear out of Culebra but eventually all was resolved and Laura and I got back to the

10

boat to find the two Chris’ from Globe Star that we had last seen in Portugal, on board talking to Helen. It was something of a
surprise as they had originally planned to stay in Gibraltar and not come across until the following year.

One of the fascinations of this life is not knowing who you are going to meet up with next. We stayed in Hillsborough a few days,
which gave us time to explore the island. Helen and I caught the bus to Windward on the other side of the island where the
Carriacou racing sloops are built on the shore. It was certainly a beautiful location for boat building. We were interested to see a
modern yacht, being built among the trees using all kinds of epoxies and exotic materials. We wandered along the waterfront.
Helen followed her ears and found someone hammering out a steel drum. We then followed a dirt track that led past a cemetery
among the trees, and arrived at an absolutely deserted reef lined beach. This was the Caribbean | had dreamed about. We swam
in complete seclusion and reveled in our surroundings with the view of Union Island, Petit St. Vincent and Petit Martinique.
While we were anchored in Hillsborough we met up with Mike.and Mary on Meriva, a classic wooden holman Pye forty-one
footer built at Tucker Browns in Burnham in 1967. As members of the Ocean Cruising Club they had been at the Virgin Islands
Rally but we hadn't really got to know them there.

Leaving hillsborough we anchored for a few hours at nearby Sandy Island, a genuine desert island two hundred yards long with
white sand, a clump of palm trees and an off lying reef. While we were there an American couple were brought out to the island
by water taxi and deposited there presumably for a few hours of genuine ‘isolation’.

It was quite rally at Sandy Island so we motored round the headland to the calm of Tyrell Bay back on Carriacou proper. Tyrell
Bay is a fascinating settlement where everything appears to move very slowly. We saw the contrast of a new lift out facility being
built complete with travel hoist, right next to a fifty footer being built on the beach by traditional methods. We spent a pleasant
couple of hours at the yacht club drinking cool fruit juices and working my way through a plentiful supply of yachting
magazines.

With the approach of the hurricane season the weather was becoming slightly more unsettled with tropical waves beginning to
move through. Meriva moved on down to Grenada. The next day we had torrential rain and managed to catch enough water in
our bimini to refill our tanks. This was a great help to us and must have been a relief to the island as previously we had been
unable to even buy water there, it was in such short supply.

We took advantage of the next break in the weather to make our way south towards Grenada. We had a fair wind and a good sail
past the rocky little island of Isle de Ronde. Slightly further on we passed, the underwater volcano Kick ‘em Jenny that lies about
seventeen metres below the surface and reputed to be getting nearer the surface all the time. It, erupted in both 1988 and 1989, I
worked out that we were close enough to peer down into the crater. I later learned that the local ferry running between Carriacou
and Grenada, steers a course well clear of the volcano.

As we reached the lee of Grenada the wind dropped and we were quickly engulfed in a torrential shower that for a few minutes
completely obliterated the coastline

Part Twenty Three - Grenada.

The rain cleared as we made our way across St. George’s Bay. We decided to keep going round Saline Point to the south coast.
As we rounded Saline Point we were taken aback by the strength of wind in our faces. We motorsailed in a heavy chop tacking
out past a small island and then in towards Prickly Bay. Prickly Bay looked rather full so at the last moment we diverted to the
neighbouring True Blue Bay where we anchored along - with just two other boats.

Helen and | celebrated our arrival by having a meal at the exclusive True Blue resort restaurant, built over the water in a corner of
the bay. We didn't know it was exclusive until we landed there. We had a superb meal particularly after Helen had asked for
more rice. We were initially served with tiny little mounds of rice. I can never work out why haute cuisine has to be served in
such meagre portions.

After a couple of days in True Blue we went round the corner to Prickly Bay where we met up with Mike and Mary on Meriva
and their friends Tim and Jean on Sassie. We spent just over two weeks in Prickly Bay. I realised then how much I had needed
to stop. We did a guided group walk into the rain forest with Selwyn Maxwell a Grenadian who had an encyclopedic knowledge
of the flora and fauna of the island. We again swam in the cool fresh water under a waterfall. We also had a tour of the island
including visits to the nutmeg factory and a rum distillery. Both plants were using technology of a hundred years ago.

The longer we spent in Grenada the more we realised that it was quickly becoming our favourite Caribbean island. The people
were incredibly warm and friendly without being the slightest bit pushy. There were no boat boys as in other islands hanging
round the boats at anchor. Once ashore you might be asked if you wanted a taxi but when you said no thanks they would just
smile and wish you a nice day. The local buses were cheap and very regular. Consisting of small mini buses they would

11

invariably be filled to capacity and beyond, but nobody ever seemed to complain. When someone wanted to get out from the
furthest corner of the bus everyone would pile out with little comment and wait patiently until they could get back in.

After two weeks anchored in Prickly Bay we moved to Mt. Hartman Bay. This bay is protected by a reef that all but blocks the
entrance. Consequently there tends to be a lot less swell there than in Prickly. By this time Meriva had moved round to the
moorings marina in Mt. Hartman. Mike and Mary were leaving her there and flying back to England for several weeks, Lau:ra
moved on board becoming an official boatsitter, and giving us all some much needed space, we couldn’t believe that we had all
been together for a year.

Mike and Mary flew back to England. The two Chris's from Globe Star hauled out at Prickly Bay and went back to England on
the same flight as Mike and Mary. On the same Friday Tim and Jean on Sassie set off on an overnighter to Trinidad. Suddenly
everything went quiet. However it was not to last. On the Sunday after everyone had moved on we decided to go by dinghy to
the weekly barbecue at Hog Island. Just before we went, Pat on Aldebaran called up to say that they were on the way down to
Grenada and would probably stop at St, George’s. We told them we were off to a barbecue. Later that afternoon we had just
finished eating when we looked up and there was Pat and Olivia. Within a few days Graham and Joan on Karma, and Richard
and Rebecca on Tutella had also anchored in Mt. Hartman Bay and we were back to happy hours and a hectic social life.

Helen and I did an expedition up to the rainforest with Pat and Olivia. After an interesting bus ride up from St. George's, during
which once again I spent a fair bit of time with my eyes shut, we arrived in the cool of the forest. We decided to tackle a fairly
ambitious walk up to the top of Mount Qua Qua. Unfortunately we had failed to take into account the heavy rainfall we had been
having lately. Some way along the path Olivia and Helen decided to walk around a volcanic lake instead. In the event their walk
proved to be fairly arduous. The walk to Mt. Qua Qua turned out to be something of a mud bath, which was a bit worrying when
you were walking along the top of a narrow ridge. The view from the top was well worth the effort, but coming back down
proved to be even harder than going up. Pat and I competed for the number of times we fell over. At one point Pat was ahead of,
me when I slipped and I went shooting past him landing in the bushes, Pat was so busy laughing he slipped over too.
While we were anchored in Mt.Hartman Bay we had the strange experience of sitting in the Marina Bar under the shelter of the
overhanging roof while the rain absolutely poured, watching tennis live from Wimbledon which was bathed in sunshine.

When we had arrived in Grenada it had been our intention to haul out for a refit if that proved to be possible. If not we would
move on to Trinidad. Initially the main haul out facility in Grenada, a new operation at St. Davids, further along the south coast
was full, but because we liked Grenada so much, we decided to stay anyway. Now we found that we could be hauled out. Once
again we had a parting of ways. Karma went off to Carriacou. Aldebaran and Tutella set off for the overnight trip to Trinidad.
The next morning we motor sailed to St. David’s where Muna was hauled out of the water for the first time for nearly a year.

As members wake up from hibernation and prepare for the new season, a cadre of members have been working hard

builder and repairer before his retirement and has worked on many members boats including my own. His repairs are
better than the original.

This edition includes the application forms for Camping Fortnight. You will note that we have changed the pricing
structure this year. Most of the costs, for example electricity, water, heating, rubbish disposal and particularly sewage
disposal are in direct proportion to the number of people camping. It seemed logical to include a fee for each person
using the facilities. Furthermore the direct and indirect costs of camping continue to rise steeply and consequently |
perceived the need to increase the fees. Its not all bad news though, we have removed the charge for cadets
camping in the cadet area, however such cadets will need to pay the ‘per person’ charge and this should be included
in the application by their responsible adult.

When it all washes through, the fees for camping will increase by an overall 30%. | must say that, in my opinion, even
with the increases, Camping Fortnight is very good value for money and considerably better and less expensive than
comparable holidays. This is only possible due to the hard work of the organisers and the small army of helpers led
by Peter Clayton, Steve Monks and Kevin Dowley. Hilary Ashley is once again undertaking her role of camping
co-ordinator and all applications will be dealt with in her usual impartial way.

Despite the fog our meeting at MASC on Thursday 15" February was well attended, members were shown three videos illustrating ‘Scenes of Essex Life’ from 1909 up to the late 50°s. This was followed by archive film from the Imperial War Museum depicting life on Osea Island during its term as a Naval Base in the early 1900’s, also action relating to their Coastal Motor Boats which were capable of 37 knots, the forerunner to the M.T.B.’s. The last video was ‘Day Trips to the Sea’ featuring trips from London Bridge down the Thames to Southend, Herne Bay and Ramsgate and also the River Medway up to Chatham featuring the pleasure steamers Royal Sovereign, Queen of the South and the Waverley, of which only the Waverly pays the occasional visit to our waters.

The last of this series of meetings will be held on Thursday 22 March when our guest speaker will be Roy Hart who will be talking about his sailing adventure from the River Crouch to the Antarctic in his yacht
Barracuda. | am sure you will find his talk both informative and entertaining.

HOW _TO START THE WORKBOAT

Several people have said that they are having trouble starting the workboat engine. The engine was marinised and fitted last Spring by three or four club members and is something that Heath Robinson would be proud of! It is easy to start if you go about it the right way.

On boarding the boat (if it is your first time, it is easier to lift off the engine box for access) visually check that the gear lever is in neutral (in the middle). Do not wiggle it backwards and forwards as this will make the clutch cones stick and make it harder to turn the engine over.

If you look on the port side of the engine where the throttle linkage joins the speed lever, you will find it marked "stop" in one direction and "run" in the other. Make sure that it is in the "run" position by moving the throttle lever by the gearbox in the appropriate direction. Move to the starboard front lower part of the engine and pull out the half-inch diameter knob painted red, a click should be heard. This is the cold start device and if it comes away in your hand then you have pulled the dip stick out so you might as well check the oil while you are about it.

The next part is where most people go wrong. To set the auto decompressor which is found a the top of the engine at the front (also painted red), rotate it clockwise to the 12o'clock position. Place the starting handle in the hold at the front and rotate if clockwise until the handle is at the 8 o'clock position. Reset the decompressor again by rotating clockwise until it is pointing to 12 o'clock, you are now ready to start.

Turn the starting handle briskly. On the fourth rotation as you pass 8 o'clock and can therefore use your should body strength, the decompressor will release and the engine will start. This last part is most important. If you start from any other position, as it hits compression your hand will fly off the starting handle and you will rap your knuckles on the engine beds and your chin on the exhaust. This may seem long-winded but takes about tend seconds to set up.

To stop the engine, close the throttle.

Changing Rooms

Visions of Carole Smilie, Anna Ryder Richardson, Lawrence Llewellyn Bowen and Handy Andy. What was this to do with
sailing I asked myself when | volunteered just after Christmas. Well it was no Gothic makeover, nor MDF fireplace surrounds
but good clean white tiles in both gents and ladies changing rooms. The design aspect did show through a bit with coloured
stripes. Good old traditional pink for girls and blue for boys. This work and expenditure was authorised by the committee in
January and a group of volunteers have spent several weeks tiling, grouting and painting. Also at floor level there is now
drainage, courtesy of Steve Glynn. No more sloshing around in inches of dirty water and much easier for cleaning.
The main bulk of tiling and grouting in the gents was courtesy of a whirlwind band of windsurfers, Phil, Brian, Duggie and
others who I was remiss at not obtaining their names. Other sterling work in both ladies and gents was by John Weedon, Ben
Ashley and Roy, plus a couple more on work party day.
Let’s hope everyone’s hard work is appreciated and that we can respect their work by doing our bit to keep things as clean and
tidy as possible. So pick up those paper towels that are dropped on the floor. Ensure that all your gear is taken home at the end of
the day and leave things as you would wish to find them.
Oh! and if anyone wants any tiling done, don’t call me, Doug Eyles, who began as a volunteer changing room re-furbisher and
finished up as tired tiler.

Commodora’s Notas
Normal service resumes this month after an email virus and other difficulties prevented my contribution reaching you last time. Most of my article was to thank Doug Eyles and his team of helpers, and most especially Steve Glynn for transforming the changing rooms. Maureen Ball did a good job thanking you, but this is thanks again lads, job well done.

You will all have seen the sign ‘No Camping Until Further Notice’ and this does look a little stark, so I will try to flesh it out a bit.
When the Foot & Mouth epidemic started, Pat Black contacted the local farmer, Spencer Klingsick, to see how it would affect the Club’s business. Spencer said that, as long as we kept ourselves and our dogs confined within our site boundaries, things would be fine. However in April one of our members crashed his vehicle through a gate and wrote off both the gate and the vehicle. This incident caused Spencer to worry that the vehicle may have transmitted disease to his land and he threatened some harsh action to protect his
livestock.
Pat began to negotiate, the upshot of which was the introduction of the disinfectant strip and the banning of camping until further notice. These actions must be seen as minor when one considers that many sailing clubs are closed by the disease and the much more onerous action Spencer was considering to protect his
stock. | have had a few emails criticising the farmer, but you must see his point of view as well. His way of
life is threatened; all we loose is a few days camping. | must thank Pat Black for his calm and mature
handling of this very emotive situation.

Now to a prediction. The F&M outbreak appears to be reaching its end. Essex has not had a case for some
weeks and the restrictions are beginning to be lifted in the county. | would be very disappointed indeed if
we could not lift our camping ban in time for the Piers Race and Camping Fortnight. When the Executive makes the decision I will give Hilary the nod to bank your cheques and notify you. Hilary tells me that everyone who applied for a camping slot will be allocated one, provided of course that the ban is lifted.

Enjoy your sailing,

Clive Shenton

Solo News Spring Points 9/10

A steady force 2/3 s/westerly greeted the seven solo sailors for the first of two races on Sunday
22nd April.
Mike Taylor was to lead for the first two laps much place changing for 2nd place between Ron Greygoose, John Salmon, Roger Smith and Steve Monks. The wind almost dropped off completely on the last lap, which resulted in some interesting wind shifts. Mike held on to the lead and finished 1st with Steve taking 2nd with the ever youthful Ron taking 3rd.It was good to see our newest solo member John Nisbet joining in the racing and enjoying himself. The wind picked up to a 4 after lunch with some strong gusts. Mike again was first of the line closely followed by John. This was to remain until the second lap when both Mike and Roger decided to go for some swimming practice on the long down wind leg from B to C mark.
(rumour has it Roger was just checking the paint work on the hull of his boat before he sells it!) This let both John and Steve though to claim 1st and 2nd with Mike in 3rd and Roger in 4th.

Steve Monks

Our Cruiser Fitting Out Supper was held at M.S.C. on Saturday 28" April and attended by a full house of 63
members. My apologies to those whose bookings we were unable to accept. Generally speaking everyone enjoyed
their meal, although unfortunately one of the tables were short of vegetables and whilst the caterers tried to retrieve
the situation with offers of double helpings of dessert, that part of the evening was spoilt for them, sorry. After the
meal we were once again entertained by members of the Erith Yacht Club fronted by our own Frank Burgess ably
assisted by Peter and Julie Bloomfield, Margaret Yeoman and Dick Papworth.

Moorings have all been laid and boats are beginning to find their way afloat and it is at times like this we must
impress upon members to park their cars in a manner that will not impede the movement of boats and trailers between
the cruiser park/cat field and the hard. This is especially important where the travel hoist is concerned; recently we
spent over an hour trying to trace members to move their cars at a time when we were launching three boats from the
cat field resulting in one missing the tide and therefore having to abort launching.

Whilst on the subject of launching, we still find there are a few members that once launched disappear up or down the
river leaving the shore party to clear up and stow the gear. Once launched members are expected to pick up a nearby
mooring if not their own and come ashore to assist with the clearing up before sailing off. [ am sorry I have had to
mention this but I have been requested by shore party members to do so.

Bookings for the “Shakedown Cruise to Burnham” are coming in, we have 14 to date with 26 members booked in for

up with VARUNA II later. Anyone else wishing to come along will be welcome, we tend to coast hop in about 6

Minutes of the Management Committee Meeting held on the 2" April 2001
Executive Meeting. The Executive Committee met on the 28" March 2001when the following matters were discussed; Grass
cutting, Cruiser road, Calor gas, Helen Brown fees, Membership, Graffham School instructor training.

Safety. Mr F Bennett commented on an article appearing in the April issue of Navigans offering advice on how to start the engine
fitted to the workboat. The Committee considered the article acceptable but recommended that future guideline notes must be
approved by the Safety Committee before publication.
Mr C Kidner is seeking advice from the Royal Life Saving Society and the Essex Ambulance Brigade with regard to the
treatment of persons suffering from suspected spinal injury and in particular recovering the casualty from the water.
Mr P Black advised the Committee that the RY A have published the following Health and Safety Guidance Notes.
Guidance Note |: For clubs with paid employees
Guidance Note 2: For clubs having premises or equipment for use by members.
Guidance Note 3: For clubs providing food and drink.

Finance. Mr F Bennett, year-end accounts being finalised.

Clubhouse and Site. Mr S Glynn, mulcher action continues.
Arab dhow refit. Mr R Greygoose has discovered the origin of the dhow, it was presented to Marconi Communications Limited in
1966 by Trading Society Alkhalid, Kuwait, on the occasion of the signing of a High Power Medium Wave Transmitter Contract
and was subsequently donated to the sailing club.
Mr P Black, Quotations have been received for the first grass cut of the season.
Calor gas, work commenced on base 28" March. Post meeting note, the installation was completed on the 3" April 2001. Action
closed
Changing Rooms, The committee thanked Mr S Glynn and his helpers for an excellent effort, a note of thanks to all concerned to
appear in Navigans. Windows, the three defective window units in the lounge have been replaced.
The fascia board at the west end of the clubhouse awaits replacement.
Mr R Greygoose noted that the doormat inside the clubhouse needs replacing.

Mr C Kidner reminded the committee that the Connie and Betty bench adjacent to the winches should not be placed in position
during the spring and autumn when cruiser launching and recovery is at its maximum. Suggested that the bench should not be in
position until mid May.
Local Fire Services, Tillingham Fire Service has a card key but Burnham Fire Service has not, Burnham to be allocated a card
key.
Mrs F Thomas noted that the galley refrigerator door lock is faulty and that the supply cable runs across the galley entrance door.

Mr M Bates, the tractor shed windows and frames have been replaced.

Roof Leaks. The race equipment container and the mast container both have severe roof leaks and the tractor-shed roof continues
to leak

Mr R Greygoose reported a complaint by a member. The caterers had parked a car on the concrete path at the front of the
clubhouse thereby forcing members to walk over the muddy grass to reach the clubhouse. The Chairman suggested that, should
this occurs again, the driver is politely requested to move the car.

Social. Mrs F Thomas. The Fitting out Party was a great success, seventy-seven tickets sold. Donation to RNLI £50. The
committee thanked Mrs Thomas and the Social Committee for their hard work.
Discos have been booked for the Cadet Party and the Fish and Chip Supper in aid of the RNLI. The theme for the August Bank
Holiday party has a South Seas flavour, pirates and hula girls.

Moorings Sub Committee. Mr P Clayton. All the club boats launched and fit for service, moorings marker buoys laid and C row
moorings laid. Man overboard practice from the barge postponed due to poor conditions. The Jack B continues to suffer battery
problems, probably due to poor positioning of auto bilge pump. The windscreen wiper blade is also broken.

Mr M Bates. The four-wheel drive tractor has been repaired. We have a number of volunteer tractor drivers in need of proficiency
certification. Writtle Agricultural College is able to run a one-day course at a cost of £400. Other training establishments to be
sought but spend agreed in principle.
The pasture mower has been repaired, thanks to M Richardson.

Sailing Sub Committee. Ms J Ball. Jenny expressed her thanks to all those who helped to prepare the Jack B for the season. The
RIB and Orkney are fit for duty. Racing has commenced
The grass in the Dinghy Park has not been cut due to the continuous wet weather; this has also hindered the planned marking of
boat parking spaces. The revised allocation of spaces has been postponed and the established first come first served system will
continue for this year.

Bar Manager. Mr N Pembleton. The MASC Club Manger has been requested to apply for extensions to bar opening times at
Stansgate for the 13 and 14” July 2001. Extension to midnight on both days.

Membership. Mr P Black. The membership now stands at 340; this shows a fall from 391 at the end of the 2000 season. The fall
is in line with the expected loss at the start of each season.

View from the Rear
Having just come back from a glorious and dry Bank Holiday weekend — (I never thought I would get to write that!) — it finally
feels like the season has properly started. It has been a bit of a blustery season so far — but the turnout at weekends has been good
and seems to be increasing in direct proportion to the levels of sunshine!

Unfortunately, we have not been able to camp at the two bank holiday weekends due to the Foot and Mouth but have been able to
make other arrangements at the Star and Sun and Anchor instead without too much inconvenience. The only casualty so far is
that we had to cancel the Small Cat Open to ensure that people did not bring motor homes onto the site — (usually the competitors
only form of transport when they come to such an event). Hopefully, we did not upset the Catapult fleet too much who were due
to bring down a fleet of boats and it was nice to see that a couple of Catapult sailors still made it down to visit us.

Wednesday night racing has just started — (which definitely means that the season has started) and we also have the Solo Open,
SeaVets visit and of course the East Coast Piers Race all coming up at an alarming rate.

I would like to thank everyone who has been manning the Race Box and Support Boats so far this season — often the weather is
quite demanding and appreciate your continued support in carrying out the required duties for the rest of the season.

We ran familiarisation session on Sunday 3 June in place of the afternoon race and offered people the opportunity to learn about
the RIB, Jack B, usage of VHF radio and Race Box/Race Management. We had around a dozen people take part in the training —
but were disadvantaged by the weather, which put more people off. I still think this is the best forum to attract people to attend
these sessions, we will fun more in the future. My thanks go to Colin Leveridge, Kate Williams, Dave Williams, John Easton and
David Bal! who all kindly volunteered to be “trainers”!

Hopefully the season will continue to bring good winds and sunshine and I look forward to seeing you all on the water!

Jenny Ball

EAST COAST WIND FARMS

I have been reading in the press of the plans for Wind Farms to be built along the East Coast. I believe that there could be
consequences for the ordinary pleasure sailor unless their interests are safe guarded.
I therefore wrote the letter below to the Royal Yachting Association and have received the reply also below.
I would like to encourage all members, whether dinghy or cruiser sailors, to write to the RYA expressing their views. Remember
that we have a number of shallow banks at the entrance to our river which in time could be seen as suitable for such wind farms.

N.T.Pembleton

The Secretary
Royal Yachting Association

Dear Sir,

I have been reading in the press about the proposals to site a number of Windfarms along the East Coast for the generation of
electricity. As a yachtsman who enjoys this stretch of coast, particularly from the River Blackwater in Essex to Great Yarmouth, I
am writing to express a number of concerns.

Whilst appreciating that it is unlikely that these developments can be halted, I hope that the RYA will be making adequate
representation to those concerned to ensure that:

Free passage inshore (Shore to 2-3 miles say) is maintained during any construction phase.
Similarly free passage inshore is available after any construction phase.

Any safety zone created around such farms is as limited as is consistent with its purpose and adequately buoyed and lit.

Such farms are constructed in a manner as to allow safe passage from the inshore channels to the offshore channels without
requiring major and lengthy deviation.

Responsibility for the maintenance and financing of all safety provisions including buoyage etc rests with the operators and does
not call on general public funding or yachtsmen in particular.

Responsibility for the safe removal and return of the seabed to its original state at the end of the working life of such farms rests
with the operators. This must include the total removal of all underwater constructions.

The operators have a legal responsibility to indemnify yachtsmen for any damage caused to the structures and all underwater
services however caused by them.

The operators have a legal responsibility to compensate yachtsmen for any damage however caused to them by the structures and
all underwater services.

The reply was:-

We have been tracking the development of this subject for some time and have attended a number of 'stakeholder’ meetings and
had informal discussions with organisations like the Crown Estates and some of the main potential site builders. If you haven't yet
located it, the industry view can be found at www.offshorewindfarms.co.uk. You will also see there is a general article in the
current issue of RYA Magazine that is both intended to inform and stimulate discussion.
Your suggested criteria are very helpful as a contribution to this process. Generally, | agree with these, and they are consistent
with the points we are putting to those involved in the development on the sites, although I doubt that the indemnification
requirements you put forward are, legally, practicable in that form.
We are hoping to use the RYA website as a means of keeping members up to date with this subject, and to gather views and
experiences.

Yours etc..

SOLOS AT MARCONI
Marconi Sailing Club held it’s annual Solo Open Meeting as part of the Eastern Travellers Series on Sunday 8 July. 29 Solos,
comprising 13 visitors and 16 club members, arrived at the club on the River Blackwater estuary in cool, showery and overcast
conditions, this followed a successful Solo training day on the Saturday tutored by Jim Hunt and Steve Ede and attended by 15
keen to learn soloists!

The race officer, John Weedon set some long courses in the tidal estuary, the wind at the start being North Westerly gusting to
force 5. This strong breeze was maintained throughout the day with occasional lapses which posed questions to the competitors
as to which course to take (o minimise the effect of the strong tide.

The first race was won by Steve Ede, only just passing Godfrey Clark from King George on the finishing line. Mike Taylor of
Marconi was third followed by the rest of the fleet enjoying the exciting conditions. There was a fair amount of place changing
down the fleet as the locals exploited the tidal conditions.

The second race, followed the same course as the first with a long fetch with the tide past Osea Island and back with a long run
and reach against the tide. Steve Ede was unfortunately late for the start due to a gear breakage, but still made his way through
the fleet to finish equal fourth. The lead changed hands a few times in the first lap with Godfrey Clark unlucky to lose a hard
earned lead by over-standing the windward mark at the start of the second lap. This let Roger Smith through to gain a first place,
followed by Ron Laure and Godfrey Clark.

After a break the third race took place with the tide changing and a slightly lighter breeze. Steve Ede romped away with this race
to finish first and win the event. The rest of the fleet had a job to work out the best route in the tidal conditions but Mike Taylor
got it right to come in second followed by Steve Monks in third. Doug Eyles and Ron Greygoose of the home club read the
conditions well to get good places in this last race.

B.J.R.C. Update

The week end of the 30" June / 1" July saw two days of BJRC events with the Stone Cruiser Cup being run of the Saturday and
the Marconi Cruiser Cup on the Sunday.

The Saturday race started well with a brisk Westerly 4 to 5. Most competitors hoisted their kites for a lively run down to the
South side of the river beyond Bradwell. With a reach across the river and the wind well forward of the beam, those who chose to
drop their kites came off best as the tide pushed the boats off course.
There were plenty of opportunities for competitors to practice their spinnaker handling over the remainder of the course that
centred around the Bench Head area of the river.
The blustery and gusty winds reached over 30 knots across the deck at some stages and this certainly favoured the bigger heavier
boats. Whistledown 2 was first across the finish line at Thirslet with Killara2 a few minutes behind.
On handicap the Marconi boat “Hartley” won the first place which was a creditable performance for there was only Ray and
Jackie on board to cope with the elements. “Carolanti” from Stone came second with “Grace and Danger” from MLSC third.

Several competitors stayed on Marconi moorings ovemight and the weather was kind enough to allow us to have a “bring your
own” barbeque. The Dell bar manned by “volounteer” Roger Camp did a roaring trade while Ray and Graham ferried the guests
back and forth to the moorings in the trusty old workboat. Ray got a very wet shirt sleeve, not sure why, but something to do with
a rope, a propeller and a mooring!

The Marconi Cruiser Cup started at | 1am the next day with a promise of plenty of sunshine but not too much wind. Dave Payne
was Race Officer with his boat “Petronella” anchored at Thirslet. We were set a course to the Wallet Spitway and back, with
various buoys to negotiate on our way there and back. Spinnakers were hoisted and fierce competition ensued in the lightish
Westerly winds.
All went well for some time, but then the wind started to die away and the fleet was left scattered all over the outer reaches of the
Blackwater trying to stem the still ebbing tide. The next few hours was frustrating for everyone as time ticked away and no
forward progress was made. Out of fourteen starters nine decided to retire, with the remainder of the fleet desperate for wind to
get them to the finish line at Marconi's before the eight hour time limit expired.

However, their persistence paid off as a light onshore wind filled in and carried them towards the finish
liné again with spinnakers flying! It seemed as though they would just make it inside the time limit, and
so it was that the first boat over the line was “Randy Robber" with less than three minutes of time left.
The fleet had by now closed up and seconds later "Grace and Danger", "Triton" and '"F-Flat"
followed. On handicap A..Sargeant in his Sonata "F-Flat"” was the winner of the Marconi Cruiser Cup,
with "Quiet Airs" and “Randy Robber" second and third respectively.
Our sincere thanks go to Dave Payne who kept a cool head (well nearly) as Race Officer throughout!

Derek Gardner (BJRC Rep)
