Minutes of the Management Committee Meeting held on the 4TM June 2001

Executive Meeting. The Executive Committee met on the 30" May and discussed the following;
Electricity supply, Commodore succession, Replacement bar till, Sewage plant, Launching trolleys, Camping and foot & mouth
disease, Navigans, Coast Guard call out, Registrar, Solo open meeting, Piers Race, showers, Support boat training, Tractor shed
roof repair, Accounts 2000-2001, Offer of extra RIB for cadet week and Piers Race.

Safety. The Coast Guard was called out to recover a Wayfarer from the Bradwell area; the boat was towed back to the Club. The
Galley fire blanket has been installed. Action closed
Mr S Glynn reported that the RIB is frequently unserviceable, Mr G Jones is to be asked for his opmion on the reasons for
breakdown and longevity of the engine. On the same subject Mr D Thomas asked when the planned replacement for the engine is
due, the information was not available at the meeting.
Changing room duckboards, the duckboards have now been fitted with non-slip rubber feet. Action closed

East Coast Piers Race. Jenny Ball reported that the TA are providing communications again this year, sufficient sponsors have
been found, Lord Faulkner has agreed to start the race. The proposal to use a double decker bus as the race control center is
awaited,
Camping is to go ahead, subject to the F & M crises, as planned starting with the Solo Open in early July.

Finance. Mr F Bennett has agreed the 2000/2001 accounts with the MASC. There has been a slight increase in the reserve
account as the scheduled electrical system assessment and update has not yet been completed thus resulting in an underspend.
The Committee thanked Mr Bennett for his diligent work over the past financial year.

Clubhouse and Site. Mr S Glynn. Disposal of hedge clippings part complete, action continues.
Mr P Bloomfield. Grass cutting, all the cutting equipment and tractors are serviceable, a number of members have been trained to
operate the tractors, a rota is required to ensure the grass is cut regularly. It was decided to call in a commercial team to cut the
grass once again pnior to controlling it ourselves
General doubts were expressed about the likely success of a scheme of voluntary tractor drivers to cut the grass; it was suggested
that a Caretaker/Groundsman might be a more efficient method.

Mr D Thomas enquired about progress on the pedestrian mower, a sum of £150 was agreed to bring it into working order.
Repairs to cruiser road, material on site work planned to start in the Autumn.
Repairs to clubhouse fascia board outstanding.
The galley refrigerator has been scrapped; the caterers have replaced it with new. The galley electric lamp has been repaired,
thanks to S Monks. It was agreed to accept a quotation for the repair of the tractor-shed roof.
Mr P Clayton, reminded the committee that the mast rack roof requires attention.

Sewage Plant. Mr P Black said that he had attended a site visit with Mr J Jiggins and was awaiting a quotation for servicing the
plant on a regular basis and also for tankering away the overload during periods of high population of the site.

The shower pump is now working but there is a problem with the push button shower controls. Replacement controls (MIRA)

Commodore’s Notes

As, obviously, you are reading this, it means that Maureen Ball has succeeded in gathering the reins of Navigans from the Dowleys, and has got this important edition out to you. We must not forget that Mike & Maggie Boreham play an important part in that process as well as they do all the copying, stuffing envelopes and everything else that is needed after Maureen produces the original magazine.

Why important? Well, apart from the benefits of good communications this is also the edition which gives you notice of theAGM and includes the nomination forms. Please use the forms, the Club could do with one or two more Committee members to bring new ideas. The other reason is that there are changes afoot with MASC. The talk is of moving from Beehive Lane to a purpose built installation in Baddow. We will keep an eye on things to ensure that the best interests of the sailing members are looked after.

It’s now September and the summer has flown by as usual. Since the last Navigans we have had the Piers Race and Camping Fortnight — both resounding successes thanks to both the organisers and the members who took part.

The Piers Race enjoyed an increased entry, but not much wind on race day. Whilst troubles with IT stocks reduced sponsorship, we will still be able to present a BIG cheque to the Cirdan Trust. I hope to do this on your:behalf before my three year tenure as Commodore comes to an end at the AGM.

I make no excuses for once again thanking Chris Davies, Charles Anderson, their Committee and everyone
who took part either by entering, raising sponsorship or in running the race support. | especially wish to
thank the mother boats whose crews were spared from seasickness in the quiet conditions this year, at the expense of a long day watching the slow progress of the competitors.

Cadet Week was another good one, and I once again enjoyed presenting the prizes to the enthusiastic and smiling competitors. Special congratulations go to the Cadet of the Week, Josh Bird, they tell me that the fact he is my nephew did not affect the judges decision. Cadet Week organisers are legion and thanks go to them all. Peter Clayton, Kevin Dowley, Steve Monks, their wives and of course Jenny Ball were the leaders. There is another unsung hero of Camping Fortnight, Hilary Ashley, who allocates the pitches and attends to all the administrationissues. Great stuff.

I am looking forward to the Laying Up Supper in early November which is at the Heybridge Hotel in Ingatestone this year. Fenella Thomas has tickets now, I’ve got mine. See you there.

CRUISER RACING NEWS

The Medusa Trophy Race

I'll tell you a story of a Budgie, strong wind warnings, dinghy chaps, 'The Green Man', and 'tail end Charlie'.

Friday evening brought much feverish activity as doom laden Met Office forecasts of 'strong wind warnings' poured in. Much telephoning and new course sheets got the fleet away on Saturday morning to sail a shortened course to the Colne via the Bench Head.

It was 'Verus Amica' who found a budgie on board soon after the start. Derek Hall and Roger Camp cared for the bird as best they could, but rumours persisted amongst the fleet that the bird had been nailed to the wheelhouse roof and encouraged to flap its wings to aid propulsion. This 'Monty Pythonesque' technique was checked in the RYA rulebook but there are no allowances for budgies, only sails and propellers. This 'loophole' in the rules we expect to see exploited next season, with either bigger or multiple birds.

Another disappointing development this year was the appearance of dinghy chaps crewing. Yet another 'loophole' has been found to get crew who actually know what they are doing. These blokes talk about 'wind angle', 'velocity made good', and they fiddle with the sails after they have been hoisted. Cruising chaps usually worry about running aground and what time the Green Man opens, which it did about 7pm and we all went in.

Dave Payne ate drank and computed at the same time. Now in the computer he found a 'tail end Charlie'. Everybody looked in the computer and agreed we should call him 'Colin Leveridge the Winner'.

View from the Rear

And so we come to the end of another sailing season and this one has seen more "opportunities" (a corporate term
meaning - problems!) than most!

When I think back to the start of the year - it seemed like we would never see a day without rain ever again and |
was contemplating exchanging my Dart 15 for an ark. Then we had a windy start to the season with a number of
weekends where it blew force 6 and 7 - just to prove how rusty we had all got over the winter. As if the weather
wasn't enough to contend with, we then had to pick our way through Foot and Mouth and the issues that brought us
in terms of relations with our neighbours and having to cancel Camping and Open meetings.

However, the positives of the season far outweigh the negatives. In true MSC style, we found ways round the
problems of Camping by relocating to local campsites. We have had a great season of sailing with very few days
when we have not been able to get on the water. We have managed our normal full calendar of events including a
successful Solo Open, Piers Race, Cruiser Race Series and a full round of Spring, Summer and Autumn points.
Cadet Week was also a great success this year and the weather was wonderful for us.

More recently, the Helm of the Year final was held on 29th September where a great day's sailing was enjoyed by
all. The results were very close and Steve Monks took a well-deserved first place overall. This was followed by
the School Night fancy dress evening which was a great success.

There are many people to thank for making all the above events happen during the course of the season. As you
will also be aware, I end my term of office as Rear Commodore this year and I have many people to thank who
have helped me over all three seasons.

I would particularly like to express my thanks and gratitude to everyone who has served on the Sailing Sub-
Committee with me during my term of office - they have all worked hard on their different tasks and
responsibilities leaving me with the much more straightforward job of just overseeing it all! The Moorings Sub-
committee, which are technically part of the Rear Commodore's remit, have continued to run themselves smoothly
and have managed to keep all the kit such as tractors, Jack B, grass cutting equipment, mooring barge etc, etc, in
good working order. I would also like to thank every Race Office team and every Support Boat helm and crew
who turn out every (well, most) weekends to ensure that the cruiser and dinghy racing can go ahead for the rest of
us.

In current life where, for many of us, time is the most precious commodity and we simply don't have enough of it -
| am particularly grateful to those people who give up their time to support the sailing activities of the club.

All that remains now is to enjoy the last few weekends’ sailing (in unseasonably warm weather) - before we start
thinking about getting all the arrangements in place for next year!!

A reminder that there will be a working party on 2nd December. We want to take this opportunity to do a big
"clear up " on the site - so please make every effort to attend and help out in whatever way you can.

Happy laying up Jenny Ball

We have reached that point in the year at which we know the outcome of the last event, have a date for the next
event and have started to plan for the next ECPR. So here is a digest of all the news:

£7000 FOR CIRDAN TRUST- this is the total raised by ECPR for the charity in 2001. An excellent result by
any standards and especially pleasing in the light of the problems posed this year by Foot and Mouth. Thanks, of
course, go to all those who made this possible — the fast rescue volunteers; the cruiser fleet; the TA: the St John
Ambulance Brigade: our corporate sponsors; the raffle organisers; those who manned the bar: the competitors who
raised personal sponsorship; the competitors who simply paid their fees; the team that sold the shirts, collected the
fees and sold the safety gear: and the people who prepared the site, ran the event and cleared up afterwards. No
names, but a lot of gratitude — thanks again to everyone who made any sort of contribution.

ECPR 2002. Setting the date is always a problem. Our tidal requirements tend to limit considerably the available

Another reminder to everyone of the byelaws affecting the River Blackwater. This 1999 legislation refers to
all pleasure craft, including sailboats. Copies of the byelaws, maps and advice are available free from the River

Over the winter months of 2000/2001, I, (Pc Ian Frakes), attended several clubs and venues to give an illustrated
talk on the history and present day workings of the Essex Police Marine and Underwater Search Unit, followed by
advice on marine crime prevention. I would like to thank everyone involved for the warm reception and the
hospitality I received at every venue. These talks are intended to be both informative and entertaining, and I shall
be recommencing them in the coming winter months. So, if you'd like to know more, or to pencil in a date, you can
contact me at the Burnham-on-Crouch office or by e-mail (see below).

Our Marine Watch Boat Registration Scheme is still up and running and stronger than ever, thanks to the efforts
of many of our co-ordinators. However, we may be able to encourage many more participants by letting everyone
know that we are constrained by the terms of the Data Protection Act and cannot as a matter of course divulge to
anyone else the information given to us by boat owners. Those who have already registered and who may have new
boats or new equipment installed may wish to update their records - or cancellation might be necessary for some.
There are no registration fees and the forms are free.

Boat/Trailer Security: Opportunist thieves are now targeting unattended trailered boats left hitched to
vehicles outside shops and pubs, etc. It takes one thief only a few seconds to unhitch a trailered boat and attach it
to another vehicle. So make it impossible to steal by staying with the vehicle or keeping it in sight, and use a good
quality heavy-duty security to lock the trailer to the vehicle. Also use hitchlocks, chains, wheel-clamps and
padlocks if boats are to be stored on trailers. Thieves are now stealing boats on wheel-clamped trailers by deflating
the clamped tyre, undoing the wheel-nuts and replacing it with a wheel of their own. We recommend the use of
locking-nuts with wheel-clamps, and I've even seen trailers secured to concrete fence posts and other immovable
objects with heavy-duty chains and padlocks. Why shouldn't you make it harder for villains to steal your hard-
earned property?

We are now an R.Y.A. training establishment, with Pc Jon Barr as the school's first instructor. The intention being
to considerably reduce our Marine-training budget and even generate an income by offering this service to other
Police Forces and agencies. Up until now all of our officers have been sent to the Northumbria Police Marine
Training School at Jarrow, for either a six-week initial course or a two-week refresher.

Laying up time is here again! Look for our posters at your club advising on security of your property and take note
of any advice given in your club's newsletters or at meetings.

‘Muna's' Travels continued - (with some editing to make Muna's progress fit into Navigans - apologies to the author!)

Part Twenty Four - Out of the Water In the Caribbean Islands, Grenada, St David's, where Muna was hauled out for the
first time in nearly a year for a refit.

Once out of the water we started on a fairly major overhaul of Muna's various systems. This proved to be harder than we had
bargained for. We had never before tried to fit out whilst living on board; the heat of Grenada was greatly intensified in the
open yard; and being a steel boat, only insulated down to the waterline, became extremely hot when out of the water. In short,
life aboard was akin to living in a steel drum. Helen in particular found conditions hard to take. We attempted to make the
best of things by starting work very early in the morning and working later in the day when it was cooler. We were helped by
the fact that the yard was equipped with very good hot and cold showers, although Helen complained that the cold water was
never cold enough! There was also a very nice bar, built right on the beach, which helped us unwind at the end of a long day.

I was pleased that we didn’t have any nasty surprises when we saw Muna's hull below the waterline, revealed for the first time
for a year. The antifouling and, more importantly, the epoxy beneath it had generally adhered well which was an enormous
relief. There was one small patch adjacent to the bottom of the keel where the epoxy had lifted. This needed grinding back
and re-treating with epoxy. Apart from that the systems had held well and the hard antifouling that I had put on underneath
several coats of erodible was holding well. The topsides were in excellent condition and continued to attract admiring
comments on the lines of 'Have you just had her resprayed?’

Ed's Note: After 3 weeks of intensive labour Malcolm and Helen flew to Canada to stay with friends from College days. They
made visits to many well-known North American locations - an interesting and varied story in itself - but for Navigans space
reasons we continue from their return to Muna:

Part Twenty Five - Back to Grenada.

After the relative cool of Canada the heat of Grenada, especially with the boat still out of the water came as a shock in spite of
the fact that we were expecting it. There was a deadline of less than a week to get the boat seaworthy again and back in the
water before my parents were due to arrive to see us. We had some frustrating delays with the company that was making us a
revised bimini. In the end we were relieved to get back into the water on the very day my parents flew into the island. We
anchored overnight in St David's Bay just outside the yard where we laid up and attempted to get ready for sea.

In the morning we had an early morning visit from the chap doing the bimini. Then I discovered that the heads was not
functioning properly after I had spent several days taking it apart and putting it back together again. We were already feeling
rather fraught after our rush to get back in the-water) Just as we were about to up anchor, we had a call on the VHF from the
yard office to say that Mike and Mary from Meriva’ had come round to St David's on the bus to see us. Their timing was
immaculate as their presence on board reducedthé tension immediately and turned the sail round to St George's into a very
pleasant one. We decided to go to the small marina at Grenada Yacht Club in the lagoon where ‘Mariva' ‘was, as it would
simplify getting over to see my parents.

We were reunited with-niy parents later that afternoon and so began what was to be a very enjoyable two weeks. My father
had not been too keen oncoming so far to see us, but was won over by Grenada almost immediately. My mother was in her
element right from the start. Far from wilting in the heat she positively revelled in it, soaking up as much sea and sun as she
possible could. We were relieved to find that, although we were moored up bows-to in the marina, my father at 89 could get
on board without too much difficulty. My mother at 82 just shamed us as usual with her boundless energy and enthusiasm.
She swam several times a day and was more than happy to go off with us on dinghy trips. One evening we took her off the
entrance to St George's Harbour to experience a sunset at sea....
We all went for a day trip in Muna, first to Grande Anse to
show them their resort from the sea. Then we sailed in a fresh 20-knot-plus breeze with both of them sitting on the coachroof
admiring the view as we sailed up the coast to Flamingo Bay where we anchored. My mother snorkelled with us off the boat
before we headed back to St. George's. While they were still in Grenada Laura completed her advanced diving course from a
centre near their resort. One of the more adventurous dives she did was 115 ft down to the deck of the 'Bianca C’' an Italian
cruise liner that had caught fire in St George's Harbour in the 60s and that had sunk just offshore whilst being towed out to sea.

When my parents flew home we began to make preparations to move on to Tobago. A brief but enjoyable reunion with
Richard and Rebecca on 'Tutella' who had just come back from Tobago made it tempting to stay on a little longer but it was
time to move on after nearly 4 months in Grenada.

Part Twenty Six - Lazy Days and Hurricanes in Tobago, and Hectic Days and Batteries in Trinidad.

We left St George's in Grenada with calm seas and little wind. As we rounded Saline Point and headed SE the seas built up a
bit but nothing like they normally seemed to be there. With less than 8 knots of wind we had little choice but to keep on
contd...

11

motoring which we did all the way to Tobago arriving at Man of War Bay about 8.30 the next morning. We haven't yet tired
of seeing an island appear at dawn and it was fascinating homing in on our destination, which was completely open to the
direction we were approaching from, as details of the coastline gradually hardened up. We were very close before we could
see any signs of civilisation in Man of War Bay. Eventually we saw a small group of yachts in Pirate's Bay and a couple of
larger yachts anchored just outside the fishing boats moored off the little town of Charlotteville. The local fishing boats were
long slim craft powered by the ubiquitous big Yamaha outboard. They had long bamboo fishing rods semi-permanently
mounted on each side with lines streaming out behind. The pilot book indicated that the anchorage off the town in Man of
War Bay was the best holding but at 20 metres was rather deep. The alternative anchorage in Pirate's Bay was shallower but
rather crowded. As we have plenty of chain I elected for the deeper water with more space. One advantage of this spot was
that we were actually nearer to the town jetty than the other boats.

Richard & Rebecca and the freebee cruising paper "All at Sea" had told us that you could now check in at Charlotteville and no
longer needed to go round to Scarborough which generally involved a hard bash against prevailing currents. | went ashore to
an almost deserted Charlotteville, being a Sunday, and found my way to the police station. A very friendly policeman took all
my details but then informed me I would have to go into Scarborough the next day by bus to check in properly. When I
showed him the article in "All at Sea" he grinned and said "Oh, yes, dat right. They will have the customs here but dey haven't
built it yet." He assured me there would be no problem and meantime we were all free to come ashore. The next morning
Helen and | caught the bus to Scarborough, and the view was spectacular as we made our way down the coast on the other side
of the island. Scarborough was an amazing place, the only busy spot in Tobago. Everything was happening there but we had
great difficulty finding anything. Nobody in the town seemed to know where anything was. We eventually found the
Immigration Department. After filling out a number of forms in quadruplicate we had a fairly lengthy interview with the
Immigration Officer. He was extremely friendly and helpful, and gave us a lengthy permit to stay in Trinidad and Tobago, that
together make up one country.

We settled into Charlotteville getting to know locals like Jabba whose excellent fruit and veg. stall was on the seafront, and the
lady who made cheese pies and rarely let me escape without buying any. Tobago has yet to experience the mass invasion of
yachts that has happened elsewhere and you feel you are seeing the place as it really is. It has a tourist industry but it is still
fairly low key, particularly in the north of the island, and the locals seem genuinely interested in getting to know you. A
relaxing place to stay, where you could potter from one tiny shop to another. Not a place where you could stock up, but for
day to day living you could always get what you needed. There were some interesting walks out of the town and snorkelling
over the reefs was excellent.

At Sharon's, the local restaurant with beautiful views over the bay, Sharon mentioned she sometimes had a yachties' night at
special rates on a quiet Sunday if enough people were there. Most of the groups in the yachts we approached at the anchorage
liked the idea of a get-together and then we realised Martin on 'Ragtime' had arrived. We had first met 'Ragtime' in Porto
Santo in the Madeiras and again in St Lucia. He had already spent some time in Tobago entertaining a variety of guests. The
evening at Sharon's was a great success and at the end of it Laura and a couple of other younger ones went off to experience
the delights of the 'Sunday School’ - an all-night event/street party held further down the island.

We were just beginning to think that it was about time we moved on to another anchorage when along came Joyce. On the
Thursday morning following the get-together, while Helen and Laura went for a walk while it was still relatively cool, I was
monitoring the weather on the SSB and was made aware that Tropical Storm Joyce had been upgraded to Hurricane Joyce.
The centre of this system was several hundred miles to our east, tracking west. Being out of the main hurricane area we had
monitored in a fairly relaxed fashion the various systems tracking well to north of us. The prediction was that Joyce would
continue on a westward path for some time and then deviate off to the north west, possibly avoiding the island chain altogether.
However, the fact that it was heading in our direction caused us to consider seeking as much shelter as we could find.

Hurricane holes are in short supply on Tobago, a small one was at Buccoo Reef which I reasoned would fill very quickly.
Some boats headed for Trinidad but the main anchorage there would be very exposed if the wind and swell came round to the
SW which would be likely if the Hurricane passed overhead. Man of War Bay where we were was fairly well sheltered from
all directions except the NW. A major concern was the swell that could built up from the SW. On Friday morning Hurricane
Joyce was moving in a SW direction, currently lying to the SE of us. It was still forecast to start tracking in a NW direction
some time during Saturday which would take it through Barbados and St Lucia. Martin came over from ‘Ragtime’ to review
the situation and we went over our limited options. Most of the other boats in our anchorage had now left, leaving just 'Rush' a
South African boat; two Norwegian boats who had only just come in and for some inexplicable reason were rafted up together:
‘Ragtime’ and ourselves.
To be continued.
Malcolm Shaft

I know it is not my imagination, every Sunday for weeks has been blowing force 6. The cats & sail boards do not
seem to mind though, and the Solos will go out in anything. Talking of Solos its good to see our President looking

Commodore’s
Report 2001 - for Club AGM on 18th November 2001, at MASC.

1.0 Introduction — I would now like to read the meeting my report on the Club for my third and last year as
Commodore. It has been a year of steady progress in many areas of the Club activity and I will attempt to summarize every
aspect of the Club. I do intend to mention names of members where they have been of particular service to the Club. Inevitably
in a Club where many of the membership contribute to the running of the Club, I will not mention everyone and I apologize in
advance for any omissions.

2.0 Sailing Sailing is the core business of the Club. I do not wish to pre-empt the Sailing Secretary’s Report, but I see
all the signs of robust good health in our Sailing Activities.

The Club enjoys extremely good sailing facilities with acres of boat storage space on land, excellent 24-hour access to wide but
still relatively sheltered sailing waters, and good back up facilities. Our members make good use of these facilities in many
divergent ways, which leads the Club to have a high usage, whatever the sailing conditions.

The Sailing Sub Committee under the chairmanship of the Rear Commodore Jenny Ball and the hard working Sailing
Secretary Dave Williams and his wife Kate control sailing. Jenny, Dave & Kate, together with the fleet captains have
arranged season long racing for all classes. This is no small exercise, each race requires seven members to man the Race Box
and run Rescue.

Our Cruiser Section ranged far and wide. One of our members was last heard of 300 miles north of New Zealand, but more
normal destinations were Chatham, Burnham and the Club’s home from home, Brightlingsea. A full range of cruiser racing
was arranged by Frank Burgess and his team with the prizes being equally spread around the participants, the exception being
Colin Leveridge.

The Board Sailors continue to use the Club when the rest of us are thinking of catching up with the gardening, ensuring full use
of our facilities.

3.0 Safety At the last two AGM’s I have told you of the formation of the Safety Committee and how it’s work is
integral in ensuring that the Club’s operations are conducted safely. Another benefit is that operations can be demonstrated as
safe to a third party such as a Health & Safety Inspector. The Safety Committee has continued with its work this year under the
Chairmanship of Colin Kidner with Peter Clayton & Murray Bates as members. Malcolm Robertson has also continued to
give his time and professional expertise to this cause.

The Safety Committee has continued to concentrate it’s efforts in the areas that have the highest potential risk. These areas are
mainly the launching and recovery of cruisers, winch and mast derrick operations, laying and recovery of moorings and the
operation of the Club’s tractor fleet. Codes of Practice have been produced and issued for implementation. Further Codes are in
preparation and still more planned.

The Committee has also produced a draft Safety Management, Monitoring and Control regime. This started with a chart
showing the relationships of the Sailing Club with it’s parent, the environmental agencies and it’s internal workings.
Pat Black and I attended a Safety Committee meeting and fully understand and agree with the principles behind the draft
proposal. It now remains to arrange the details of implementation, including the appointment of a Performance Monitoring
Officer. In my experience the work of Safety Committees are often misunderstood. They do not exist to place draconian and
unnecessary regulations upon us. Neither is their sole objective to protect management, or, in our case, the Flag Officers in the
event of a possible prosecution by the HSE, although they do accomplish this most effectively. The prime objective is to
advise, educate and monitor potentially hazardous operations to ensure that our enjoyment of sailing is not marred by
avoidable accidents.

I thank the members of the Safety Committee most sincerely, and encourage them to continue their good work.

4.0 Rescue The Club continues to run three support boats, the Rib, Jack B and the Orkney. The Rib is our most
effective rescue boat. However it has seen a lot of service and has needed heavy maintenance during the year. Some
breakdown time has affected its operation. Although these problems have been overcome by the Rib Bosun, Roy Hardwick
with the help of Graham Jones, the Club must recognise that it is nine years since this equipment was purchased second-hand,
and replacement is now due. I know that the Sailing Sub Committee are preparing a proposal to put to the Management
Committee. The Jack B has served the Club well over many years and has many more years service left in her. Geoff Josey
has serviced the engine and kept it sweet. Last season it was not possible to carry out much work on the hull, but last winter a
major refit was undertaken, starting with epoxy paint to the hull. Prime mover in this was Roy Bellord with many others
involved including Mike Smith, Ray & Jenny Ball. A new rudder was also made by Brian Piggott and fitted by Peter.
Culling & Mick Richardson. The Jack B Bosun, Eric Cockerton, was in evidence throughout the winter months, sometimes
staying on his boat so as to be on hand to attend to the infra red heaters, key to the epoxy work. The Orkney is relatively new
and continued to perform well throughout the season. It is especially useful during Cadet training sessions when its
controllability make it possible to give close quarters support. Tim Sweet & Barry Glynn have looked after the Orkney this
season.

The system of rostering and notifying Support Boat crews was brought in last year and has been successfully managed this
year by Tony Ferguson, Barry Hutt and Dennis Gilbey. However we do need more drivers, particularly for the Jack B. lam

sure the Sailing Secretary will say more. Robin and Sam Shenton undertook many duties on the RIB, releasing the rest of us
for sailing.

The RIB and Orkney run on petrol which has to be purchased regularly and transported to the Club. My thanks to Dave
Bladon who has been quietly & efficiently doing this job for several years.

5.0 Cruisers Cruisers make up almost half of the boats registered at the Club. Members who own cruisers enjoy good
facilities at a fraction of the fees charged by professional boatyards elsewhere on the East Coast. This pricing structure is only
made possible by the members themselves undertaking many jobs that are dirty, wet and physically hard. These self help
efforts alone would not be enough without the leadership of the Fleet Captain, Derek Kirby, and the work of the Moorings
Sub Committee under Peter Clayton and Murray Bates, which channels and manages the efforts of the members to achieve
the objective.

Tractors continue to be the most important single resource for handling boats on the shore. None of our tractors are new and
much work is necessary to keep them serviceable. Considerable effort has been expended by Murray Bates, Jack Goody,
Gerry Champion and Harold Griffiths. I suspect more than a sense of duty is driving them, they obviously derive much
satisfaction from keeping these marvellous near vintage machines running.

The travel hoist continues to prove its worth with 25 boats using this facility. These boats do not therefore need to maintain
their own trailer, which, in turn, releases the storage space that would otherwise be taken up. Murray Bates & Mick
Richardson installed a hydraulic steering system this year, all part of a policy of progressive improvement. The moorings are
laid and lifted each year by the members using the mooring barge. The investment made some years ago in this barge
continues to deliver efficient and low cost service to our members. The hull was epoxy painted at the same time as Jack B, with
the same members involved. Our winches have been converted to hydraulic power from donated parts at minimal cost except
in time and effort by Murray Bates. This equipment has made the operation of winches both safer and easier and was made at
the recommendation of the Safety Committee.

6.0 The East Coast Piers Race During the last few weeks I was privileged to present a BIG cheque in the sum of
£7,000 to the President of the Cirdan Trust. Race Chairman Chris Davies, together with Race Committee members Chris
Hutt, Kate Williams and Charles Anderson, attended. I was particularly pleased that Derek Kirby was able to join us to
represent the Cruiser Fleet who do such good work on Race Day. The Race could not take place without the safety cover they
provide.
The presentation took place at the official opening of the Trust’s new offices on Hythe key, rented at a peppercorn rate from
the developers. I always feel a bit of a fraud at this presentation, as apart from entering the race. I do little of the work.
Nevertheless as your Commodore I am proud to represent you all because this unique event in aid of charity is something in
which the Club can take much pride. Mike Turner once again did his usual excellent job as Race Officer with the added
benefit of working from one of the Trust’s barges, which greatly adds to the character of the event.

The date for next year’s race is Sunday 30" June, so put it in your diaries.

7.0 Cadets & Camping Fortnight | One of my most enjoyable and arduous duties this year was to present the Prizes
at the end of Cadet week. Peter Clayton, Steve Monks and Kevin Dowley took on the organization again this year. They
were aided and abetted by Steve and Debbie Glynn who never seem far away from the centre of Club events. Many other
members put in much work to make Cadet week the success it is. Probably the most important group are the tutors who give up
their holidays to work unpaid, often missing out on major championships in the process. One of the real benefits of having a
mature Cadet Instruction Programme is that the youngsters we were teaching a few years ago are now instructors themselves.
I am also pleased to note that the girls are much in evidence throughout the Cadets. Jenny Miller was an excellent Cadet
Captain last year, Michaela Glynn (Ed's note: & Andrew Dowley?) has taken over this year, and, of course, Jenny Ball our
Rear Commodore makes a major contribution to the week. The medium and long-term future of any Club can be found in the
enthusiasm of its Cadets. The future of Marconi Sailing Club therefore must be assured.

Cadet Week constitutes but half of Camping Fortnight. I must thank Hilary Ashley for managing the applications once again.
The Management Committee decided to increase the fees for Camping this year. This had the desired effect of ensuring our
margin remained stable in the face of steeply rising costs, and also slightly damped down demand for spaces.
We were fully subscribed however.

8.0 Entertainments. Fenella Thomas took over as Social Manager this year. She has arranged a number of
enjoyable events throughout the year and has shown a good flexibility of approach, succeeding in accurately judging what will
be well supported and successful. Fenella has had support and encouragement from Chris Hutt and Belinda Dowley
throughout the year and I thank you all ladies. Many celebrated the New Year at the Club. March saw the Clubhouse as full
as I have seen it for the Fitting Out Supper. A fish & chip Supper and a Bangers & Mash bash were organised by Tony &
Sally Ferguson. The Murder Mystery evening was courtesy of Mike & Maggie Boreham, and Jenny Mead joined the team
for the Back to School evening centred on the Helm of the Year weekend.

The last event of the year was held two weeks ago at the Heybridge Hotel Ingatestone. It was, of course the Laying Up Supper.
Its good to give the Dinner Jacket its once a year airing. There was a good turnout considering it was Guy Fawkes weekend,
this and the new venue contributed to an excellent evening.

9.0 Membership Our Membership has remained stable through the year just below the 400 mark. Many are Family
members whose membership permits partners and children to use the Club facilities at no extra charge. This means at least
1000 people make a call on the Club services. The Management Committee believe that the Club can support a modest
increase in membership thus bringing both financial and other benefits. Margaret Yeoman mounted a campaign to achieve
this aim. It was an efficient and far reaching effort. The fact that our membership remained stable in a very difficult year of
record spring rains and the constant threat of closure due to Foot and Mouth disease is testament to its success.
The Club also has a web site which has been created and maintained by Colin Kidner for some years. This site has also
significantly contributed to attracting new members. After many years of sterling service as Fleet Captain, Rear Commodore,
Commodore and latterly as Vice President with special responsibility for Safety, Colin is stepping down from Club activity to
pursue his new pastime of parascending. We wish you luck in the future and thank you for past service.

10.0 The Site and Clubhouse In the Club’s organisation structure responsibility for the Clubhouse and site is delegated
to the Vice Commodore and the Clubhouse Secretary. After three years as Vice Commodore Peter Bloomfield stepped down
last year, however, as a replacement Vice Commodore was not forthcoming, he continued to execute those duties as Vice
President.
The Clubhouse Secretary was Mick Richardson he worked hard dealing with day to day problems. Steve Glynn, Frank
Bennett and Pat Black have also contributed their time and expertise in many ways.
This year saw a change in organisation in that Darren, our long time sole employee resigned. His cleaning duties were taken
over by Jan who has made the Clubhouse shine. We had intended that grass cutting would be undertaken by a rota of members
using Club tractors and mowers. This worked well in the second half of the year after the spring rains gave way to summer, but
we were forced to employ outside contractors to deal with the lush early growth.

As the first component of the Five Year Plan both the Ladies and Gentlemen’s changing rooms were extensively improved.
Steve Glynn contributed the time, plant and expertise of his Building Company to install new floor drains at no cost to the
Club. Steve also championed the whole project. The new wall tiling that so improves the look of these essential areas was fixed
by a small team of members led by Doug Eyles. The results are most worthwhile.

Tony and Wendy operated the Galley concession throughout the year. They can provide anything from a cup of tea to a three
course meal and their service is much appreciated by most members.

As well as attending to many day to day electrical problems, Frank Bennett instigated a thorough inspection and test of all the
Club’s electrical installations. This is necessary under Health & Safety Regulations. The full results are not yet available, but it
seems probable that we will need to up rate our electrical infrastructure. A full proposal will be made through the Management
Committee.

Neil Pembleton once again undertook the duties of the Bar Manager. The bar makes a modest profit and greatly adds to the
amenity value of the Club. Neil will shortly become Commodore and cannot possibly combine that role with that of Bar
Manager. I am grateful to Mike Smith & Malcolm Yeoman who have undertaken to share responsibility of the Bar next year.

11.0 The Five Year Plan The first, and most fundamental element of any Five-Year Plan must be that the
Organization should continue to exist at the end of the period of the plan. To that end we have closely followed the ebb and
flow of events with our parent MASC and our ‘grand parent’ BAe. You have all recently received a letter which, in effect,
says that BAe have applied for Planning Permission to build houses on the Beehive Lane site. However to satisfy conditions
that will be imposed by the Planning Authority, BAe intend to donate land within their Great Baddow complex for the building
of new facilities. Pat Black, Frank Bennett and I recently attended the MASC AGM. It was a poorly supported and short
affair, but I did detect an air of optimism from the Club Manager Ralph Coates and Rupert Boyle the President. They consider
that they have a great opportunity to plan for the future, although, with the withdrawal of subsidy from the grand-parent the
MASC will need to become commercially viable, which it is not at present. Changes in the organisation will be inevitable and
it is far too early to say how the sailing club will feature in the future of MASC.

You will remember that I told you at last year’s AGM that David Thomas, Chris Davies and John Bird joined Frank Bennett,
Pat Black and myself in preparing a Business Plan which shows that the sailing Club can survive and prosper alone if our
parent casts us from the nest. This may not be necessary, but it gives me comfort to know that it is viable and already in place
should it be needed. Planning issues take years to evolve, so, provided your Executive keep in touch with the changing
situation we should be able to influence events.

In order to get early warning of outside influences that may affect the Club we have continued our policy of serving on local
Committees that deal with the future of the Blackwater. Ron Greygoose and I have attended the quarterly BACSPA meetings.
BACSPA is a local Committee of the RYA and is dedicated to protect our right to sail on the Blackwater. I believe that by
attending such meetings we will be able to influence opinion and policy on matters which are of direct concern to the Club’s
future.

Last year we had several meetings and conducted an opinion poll to determine the spending priorities of our Five Year Plan.
We have a relatively small amount of money available for capital expenditure after all running expenses and depreciations
have been covered. The first year objective of refurbishing the changing rooms has been achieved and I look forward to the
fabrication of the veranda which is next year’s target. I must give a ‘health warning’ here. We can only spend the money if we
have it, if an unforeseen expense or a drop in income occurs, then we may have to adjust our expectations.

12.0 The Secretariat The Secretariat is made up of our Hon. Treasurer, Frank Bennett, our Hon. Secretary Pat Black and
the Membership Secretary. For almost three years Linda Chaplin has carried out the duties of Membership Secretary. During
this year a progressive change was made and now Nick Beavins and Jan are fully in charge of task. I wish Nick & Jan luck
with this essential job and thank Linda for three years hard work.

Frank and Pat are key to all Club activities. They not only attend two meetings a month but do all the day to day administration
of the Club. I cannot stress too highly the massive debt that the Club owes these two dedicated members. If these were not
Honorary positions, the Club would have to pay salaries of tens of thousand a year to buy equivalent services. I have worked
closely with them on Executive over the last six years and thank them for all the advice and support they have given me
personally during that time.

Another important task is that of Navigans Editor, Kevin and Belinda Dowley recently stepped down from the role after some
three years. In that time they have produced a continually high quality newsletter which is the envy of most other sailing clubs.
Maureen Ball was Editor for many years before the Dowleys took over, and she has kindly acting as temporary Editor while
we recruit a permanent replacement. If you wish to give a major input to the quality of Club life I urge you to take on the role
of Navigans Editor. Your work would be read and appreciated throughout the membership. Mike & Maggie Boreham have
been distributing the newsletter for over a year and now deal with all the printing as well. This is a big job which used to fall in
part to the Editor. Navigans is a vital organ of the Club, building enthusiasm and informing members, and I thank Maureen,
Belinda, Kevin, Maggie and Mike for their dedication.

13.0 Club President At this AGM one of our most venerable members, our President Ron Greygoose will be standing
down from his position as President. No one, not even Ron, can remember quite how many years he has served the Club. As
many of us know, Ron had major surgery in the summer and it is a tribute both to the skill of Bart’s hospital and Ron’s
determination to be sailing again that he looks so fit. I know we all wish to thank Ron for the years of service and wish him
many more years sailing his Solo at the Club. I also thank Mary for the years of support she has given both Ron and the Club.

The Committee have debated and reached agreement on our next President. Ron was therefore tasked with approaching our
famous neighbour, Tony Benn, to offer him the position. I am very pleased to tell you that Tony Benn recently accepted the
offer and said that he felt honoured and flattered to be considered. I believe that having such a nationally known and powerful
President will give us influence in circles above and beyond those available to most of our Committee Members. I also hope
that Tony gains enjoyment from “hopping over the fence’ for a beer and a chat. Who knows, he may take up sailing.

14.0 Management Committee I would like to end my Report by thanking those members who have served on
the Management Committee during the year. | will not list them all by name as over twenty members serve on that Committee.
The meetings have been well attended and the wide range of opinions expressed were most helpful to the running of the Club. |
have already mentioned & thanked Ron Greygoose, the Dowleys, Linda Chaplin and Colin Kidner who will stand down this
year. Roger Camp & Nick Beavins will join the Committee next year. Good luck to them.

The Executive have also met every month and have often sat late into the evening while discussing the Club’s business and
future. The Rear Commodore Jenny Ball has kept the core business of the Club running most efficiently, aided and abetted
by the Sailing Sub Committee. Like me, Jenny must stand down this year. I am pleased to hear of her intention to remain a
prime mover in the Cadet activities of the Club. I thank Jenny for the hard work and expertise she has applied to her job, and
hope that she will aspire to Flag rank again in the future when career considerations permit. As acting Vice Commodore,
Peter Bloomfield has sat on Executive this year. Dave Payne has volunteered to be Vice Commodore next year. As his
nomination did not reach us in time for publication in the Notice of AGM he will be co opted into this position at the next
Management Meeting.
I thank Peter for four years good work and look forward to joining him as a Vice President in the coming year.

15.0 Commodore’s Trophy _ I now wish to take this opportunity to present the Commodore’s Trophy. Last year I
decided that Malcolm Robertson had made a tremendous contribution to the Safety Committee and I had his name engraved on
the Trophy before the AGM. However it was some months before I was able to track him down to make the presentation.
1 don’t want to make the same mistake this year. The Commodore’s trophy is just that. It is in the sole gift of the Commodore
to a member who has impressed him during the year. This year I have considered several members each of whom deserve the
Trophy. Derek Kirby has served as Cruiser Fleet Captain for 9 years and together with Doreen has made the job his own. I
had the pleasure of making a presentation to him at the Cruiser Fleet AGM on Thursday. It is difficult to find a Club activity
that Peter Clayton is not involved in. Jack B, Moorings, tractors, winches, leader of Cadet Week all benefit from his tireless
energy. He is also a fearless and vocal promoter of his views at Committee meetings. We have had many a ‘frank and earnest’
discussion. But I have not chosen him either — Sorry Peter.

So which member have I chosen?

The Club has had a difficult year, especially with regard to the Foot & Mouth epidemic. Many Sailing Clubs were closed for
several months. There was obvious potential for our Club to suffer the same fate, but thanks to the calm negotiating skills of
my choice our relationship with the local farmer, Spencer Klingsick, remained stable. At one time relations were sorely tested
when one of our members crashed his Land Rover into a field, but this member kept things under control. This member has
also served the Club in many capacities over the years. I have come to rely on his advice, judgement and sheer capacity for
hard work during my time on the Executive. It should make every member comfortable with the future to know that he is once
again up for re election as Hon. Secretary, he is, of course PAT BLACK.

16.0 Closing Statement I will shortly hand the Club on to the care of a new Commodore. I do so in good
conscience believing that the Club is as healthy as it was whenI took over, even a little better possibly. I have seen eye to eye
with Neil on most issues and I have appreciated his clear thinking support during my term. I now look forward to returning the
compliment by serving him as Vice President next year.

Good Luck Neil and good sailing to all of you. Clive Shenton

Cruiser News - AGM, held Thursday 15th November 2001, at MASC.

Fifty two members, representing 42 boats, attended the Cruiser AGM. Apologies for absence were received from
Neil Pembleton, Peter Clayton & Jenny Ball. Derek Kirby welcomed the members to his last AGM in his post as
Fleet Captain and reminded those present that he was standing down before reviewing the 2001 sailing programme.

Cruising
& Social Events: The Fitting Out Party was held in April attended by 63 members who were entertained
by the Erith Minstrels. On 26" to 28" May, 19 boats sailed to Burnham where 58 members dined in the Swallow
Tail. On 21* to 25" July, 10 boats made the trip to St. Katharine’s Dock via Queenborough, returning after a few
days to Chatham, before heading back, via Brightlingsea, to the Club. On the week beginning 25" August, 21

Cruiser News contd......

boats sailed to Shotley where 56 members ate in the Shipwreck, including additional members of the RNSA. From
Shotley the fleet separated, with 16 boats going on to Ipswich. The fleet met up again in Brightlingsea the
following Saturday with additional boats joining them from the Club and other ports.

Cruiser Racing: Frank Burgess summed up a successful 2001 racing season and Derek Kirby thanked Frank for his
efforts in organising the events.

The Mamgu Trophy was presented by Clive Shenton for the best log, won by Malcolm Shaft on Muna. The trophy
was accepted on the winner's behalf by Malcolm Yeoman - Muna and her crew being in the vicinity of New
Zealand at this time.

The Big Cock Trophy had several contenders, the winner being the one who unintentionally abandoned ship and
was somewhat slow in re-boarding. Among the runners up was the person who has learned not to wash his lower
regions with white spirit and the person who, next year I am sure, will remember to release all lines before floating
off his trailer. (A veil ofsecrecy is drawn over contenders for this trophy - to save some blushes! - Ed.)

Hauling Out: Thanks to the organisation of Murray Bates and his team, there have been no incidents or accidents
this year during the haul out for winter storage. Concern was expressed about the high number of breakaway boats
from their moorings, particularly from drying moorings. These have mainly been due to shackle failure. Murray
urged cruiser owners to buy their shackles from our club supplier Don Holdsworth who only sells tested shackles.
The fleet was reminded not to leave unattended cars in the cruiser park, especially when they are away sailing due
to problems with blocked-in trailers and difficulties of manoeuvring boats when being towed around the site.

i Derek was standing down after nine years in the post and he
expressed his thanks to Malcolm Yeoman for his long-term support. He thanked the cruiser race organising team
of Frank Burgess, Dave Payne and Derek Gardner for their work. Roger Camp and John Walker were nominated
and elected to the posts of Fleet Captain and Fleet Vice Captain, and the cruiser race committee was re-elected. At
the end of the meeting Clive Shenton, the club Commodore, presented Derek and Doreen with a well stocked
globe bar as a thank you for all their hard work on behalf of the cruiser fleet for the last nine years.

Working Party: Peter Bloomfield outlined the tasks listed to be carried out on Sunday 2TM December and asked that
as many members as possible turn out to help with hedge trimming and rooting out of the scrap left on the site.

Paint Orders: Gordon Preston informed the meeting that the discount for International paint this year will be a
lower 29% while Blakes will remain at 33%. The target to achieve this discount is an order totalling £4,000.

Chain, etc: Don Holdsworth urged everybody needing mooring chain, shackles or anodes to contact him early as
he will be unavailable from 17th January until 17th March. (See item following Cruiser news).

Proposals for the 2002 sailing season were made and met with approval (see programme on P.10). Winter
meetings will be held on 17" January, 21" February and 21“ March. Murray Bates and Mike Smith will be
organising a light hearted quiz evening for the February meeting. The Fitting Out Party will be held on 1 1TM May at
the sailing club. The shakedown cruise to Burnham will be held from 1* to 4 June which will consist of a sail
from the club to Burnham, a lay day, Burnham to Brightlingsea and Brightlingsea to the club.

There will be a cruise in company to Brightlingsea on 22" June to encourage members new to this area, or new to
cruiser sailing, to visit our second port, in company with the old hands who will be able to assist and advise. The
East Coast Piers Race will take place on 30" June, and as Cruiser volunteers as mother boats are essential for the
success of this race, members were asked to please help if they can. The week commencing 27" July a cruise to
Ramsgate, Dover, and possibly France, via Chatham - details to be announced later. The cruise to Shotley will take
place on 24 August with additional places to be visited similar to those of 2001 but will probably also include
Ipswich. RNSA plan to visit MSC on 7" September for a barbeque. On 21" and 22TM September the ‘Watercress
Run' to Heybridge Basin has been booked. Those who are not racing should take their dinghies to use for a trip
along the canal.

I would like to record my personal thanks to Derek and Doreen and Malcolm and Margaret for the help that they
have given me in the last two months in preparation for taking over the role of fleet captain. Derek has very kindly

offered to give me whatever advice I require over the next year which I will be making use of. The cruising and
racing programme is reproduced in this Navigans (P.10) and some of the races are incorporated within the cruising

The advantage of staying where we were was that we had plenty of swinging room, and both Martin and I decided to sit it out.
Saturday morning brought news that Joyce was still to the SE of us and tracking west, clearly a Hurricane that hadn't read the
rule book about Hurricane zones. Martin decided to move away from his spot close to the rocks. We all had a tour of the
on 'Ragtime' looking for the best place to anchor. An area to the SW of the pier, that had plenty of swinging room but shown
on the chart as shallower than where we were, proved to be much deeper than expected. It was normally a fishing area but the
fishermen we had spoken to had said it would be fine for us to go there. Martin decided to re-anchor just a little further out
than he had been before, while we on Muna decided to stay where we were and add yet more chain. Having helped Martin set
two anchors in tandem for 'Ragtimc' we returned to Muna and set about extending our chain. An extra 100 metre length of
chain I had invested in during the refit was shackled onto Muna's original 55 metres and before long we were hanging on no
less than 130 metres of chain, with more in the chain locker as backup. We then set about making the boat as shipshape as we
could.
That evening we heard that Joyce was now set to pass right overhead in the early hours of the morning. The good news was
that she was now downgraded to a Tropical Storm, but with predicted winds of 50 - 60 knots we still had no cause to relax.
That night was slightly nerve-racking and passed without my usual long uninterrupted sleep. There was little wind but an
increasingly heavy swell. At about 5.30 on Sunday morning I sat in the cockpit in the early morning light. With the swell, and
the rumbling of thunder with occasional flashes of lightning, there was a distinctly ominous feel. As the morning progressed

12

and the system moved slowly westwards, the wind increased and the rain set in. The wind settled in direction as it built up and
stayed in the SE for most of the day. We began to experience squalls of up to 35 knots. As the wind increased the swell
lessened and it actually became more comfortable. The rain settled into a pretty constant downpour - unlike the more usual
pattern of sudden heavy downpours that stop as quickly as they start. It all became much like sitting out a gale in an English
harbour. We pottered about in the cabin feeling distinctly relieved. It was to be another day before the weather cleared. When
we went ashore again there was a definite feeling of relief, though parts of the island had been hit quite badly by floods.
Everything gradually returned to normal and we recovered our extra chain, thankful that it hadn't been tested in real anger.

Later in the week we set off, with 'Ragtime' as our pilot, round the north of the island, passing inside some offlying islands,
including London Bridge, so named because of its very conspicuous arch. We anchored, after some procrastination on my
part, alongside 'Ragtime' in the cosy anchorage of Anse Bateaux. The next day we were joined by the crew of 'Rush' who
came over on the bus, and we all went in Martin's dinghy to the offlying island of Little Tobago that has been a bird sanctuary
for many years. On the way we passed Goat Island which for many years was home to Ian Fleming. This area is superbly
clear and snorkelling was a delight. From Anse Bateaux we made our way round the small offlying islands to the north of
Tobago. We then returned to Charlotteville, anchoring in the shallower water of Pirate's Cove to discover that Sharon's
restaurant where we had had our superb yachties' evening was burned to the ground. Speculation was rife as to the possible
cause.

We sailed in light airs down the west coast of Tobago to the delightful Englishman's Bay, well sheltered with an almost perfect
beach, as yet unspoilt by any kind of development apart from one small bar. Many people say that Tobago is reminiscent of
the Caribbean of 20 years go or more and we can see why. From the beach we ventured inland to find that every little stream
we followed invariably led us to a waterfall where we could have a freshwater shower or swim in complete privacy. In
Englishman's Bay we met up with 'Nova' whose skipper had been a high altitude pilot for the US Air Force, and 'Miss Sophie'
a wooden German boat, smaller than ‘Muna’. Martin took us in his dinghy around the corner to Parlivutier where we found yet
another superb waterfall and a fascinating shop, run by Mr Chance, jam packed with just about anything you might want, a
veritable Aladdin's Cave. If you wanted anything not in stock, Mr Chance was extremely reluctant to say so and would try and
sell you the nearest thing he had.

After 5 glorious weeks in Tobago we moved on to Trinidad still in company with 'Ragtime’ who was booked up with visitors
until after Christmas. It was now mid-October and he was visiting Trinidad to stock up. By anchoring overnight in La Vache
Bay on the north coast of Trinidad we managed the trip in two day-hops rather than an overnighter. Arriving in Chagaramus,
the main yachting centre in Trinidad we managed to check in, stock up with essentials like beer, refuel and motor across to the
island of Chacachacare to meet up with 'Aldebaran'. Chacachacare is an amazing place. a beautiful, horseshoe-shaped island,
for many years a leper colony, until its closure in the early 70s. The whole place was simply evacuated, since when nature has
done its best to regain control. After fighting through the undergrowth you can explore the leper colony buildings spread
around the island, including the particularly eerie hospital building with the patient records and medicines just left lying about
and, in the main hall, a film projector still standing ready for the next film show. After a lively evening celebrating the
birthday of Olivia from 'Aldebaran' that night's sleep was disturbed by a bat flying into and around the cabin and in the
morning a half-eaten banana confirmed it had been a fruit bat.

The next day, after spending the morning sorting through a mound of Pacific Charts that had been photocopied for us (legal in
Trinidad) we made our way back to Chagaramus. We were determined not to stay long in Trinidad which, though a
fascinating place in its own right, has become a major yachting centre and a bit too hectic after our quiet time in Tobago. We
made a visit to a Hindu area to share in the celebration of Divali, so see nearly every house decorated with hundreds of candles
or oil lamps laid out in a wide variety of imaginative patterns. As we wandered along the streets admiring the displays we
would be invited into people's homes to share in the celebrations. On the Sunday Laura and I joined in a hike led by a
colourful character known as 'Snake' for his propensity for wrapping live snakes around himself. A fairly energetic walk
brought us to an impressive waterfall with a large, deep pool where we cooled off. Snake jumped into the pool from a fairly
high position on the rocks, fully dressed and wearing a large pair of welly boots. Our stay in Trinidad was longer than we
intended. Our batteries were no longer holding a charge and, though barely 18 months old, we had to replace them and I
decided that it would be a good time to upgrade our engine charging system. By the time we had been persuaded that our
needs would be best met by a set of 'golf cart’ batteries that needed a fair bit of surgery to install, we were committed to three
weeks' upheaval with the entire contents of our cockpit locker stored on the foredeck. All this, combined with the intense heat
and the intermittent heavy rain of Trinidad, made our stay something less than relaxing. Once the installation was complete we
escaped to the peace of Scotland Bay to test the system and restore the boat to order. We returned to Chagaramus to check out
and refuel before setting off for Venezuela, after stopping off at the island of Chacachacare for the night. In the morning we
motored out of the Gulf of Paraeos with little wind and a glassy swell for the short hop to Cabo San Francisco and our first
taste of Venezuela.

Part Twenty Seven - Venezuelan Islands

We left Trinidad for Venezuela on 29th November, later than originally intended, and made landfall on the Venezuelan
mainland at San Francisco, a remote bay with a small fishing encampment the only signs of civilisation. We arrived soon after
midday, anchored in fairly deep water and ventured ashore, braving the surf and discovering a stream where we could enjoy a
freshwater shower. Back on 'Muna' we found the anchorage bit rally so decided to start our overnighter to the the offlying

13

islands of Los Testigos. Leaving just after dark, we motored in a flat calm but after a few hours the wind gradually picked up
and we enjoyed a lively sail with both wind and seas picking up around dawn. As we sailed into the strait between the two
main islands the wind really whistled through. We anchored in the lee of Testigo Grande anda little later motored the dinghy
across to the island on the other side of the strait, where a coastguard officer was based, to check in. Both main islands are
home to a small group of fishermen and their families who take their boats across to the mainland every few weeks to stock up.

The next morning we went ashore on Testigos Grande intending to climb to the highest point where there is a battery-powered
lighthouse. Apparently for many years, as soon as new batteries were installed someone would climb up and remove them,
With no clear path through the undergrowth we reluctantly gave up our climb and turned back. Helen stood on a cactus whose
spikes stuck into her toes, from when I watched my feet with great concentration, and completely missed a cactus hovering at
head height. Throughout this trip I have had a lot of trouble with cactus. I am convinced that they lie in wait for me, ready to
pounce at every opportunity. This one got me smack in the face. Within a few seconds I had a searing pain in my left eye,
within minutes I couldn't open the eye at all. We got back to the boat as quickly as possible to try fresh water and eyedrops,
which had no effect. Laura collected the crew from a neighbouring French boat who spoke Spanish and they went ashore with
us. A local then took Helen and me at high speed in his pirogue (/large canoe) to the other island where the coastguard was
also the medic for the island. He fortunately knew all about cactus and gave me drops to put in the eye which eventually did
the trick, though it was a good while before the stinging stopped.

From Los Testigos we had a long day-sail with a strong following wind to Porlamar on the island of Margarita. Margarita
came as something of a surprise. A tax-free haven, it has been the base for much speculation, with a skyline of high-rise
properties which turned out to be illusory, closer examination revealed at least some of these to be empty shells. The shopping
malls were no illusion with bargains like gin at £1 a bottle that were hard to resist. It was in Porlamar that we finally met
Alex to whose daily SSB net we had been listening to for some time as a good way of getting latest weather reports and of
getting in touch with other yachts. Alex and Yetta had left their native Norway 15 years ago in their ex-steam pinnace
‘Albatross’. It was during their 9-year stay in the Canaries that Alex started a radio net, then came across to the Caribbean 6
years ago still running his net on a daily bases without a single break. They spend most of their time in Venezuela with the
occasional trip to Trinidad. 'Albatross' is kept in immaculate condition and makes a stirring sight with a pelican perched
almost permanently on her long varnished bowsprit. We visited the capital of Porlamar, Ascencia, the outward journey on one
of the ageing American cars that serve as taxis on the island. The town proved to be a delight, and we visited the old Spanish
fort in time to savour the atmosphere before the organised tours arrived and listening in to the guides gave us an insight into
snippets from the fort's somewhat gory past. Before leaving Porlamar we topped up with diesel from the fuel boat, run by an
old chap who had the interesting system of bringing a large container on to your deck and then syphoning the diesel into your
tanks, For someone doing this all the time he didn't seem to be very good at it. When he finally got the syphon to work, he
ended up with a mouthful of diesel for which the obviously well-practised cure was a cold beer.

After spending some time restocking in Porlamar it was a relief to sail on to some of the smaller islands. Our first stop was
Coche, followed the next day by Cobagua, the site of the first Spanish settlement in South America, where foundations of the
first buildings can still be seen. From Cobagua we made our way to an anchorage on the western end of Margarita from where
we planned to make an early start the next day for the 180 mile overnight trip to Los Roques. We were woken at 2.30am by
persistent shouting to find a fisherman circling round us in his small open boat. We gathered that we were anchored just where
he wanted to fish, nowhere else would do. Not wanting to risk re-anchoring in the dark we upped anchor and headed out to
sea. Using our downwind rig we drifted gently in the unusually light breeze. As day broke the wind increased and shifted to N
giving us a beam reach which needed the normal fore-and-aft rig. The wind fluctuated for the rest of the day and that night,
but it decided to get up the next morning just as we had Los Roques in sight.

to be continued ... ..... Malcolm Shaft

Want to be Rear Commodore?

A Year in the Life of a Rear Commodore

As you will be aware, my three year tenure as Rear Commodore has just come to an end. As such, one of you now needs to
volunteer to take on this important and interesting position. The purpose of this article is to give you an idea of the type of
things you can expect if you volunteer to be Rear-Commodore.

Key Purpose of Rear Commodore:

The role of Rear Commodore - whilst important, is not as arduous as you may think. This is due to the raft of other club
volunteers who are in place to support you. Your primary function as a Rear Commodore is to oversee sailing activity for the
club - your secondary function is to ensure that the views of all club fleets are fairly represented to the Exec Committee and the
Main Committee.

Benefits:
= you get a very good insight into the workings of the club
= you get to play a key role in determining its future direction
= you get to work with some great people
= you get the satisfaction of seeing club members enjoy a full programme of sailing as a result of your efforts

The following is an overview of the role of the Rear Commodore:

1. Chair Sailing Sub-Committee

Sailing Sub-Committee meets monthly and consists of sailing secretary, fleet captains and support boat co-ordinator.
This committee is the hub of organising sailing programmes - the role of the Rear Commodore is to ensure that all aspects
are covered and that tasks are shared out amongst the Sub-Committee members.

Member of Executive Committee

&V V Exec Committee meets monthly and consists of Commodore, Vice and Rear Commodores, Treasurer and Secretary.
This committee is the core team of the club and discusses all matters relating to MSC - both current and future.
Your role as Rear Commodore is to input the views of the fleets and to keep the Exec informed on sailing matters. You
may also be assigned specific tasks or projects from time to time.

Member of Main Committee

Your role on the Main Committee is to report out on the activities of the Sailing Sub Committee. It is also the
opportunity for Committee members to raise any sailing queries or matters with you.

4. Moorings Sub Committee

Although the Rear Commodore technically oversees the activities of the Moorings Sub-Committee - the reality is that this
group run themselves under the able leadership of Pete Clayton and Murray Bates. The Moorings Sub-Committee are
responsible for all matters relating to the mooring, launching and recovery of cruisers and they complete a tremendous
amount of work each year. However, the input required from the Rear Commodore has been absolutely minimal during
my time.

I should also add that, although I personally spend quite a lot of time on Cadet activities - this does not form part of the Rear
Commodore role - Cadet activities are co-ordinated separately by the Cadet Fleet Captain and the Cadet Committee.

I would encourage any of you to consider taking on the role of Rear Commodore. It is one of the less difficult positions within
the club and also the position that receives the most support from other club officers / co-ordinators. I would be happy to
discuss the role further with any of you who may be interested - so please feel free to call me to find out more.

As a final plea - this role is essential if we want to continue to have the sailing facilities and programme that we all enjoy. I
know the Exec Committee will take a very serious look at whether we can continue normal sailing activities next year if this
role is not filled. Please consider whether you would be able to help out.

Thanks, Jenny Ball [redacted]

Sailing
Secretary's
Report 2001 (from the AGM)

The 2001 sailing season included the usual programme of club racing for the Dinghy and Catamaran Fleets. New racing rules
of sailing were due out for the start of the season. Unfortunately these were late being published and so the Sailing Sub
Committee decided to run our Spring Points series using the old rules. The new rules were introduced in time to be
incorporated into our sailing instructions for the summer. I would like to thank Roger Smith for attending seminars and
redrafting the club's standard sailing instructions for the new rules.

With 82 different races organised for club members only 2 were cancelled due to adverse weather conditions. This must be a
record for recent years. Do we see the onset of global climate change or are we all getting older but less wise? With 93
different helmsmen across the whole year it would appear that the club racing is in a strong position.

Turnout in the Solo and Handicap fleets was similar to last season. There was some increase in numbers in the Fast cat fleet
after a slow start to the season. Unfortunately there was a reduced turnout in Medium cats and the Dart 15's. A decision was
taken early in the season to combine the Medium and Fast catamaran fleets, encouraging good competition for all competitors.
The Cadet fleet numbers peaked in mid summer, as usual, but were somewhat lower as we neared the end of the season.
However, one of the reasons for this was a number of cadets switching week by week from the Cadet fleet to race in the Dart
15, Handicap and Cat fleets all of whom will keep the rest of us on our toes next season.

The now firmly established Cruiser racing fleet organised their usual series of races with a similar number of entrants to last
year's record season. A similar series is already planned for next year in co-operation with the established BJRC cruiser racing
that takes place on the estuary.

August again brought with it another camping fortnight and another hugely successful Cadet week. For the second year, in
addition to the Cadets, tuition was organised for the "Senior Service" group although on a slightly reduced scale compared to
last year.

As I am sure you all remember the season started under the cloud of Foot and Mouth disease. We were very fortunate that,
unlike many of the other clubs in the country, we were able to start our club-racing season on time. Unfortunately the Small
Cat. Open meeting planned for the Spring Bank holiday weekend had to be cancelled. This was to be the first running of this
event, which had been planned to replace the Dart 15 open. Plans are already underway to ensure that this event will not be lost
to our members. Easing of Foot and Mouth restrictions in the county allowed us to proceed with our other open events. The
Solo open meeting was extended to two days by adding a training day on the Saturday. The event itself attracted a turnout of
29 competitors this being the best attended Eastern Area open meeting this season. | think congratulations should go to the
fleet captain for his efforts in getting as many club boats out as possible and to his organising committee for attracting such a
large visiting fleet. The Kestrel fleet visited us over the August Bank holiday weekend and a small fleet of visiting Hamble
Stars threatened to join our club racing but found the lure of the bright lights of Maldon to much to resist. The East Coast Piers
Race, saved from foot and mouth, attracted 60 entries. I am sure you will have heard about the funds raised from previous
speakers.

The next section I shall call 'Marconi Sailors Abroad’. Although ‘abroad’ will include such destinations as Thorpe Bay and
Lawling Creek. A number of our Solo fleet members contested races in the Solo open circuit, with Roger Smith securing third
place in the Solo Scottish National Championships. Our Catamaran sailors were out and about this season with Hurricanes and
Formula 18's competing on the circuit. Highlights of the season were Tim Wallace following up his 2nd in the ECPR with a
third place at the Thorpe Bay Open (part of the Hurricane GP circuit). While Phil Longhurst became Hurricane Spinnaker
National champion with Lee Harrison runner up.

Finally, with seven of the Sailing Sub Committee standing down this year I would like to thank them on your behalf for all
their hard work, in some cases over many years
