‘Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Five - 2001 Pacific Odyssey (or should that be Oddity?)

It is much harder to define a Pacific crossing than an Atlantic one. It is generally accepted that when you sail from the
Canaries or even the Cap Verdes to one of the Caribbean Islands you have crossed the Atlantic. With the Pacific it is far less
clear cut. However, following the Coconut Milk Run (or Coconut Milk-Shake Run as it can be), the longest single leg is from
the Galapagos to the Marquesas and, at just under 3000 miles, is a couple of hundred miles longer than a direct course
between the Canaries and one of the Caribbean Islands. By Thursday Sth April, conditions seemed right for departure. The
Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) had moved north, indicating the likelihood of favourable wind in the area just south
of the Equator that we would be crossing. Although winds were light just off the Galpagos Islands, this was often the case. A
number of boats were gearing up to go at a similar time to us. ‘Lazyjack' and 'Fair Hippolyta’ had left the previous day and had
found wind almost right away. Unfortunately Helen had been under the weather for 2 or 3 days with symptoms of tonsillitis but
seemed to be on the mend and we decided she would be as comfortable at sea as in harbour. Several American boats left just
before us, one of them 'Aldeberan of Milwalkey' whose owner, Fred, a dentist, had done an emergency filling for Helen a
couple of days earlier. Pat and Olivia on the other 'Aldebaran' left just ahead of us and 'Cap d'Or' a little while after.

15

Once clear of the anchorage we hoisted sail and were rewarded with a fair breeze of 10-15 knots which got us off to a good start. The
advice in 'World Cruising Notes' is to head south initially to pick up the SE trades rather than set a direct course for the Marquesas.
We initially headed just south of a direct course. Pat on 'Aldebaran' set his cruising chute and pulled ahead while, during the
afternoon, 'Cap D'Or' gradually overhauled us. That evening Richard on ‘Fair Hippolyta' warmed us that the previous night, they had
become entangled with a fishing net and had had to cut themselves free. In an attempt to avoid this area we started heading further
south. Even so, we still managed to meet a fishing boat later in the night. The wind died away overnight and in the morning we ran
the engine for a couple of hours to charge the batteries and make some progress. The wind got up just enough for us to start sailing
again. During the afternoon what little wind there was died away again and we decided to motor again. We did not have enough fuel
to motor indefinitely but as our batteries were not yet fully charged, we thought we might as well try and look for some wind.

When I did my usual checks prior to starting the engine, I discovered that the freshwater cooling system had drained itself into the
drip tray under the engine. After I had got over the initial shock, I took off the alternator drive belt and the timing belt housing to try
and discover where the water was coming from. As far as I could tell, it appeared to be coming from the fresh water pump, dripping
off the pump drive pulley. On the evening net I received a wide range of advice. Richard on 'Fair Hippolyta" had had a similar
problem with his Perkins Prima when it was only 3 weeks old. He was able to warm me that getting to the pump involved disturbing
the timing belt. There was a general consensus that running the engine with the water filler cap removed might reduce pressure on
the system. Meanwhile we had to consider our position. We were only just over 100 miles from the Galapagos and had the best part
of 3000 miles to go to the Marquesas. To head back would seem to have been a sensible option, except that it would mean sailing
against the current and prevailing wind (if and when it returned). Getting safely into harbour was going to be a problem whichever
option we chose. Carrying on presented problems in terms of charging the batteries unless we had enough wind to get the wind
generator moving. In the end there was no real contest as going on felt a lot more positive than turning back.

I will admit to feeling pretty fed up that day. We are well aware of Sod's Law, but for something like that to happen on the first day
out on a long passage just seemed a bit much. It might not have seemed so bad if we had at least been making progress in the right
direction. As it was, we spent that night in a flat calm with absolutely no wind. It just served to emphasise our position. Unlike the
calms we had experienced on the way to the Galapagos, here there was still a swell, so much so, that we took the sails down to stop
them slatting and we put up the anchor light. We still kept a full watch as we were able to do with three of us on board, and
overnight, I rationalised on our position. I had long admired those who ventured to sea without the backup of engine power and,
although I had no desire to emulate them, I knew it could be done. We were a sailing boat after all. During my watch in the stillness
I became aware of a rumbling noise a little way off. Peering into the darkness I could just make out the shape of a whale. A little
while later it disappeared, but reappeared just before dawn the next morning. In the morning I had a go at running the engine. By
pouring water into the heat exchanger I could just about keep the level up but water was spraying from the drive pulley all over me,
the galley and the chart area. The logbook quickly looked as if it had been through a storm. | then tried replacing the cap and found
that it actually reduced the leak rate. The procedure after that was to start the engine, quickly fill the system and then replace the cap.
After a few minutes I would remove the cap to top up the system and carry on from there. I now knew that, with care, I should be
able to run the engine to help charge the batteries. | didn't like to risk running in gear with the much heavier load that that would
entail. One issue was the amount of water that would be needed. This was partly resolved by recycling at least some of the water by
collecting it as it came out of the pump.

The wind got up sufficiently to allow us to get the chute up and flying. The winds were light but at least we were moving in the right
direction. We managed to keep the cruising chute up for two days before, on the Monday morning, four days out, the skies became
very threatening. We were surrounded by thunder and lightning just before we were hit by a squall. We got the chute down just in
time. Soon after, the wind died away completely before getting up from the north a little. while later. We appeared to be having
typical ITCZ weather. This carried on for the next few days which were generally overcast and the wind varied from nothing to
squalls of 30 knots. One bonus was that these squalls were often accompanied by heavy downpours which gave us the chance of
collecting some much-needed water. In the squalls our rain-catching system, based on the bimini, was useless, so we resorted to Eric
Hiscock's tried and tested system ofhanging a bucket from the gooseneck. It's amazing just how effective this method is. At times
We were getting a bucketful in just a few minutes. The rain squalls, of course, tended to come at night. One pitch black night, with
30 knots over the deck, I was tottering along the deck emptying bucketful after bucketful into the tanks. Before leaving England
Helen and I had splashed out on top-of-the-range Musto HPX breathable 'oilies'. Breathable they might be, but on this occasion I
was soaked to the skin. At least it was warm.

After a week out, conditions began to settle. The skies cleared and the winds became steadier, settling into Easterlies. We achieved a
24-hour run of 131 miles, which after our initial progress, was wonderful. | also spoke to Jim on the trawler yacht ‘Atlas’, still in
Vilamil, who told me that a crew member of his who was coming out from Australia would try and get the parts we needed for the
water pump. They would be leaving for the Marquesas later in the month. All through this second week we continued to make good
progress. We were now sailing just off downwind with the main and boomed-out yankee, wing and wing. Surprisingly, we were
going even faster when the wind almost came round to the beam even with the yankee poled out. We were now sailing mainly in
sunshine but still getting occasional downpours which were keeping our tanks topped up. The stronger winds meant that the wind
generator was working well, so during this period I only had to run the engine about once a week. This was a great relief as running
the engine still caused a major mess. All in all we were now enjoying the passage in spite of continuing anxiety over the engine
situation. Helen had taken a long time to fully recover from whatever it was that had laid her low before the start of the trip, but by
now she was much better and almost back to normal.

We had got into a good routine and were even managing to get various jobs of routine maintenance done. Between them, Laura and
Helen were producing some superb meals and life was good. By the second week we had covered nearly 1500 miles, more then 850
of them coming in the second week. In addition, thanks to the showers we were getting, we still had full water tanks. The wind was

16

tending to be more easterly than south-easterly and therefore putting us dead downwind. We had previously debated putting the full
downwind rig of boomed-out yankee and genny up. Now we realised that the mainsail was chafing on the shrouds so we lowered it
and set up the twins. The great advantage of this rig was that we could sail dead downwind and the wind could veer from one side to
the other without causing us any concern whatever. In addition the monitor had no trouble steering whereas previously it would be
occasionally overwhelmed. The only drawback was an increase in the already pronounced rolling we were experiencing. All in all
the sailing was more relaxed with seemingly less stress and strain on the rig. Eighteen days out we passed a fishing boat which was
the first sign of life that we had seen since our first night out. It was a bit of shock after a succession of night watches when the
main concern had been which tape to play on the walkman. We now went through several days of quite large seas. However the
skies were clear and the rain squalls had stopped. At times it was almost reminiscent of the boisterous trade wind sailing we had had
in the Atlantic. Twenty five days out the wind dropped and the seas calmed. We took the opportunity for Laura to climb the mast
and carry out a check. Everything seemed in order. One of the American boats crossing at the same time as us had had a major
problem when their forestay parted. An amazing rendezvous of four boats at sea resulted in the mast being saved.

By this time we had just 300 miles to run to Nuku Hiva, the main island in the Marquesas. Like most people we had originally been
heading for Fatu Hiva, a little island to the SE of Nuku Hiva. However our engine problem had, not surprisingly, persuaded us to
head for the more sheltered anchorage and the one place in the islands with reasonable communications. We now watched as our
daily run once again dropped. We began to have visions of being becalmed just off the islands. Fortunately, although the winds went
light, they didn't die away altogether. Twenty seven days out, we had our first sighting of land. Way to the south we spotted the little
island of Fatu Huku, then just before dark we could see almost ahead the island of Ua Huka that lies some 25 miles to the east of
Nuku Hiva. Under normal circumstances we would probably have chosen this time to reduce sail to slow down to ensure that we
didn't arrive at our destination before dawn. However I was so concerned about being becalmed that I didn't want to waste the wind
while we had it. Instead of decreasing as it had been forecast to, the wind actually got up. Because of the proximity to land, our night
watches weren't as relaxed as they had been. We arrived at our waypoint off the harbour at Taiohae Bay on Nuku Hiva while it was
still dark. I had been snatching some extra sleep and we were a bit slow in dismantling the downwind rig. We then discovered that
the yankee wouldn't roll up. Luckily, Laura spotted that a halliard had wrapped round the top of the stay and we managed to get it
clear. We got the main up just in time before the current took us past the entrance.

By this time it was just getting light and we could see the imposing entrance to Taiohae Bay lying between two offlying islands called
the Sentinels. The bay is an ancient volcanic crater with towering cliffs each side. It makes an imposing sight, especially after 28
days at sea. With 18 knots on the beam we had a fast run in. However, once in the lee of the cliffs the wind began to do very strange
things. With about 2 miles to run into the bay the wind went round 360° several times with speeds between 0 and 25 knots. By the
time we got to the anchorage we were exhausted. We managed to keep going however. Several boats were keeping an eye out for us
and David and Eric from ‘Peace and Aloah' came out in their dinghy to see if we needed a hand. The anchorage is well spread out
and we headed for a likely looking place, dropped the hook and we were anchored. We were actually very well positioned. Helen
reckoned it was the best bit of anchoring that I had done for a long time!

Top of the Thames and Back!

A much postponed safe single handed retirement cruise had at last got under way in my small retirement cruiser ‘Liesl’, a Mirror
Offshore diesel yacht of 1960s design and a boat which I first considered and rejected for a variety of reasons in those early days.
However, now many years into retirement and several family boats later, my aspirations and crew size have changed, as have my
confidence and ability. ;
For inland waterways the small MD1 Volvo Penta diesel is ideal once the difficulty with the no-longer-availability of spares can be
overcome or coped with, as well as the inaccessibility of the engine's maintenance areas in the Mirror Offshore's installation. I have a
cunning plan for these drawbacks when necessary!

Leaving the South Woodham Ferrers Sailing Club near the head of navigation on the River Crouch in Essex I used the ebb tide, and
some hours later simultaneously ran out of water and daylight adjacent to Potten Island, midway between the River Roach and the
Havengore Lifting Bridge in Essex. This well known short cut into the River Thames, crossing drying sands and experimental gun
testing ranges, is something | have previously avoided during the last 35 years of sailing in the south east. I settled down for the first
night in the mud in company with five antisocial seals only a few yards away!

Always a bit apprehensive when leaving the first mate alone for long periods | found it difficult to sleep. Once afloat again, although
still completely dark, I motored dead slow towards the Havengore Bridge which is about a quarter of a mile from the creek entrance
where | intended to anchor again.
It was a complete surprise when the lights came on and the bridge lifted, although the books clamed it was only manned and lifted
during the hours of daylight. I had no plans for this eventuality! I went through, shouting to the bridgemaster that I could not hear
his instruction above the noise of my engine which I dare not stop in such a position.
My first mistake was in not anchoring until daylight between the seaward side of the bridge and the creek mouth; I had previously
read of many underwater obstructions. Emerging from the creek, the echo sounder revealed near minimum water depth requirements
and it was quite bouncy!

7

The second mistake was also obvious - the boat was open, washboards and hatch cover stored in the cabin due to the warm weather;
the spray was flying in the rising wind and, in keeping the correct heading (due south by compass), I could not leave the tiller even
for a moment. some planning revisions were clearly necessary as soon as possible! The next hour was wet and horrible and my
morale and confidence were severely shaken!
The tide was ebbing before I reached the Thames near East Shoebury buoy and it took some time before I picked up a vacant mooring
opposite Shoebury coastguard station, and by sheer coincidence right next to my first real boat, a Macwester 26 names 'Vanellus',
looking much smarter and better equipped than when I owned her about 20 years earlier.
After a few hours' rest, some reorganisation and a rethink, I enjoyed a good sail for a few hours past Canvey Island to the Gravesend
area and took the visitor's mooring at Thurrock Yacht Club for a good night's sleep(?) However the moorings are exposed to the
prevailing south west winds and, at first light, I motored under the high M25 bridge to the Erith Yacht Club moorings situated on the
south bank and therefore sheltered in the prevailing conditions.

On the third afternoon's flood tide I motored to St Katharine Docks adjacent to Tower Bridge where I planned to demast and secure as
yachts do in situations of low bridges. While waiting for the marina to open I decided to start the process on their waiting mooring.
The process went like clockwork and was completed and secure just as the marina lock opened.
With renewed confidence I decided to press on through London, passing under 16 bridges on the tidal Thames with many things and
sights of interest to see.
With no planned stopover for this section of the river and being wamed off a couple of likely places due to possible complications
during the low tide period in the dark, it was then long after dark when I picked up a vacant mooring at Richmond Lock -
the end of
the tidal Thames.

The next morning the first stop was Teddington Lock to acquire the temporary licences (one month for cruiser and tender - the latter,
an extra £10!)
My sea toilet had been removed prior to this tip and replaced with a small self contained portable caravan type, since I would travel
through 260 miles of London's drinking water. No inspection of my boat facilities was conducted!
Having no further need for the tender in tranquil water, leaving it somewhere safe proved difficult. Eventually I hit on a suitable line
ofpatter and, so that ] would remember which lock keeper had agreed, | wrote "TLH' (tender left here) on my river map. There were
44 locks to be negotiated each way! More about that later.

Stanford's River Thames Map 1'4" = | mile provided all the river information required. NRA (National Rivers Authority) Thames
Region and 'British Marine Industries Federation’ data was also very useful.
Apart from the locks to be negotiated, there were a further 80 bridges to pass under in the fresh water Thames, of all ages, designs,
construction details and materials. I had a good look at each from both directional passes, especially those older stone arch types,
some very significant in English history. I counted 15 arches on one particular bridge where the river was wide with adjoining flood
lains.
The locks with a rise and fall varying between 3 and 9 feet necessitated a quick learning curve for a single hander who was only
rarely offered help controlling the boat's both fore and aft lines simultaneously. No problem in an otherwise empty lock, but fill it up
with large-beamed broads-type cruisers and canal-type narrow boats, plus the odd larger shiny gin palace, all with large superior
crews watching ever so carefully, can be intimidating, but in that area at least I was superb!
One other facet (during locking) was another problem in that engines had to be stopped in each lock; this was more complicated for
me than for others in my particular installation, with unhealthy noise problems starting to occur from the dyno-starter motor.
During the ascent to head of navigation (126 miles from Teddington), in my case somewhat further and well past the village of
Inglesham, | planned the places I would visit/explore in detail on the return trip. This system worked well.

I only saw, perhaps, a half dozen other sailing cruisers being used as motor cruisers and none at all in the last 35 miles above Oxford
which had very little traffic during my period of transit. Mirror Offshore owners may be amused to read that one lockmaster told me
it Was great to see a real boat in his lock for a change!!
In the midst of the foot and mouth epidemic, the large numbers of cattle and sheep in the farmland areas adjacent to the river was
quite a surprise.
Final practices for the Henley Regatta period were at their height as | passed through on the penultimate evening. My unplanned
timing was a mistake, and it showed! However I was most impressed with this highly disciplined sport, especially in the longer
multi-crewed boats.

Boatyards are more than plentiful along the Thames but they don't provide showers. Marinas are scarce, only Bray and Reading
marinas list showers on the river map. Abingdon's free 24 hour moorings adjoin a heated outdoor swimming pool in superb parkland
and the changing room showers are excellent. An essential stopover in both directions!
Between Oxford and the head of navigation | had prop weed problems, which on two occasions improved my hot weather hygiene
via unplanned swimming, quite enjoyable if a little dangerous in my complete isolation. The abundance of weed was apparently due
to the early season lack of traffic and the foot and mouth epidemic. I suspected, perhaps, variable patterns of fertilisation?
The Osney bridge at Oxford has a maximum span height of 2.28 metres but river height can have some variations. My mast etc.
support crutch just cleared, having got my sums right for a change.
While this report is not intended to describe the many well known venues which can be visited by road, e.g. Hampton Court, Windsor
and Eton, Oxford, Runnymede, etc. | think it worth noting a couple of features not so obvious or well known.
Firstly, the fabulously rich homes with gardens down to the river are almost certainly best observed from the river, but, even in
excellent weather conditions, why were the incumbents never to be seen enjoying their privileges as I was passing both ways? Could
it be something to do with being British?

18

With some experience travelling British canals and even more on the Dutch canals my conclusions are that the Thames easily
surpasses both in the generally accepted tourism criteria.

Lastly, on a historical note, one particular site not so well known because of its location, concerns features near the village of
Dorchester, Oxfordshire, noted for its 7th century abbey. (This site is not to be confused with Dorchester in Dorset and the nearby
ancient earthworks and fortifications of Maiden Castle.) About midway in the mile or so walk from Days Lock to the village is a
system of iron age earthwork defences (moats now dry) where more recent additional defences of 1940s vintage were added. Most of
these concrete pillboxes scattered everywhere along the Thames in open areas will, no doubt, like their predecessors, always be a
feature amongst our historical sites. Although the latter defences were, thankfully, never required it is doubtful if their predecessors
were so lucky, as the site is so close to Wallingford, a crossing which records as being fought for by Celts, Romans, Saxons and
Danes, and even William the Conqueror's army passed there.

Since this is a 'warts and all' report I am reluctant to mention going back through the lock concerned and forgetting my tender, as
there had been no need to look at the map/chart where I'd written 'TLH'. This resulted in an about-tum and some jokes at the
lockmaster's house. However, he didn't have to visit the pub that night!
Not many days later I was seeing the sights of central London again from a riverside perspective and was once again surprised at how
rough the water is when in a small boat. It can't all be down to the fast water taxis - wind against tide, perhaps? I had never noticed
such disturbance from the embankments.
The rig was reinstated on the mooring at Erith Yacht Club after passing the usual points-of interest in the reverse direction, e.g. the
London Eye, Cutty Sark, Dome, Thames Flood Barrier, etc.
Sailing past Canvey Island towards Southend in a strong wind (getting a bit hairy in fact) there was a big bang/bump underneath. The
deep (unsupported low down) spade rudder was now at an acute angle, only hanging on by the top pintle. I was in the shipping
channel, and control was almost impossible with the rudder angled on top pivot only. I used my mobile for a 999 call and about half
an hour later (it seemed longer) Southend RNLI from Southend pier arrived and agreed to tow me to a drying mooring sheltered
behind Canvey Island (they were not completely happy). At low tide I effected a botch-up temporary repair to support the rudder at
the lower pivot point on the transom.

Early next morning as I was about to leave on the top of the tide, I found the Lifeboat crew had arrived and were circling my boat.
This was quite a surprise to me. "We came to see if you were alright," I heard. | pointed out my temporary repairs but did not inform
the crew I was preparing to leave. The weather was fine and bright with a nice prevailing breeze from the south west, but the forecast
Was more pessimistic!
With tide and a decent wind on a broad reach, even a Mirror Offshore can pick up her skirts. Southend pier (the longest in the world)
was soon astern and about three hours later I tucked in behind the western end of the artificial island via the small channel I had
spotted in the now exposed sands.
Anchored in a small deep lagoon close in on a sheltered weather shore it was time to sleep while awaiting the next high water before
crossing the sands/firing range to Havengore creek. But no! The multitude of nesting sea birds were just waiting to be photographed
and the island explored.

I rowed ashore for this proposed quick assessment of the island's stone and bird varieties, photographing nesting chicks in
uncomfortable nests (no grass), forgetting time, when, from the far end, I noticed the tender being blown northwards past the
anchored cruiser! Racing back as best I could on the loose surface and completely out of condition from the long days of small boat
confinement, I stripped off, leaving clothes/camera etc. high up and swam out to the cruiser, started engine, upped the anchor, top
speed after the distant tender! Thankfully, I never grounded as expected, and after recapture, returned to my anchorage, towing the
tender, cold, starkers and very depressed at my catalogue of recent failures, in nothing but basic common sense more often than not!
The books all advise that the Havengore should only be crossed at spring tides and by shallow draft boats, preferably with a northerly
wind. The first and last of those variables were not fulfilled on that date, quite the opposite in fact! I would have had to stay put until
the next day for the correct tidal directions and daylight had I changed my plan and taken the long route around the Whitaker Beacon.
Both options had little appeal at that time. I subsequently decided to stick to the original plan especially as I had saved my unsinkable
tender.
Being in the shallowest place at the top ofthe tide was essential so I set off early and slowly, but had a couple of short stops through
grounding in the rising tide.
Finding the creek entrance first time coming in from the sea was quite a problem as the entrance and the bridge can only be seen
when opposite the opening. I didn't know this and reached a stage where I needed advice about whether to search in a northerly or
southerly direction. A phone call to the bridgemaster confirmed that he could not see me either, but he solved my problem by raising
the bridge to the vertical when clear, and all was revealed. Passing the bridge later, | returned his big grins from the control platform
with my profuse thanks.

The next day I was safely home and promising to confine my sailing in the future to local areas, where unknown variables will not be
a factor!
The total distance covered during this venture is calculated as approaching 400 miles.

Ronald V. Phillips, November 2001].

COMMODORES NOTES

IMPORTANT CHANGES AT MARCONI ATHLETIC AND SOCIAL CLUB
Since I wrote the last set of Commodore's Notes there have been some important and significant changes at the Marconi Athletic and Social Club.
On 15" July a Special General Meeting was held to approve a new set of rules and membership fee
structure.
The first change is to the name, which is now MASC.
The second and a major one as far as the Sailing Club is concerned, was to change the classes of membership. Basically there are now two classes, Ordinary, covering an individual, and Family, which covers the individual plus partner and up to three children under the age of sixteen. This change brings the MASC very much in line with our membership within the Sailing Club where we have Member, for an individual and Family membership covering the Individual with his partner and children as permanent guests.
Thirdly, there is now no distinction between Company Employees and Associate members. All members have the same rights and are able to seek election to the MASC Main Committee.
At the same meeting a new membership fee structure was also adopted which has resulted in a reduction for most people for renewals since 1* September.
The new fees are £21.15 for an Ordinary Member and £55.25 for Family member, which will mean
a saving for most of our members. However they have also decided that the Section will collect a fee of £16.00 per member to be paid to the MASC which will obviously result in an increase in our own fees.
Increasingly we are seeing also that our revenue costs are rising significantly in the Sailing Club as we are forced to ensure that the facilities meet modern legal requirements. A few examples are the need for annual inspections and re-testing of equipment, training costs to ensure that Support Craft and tractor drivers are qualified, and removal of waste material and sewage. Also, the need to refurbish areas of the Club, the latest being the galley, which must be carried out before Maldon Council will renew the hygiene certificate.
Normally we see a rise in the combined total cost of membership of the masc and Sailing Club each year. Although we have not yet finalised the budget for next year, I am hoping that with the changes at the MASC and our own prudent housekeeping we may be able to hold the combined cost to the same level as last year for the majority of members.

As those who camped at the Club in early August are aware, the arrangements for cleaning the clubhouse totally failed and I would like to thank all who did their bit to help out. I can only apologise for the situation and the Committee has agreed that there will be a refund of £5.00 per week per pitch. This will be posted to the person who booked the pitch as soon as arrangements can be finalised.

The successful completion of another Cadet week and Camping fortnight is due entirely to the support that is given to those who organise the event by those who attend. It is a tribute to the spirit of co-operation that exists in the Club.
Further evidence of this was provided when the Cat Fleet laid on an excellent BBQ and wine evening inviting those members of the Cruiser Fleet who had assisted at the East Coast Piers Race.

While I was away with the Cruiser Fleet over the Bank Holiday weekend, John Salmon had the chance to show our President, Tony Benn, around the site before Tony took centre stage and presented the prizes for the Kestrel Open. Again another resounding success for those involved in its organisation and I understand that the Kestrels have already booked for next year.

CRUISER RACING NEWS

——

Ten Marconi yachts were started by Doreen and Derek Kirby from ‘Happy Medium’ for the Medusa Race on Sat 20" July.
The fleet started close hauled down river en route for the ‘Medusa’ buoy off Walton, in light airs. ‘Killara 2’ pulled away to an early lead, followed by ‘Ocean Slipper’, and ‘Lucy 2’, then ‘Reflection’ ‘Moon Fleet’ and ‘Juno’, ‘Out of Focus’, ‘Bluster’, ‘Dreamer’, ‘Petronella’ all trying to find the best route out of the river. As the fleet worked its way past Mersea, Lucy 2 continued to draw away followed by ‘Reflection’, ‘Moon Fleet’ and ‘Out of Focus’, with Killara now out of sight!
In the early afternoon the wind fell away, and large black clouds developed over Clacton and Walton followed by spectacular displays of thunder and lightning, and then torrential rain, all this coinciding with the start of the flood tide.
The fleet was by this time dotted throughout the Wallet from ‘Bluster’ at Clacton Pier‘ to ‘Lucy 2’, ‘Reflection’ and ‘Moon Fleet’ in sight of the Medusa buoy, but all struggling to make ground against the strengthening tide.
Then the news....Killara 2 had rounded the Medusa! and suddenly we could see her pink spinnaker as she
ran inshore back up the Wallet for the finish at Bradwell, encountering a 40 knot gust of wind on the way! So there we are, all the rest of the fleet retired, and we returned to the Green Man at Bradwell to commiserate with each other, drink beer, and congratulate the crew of Killara.

Which goes to prove that sometimes....just sometimes. ....size does matter!

Kestrel Open Meeting

The Kestrel Association wishes to thank the Club for hosting their Open Meeting over the August Bank Holiday weekend. Everyone, including 10 visitors appreciated the facilities and race management. The honour of having our president, Tony Benn, present the prizes was an added bonus.
The Kestrels have a long standing agreement that the 3TM boat overall at a meeting has the task of preparing the report of that meeting. The following therefore was issued to Yachts and Yachting

11 Kestrels contested the Open Meeting held on the 25"/26" August 2002.

Race 1 was held in a light easterly breeze with the first leg against a strong flooding tide. Kate Hearsun and Paul Jarvey got the best start but confusion about the exact location of the first mark allowed Dave Pearson and James Jarvey to take the lead. A close tussle for third place with Rob and John Howell getting the better of Andrew Richards and Alan Bourne who crossed the line to silence for being OCS moving John Weedon and David Tully up to fourth place.

Race 2 was sailed in a force 2-3 North Easterly with Kate and Paul once again leading the way to the first mark and going on to take first place. A close race for second took place between Dave and James and John and Rob with the former taking advantage on the second beat after splitting tacks. Steve and Lynn Worf took fourth place from John Weedon and David Tully.

On Monday the wind had freshened to a 4 -5 Northerly. Dave Hearsum's crack of dawn tweaking paid off as he stormed into an unassailable lead to win. John and Rob Howell snatched second place from Kate and Paul after daring to fly their kite on the penultimate leg. This time John Weedon beat Steve and Lynn Worf to fourth place.

In the afternoon the wind had increased to a force 5 gusting 6. The fleet was sent up the river to the north of Osea Island which lead to some considerable confusion in finding the second mark. This resulted in the whole fleet bunching but it was Dave and James who pulled away from Kate and Paul. After a close race John and Rob Howell took third from Steve and Lynn Worf.

10

We set out for Harwich from Marconi Sailing Club in the Blackwater at 9am on

mooring... During the day, we considered the shingle bank shape and
believe that if we had continued we would have gone straight over...

Is it Jez Rowles - "captain of the boat", for failing to brief his crew and not keeping an
eye on the shallows he knows about and then ordering the U-turn...
Is it Nick Rowles - "the cabin boy", for being in charge whilst Jez was fixing the
engine, not being aware of the shallows and leaving the helm to an out-of-practise

impact and not having read the chart before setting off.

Summers do go with a rush, don’t they! Here we are already deep into Autumn Points racing, with evenings closing in again, and talk is of recovering cruisers for the winter, and Laying-Up Suppers and all that stuff. I can’t keep up with it.
One result of shorter days has been the conclusion of our Wednesday night pursuit series. This series remains as popular as ever, with the informal nature of the event appreciated by most, if not all, participants. It was organised and run with great efficiency once again this year, by John Weedon, with able support from Mavis, and of course the two stalwarts of the Jack B, Colin Leveridge and Colin Phillips. Great job guys! August Bank Holiday weekend saw the conclusion of our Bank Holiday Series for Monohulls. Cats, and Cadets, as well as an event for visiting Kestrels, which provided some good racing over the two days under varied conditions. The events were topped off by a visit from our President, Tony Benn. who presented the permanent trophies and the Open Meeting prizes.
Another major event coming up is the “Helm of the Year” finals on Saturday Sept 21, competed for by the champions of each of our regular racing classes. This will be a series of short races, in single-handed Bytes, held close to the Club site. Spectators as always will be welcome.

'Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Six - The Marquesas (French Polynesia)

Having sailed engineless into Nuka Hiva we very quickly became enamoured with this first part of French Polynesia. The first
morning we were there we visited the Gendarme and were pleased to discover that entry was straightforward and stress-free.
Everyone we met was friendly and extremely helpful Taiohae Bay is the main settlement on the island. there is a bank, a
hospital and several shops, but the little town is so spread out that at first sight there appears to be very little there and it took
us several days to discover all the shops. There was a bit of a swell in the bay but we found it quite relaxing. After rolling
down the trades on the milk-shake min, a total lack of motion would have come as a bit of a shock! Nuku Hiva was a very
relaxing place to arrive but it wasn't all rest as we had the most amazing mess to clear off the hull. Round the waterline we had
been colonised with goose barnacles. These are basically stowaways, and fortunately once you stop moving they tend to jump
ship!. Above the waterline, however, where the topsides had dipped with the rhythmic rolling, the hull was a glorious yellowy
green with patches of weed as extra decoration. Getting all this off turned out to be a major operation that we managed to
make last for several weeks. :

We stayed in Taiohae Bay for 10 days. It was a week before the trawler yacht 'Atlas' arrived with our replacement pump for
the engine. The story of our pump had become quite a saga. When he had heard about our problem, Jim had e-mailed his
crew Jan who was still in Australia at the time. Ian had got the high-up in Perkins Australia who located the part at a dealer's
several hundred miles away and had it flown in to Ian just a few hours before he was due to leave. Within a few days Rauol, a
French yachtsman who had been in the Marquesas for a year, managed the far from easy task of fitting the pump. In fact,
fitting the pump was easy, it was getting to it in the first place that was the difficult part. As soon as we started the engine
again we realised that the bearing on the pump must have been failing for several months. Helen had been saying for a long
time that the engine was noisier than it had been. Now we realised why. We were now free to move on. However, our time in
Taiohae Bay had been far from wasted. We had done several walks into the hills and discovered our first Tiki Sites. Tikis are
old stone carvings. They tend to have goggle-eyed expressions which have a look of aliens about them. An archaeologist we
met said that the expressions probably originated from the fact that the statues were modelled on the victims of ritual sacrifice.
The Tikis also featured large erect phalluses - however, most of these had been removed on the instructions of the early
missionaries that had arrived on the islands in the 18th and 19th centuries. Some of these missionaries had not survived long.
It was fascinating to discover that cannibalism had been perpetuated here until less than a hundred years ago. On one occasion
we were treated to an impressive display of tribal dancing, one of these being a form of greeting. It featured a lot of chanting
and repetition of your name along with chest banging and elbow gesturing. Entertaining though it was, if I had been greeted
like that a couple of hundred years ago | think I would have beaten a hasty retreat.

After we had been in Taiohae Bay about a week we had been joined by Pat and Olivia on 'Aldebaran'. We set off together on
a circumnavigation of the island. Our first stop was Controller Bay where we had the anchorage to ourselves, nestled deep
between dark forbidding cliffs. Going ashore we walked through the tiny village, almost buried amid the typically lush
surroundings. All the vegetation seemed larger than life. I asked a girl if there was anywhere we could buy bananas. She took
us to her home where her family entertained us and showed us round their extensive garden. As well as a hand of bananas they
loaded us down with pamplemousse, breadfruit and various other fruit and veg. Before arriving in French Polynesia I had
never encountered pamplemousse, a type of grapefruit which quickly became one of my favourite fruit. When we came to
leave we tried to pay for these but they refused to accept anything. This was the sort of generosity that we were to experience
time and time again in the Marquesas.

The next morning we came ashore to attend a service in the local church. The main purpose being to experience the superb
Polynesian singing that characterises church services here. Unfortunately the surf was running higher in the morning and by
the time we had all got ashore in our dinghy we were all absolutely drenched. When we got to the tiny church it was already
pretty full and Pat and I ended up squeezed into a pew near the back. After a while I was aware of a dripping noise and
realised that we were making rather a mess on the floor. Pat had taken his socks and sandals off and was attempting to mop
the floor with his sock under his bare foot. After a while he bent down and picked his sock up and wrung it out of the window.
While this bizarre behaviour was going on the small congregation gave us the benefit of some glorious singing. The whole
service was conducted in Polynesian. At the end of the service everyone was really friendly, totally ignoring the fact that we
had invaded their service like drowned rats and had proceeded to exhibit some very odd behaviour. We were shown carved
wooden tikis and exquisite jewellery . We also had the chance to give some small presents to the children of the family that
had been so kind to us the day before.

We then moved round to the middle of three inlets that, together, make up Controller Bay. From there we were able to make
our way through some dense vegetation to one of the most spectacular tiki ceremonial sites we were to see. On the way we
saw a great deal of evidence of earlier Polynesian dwellings. A few hundred years ago the population of these islands was far
higher than it is today. Descending from the site we were engulfed in torrential rain which did nothing to dampen our spirits.
In fact in this climate it was quite refreshing. The one thing that is cold round here
is the rain. On returning to the boats we
were cool enough to enjoy hot toddies. The next day we set off round the east coast of the island while Laura for some reason
chose to cross the island on foot. As we sailed up the impressive coast about half a mile offshore our GPS plotted on the chart
put us at least half a mile inland! The north coast of the island presented even more deep bays. The one we were headed
for,
Anaho Bay, provided one of the best anchorages we had ever seen, sheltered as it was by an inner headland, making the
anchorage invisible from seaward. A resort nestled behind the beach, but it was so low-key that we only ever saw two guests.

1?

There were only one or two locals living in the bay, one of whom insisted on heaping gifts of fruit on Laura. The only thing he
wanted in exchange was her promise to marry him. I never could understand why Laura was so much more successful in being
given fruit than me. This also applied when it came to getting lifts. On her walk across the island Laura had turned down lifts
from every vehicle that passed her. From this bay we undertook an epic walk with Pat across the headland to the next bay to
visit yet another tiki site. Olivia, wisely as it turned out, had elected to stay behind on the boat. In our enthusiasm to find it we
overshot our target and ended up miles out of our way, but in the process managed to see three more bays. The problem was
that the coast road was very open and we were fully exposed to the midday sun. Eventually | met a beer delivery truck coming
the other way. They told me I was all wrong and told me to get in. On the way back they picked up Pat and Helen and very
kindly took us right up to the tiki site, which turned out to be a very elaborate one. | blamed Pat for taking us so far in the
wrong direction and Pat and Helen blamed me - so much for loyalty.

The next day we motored 'Muna' round to the bay and returned to the Tiki site where an archaeologist was giving a very
interesting talk that answered a lot of the questions we had been asking about the Polynesian civilisation. We carried on our
anti-clockwise circumnavigation of Nuku Hiva, having a cracking sail round to Daniel's Bay where Daniel has been
entertaining yachties for the past 28 years. From there we had a fascinating walk through dense vegetation up to a waterfall.
We swam in the pool, having negotiated the path under several fallen boulders. The route up to the waterfall was littered with
overgrown pai pai's or platforms made of large boulders as evidence of what had once been a teeming metropolis. We
completed our circumnavigation of the island by returning to Taiohae Bay from where we sailed 25 miles to the island of Ua
Pou, anchoring behind the breakwater in the main harbour in Baie D'Hakahau. This was another lovely island with an
incredible skyline. The phallus shaped peaks only rarely appeared from behind the clouds. It was here that Laura left us
temporarily. Henry on 'Maritime Express’ a Canadian yacht had broken his wrist while climbing to the waterfall in Daniel's
Bay. He had had to have pins put in and was therefore somewhat disadvantaged. Laura offered to help out. Our time in this
anchorage was enlivened by the fact that the local boat club had a team entered in the Round Moorea outrigger canoe race, due
to take place in Tahiti in July. This was a six-man event but for the marathon 80 km race, each canoe has a support boat with a
relief crew. Once the race has got under way the crews can change as often as they like. We watched the Ua Pou team
practising this changeover. The support boat would drop the relief crew in line in front of the canoe. The canoe would then go
alongside the six in the water so they were between the canoe and the outrigger. The ones in the canoe would then leap out the
other side, while the new crew clambered in. The Sunday before we moved on, the boat club put on a traditional pig roast,
which turned out to be a very sociable occasion and an opportunity to experience traditional Polynesian food.

Part Thirty Seven - Marquesas to the Tuamotus

We now had 500 miles to cover to reach the Tuamotus. This was the first significant passage that Helen and I had been on on
our own for some time. We set off with 'Aldebaran' and rounded the island. As we passed a bay further round we were joined
by 'Cap d'Or' and 'Silver Fin’. So it was that four of the five boat that had set off from Los Perles together, were reunited. it
was very pleasant on these passages to be able to communicate with other boats via the radio. Once out of VHF range, we
normally set up a schedule for an informal 'net' on the SSB. After a quiet start the wind built up enough to give us good
progress and pleasant sailing. We settled down to a comfortable beam reach as we were now heading almost south westerly.
The second day out we were startled to see what we reckoned to be a sperm whale a good 45' long, placidly swimming
alongside us no more than 100" away, blowing merrily. Fascinating though it was, it was quite a relief when it decided to leave
us. The first two or three days were generally fairly pleasant. On the fourth day when we had been out for 3 nights, the winds
went light on us. We drifted along all day with just a couple of brief squalls to liven things up. By this time 'Cap d'Or' and
‘Aldebaran' were far enough ahead to press on for landfall that day. ‘Silver Fin' and ourselves were committed to another night
at sea. The Tuamotus are not a place you would choose to arrive at night. That day there were rather ominous reports of bad
weather on the French Polynesian forecast. After nightfall there was still very little wind. About 10 o'clock the little wind
there was died away completely. I reluctantly started the engine as the motion was so uncomfortable. Within minutes we had,
out of nowhere, 35 knots of wind well ahead of the beam. This was to continue, slightly abated, all night and all the next day.
After wallowing about with all sail up we set off like a scalded cat. Initially thinking it was just another short-lived squall I
hung on to full sail for a while. The auto helm which, up to then, had been doing the steering on this trip, was overwhelmed so
we were now committed to hand steering. As the night wore on I put first one, then two reefs in the main. With the headsails
partially furled we found that, left to her own devices, ‘'Muna' could steer herself. This is the sort of weather when we are
really grateful for 'Muna's' weight and full-bodied design and we had a remarkably comfortable night, all things considered.

As it got light I realised that at our current rate of progress we would have a job reaching our destination by nightfall. I
therefore reassessed the rig, put up more sail and started hand steering. We started powering along at 6-7 knots through large
seas, just holding our course. It turned out to be a cracking sail and after minimal sleep overnight I really began to enjoy
myself. By cracking on we reached the pass at Makemo at dead slack water and had a tranquil passage through, in contrast to
‘Cap d'Or' and 'Aldebaran' who had had quite a bash the day before, entering on the ebb. Once through the pass we headed
across the lagoon to an anchorage on the far side. The water in the lagoon was surprisingly rough and we had to be on the alert
for isolated coral heads that rose vertically from the 20-30 metre depths. All the atolls in the Tuamotus are basically reef-lined
lagoons with small islands, or Motus , scattered about the reefs. These atolls were originally volcanic islands that attracted a
fringe of coral reefs. The islands eroded away leaving the coral reef behind.
to be continued Malcolm Shaft

COMMODORE'S NOTES

We are rapidly approaching that time of year when the sailing comes to an end and our thoughts turn to the long
winter evenings and the prospects for next season.

However we still have the Annual General Meeting at 10:30hrs, 3°’ November at the MASC on Beehive Lane
which will be followed by prize giving as normal.

As I explained in my last Commodores notes the MASC has changed its membership fee structure.
Last year an Associate member paid an MASC subscription of £52.00 and then the fees to the Sailing Club. From
1* September the MASC membership fee is £21.15 for an individual and then the Section is charged £16.00 by the
MASC making a total of £37.15 leaving a "Saving" of £14.85.

The Executive have recommended to the Main Committee that the only increase this year will be on the
membership Subscription fee which will be increased by £16.00, which we have to pay to MASC, and the "Saving"
of £14.85 (pro rata for Junior, Student and Retired Members) with no increase on any other fees.
This should mean that for the majority of members their combined MASC and Sailing Club fees for last year will
be equal to their combined fees for the coming year. The Main Committee have approved this proposal and I hope
that you will at the AGM, as this will enable us to continue to maintain and improve the facilities which we all
enjoy.

Elsewhere in Navigans, you will find a table to allow you to check the result for yourself. (Ed's Note: Next Page)

The weekend following the AGM, Sunday 10" November, we have the working party to shut the clubhouse and
site down for the Closed Season, unless of course you join the Windsurfers who seem to come out as the wind
strength increases. The tasks we will be tackling that weekend are listed elsewhere in Navigans and I hope to see
many of you there.

During the winter there are a number of other tasks to be completed but these are being split among groups and
fleets to tackle at times that are convenient to them.

We will be holding a working party to shake off the Christmas festivities on Sunday 29 December. This will
concentrate purely on "Hedging and Ditching" with the prospect of Mince Pies and Mulled Wine in the lunch break

Finally can I remind everyone that Fenella is beavering away to organise the Laying Up Supper at the
Waterfront on Saturday 16" November. Based on the other events that she has put on this year a grand evening
is in prospect and I believe that some tickets are still available.

Neil Pembleton

Tail-piece

My attention was instantly caught by the article in October Navigans about Juno on Thirslet spit, as I had a
somewhat parallel experience last month myself, and can certainly identify with the various viewpoints expressed,
albeit lightheartedly, about responsibility.

I was helming a friend’s (still friends I think!) cruiser down the Crouch on a falling tide after a pleasant trip up to
Brandy Hole Y.C. for lunch, and parked it on the mud near Fambridge. Our quick and frantic efforts to dislodge it
failed and we were stuck until the next tide which refloated us at about 1 am the following morning. Getting home
after 03.00 and up again at 07.00 was not best preparation for my task that day - Race Officer for our Helm of the
Year finals! However, that event went reasonably smoothly and was enjoyed, | think. by all who participated. The
Club is indebted to all who lent a hand in support of HoY and it’s preparation, and particularly to those who
allowed the use of their Byte dinghies for the racing.

As our sailing season draws to a close it is appropriate to acknowledge the work done by the Sailing Sub-
Committee to make it all happen. My thanks to all who supported this team over the year, and particularly to our
Sailing Secretary, Dave Williams, who with Kate’s help has been a great strength to the Club.

All those with boats and equipment in the dinghy park are requested to ensure that they are removed promptly this
year, as trenches need to be cut in support of the major electrical works at the club commencing Nov 11.
Hope to see you all at AGM, Prize-giving, and Laying-up Supper.

John Salmon

This prestigious event was held this year on Saturday 21 September. The day was dry and blessed with occasional
sunshine, with initially light winds increasing to force 4 at times in the afternoon. The format for recent years was
retained with a series of races in single handers where competitors sail a different boat in each race. This year
Bytes were used for the first time, with boats kindly loaned for the occasion by club members.

The Champions of six fleets were invited to take part, and this year they were : Dave Williams (H’cap); Steve
Monks (Solo); Jenny Ball (Dart 15); Roy Hardwicke (Cruiser); Paul Harrison (Catamaran); and Alex Dowsett
(Cadet). Due to the light winds the fleet was taken around Stansgate point, to gain some protection from the tide,
where a short triangle / sausage course was laid for the first 3 races.

Morning Races: The start of Race 1 saw Alex charge the line a little early, he was recalled. The rest of the fleet
made a clean start with Steve establishing a good lead by the windward mark, followed by Jenny, Paul, Dave, Alex
and Roy. Jenny and Alex lost some ground when they missed the start line gate at the end of the first lap, but
quickly recovered. Dave passed Paul on the beat and final finishing order was Steve, Dave Paul, Jenny, Alex, and
Roy. A clean start to Race 2 was led away by Steve, Alex and Jenny, but a good windward leg by Dave took him
through to second. Alex re-passed him on the reach before a disastrous second beat dropped him to 5". Jenny
closed steadily on Dave to pass on the run, while Steve remained unchallenged in the lead. Finishing order : Steve,
Jenny, Dave, Paul, Alex, Roy. The first beat of Race 3 saw the closest racing yet, with Alex just pipping Steve to
the first mark, and forcing an extra tack from him to establish a useful lead. Jenny, Paul and Dave rounded close
together. The feature of the race was Steve’s chase of Alex for the lead, but despite closing the gap it was Alex’s
offwind speed which prevailed. Finishing order was Alex, Steve, Jenny, Paul, Dave, Roy.

The wind had been gradually picking up through the morning, so after the lunch break it was decided to set new,
spectator-friendly, courses with the start line and leeward mark immediately in front of the clubhouse. So for the
final 3 races spectators had a grandstand view.

Afternoon Races: In Race 4 Steve again led at the windward mark followed closely by Jenny, Dave, Paul, Alex,
and Roy. Alex again generated enough extra offwind speed to just steal second from Jenny and Dave at the
leeward mark, but Dave passed him again on the second beat. Roy, who had been struggling with a back problem
throughout the event, capsized on the run as the wind picked up to a gusty force 4, and retired. Steve was
stretching away in a comfortable lead, but the close fight for second was only resolved on the final reach when
Jenny and Alex both took a dip leaving Dave safe in that position. They finished: Steve, Dave, Paul, Jenny, Alex.
In Race 5 Paul led through the start, but capsized half way up the beat to relegate himself to last place. At the end
of the first lap Steve and Alex were disputing the lead well clear of Dave and Jenny, with Paul struggling to catch
up. Steve incurred a penalty at the windward mark, which let Alex into the lead, but Steve again showed excellent
speed and control on the reaches to catch and re-pass Alex and claim the race. They finished: Steve, Alex, Jenny,
Dave, Paul. In the final Race 6 Steve again led away and extended his lead throughout, with Jenny secure in
second. Alex passed Paul and Dave on the run to move into third which he held to the finish. Final order was:
Steve, Jenny, Alex, Paul, Dave.

With 5 wins in 6 races, Steve had once again claimed the title of Helm of the Year. Well done Steve!

COMMODORE'S NOTES

By the time that you read this, we will have held our last official function of the Year, the Laying Up Supper and I
hope that all who came to it had an enjoyable evening. Elsewhere in this issue, you will find my report to the well
attended Annual General Meeting reviewing the year from my stand point.

As you are aware during the gales at the end of October, we unfortunately lost the clubhouse roof. Thankfully no
one was seriously injured and I would like to thank those who helped when a person was trapped under its remains.
The Club continues to flourish and many members contribute in many different ways. I would like to thank
everyone who attended the club on a very wet Sunday 10" November for the working party. Despite the conditions,
the dinghy park has been cleared, the tender rack sorted out, a number of cruisers moved, the Race Box shut down
and the external furniture placed in safe storage in race reception. In addition a small dedicated band working in the
dry and comfort, stripped the Galley ready for its rebuild. All of us would like to thank Maureen and Leonie for the
hot soup and rolls at lunch time.

Although we are now in the quiet season (no sailing unless you are a wind surfer), many members are involved in
the various committees planning for next year's season and carrying out or organising maintenance work at the club
over the next few months.

Many of you may find yourselves approached by the fleet captains to help with a number of maintenance tasks at
the club. We are trying the approach of asking each fleet to complete one or two jobs over the winter on weekends
convenient to their members rather than attempting to carry out many different tasks at one or two "all in" working
parties.

But please note that we are holding the traditional Christmas break working party on SUNDAY 29"
DECEMBER concentrating purely on hedging and ditching, (Mulled Wine and Mince Pies as well as soup
and rolls).

We still need one or two people to come forward so that we can nominate them to serve on the MASC Main
committee and thereby ensure the future prosperity and well being of the Sailing Club.

This edition is probably the last one to land on your doorsteps before Christmas and I wish you all a Happy
Christmas, enjoyable New Year and successful sailing season to come.

Neil Pembleton

CATAMARAN FLEET - Where did this season go?

The old saying says it all. That time flies by when you're having fun. We have had some good sailing throughout
the season although unfortunately we did lose a couple of long distance races due to the weather.

With the courses available, it does allow us to race a mixed fleet of 2 sail + 2 sail and reacher catamarans together,
due to the fact that depending on wind direction it doesn’t suit cither or perfectly every weekend. But it does seem
to even itself out over the season.

For me personally the exhilaration of sailing with the reacher 1s a must, having said that as I approach the leeward
mark and then continue past it for a further 50yds whilst | untangle my downhaul, the 2 sail mode does seem more
appealing.

This years E.C.P.R was well attended with some 50+ visitors swelling the clubs own entries; thank you once again
to all the volunteers on and off the water, in particular the “mother boats” who had an uncomfortable day on
station as the weather deteriorated during the race. Many thanks also to those who donated prizes for the raffle,
which with the entry fees and sponsorship donations helps to give sailing opportunities to people less fortunate than
themselves.

It is with this thought in mind the E.C.P.R Committee is already planning for next year’s event (5"/6" July 2003.)
We are currently looking for additional sponsors, so if you have a company or individual who would be willing to
add their weight behind the event please let me know.

Christina Hutt has again “volunteered” to arrange the raffle and to broaden the appeal and to hopefully increase
ticket sales to non-sailing people. She is looking for 2 or 3 main prizes unattached to sailing; please contact
Christina with any ideas or donations.

Open Meetings

4 Formula 18’s and 1 Spitfire attended the National Championships at Netley SC on Southampton Water and with
the Sunday racing coinciding with the last day of Cowes week, this did get a little congested. Netley “stood in” at
the last minute to host the event which, with race officer Don Findlay in charge was very well run.

Mitchell Glynn and Rob Mead won the youngest combined age trophy; which was no mean feat given the final day
was sailed in very windy conditions. We also had several Hurricanes at Stone SC. But Paul and Michelle Harrison
and Lee and Davina Harrison have topped everything by shipping their boats to Aruba in the Caribbean for a
catamaran open with entrants coming from all over the world.

Welcome to Simon Hay (Hobie) , John Higgs (Hobie Tiger) and Laurie Hanson (Hurricane 5.9) to the fleet; we
would like to see more boats out, so if you are thinking of purchasing a catamaran but would like to try one out
first, then please don’t hesitate to contact me, - there is plenty of advice on hand from current sailors.

Finally I would normally be saying at this point if you haven’t already taken your mast down for the winter, please
do so immediately. But we have saved you a job on 25" October; we experienced the strongest winds since the
storm of ’87- Force 11 recorded in the clubhouse. So with those at hand we dropped all the masts in the park- if you

haven’t been down for a while please go and tidy things up because the mast has only been laid beside your boat.
Thank you for all those who helped with this task.

It remains for me to wish you a Happy Christmas and a Happy New Year. Look forward to seeing you on the water
next season.

HANDICAP FLEET.

Well, the racing has come to an end, the boats are packed up for the winter, and it’s AGM season...

In a break with the Handicap Fleet tradition of recent years, this will take place before Christmas (just), on Tuesday
10" December, at MASC. I wrote a few weeks ago to the 123 Handicap Fleet members, as identified by Nick
Beavins’ magical membership list, so I hope that you are all aware of it. Do join us for 7.30pm for the meeting, or 7
pm if you need some Dutch courage to cope with such an ordeal.

It would be particularly good to see monohulls sailors who don’t restrict themselves to Sundays and club racing. So
if your preference is cruising in a Wayfarer, creek crawling in a Mirror or touring the Open Meeting circuit, come
along and share your views and experiences of the season.

I am certain that this will have been said elsewhere in this edition of Navigans, but I would like to thank everyone
who helped to secure the dinghy park, and elsewhere on site, during the gales of 27th October (technically not
gales, but a force 11 ‘near- hurricane’, I believe. I can’t prove that, but I did spot one photographer waiting to
capture the moment on the club anemometer...). When J arrived at the club, three dinghies that had fallen had
already been secured, and phone-calls made where the owners could be identified. Numerous other dinghies’
fastenings were tightened, stakes stamped back in, and trolleys re-inserted. Amazingly, every single cat mast had
been lowered and at least one cruiser secured by tying it to a tractor. Some damage was sustained in the fleet, with
John and Mavis Weedon particularly sickened by the loss of yet another mast. The damage all around the club
could easily have been much worse though, and my thanks again to all who ensured that it wasn’t.

I look forward to seeing you at the AGM, and maybe even at a fleet social — watch this space...

The Support Boat Roster — How it works!

As you are all aware, the club racing programme is very dependent on an army of volunteers who helm and crew
the support boats. On the whole, this process runs smoothly but like the swan, an awful lot of frantic paddling goes
on under the surface!

I thought it would be worthwhile just explaining the process that we use and the responsibilities of the various
people involved so that the machine continues to run as smoothly as we would all want.

At the beginning of the sailing season a Roster of support boat cover is published in Navigans. This identifies the
crews and helms for Jack B and the RIB against dates and events. The Roster will have the names of those club
