Commodore's AGM Report.

Welcome to what I believe is the 50th Annual General Meeting of our Club. Since its founding in 1952 the Club
has come a long from its beginnings in a hut on the allotments at Heybridge via the barge Mamgu to its present
home here at Stansgate. This could not have been achieved without the vision and foresight of numerous members
who have served on committees, undertaken projects to acquire, and I use that term in its loosest sense, equipment
and buildings for the site and all those who have turned out at numerous working parties over these fifty years. We
also need to remember the very real assistance given by the MASC during this time. Without the backing of its
main committee and its considerable financial facility at that time, the site could not have been purchased and
subsequently the clubhouse built.

I believe that the greatest asset that the club has acquired over the fifty years is not this site but the members'
willingness to recognise that we are all wanting the best for the club whilst each having a different needs from the
club. It is this spirit of co-operation that has enabled us to build a club able to provide one of the most diverse
sailing sites on the East Coast. This has not always been achieved without considerable debate and intelligent
discussion along the way but the committees over the years have been able to move the club forward with the full
support of the members after such debate.

One of the luxuries we have on our site is space. However this does bring its own problems. It is often easier to
allow unwanted items to accumulate than tackle the problems of disposing of them. Last winter committee decided
that the time had come to tackle this particular area. A start was made by cutting up and removing a vast amount of

trailers and other metal from the site. At the same time Jenny Ball has been attempting to identify the owners of a
number of dinghies that appear to be abandoned on the site. It is now intended to dispose of these in the next few
months. Once this has been done, the committee will be enforcing the rules relating to the payment of fees or in the
last resort the recovery of fees by the sale of such items. In the case of the cruiser fleet, this is already starting with
the charging of members to scrap old trailers. By the way, the money raised does not go to the people who provide
the labour but to the considerable cost of hiring equipment and more importantly the skips and subsequent disposal
of the scrap. Increasingly we are faced with not only higher costs for disposal of waste from the site but greater
legislation regarding the method. For example the skip provided throughout the year must not be used for the
disposal of metal and garden waste, this has to be separated out.

One of the main topics that the committee has had to deal with related to the electrical system. Again it is the
requirements of today's legislation that highlighted the problem. The club needs to have its system certified as safe,
however, when tested it did not meet today's definition - please do not get the impression that we are using a
dangerous system. We were faced then with a number of options; should we do the minimum needed to obtain a
certificate, replace like for like, or take a longer term view of replacing the entire system and allow for growth over
the next ten, fifteen, or twenty years? I would like to thank Clive Shenton, Frank Bennett, Dave Payne, Dave
Steward and all those they consulted for the time and effort freely given on the project to date. As a result of their
efforts it was apparent that the most cost-effective long-term solution was its total replacement and expansion.
Next they addressed the problem of how to do it. We pride ourselves on being a self help club but sometimes it is
right to act as project managers and let the professionals do the work. We decided this was such a case.

The latest major infra structure problem has again been highlighted by legislation. I refer to the Galley where the
hygiene certificate has not been renewed - again please do not get the impression that we are all about to get food
poisoning. So we need to totally refurbish this over the winter. In this case the project can be handled using the
club's self help philosophy. Dave Payne has consulted with Belinda Dowley and the certifying authority, he has
spoken to various people to acquire the necessary equipment, not necessarily for free but at very reduced cost, and
he assures me that he has a team of very willing volunteers to carry out the work. Once this has been done, we are
going to have to keep the Galley locked to comply with the legislation. We are currently looking at methods of
providing facilities for making hot drinks in another area. Before leaving the subject of the galley, I am sure that
you all would like me to thank Belinda and her team for the excellent fare this year.

We have continued to invest in replacement of facilities at the club during the year. The most significant being the
new RIB, which I understand, is most successful. Jenny Ball carried out much of the initial research and
negotiation, and then John salmon and Roy Hardwicke took up the mantle. All of them and the drivers are to be
congratulated on the smooth introduction of the boat.

As [ have already said in Navigans, we can only apologise for the lack of cleaning during Camping Fortnight.
This was due to a lack of communication within the Executive. Having examined all the methods available to us to
make the refund, it has been decided to do this as part of the renewal process in January.

On the sailing side I will only make a passing comment on the East Coast Piers Race and leave the sailing
Secretary to report on this later in the meeting. This year's race must rank as one of the fastest ever sailed. Chris
Davies and his team did a splendid job but as always some areas for improvement were identified and are being
worked on. On occasions I hear the odd comment that the race is run only for the benefit of a few cat sailors from
our club. Just to put the record straight, the entry this year comprised 55 boats from outside the club and 17 from
within. I believe this reflects well on the ability of the entire club to stage the event and the commitment of all
areas of the club to help each other. I would like to see us aiming for 15 to 20% growth in the numbers sailing the
race for each of the next three years.

Mike Smith and Malcolm Yeoman introduced a major innovation this year when they dispensed with keg beer and
went to bottled in the bar. I believe that this has been a successful move although not without some problems,
which they are looking at.

MASC AGM [am lucky with our AGM in that a large proportion of the membership attends, it does ask
questions and express views, which, whilst it can be uncomfortable at times, does allow the Executive and Main
Committee to understand the feelings you have. Unfortunately the MASC suffers from a lack of attendance of
members at its AGM. This is in part to due to their failure to publicise the date. This year's Annual General
Meeting is on Wednesday 13 November starting at 7:30 at Beehive Lane. As I said earlier the MASC has in the
past been very supportive in the development of our site. I would urge as many of you as possible to attend their

meeting and ask any questions you want to. The other area we need to address is representation on their Main
Committee; we need at least one but preferably two persons to serve on it. It is only by having this that our views
can be expressed and heard, and just as importantly we can know what is being planned for the future. I hope that
some of you will contact one of the executive to volunteer to represent us on that committee.

As you all are aware the first phase of the replacement of the electrical supply will start in November with the
work being carried out in the area of the Dinghy Park, Clubhouse and Tractor shed. The second phase is
scheduled to start in May next year mainly affecting the Cruiser Park, Race Reception areas. This work will
require our co-operation to clear areas as required and we will inevitably need to carry out some reinstatement work
afterwards. Please check in Navigans for advance warning and the need to help with moving of boats etc.

Last year a considerable number of people retired from the committee and other positions within the Club so there
has been quite a learning curve for many of the replacements and we apologise for any problems experienced as a
result. This year we have a much more stable situation but there are some significant gaps to fill.

Bob Collins took on the role of Navigans Editor last year, and then unfortunately for us was promoted within the
education system and has had to move out of the area.

Camping: Hilary Ashley a number of years ago decided that a better method of allocating pitches was required
than the First Come First Pitched approach. Quietly and single handedly at that time she set about devising and
implementing the system that we see today. After all this time, she has decided to retire from this self-created
position and I ask you all to show your appreciation for the time and effort that she and her helpers have put in.

Last and most significant is the retirement of Frank Bennett. Subject to your approval later in the meeting John
Bird will succeed him . Frank has served as Treasurer for fourteen years and during that time the Club has
improved its facilities, the reserve account has grown to a healthy balance to allow major capital expenditure year
on year whilst the increase in fees has largely matched inflation. Aside from this, Frank has been a true friend to all
who have served with him on the Club's committees over the years. I wish him a long and happy retirement and
hope that we will see him around the Club for many years to come.

Finally I would like to congratulate Fenella on the programme of social] events she has organised this year. One of
my first memories when I joined the club was the Mid Summer Barbecue. Fenella suggested celebrating fifty years
of the club by reviving it. She along with members from all sections of the club made a resounding success of the
day and evening. All are to be congratulated and I hope that we may see it repeated next year.

As I said at the start of my report, the Club has a long tradition of co-operation and friendship between individuals,
groups, and fleets. It is also proud of its ability to improve itself by self-help. I firmly believe that these have been
paramount to its success in the last fifty years and, if continued, will see its continuing success for at least another
fifty years.
That ends my report for this year.

Commodore's thanks to Frank Bennett, retiring Treasurer.

Finally before I close the meeting, I must return to Frank Bennett. It was just over fourteen years ago that I stood
down from the post of Treasurer and was introduced to a young lad wearing shorts, quite obviously fresh out of
school. In the last fourteen years this lad has blossomed into the fine figure that we know today. I cannot believe
that there is an area of the club which has not received his magic touch, be it from chucking lighted paper into the
hole we dug to replace the water main to check that we had not punctured the gas pipe, designing and building the
gate and clubhouse locking system, maintaining the sewage system and many other jobs. At the same time there
cannot be many members who have not benefited from Frank's knowledge and experience. I personally, and I am
sure that all other previous Commodores, members of the Executive and main committees, have welcomed his
calm, careful analysis and advice over the fourteen years.

In addition to this he also found time to carry out the duties of treasurer, a role mainly in the background but most
essential to the well being of the club. Without his careful husbanding of the club's finances we would either be
paying very much higher fees or be unable to renew and develop the facilities the way that we have. The fact that
we are able to move forward with the replacement of the electrical system, whilst reducing our reserve for the next
two or three years, and not had to take the alternative route of closing the site is largely due to his skill in making
every pound that we pay, stretch and work for all our benefit.

On behalf of those people who have worked with you on the committees over the years, I would ask you to accept
this gift. (A barometer and watch were then presented to Frank by Murray Bates on behalf of present and past
Committee members.)
Neil Pembleton

Our final scheduled club race for the year was the “Last Fling” on 27" October. Plenty was “flung” on that day, but
unfortunately sailing was definitely off. As most of you will instantly identify, it was the day of the big storm,
when very high winds threatened to create havoc, and most of the felting was ripped off the clubhouse roof.
A lot of quick work was put in that day in the boat parks, to lower masts and re-secure boats, thus preventing more
damage. Thanks to all who took action.

these boats, the responsibility remains with owners to either remove them promptly, or lower masts, secure for
winter, label them with name and telephone number, and pay the winter storage fee. If you are one of these owners,

‘Muna's Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Six - The Marquesas (French Polynesia)

Having sailed engineless into Nuka Hiva we very quickly became enamoured with this first part of French Polynesia. The first
morning we were there we visited the Gendarme and were pleased to discover that entry was straightforward and stress-free.
Everyone we met was friendly and extremely helpful Taiohae Bay is the main settlement on the island. there is a bank, a
hospital and several shops, but the little town is so spread out that at first sight there appears to be very little there and it took
us several days to discover all the shops. There was a bit of a swell in the bay but we found it quite relaxing. After rolling
down the trades on the milk-shake run, a total lack of motion would have come as a bit of a shock! Nuku Hiva was a very

12

relaxing place to arrive but it wasn't all rest as we had the most amazing mess to clear off the hull. Round the waterline we had
been colonised with goose barnacles. These are basically stowaways, and fortunately once you stop moving they tend to jump
ship! Above the waterline, however, where the topsides had dipped with the rhythmic rolling, the hull was a glorious yellowy
green with patches of weed as extra decoration. Getting all this off turned out to be a major operation that we managed to
make last for several weeks.

We stayed in Taiohae Bay for 10 days. It was a week before the trawler yacht 'Atlas' arrived with our replacement pump for
the engine. The story of our pump had become quite a saga. When he had heard about our problem, Jim had e-mailed his
crew Ian who was still in Australia at the time. Ian had got the high-up in Perkins Australia who located the part at a dealer's
several hundred miles away and had it flown in to Ian just a few hours before he was due to leave. Within a few days Rauol, a
French yachtsman who had been in the Marquesas for a year, managed the far from easy task of fitting the pump. In fact,
fitting the pump was easy, it was getting to it in the first place that was the difficult part. As soon as we started the engine
again we realised that the bearing on the pump must have been failing for several months. Helen had been saying for a long
time that the engine was noisier than it had been. Now we realised why. We were now free to move on. However, our time in
Taiohae Bay had been far from wasted. We had done several walks into the hills and discovered our first Tiki Sites. Tikis are
old stone carvings. They tend to have goggle-eyed expressions which have a look of aliens about them. An archaeologist we
met said that the expressions probably originated from the fact that the statues were modelled on the victims of ritual sacrifice.
The Tikis also featured large erect phalluses - however, most of these had been removed on the instructions of the early
missionaries that had arrived on the islands in the 18th and 19th centuries. Some of these missionaries had not survived long.
It was fascinating to discover that cannibalism had been perpetuated here until less than a hundred years ago. On one occasion
we were treated to an impressive display of tribal dancing, one of these being a form of greeting. It featured a lot of chanting
and repetition of your name along with chest banging and elbow gesturing. Entertaining though it was, if I had been greeted
like that a couple of hundred years ago I think I would have beaten a hasty retreat.

After we had been in Taiohae Bay about a week we had been joined by Pat and Olivia on 'Aldebaran'. We set off together on
a circumnavigation of the island. Our first stop was Controller Bay where we had the anchorage to ourselves, nestled deep
between dark forbidding cliffs. Going ashore we walked through the tiny village, almost buried amid the typically lush
surroundings. All the vegetation seemed larger than life. I asked a girl if there was anywhere we could buy bananas. She took
us to her home where her family entertained us and showed us round their extensive garden. As well as a hand of bananas they
loaded us down with pamplemousse, breadfruit and various other fruit and veg. Before arriving in French Polynesia I had
never encountered pamplemousse, a type of grapefruit which quickly became one of my favourite fruit. When we came to
leave we tried to pay for these but they refused to accept anything. This was the sort of generosity that we were to experience
time and time again in the Marquesas.

The next morning we came ashore to attend a service in the local church. The main purpose being to experience the superb
Polynesian singing that characterises church services here. Unfortunately the surf was running higher in the morning and by
the time we had all got ashore in our dinghy we were all absolutely drenched. When we got to the tiny church it was already
pretty full and Pat and I ended up squeezed into a pew near the back. After a while I was aware of a dripping noise and
realised that we were making rather a mess on the floor. Pat had taken his socks and sandals off and was attempting to mop
the floor with his sock under his bare foot. After a while he bent down and picked his sock up and wrung it out of the window.
While this bizarre behaviour was going on the small congregation gave us the benefit of some glorious singing. The whole
service was conducted in Polynesian. At the end of the service everyone was really friendly, totally ignoring the fact that we
had invaded their service like drowned rats and had proceeded to exhibit some very odd behaviour. We were shown carved
wooden tikis and exquisite jewellery . We also had the chance to give some small presents to the children of the family that
had been so kind to us the day before.

We then moved round to the middle of three inlets that, together, make up Controller Bay. From there we were able to make
our way through some dense vegetation to one of the most spectacular tiki ceremonial sites we were to see. On the way we
saw a great deal of evidence of earlier Polynesian dwellings. A few hundred years ago the population of these islands was far
higher than it is today. Descending from the site we were engulfed in torrential rain which did nothing to dampen our spirits.
In fact in this climate it was quite refreshing. The one thing that is cold round here is the rain. On returning to the boats we
were cool enough to enjoy hot toddies. The next day we set off round the east coast of the island while Laura for some reason
chose to cross the island on foot. As we sailed up the impressive coast about half a mile offshore our GPS plotted on the chart
put us at least half a mile inland! The north coast of the island presented even more deep bays. The one we were headed for,
Anaho Bay, provided one of the best anchorages we had ever seen, sheltered as it was by an inner headland, making the
anchorage invisible from seaward. A resort nestled behind the beach, but it was so low-key that we only ever saw two guests.
There were only one or two locals living in the bay, one of whom insisted on heaping gifts of fruit on Laura. The only thing he
wanted in exchange was her promise to marry him. I never could understand why Laura was so much more successful in being
given fruit than me. This also applied when it came to getting lifts. On her walk across the island Laura had turned down lifts
from every vehicle that passed her. From this bay we undertook an epic walk with Pat across the headland to the next bay to
visit yet another tiki site. Olivia, wisely as it turned out, had elected to stay behind on the boat. In our enthusiasm to find it we
overshot our target and ended up miles out of our way, but in the process managed to see three more bays. The problem was
that the coast road was very open and we were fully exposed to the midday sun. Eventually I met a beer delivery truck coming
the other way. They told me I was all wrong and told me to get in. On the way back they picked up Pat and Helen and very

kindly took us right up to the tiki site, which turned out to be a very elaborate one. I blamed Pat for taking us so far in the
13

wrong direction and Pat and Helen blamed me - so much for loyalty.

The next day we motored 'Muna' round to the bay and returned to the Tiki site where an archaeologist was giving a very
interesting talk that answered a lot of the questions we had been asking about the Polynesian civilisation. We carried on our
anti-clockwise circumnavigation of Nuku Hiva, having a cracking sail round to Daniel's Bay where Daniels has been
entertaining yachties for the past 28 years. From there we had a fascinating walk through dense vegetation up to a waterfall.
We swam in the pool, having negotiated the path under several fallen boulders. The route up to the waterfall was littered with
overgrown pai pai's or platforms made of large boulders as evidence of what had once been a teeming metropolis. We
completed our circumnavigation of the island by returning to Taiohae Bay from where we sailed 25 miles to the island of Ua
Pou, anchoring behind the breakwater in the main harbour in Baie D'Hakahau. This was another lovely island with an
incredible skyline. The phallus shaped peaks only rarely appeared from behind the clouds. It was here that Laura left us
temporarily. Henry on Maritime Express' a Canadian yacht had broken his wrist while climbing to the waterfall in Daniel's
Bay. He had had to have pins put in and was therefore somewhat disadvantaged. Laura offered to help out. Our time in this
anchorage was enlivened by the fact that the local boat club had a team entered in the Round Moorea outrigger canoe race, due
to take place in Tahiti in July. This was a six-man event but for the marathon 80 km race, each canoe has a support boat with a
relief crew. Once the race has got under way the crews can change as often as they like. We watched the Ua Pou team
practising this changeover. The support boat would drop the relief crew in line in front of the canoe. The canoe would then go
alongside the six in the water so they were between the canoe and the outrigger. The ones in the canoe would then leap out the
other side, while the new crew clambered in. The Sunday before we moved on, the boat club put one traditional pig roast,
which turned out to be a very sociable occasion and an opportunity to experience traditional Polynesian food.

Part Thirty Seven - Marquesas to the Tuamotus

We now had 500 miles to cover to reach the Tuamotus. This was the first significant passage that Helen and I had been on on
our own for some time. We set off with 'Aldebaran' and rounded the island. As we passed a bay further round we were joined
by 'Cap d'Or' and 'Silver Fin’. So it was that four of the five boat that had set off from Los Perles together, were reunited. it
was very pleasant on these passages to be able to communicate with other boats via the radio. Once out of VHF range, we
normally set up a schedule for an informal 'net' on the SSB. After a quiet start the wind built up enough to give us good
progress and pleasant sailing. We settled down to a comfortable beam reach as we were now heading almost south westerly.
The second day out we were startled to see what we reckoned to be a sperm whale a good 45' long, placidly swimming
alongside us no more than 100' away, blowing merrily. Fascinating though it was, it was quite a relief when it decided to leave
us. The first two or three days were generally fairly pleasant. On the fourth day when we had been out of 3 nights, the winds
went light onus. We drifted along all day with just a couple of brief squalls to liven things up. By this time 'Cap d'Or' and
‘Aldebaran' were far enough ahead to press on for landfall that day. 'Silver Fin' and ourselves were committed to another night
at sea. The Tuamotus are not a place you would choose to arrive at night. That day there were rather ominous reports of bad
weather on the French Polynesian forecast. After nightfall there was still very little wind. About 10 o'clock the little wind
there was died away completely. I reluctantly started the engine as the motion was so uncomfortable. Within minutes we had,
out of nowhere, 35 knots of wind well ahead of the beam. This was to continue, slightly abated, all night and all the next day.
After wallowing about with all sail up we set off like a scalded cat. Initially thinking it was just another short-lived squall I
hung on to full sail for a while. The auto helm which, up to then, had been doing the steering on this trip, was overwhelmed so
we were now committed to hand steering. As the night wore on I put first one, then two reefs in the main. With the headsails
partially furled we found that, left to her own devices, 'Muna' could steer herself. This is the sort of weather when we are
really grateful for 'Muna's' weight and full-bodied design and we had a remarkably comfortable night, all things considered.

As it got light I realised that at our current rate of progress we would have a job reaching our destination by nightfall. I
therefore reassessed the rig, put up more sail and started hand steering. We started powering along at 6-7 knots through large
seas, just holding our course. It turned out to be a cracking sail and after minimal sleep overnight I really began to enjoy
myself. By cracking on we reached the pass at Makemo at dead slack water and had a tranquil passage through, in contrast to
‘Cap d'Or' and 'Aldebaran' who had had quite a bash the day before, entering on the ebb. Once through the pass we headed
across the lagoon to an anchorage on the far side. The water in the lagoon was surprisingly rough and we had to be on the alert
for isolated coral heads that rose vertically from the 20-30 metre depths. All the atolls in the Tuamotus are basically reef-lined
lagoons with small islands, or Motus , scattered about the reefs. These atolls were originally volcanic islands that attracted a
fringe of coral reefs. The islands eroded away leaving the coral reef behind.
to be continued Malcolm Shaft

Club Notes

Commodores notes. On behalf of all those who attended the Laying Up Supper, I would like to thank Fenella for
organising a splendid evening in a pleasant location; also the other members of the Club who undertook various
functions on the night. I would like to thank the Club and Mavis Weedon for the bouquet of flowers presented to
my wife; without her patience and support the job of Commodore would be far more onerous.
The Committee and I have been supported by many other members without whose help the Club cannot function.
In saying Thank You to them on your behalf, I would like to include the many other partners who tolerate the time
that we devote to running the Club.
Finally, thanks to all those who come to the Club and enjoy its facilities and the sailing. Without you the
Blackwater would lose its friendliest and most diverse club.

As some of you may be aware, a suggestion was put forward that there should be some method by which members
who were Time but not Cash restrained could make some form of payment in lieu of helping at working parties or
in other ways. Earlier this year the Committee asked Clive Shenton and Steve Glynn to explore the possibility and
present a proposal to it for consideration. At the last Committee meeting, Clive reported that whilst the idea had a
number of benefits to members and the Club, they could not devise a simple and practical method of implementing
such a scheme. As a result the Committee has had to abandon the idea for the foreseeable future.

We are still looking for someone to join David Thomas on the MASC Main Committee. As many of you are aware
the members of the MASC own the Sailing Club site, it is the only asset that they own. It is therefore very much in
our interests to ensure that the MASC is well managed and run to ensure that we can continue to enjoy the use of
the site. This extends beyond simply paying our fees etc to the MASC to include being actively involved in its
management. Any member of the MASC can serve on its Main Committee and I am sure that there must be
someone in the Club not actively involved in its management/running at present who can help David one, or very
occasionally two evenings, a month to look after our interests. Please do not assume that someone else has stepped
forward but contact myself, any other member of the Committee or David if you can spare the time.

On the basis that this issue will not hit the doormats before the New Year, I would like to thank all who came to the
Hedging and Ditching party on Sunday 29" December 2002.

Only three more months before we start to go sailing again.

Neil Pembleton

and trailers in the cat field.

Cruiser AGM held on Thursday 21 November, 2002 with 46 members attending.

1. Apologies for absence were received from Chris Davies, John Easton, Carole Clark, Danny Ainge, Peter Clayton
Derek Hall, Mike Smith and Dave Onions.

2. Sailing Programme 2002. Burnham 1* June with 16 boats and 36 for a meal. Brightlingsea 22TM June with 16
boats. Ramsgate 27" July 7 boats, Shotley 21 boats with 40 sitting down for a meal. 21 September Watercress
(Heybridge Basin) 18 boats followed by barbeque.

3. Review of Racing and Prize Giving, Frank Burgess. Medusa wind died and Killara was the only boat to finish.
Mike Turner (navigator tactician) had lot of success on Forza. Roy Hardwick represented the cruiser fleet in
helmsman of the year. John Easton won the Brown Cup in BJRC.

Thanks to Dave Payne for results, Derek Gardiner for rep BJRC and Murray Bates for engraving trophies. Dave
Williams for co-ordinating starts.
Full results were published in the previous Navigans.
Next year the intention is to run the same series. The Upriver race will run in conjunction with the Jackpot trophy
dinghy race. There will also be a single handed race down river.

4. Election of Fleet Captain, Vice and Officers. Roger Camp, John Walker and Frank Burgess were re elected.

5. Winter Storage and Cruiser Park. This year we had 37 boats coming out on the travel hoist as opposed to 29 last
year. We have 26 boats stored in the cat field, 18 on the old ditch, 35 in row A and 30 in row B with 4 large boats
at the end of the park and a few odd ones scattered about giving a total of 119 laid up at the club. With the
increasing number of boats using the travel hoist and the decreasing number of boats on trailers, we are going to
have to start utilising the main body of the cruiser park for travel hoist boat storage. This year we have used the old
ditch area to store boats off the travel hoist but there is limited room for manoeuvring. One possibility will be to
use the ditch area for trailer boats up to 26 foot. We could probably get 24 trailer boats in the ditch area. Row A
for the big boats, pretty much as it is now, and row B would progressively get taken over by travel hoist boats. The
logical time to start this programme would be towards the end of May when the cruiser park will have to be
emptied to allow the electrical contractors access. The final decision will not be made until the spring so if anyone
has any comments, suggestions or ideas do not hesitate to contact me.

The modifications to the cruiser park will include 18 new power points down the centre of the cruiser park and
along both sides of the hedge. In theory no one should be more than 30 foot from a power point. These will be the
marina type posts with 4 sockets on each. The water taps in the ditch area will be moved back against the hedge
and replacement services will be run down to the race box and a layer of crushed concrete on the ditch area.

6. Tractors and Haul Out. All went well. Thanks to Murray and his crew for maintaining the equipment in such
good order. Any breakdowns were repaired within a few days.

7. Moorings. There have been no breakaways this year. Ted Barnes will be checking all the drying moorings to see
that they conform to the club guidelines, just as deep water moorings are checked prior to laying. This examination
will take place in May. Please contact Ted for any advice or queries on drying moorings.

8. Chain. Don has chain. The price goes up in January but Don still has some at the old price.

9. Paint and Anti Fouling, Gordon Preston. Discount is the same as last year with some changes. See Navigans for
details. Date for orders to be in is 10" Jan. Delivery date in early March.

10. Next Season Cruising Programme and winter meetings. On 23TM January the Port of London Authority Harbour
Master will give a talk on the tidal Thames. On 20" February Icom will give a talk about DSC Radio and on 20"
March there will be a light hearted quiz as last year.
10 May the Cruiser Fitting out supper will be held at the Sailing Club. 24" May, a Bank holiday cruise to
Burnham with a meal at the Swallowtail. 14" to 15" June there will be a trip to Brightlingsea. 6" July ECPR. Neil
on behalf of Chris Davies thanked everyone for last year and hopes for support this year. 12" July Watercress Run
to Heybridge, followed by barbeque. 2" August for one week, cruiser to St Katherine’s and Medway. 23" August,
Bank Holiday cruise up the East Coast. There was a discussion on Shotley versus Ipswich.

11. Cock Up Trophy. There were various contenders but the winner couldn’t have made a more public cock up, his
crew mutinied and the resulting spectacle was widely discussed in the yachting press.

12. Mooring Parties. Thanks to Derek and Doreen for providing hot drinks and snacks for the mooring teams.

13. Any Other Business. Victory Marina in the Medway was recommended as a possible club stop over. Colin
Leveridge proposed thanks for the tractor and winch teams. Malcolm Yeoman concerned about access road re
electrics. Dave Payne assured him it would be reinstated.

Neil, on behalf of the fleet, thanked Roger.
Meeting closed at 21.15.

If anybody has lost a set of tractor keys, please contact me. We still have a number of homeless dinghies to be
claimed behind the mast container. Please avoid driving in the cat field as it is very boggy at the moment. The
next event will be a talk by Gordon Dickens, Harbourmaster of the tidal Thames, on pleasure boating on the river
Thames from sea reach to Tower Bridge. This will be on Thursday 23" January at 19:30 at the MASC in Beehive
Lane.

I would like to wish everybody a merry Christmas and a happy New Year.

Roger Camp

Not much to report on the sailing front at this time of year. One or two members who cannot get enough of it, are
tackling Winter Series at other clubs, notably Kate and Dave Williams. I am told they are going great guns at
Maylandsea Bay.
Most of you will no doubt be servicing boats and equipment, and making your plans for next season. Good for you.
Much better than waiting till the last minute isn’t it!
The Club programme for 2003 is now finalised, and it will not be long before we can get started.
The Sailing Sub Committee continues to meet over the winter, with one or two new Fleet Captains emerging to add
new ideas and energy to the process.

There is now a new Medium Cat Fleet established which takes the place of the diminishing Dart 15 fleet, while still
offering D15 and others of the smaller sized catamarans in the Club, a fleet to race in. Joe Bird is the Fleet Captain
for the new fleet, so contact him if you need more details.

Last month I announced the Club’s intention to fund RYA First Aid training for support boat crews (drivers and
crew members). The take-up response to this offer has to date been disappointing, the training will only take one
day of your time and it is an opportunity for you to make a greater contribution to the Club’s overall competence
and well-being. Please let me know if you are prepared to take part in the training.
I hope you all enjoy your Christmas festivities, and that the New Year heralds some great sailing for all club
members.

Handicap Fleet

Many thanks to those members of the fleet who were able to make the AGM in December. A number of current
issues were brought up, most of which will be fed back to the Sailing Sub-Committee for consideration. The two
most important items were:

Social Events This is an area where other fleets definitely take the lead! We discussed organising fleet socials both
in and out of season, and you can look forward to barbecues and some fleet cruising during the summer (unless
anyone fancies a winter barbecue?). In the immediate future, open your diaries at Friday, 28" February for bowling
at the Chelmsford Super Bowl. I vaguely recollect challenging the Solo Fleet at bowling during a Sailing-Sub
meeting, and I reckon we should get some practice in! If you could let me know if you’re interested, and I will
make sure that we have enough lanes.

Dinghy Park A more serious matter needs all our input. The dinghy park now has a shiny new electricity cable
running a foot below the surface. As a result, we can NO LONGER USE 18” STAKES in the dinghy park as per
previous club rules. The club is proposing to use the more permanent anchors as used in the Cat Park. This means
that we need to develop a way of laying out the Dinghy Park more permanently. After discussing the issue at the

members tie their boats down to the secured chain, rather than using their own stakes. Barry is working on the
layout required in order to make this work, as once the chains are laid they will be hard to remove.

This ties in well with plans for a Fleet Working Party: laying out the Dinghy Park will require some help. We
would be very grateful if you could spare us a few hours on Sunday, 23" February, from 9.30 am, in order to

Club Notes

Commodore

THIS IS IMPORTANT — IT CONCERNS YOUR SUBSCRIPTIONS

Occasionally the Executive and Management Committees of the Sailing Club find themselves sitting on the ‘Horns
of a Dilemma’. This is just such a time and I need to explain the difficulties we are dealing with. This problem
concerns our relationship with Marconi Athletic and Social Club (MASC).

Firstly, we must recognise that, as a section of MASC we have an obligation to operate within that structure. We
also clearly have an obligation to do all that we can to protect the interests of our own members within the Sailing
Club. We now find that these twin requirements are in conflict.

Accounts published by MASC at the recent AGM in November 2002 showed that it incurred a trading loss in
2001/2002. Previous discussions and pronouncements had led us to understand that actions had been taken to
address the underlying problems; the new subscription structure and the new gym were intended to ensure that the
situation was reversed. It had been said that the deficit would be reduced and even suggested that a small profit
could be produced for 2002/2003. Clear indications now are that MASC will create an even larger trading loss in
that period and, more significantly, that the loss-making trend continues unchecked.

When we look back at the MASC Main Committee minutes for December 2002 (after the AGM) we find two items
that only serve to add to our concern:

I quote from the minutes:
"Financial Situation
Le The General Manager, after making Les Murray (MASC President) aware of the financial situation, has
set up a meeting with himself, President, Trustee and MASC Treasurer for Friday 1 3 December.
A committee member stated that it’s very clear that the income of the Club does not meet with expenditure
and that the Management must take steps to rectify this situation. Proposals to be presented.
Treasurers Report
ms The Treasurer presented the accounts for September, who pointed out the increasing trading deficit.
All areas of Club activities are down on previous years in particular catering which is now showing a
£5000.00 deficit.
There will be no further capital expenditure for the Club or Sections until the position improves."

Our discomfort arises from the fact that, as a Section of MASC, we are obliged to hold all our funds within MASC.
This means that the cash to meet our week by week expenses and the Reserve Fund which is used to cover our
major expenditure is with MASC; we are not allowed to have an independent bank account under the constitution
as it stands. Our Reserve Fund is projected to be £30000 at the end of the present financial year and a substantial
portion of that is earmarked for the major overhaul of the electricity system, which is ongoing. We need to be
satisfied that our funds are not threatened by the apparent financial weakness of our parent.

As soon as the above facts became clear to our Executive I was tasked with writing to the senior managers of
MASC to seek an explanation and assurance that matters were being properly dealt with. Informal discussions with
officers of MASC had not produced the answers we need. I wrote a letter to the MASC Trustee, President,
Chairman and General Manager on 28" January 2003. To date, and in spite of prompting, I have received neither
acknowledgement nor reply from any of these people.

The Executive Committee is clear in the view that, although we would not wish to do anything to harm MASC or
our relationship with them, our first duty is to protect as far as possible the interests of our own members. The
Management Committee fully supports this view and has decided that it will be sensible to stage Sailing Club
subscription payments for 2003. This approach will afford some measure of protection and underline our serious
concerns. We plan to collect half the subscription value at the normal time and the balance during June 2003.

Those members who have already sent a renewal payment to the Membership Secretary will have their cheques
returned with a request that they re-issue two cheques of equal value. One of these cheques should be post-dated

30" June 2003. Those who have yet to renew (and the normal deadline applies) should split their payments in the
same way.

We obviously regret the need for this sort of action and very much hope that we can quickly restore normal
relationships with MASC. We are confident, however, that members will support the view that this is a situation
that could not go unchallenged. This action is designed to be both protective and remedial; we will, however,
continue to review the situation and be prepared to act appropriately in the event that we do not receive the required
response from MASC.

Neil Pembleton

Ships Log

Woody and Frank, to the Caribbean.

For ‘Woody’ and I, our journey to the Caribbean started at 5am in a snowstorm on a dark M25, to Gatwick, to
catch a JMC Airbus A330 charter flight. 8 hours later we landed at Port Salines on Grenada, and on reaching the
open door of the plane we descended the steps in a blast of heat and bright sunshine.
Customs in Grenada are typical in taking their time with much questioning, and rubber-stamping of documents, but
we waited our turn, they let us in, so we left the airport building before they changed their mind, and found a
ramshackle taxi to Spice Island Marina, Prickly Bay.
Our boat for the holiday was ‘Essex Girl’ a C&C 30 built in Ontario Canada and owned by Graham from
Blackwater Sailing Club.
An evening meal in the marina restaurant followed by sleep, and on Sunday morning we motored round to ‘Hog
Island’ a sheltered anchorage favoured by ‘live aboards’. ‘Hog’ is famous for ‘Roger’s Rum Shack’ set amongst the
trees on a beach of white sand, and on Sundays there is always a barbecue, fortified by strong rum and cokes and
the local ‘Carib’ beer. Our friend ‘Thilo’ the Mad German joined us. Thilo lives aboard a 40ft Wharram catamaran
during long holidays from Cologne. I afraid we all got steadily merrier. Late that night we went to bed soon to be
awakened by a splash. ‘Woody’, sleeping in the cockpit had got up to take a leak and had fallen in! Graham and I
scrambled to the cockpit to find Woody appearing over the stern dripping but none the worse for his dip.
The Grenadines are split into different countries and so on Monday we called at Prickly Bay Customs to officially
book out. We then continued to St Georges the main town of Grenada to visit the supermarket, fill up with water
and diesel, and change some money at the Bank. The Grenadines currency is the Eastern Caribbean Dollar, which
is unobtainable in the UK so we took Sterling plus a small amount of US Dollars (which are accepted). A visit to
the market for fresh fruit and the Grenada Yacht Club for showers, then back to ‘Essex Girl’ for a short passage up
to ‘Halifax Bay’ where we anchored, dined, and watched the locals fishing, accompanied by a huge elegant yacht
with a paid crew waiting on the guests.

We left at 9am in the morning for a 6-hour beat North to Tyrell Bay on Carriacou passing over ‘Kick em Jenny’ the
site of a volcano. Tyrell is a good sheltered anchorage and features a mangrove swamp where we explored 2
abandoned yachts. Then we visited the Carriacou YC for showers and dinner. Woody found a cockroach in his
shower and chased it round the bathroom bashing it with a broom.
The next day we sailed round to ’Sandy Island’, about 100 yards long the archetypal island with azure blue water,
white sand, palm trees, and a reef for snorkelling. In the evening we were invited aboard a Sigma 41 from BSC
Maldon, which had completed the Atlantic Rally for Cruisers. That night it rained and ‘Woody’ was forced to leave
his cockpit berth and sleep with me!

Next day, up anchor, and off to Clifton Town on Union Island where you run the gauntlet of boat boys selling
moorings, fish, etc, to book in with Customs and Immigration for this group of islands, then over to Mayreau,
Saltwhistle Bay...more swimming and dinner under the moon.

Morning came, up anchor, and off to Tobago Cays, a paradise, of islands and reefs protecting the anchorage from
3000 miles of ocean. Woody and I paddled the dinghy onto the reef and tied it a mooring provided. Then over the
side for the best snorkelling ever. Evening came, a fish dinner, with the sound of the waves breaking on the reef,
the Trade winds blowing strongly, and Woody in the cockpit again, playing spinnakers with his bed sheet!
In the mooring we re-anchored in the lee of ‘Petit Bateau Island’ where passengers from the cruise liner ‘Club Med
2’ were landed for swimming. Woody found a lobster in the reef and set of in pursuit for our lunch.... After a lunch
of egg butties, we sailed North to Charles Bay, Canouan, the most northerly point of our cruise. More swimming,

and in the evening ashore, past an empty luxury hotel, and on to Annie’s the local bar. Here we met 2 guys from
Poole who had sailed across in their 29 ft Albin Ballad. We then drank too much and on returning to our now
deflated engine less dinghy we blagged a tow from the crew of a J boat Jeau d’Espirit, which had also done the
ARC.

We were a bit slow to get up in the morning........ but we upped anchor and sailed fast back to Union Island for
Customs check out, more shopping and a conch rota, a sort of curried pasty made from conch a huge welk, very
good!

Away from Union and over to Hillsborough town on Carriacou to clear in with Customs and Immigration for
Grenada. During the night Woody got rained out of the cockpit and morning found him asleep on the saloon floor.
Up anchor, then off to Petit Martinique, where skip served up mangos, followed by avocado, and tomato. Woody
and I went ashore and climbed the hill for a magnificent view of Tobago Cays Union, Canouan, Mayreau, and Petit
St Vincent and further North the distant St Vincent and Bequia. Woody comments in the log here that, ‘we were in
bed by 7.45pm ....’Essex Girl’ is becoming like an old peoples home!’

We left Petit Martinique early en route for Grenada, and sailing fast arrived off another Sandy Island, this one
being where the ‘Bounty’ adverts are filmed. However it was too dodgy to anchor, so we sailed on towards the NE
of Grenada. Ever since leaving Grenada, we had been towing a fishing lure with no luck, but suddenly the line was
running and the reel screeching. Skipper Graham grabbed the rod, yelled at us to; ‘stop the ****** boat and get the
gaff ..’ a lot of heaving and grunting and over the side came a beautiful Tuna. ‘Get the rum! What for?
...Give it a drink’, I shoved the bottle down it’s mouth....that’s how they do it....stuns the fish so you don’t have to
bash it with the winch handle! ......... Ok, calm down, get underway, ...half an hour later the reel’s going
again....more panic, more rum and this time it is a very big ‘King Fish’ nearly 4 ft long!

Well that was the end of fishing for that day and by evening we had entered Clarkes Court Bay on Grenada, and
anchored for the night off Woburn village. Graham called up ‘Little Dipper’ a Rasta restaurant...’Can you cook our
fish?...No problem man bring him along’. Suddenly there was ‘Thilo’...remember him? ....the Mad
German...’come and have dinner Thilo...OK Man’.
Now Thilo needed to go back over the reef to his Wharram, so we waited for him. Eventually he returned, with a
cut over his eye and a large bump on his head. ‘What happened to you?’ .......... *Well.... (in a German/South
African accent)...I missed my way in the dark...the engine hit the reef, and I fell over the bow and head butted the
TOOL
>Oh deary deary me’....we said... “you’d better have a drink!’
And so we went ashore, climbed the hill to Little Dipper and had the best meal of my life....for 3 quid!...then the
trouble started, because Woburn is noted for Nimrod’s Bar. Now old man Nimrod had died just 3 weeks before, but
his son had continued the tradition of serving yachtsmen. The bar is just a concrete shack, which sells groceries
rum and beer. Behind the bar there are several visitor books signed by a generation of yachtsmen from all over the
world. However you must ’cross the bridge’ which entails drinking a shot of 140% proof rum followed by a drink
of water. If you survive this you can continue with the other local customs, which I had better not mention here!

Next day we sailed round to Prickly Bay to anchor alongside ‘Jo’ a 26 year old from Norway. He had come via
Caledonian Canal, Belfast, Isle of Man and Cork in a 31 footer. I must admit to feeling somewhat humble, as this
quiet man casually mentioned the cockpit filling with water during the Atlantic crossing!

For our last day we visited St Georges for souvenirs, followed by beers in the Nutmeg restaurant on the harbour
side. We visited the Grenada YC on our return, and could not resist going over an old Westerly Conway for sale.
The rest of the day we pondered the pro’s and con’s of boat ownership in the West Indies, and for our last night at
the marina, we drank beer, listened to the Steel Band and the Reggae Band till 2 am, with Jo, and I think we invited
him to visit MSC, on his back to Norway.....I think.....you see, we were very tired, and very

Frank Burgess

BACSPA

Last December I attended a meeting of the BLACKWATER & COLNE SAILING PROTECTION ASSOCIATION and as on previous occasions I am reporting on matters raised which I feel may be of interest to you.

Under the Eastern Region RYA Committee Report, reference was made to the McKinsey RYA Organisation & Governance Recommendations which in essence proposes the streaminlining of the Council and that Regional Chairmen are always to be Council Members. It proposes changes to RYA Central Committee that include a general reduction in size and less frequent meetings. The Chairman of BACSPA is not convinced of the efficacy of this and fears it reduces the input of the Clubs and Members and strengthens that of the staff,and has written an appraisal expressing these concerns i.e. the idea that it is necessary to reduce the influence of the clubs on Council as against the personal membership seems to be based entirely on the perceived mismatch in numbers and hoped the Council will recognise the weaknesses in this report and the danger of creating a more centrist arrangement that does not make best use of the people with experience based in the Regions. Asked whether there would be any opportunity to object to the proposals,
the
Chairman answered no ! It was pointed out by me that people joined clubs so that their voices could be heard. Peter Woods BIRD Cruiser Group announced he had resigned from his post on the Cruising Committee in protest at these changes. No one at the meeting had seen a copy of the RYA Briefing. It was pointed out the RYA Eastern Newsletter was available on the Internet.

March is here already, and with it the start of the new sailing season. In case you have not noticed — Spring Points
racing starts on Sunday 23 March. I hope we can start with a good turn out from all fleets as a suitable reward for
all the work that has been put in by committee and working parties to enable this to happen. It may be tempting fate
to say it, but the weather is often excellent for the opening day.

After much deliberation, the plan for protection of the new electricity cables beneath the dinghy park has been
decided. This consists of paving over the cable routes to prevent inadvertent damage from dinghy securing stakes.
It is not anticipated that this will prevent any dinghies from being adequately secured, but care must be taken not to
move or damage any of the paving slabs after they have been put in place. Thanks are due to the anne Fleet
who have devised this plan and agreed to lead a working party to carry out the work.

I know that Barry Hutt is working on a new layout for the dinghy park, so when you bring your boats down to the
club at the start of the season, please be careful to comply with instructions for their location, to ensure that the new
layout is adopted with the minimum of hassle. If in doubt, consult with Barry.

It is quite a long time since the MSC Race Officers last got together to debate concerns and issues, and discuss
possible improvements to the way in which we run our races. For this reason Dave Williams has issued an
invitation to all R.O.s for a meeting at MASC, Beehive Lane, at 19.45 on Thurs 13 March. This type of event has
proved to be very useful, informative and good fun in the past, so I would like to encourage all R.O.s, assistant
R.O.s, and indeed anyone who is interested in the way that our racing is administered, to attend.

All the best for a great sailing season!

The Cirdan Sailing Trust was founded in 1983. Since that time we have taken over 16,000 young
people sailing on one of our four traditional sailing vessels operating from various ports around the
country.

The Trust works principally with groups of young people, upwards of 10 years old in particular those young people who are socially, mentally or physically disadvantaged. We aim to provide an opportunity for the groups to experience the adventure and challenge of life at sea by taking an active role in running and sailing the vessel. Few other environments can match a large sailing vessel for providing young people with the opportunity to develop life skills and stretch personal boundaries.

To assist with the fund raising activities for our Queen Galadriel Refit project Charles and Rupert Anderson have very kindly offered to run in The London Marathon on behalf of The Trust.

We would like to wish them both good luck and ask that you support our work through their endeavours on April 13 2003 and in turn, disadvantaged young people. Thank you.

Commodore

Over the winter period, a great deal of work has been carried out at Stansgate to maintain and improve the
Clubhouse and site.
This has included the installation of the new power cable to the Clubhouse and the provision of power sockets
around the exterior of the building. This left the problem of protecting it across the dinghy park at which moment
Claire Davies came forward with the idea of laying the slabs, much more cost effective than any ideas from the
Executive Committee and providing a permanent mark. The Handicap and Windsurfer Fleets then held their own
working party the week before the main one and carried out the work.
In the meantime David Payne decided that he and a small band of very willing helpers (he assures me although I
am told otherwise) decided to destroy the Galley and then rebuild it. As we can all see the result is a tremendous
improvement and we have been able to renew the necessary certificate from Maldon Council so that Belinda
Dowley and her team can continue to keep us fed and watered.
At this point Fenella Thomas decided that she would set about improving the saloon. From somewhere she found a
team to tackle the project. They stripped the area, prepared and washed all the walls before redecorating and
making new curtains.
Last Sunday, we were all able to see the results at the working party. This was one of the best attended that I have
seen for many a year. All the fleets were well represented and it was just as well that the Handicap and Windsurfers
had their go the week before. We could not have accommodated everyone in the Clubhouse. On a glorious day the
Cat Fleet set about a major clearance of the cat field, the Cruiser Fleet destroyed a few old trailers, the Solo Fleet
put the Race Box together along with moving all the outside furniture into position. In addition a wealth of other
tasks were completed.

While all this activity at Stansgate has been going on the Executive and Main Committee were debating the best
way to protect our members fees which we have to pay to the MASC. The response by you, the members, to our
request for you to send us two cheques has been overwhelming. We had anticipated that some members would
have considerable doubts and might not renew, in the event Nick and Jan had the major problem of emptying their
over full letter box each day and almost everyone had supplied the replacement cheques within ten days of the
letter going out.
As your Commodore, I feel very privileged to be a member of a Club which wholeheartedly supports its ethos of
self help and which has demonstrated such overwhelming support for the decisions taken by the Main Committee.
Given this support, I am convinced that we will weather the current problems at the MASC and that the Club will
continue to flourish and grow into the future.
Finally the time is rapidly approaching to dig out those sailing clothes and get back on the water. I hope that we all
have a successful and enjoyable season.

THANKS TO YOU ALL
This list does not pretend to include everyone who has put time in at the Club over the winter but I would
particularly like to thank those who worked on the Galley, Saloon and Dinghy Park which included:
Jenny Ball, Jenny Miller, Nick Miller, Michael Miller, Malcolm Thomas, Les Hurrell-Smith, Dave Williams, Kate
Williams, Dave Steward, John Weedon, Glenis Monks, Steve Monks, Steve Ash, Christina Hutt, Belinda Dowley,

Membership Registrars Annual Report

In December 2002, 388 membership forms were produced via a report and sent out to members.

As of this date (14/3/2003) we have 340 members who have renewed with 12 of those still owing the two cheques
as requested in the Commodores letter dated 15 Feb 2003. In general, members response to that letter was very
positive and on behalf of the Commodore and the Main Committee I would like to thank you all.

We now have the e-mail addresses of 144 members, more than 40% of the total membership.

There are currently 48 members from last year who have not renewed. I will be writing to these ex-members.

Last year we were new to the process and were a little flexible over the renewal closing date as stated in rule 8e.
We had intended to stick rigidly to the rules this year but the late changes to the payment requirements meant that it
made sense to be flexible. Several letters have now been sent to members who have not come back with the two
cheques.

One issue that I would like to remind members of is the requirement to keep us up to date with address and boat
details. Several membership forms went to the wrong address and some members only notified us of additional or
changed boat details that had occurred during the previous year on their renewal forms. Renewal forms were
therefore produced with the wrong information that caused extra work in levying the adjusted fees.

We will try again next year to apply the rules as they are stated in the yearbook. Thus far I can only offer thanks to
late paying members for adding to club funds but no thanks for extending an already lengthy task for Jan and I.

If any member has any problems with their membership pack please do not hesitate to contact me.

Handicap Fleet News

At last, the sailing season is here! Those you who have been down to the club to deposit or move your boats will
have noticed some major changes on the site, not least the lovely new terrace across the dinghy park...

First and foremost, many, many thanks to those handicap and windsurf fleet members who joined us for the
working party to lay the slabs — I’ve never seen a job completed so quickly. We had a good day for it, and a chain
was quickly established, with diggers, slab-layers, slab-movers and cement-mixers all working together along the
line to get the job done.

For those who are wondering what I’m talking about, I wrote in the January Navigans about the need to protect an
electric cable that has been laid beneath the dinghy park. After much deliberation and tapping of calculators, it was
agreed that the earlier plan involving ground anchors and chains was too costly, and so a permanent and solid
protection has been laid above the cable to prevent the possibility of striking it with a metal boat stake. There
remains a stretch to be covered beyond the boundary of the dinghy park, but we have for now made the park safe.

You will also find that the layout of the dinghy park has altered somewhat. Essentially the boat spaces have been
turned through 90°, creating some 40 additional spaces. The various sizes of space will be clearly marked on the
plan in the clubhouse. Please ensure that you park your boat in a space of an appropriate size. Don’t forget your 18”
stakes, to mark your name on the plan, and to ensure that your boat is properly marked with your name, contact
number and year sticker. The park has been mowed in preparation, but please do look after your space as the season
progresses.

booked and cleaning rotas will have been finalised. All of this activity is in the hands of various club officers - but
none of them are campers.

We need a couple of volunteers to share OOD-type responsibility for the on-shore aspects of the fortnight. They
would need to take responsibility for knowing who should be doing what and when they should be doing it — and
then have the information to enable them to co-ordinate a proper response if things do not go quite according to
plan. We are quite definitely not looking for someone to undertake cleaning or bar work or rubbish removal - just
someone with the means and the will to make sure those things happen as they should.

I don't expect to hear from anyone who is heavily involved with Cadet Week and it might not be reasonable to rope
in a member who already has extensive responsibilities elsewhere within the club ... but that does actually leave us
with quite a few suitable candidates.

Please think seriously about taking on an important role in support of an important event in our calendar. You can
make a significant contribution to the success of the event without seriously affecting your own involvement or
enjoyment - job sharing and mobile phones should minimise any potential inconvenience.

Please call for an informal chat about this exciting opportunity (without obligation).

East Coast Piers Race — The Charity Angle

Elsewhere in this issue you will find an appeal for help in running ECPR 2003 and we are all keenly aware of the
valuable charity support that the Club creates through this event.

With impeccable timing Cirdan Sailing Trust have recently written to our Commodore a fulsome letter of thanks
for our £6500 support in 2002. The detailed information contained with that letter comprehensively underlines the
value of what we are doing in supporting such a cause.

The breakdown of bursaries provided through ECPR donations last year reveals that our funding helped to provide
sailing adventure experience for:

Eleven young Kent people with severe learning difficulties
Twelve 18-24 year old long-term unemployed people from NE England
Twelve local youngsters from a Maldon church group dealing with low income families
A group of 12 students from a Midlands college specialising in the education of disaffected young people
A 12 strong team from a Lancashire inner-city youth group
Another 12 youngsters from inner-city Newcastle, as part of an ‘Excellence in Cities’ programme.
12 young people from deprived wards in South Tyneside
A group of 15 youngsters based in Southend, most of whom have experienced homelessness and are care
- leavers.

All of this detail is accompanied by a fascinating collection of logs and notes that clearly illustrate the enjoyment
and challenge to which we have contributed and, perhaps, hint at some far deeper changes too. Watch out for a
display of all this material in the clubhouse — or have a look at the Marconi ECPR website where we will shortly
display a selection of the material.

Thank you for your ongoing support.

Chris Davies
Chair ECPR Committee

ECPR - A call for support — 5" /6" July

Last year
Once again, we are at the point when we galvanise support for the Piers Race weekend. Chris Davis is in the chair
again ably assisted by the Piers Race Committee.

The Race
The race, a long distance catamaran event starting from Osea Pier and sailing to Walton-on-the-Naze Pier
and then back, is once again expected to attract top catamaran sailors from across Britain and Europe.
This year the race will be started by Reg White OBE, Tornado Olympic Gold medallist.

The Charity
Possibly one of the most significant differences the Piers Race has over other sailing events, is the generation of
funds for our own locally based sailing charity “The Cirdan Trust”. You may be familiar with their Thames Barge
‘Xylonite’ which operates out of the Blackwater for most of the season. In addition, their other boats include the
Robert Clark designed ‘Hartlepool Renaissance’, a classic Edwardian yacht called ‘Duet’ and The Queen Galadriel
a fine old Baltic Trader. While Maldon remains their base, they ply the waters of the north east/Scotland, the south
coast and the south west/Channel Islands and Scilly Isles respectably.

The Cirdan Sailing Trust provides sailing breaks for the disabled, disadvantaged as well as their helpers (not
necessarily together). The money we raise goes towards bursaries which help those less able to pay make use of the
charity’s services. You may recall some of the letters of appreciation published in a previous edition of Navigans
and the impact of what we were able to do for some of the youngsters involved.

While in previous years we have supported the RNLI, Sailability (the RYA charity for disabled sailors) we have
provided over £70,000 for charities in total. No mean feat for a sailing club and something we all should be proud
of.

Backbone
Again as usual, a copy of the weekend’s questionnaire is in this issue; please don’t forget that if you do respond,
your offer will be taken up so keep an eye on Navigans news about the weekend and definitely please do turn
up at the weekend.
For cruiser owners, we will continue to use MII/ch80 for routine comms although we can accommodate those of
you still on MI. If you do have a cruiser and would like to do a bit more with the weekend I would love to hear
from you.

While cruisers provide the backbone for the weekend’s support we always need additional help with running the
bar, reception, runners, spotters, trolleys, rescue crews and so on.

There is input from across the club so don’t feel bashful about lending a hand.

Special race with special support

We are all justifiably proud of the contribution we make to Cirdan and as mentioned, it is unique in the sailing
world. Other long distance events have sprung up since MSC established the Piers Race 17 years ago but we
remain the only one with the charity link as well as establishing standards that other events wish to emulate. We
have made a big difference to disabled sailors over the years and we really appreciate the help and support we
receive from you all.

Once again I thank all of you who have helped in the past and my deepest gratitude goes out to those able to make a
contribution this year.

Charles Anderson

Hello again........ in this issue of the newsletter you will find the new 2003 Programme of Cruiser Racing Events
listing both M.S.C and B.J.R.C. As always if you fancy a try and have questions, then call me, Frank Burgess for

mind, i.e., down river in open water with minimal marks.

Steady Guys...... It won’t be long now...you’ll soon be on the water!

Solo Matters

Dear All, Roger has submitted a brief write up of the evening down at the clubhouse over the 5" and 6" of April as
follows:

“We had a good thrash on Saturday (well for us oldies anyway!) - The new Clubhouse decor was much appreciated
by all and Belinda's food was superb. The home made Black Forest Gateaux was even better (but we would say that
- don't tell Belinda!). Dennis and Tim thought of new ways to humiliate us all, ranging from quizzes to football

penalty shoot outs and miming to the Rolling Stones. The fancy dress was very good with Diane and Jack
Rusbridge as clear winners with the hippie ban the bomb theme.

Thanks Rog.”

I'm sure you all know by now that we have an Open meeting on the Sunday Ist of June. There's no such thing as
bad publicity however, so here it is again! Last year's event was very successful with a high turnout from our own
fleet and a good number of visitors from a variety of clubs. This was due in large part to all the hard work behind
the scenes put in by a small (but perfectly formed) group of our guy's efforts.

This year we have taken stock of last year's strengths and weaknesses and hope in tum to improve an already
excellent weekend's sailing. So what do we have planned for you?

We kick off with Saturday morning with a training day starting at around 11.00am with rescue cover and we will
be organising short course racing etc. as we have done before. This is a good limber up for the Sunday,
unfortunately I need about a week of this to do any good but there you are!

Saturday evening we can light the barbeque and maybe even to cook something on it! Bring along your favourite
cuts and char them to a cinder in the traditional fashion. Or join me down at the local for some decent cooking...

Sunday morning our core team of organisers will be around from 8.30 or so. If you are sailing, as most of you
wall want to be, then it will be worth getting there in good time say 09.00, a) to grab one of Belinda's now
legendary bacon rolls and b) to be around to welcome and assist any of the huge number of visiting competitors
we are expecting to turn up. The rest of the day will follow the usual formula. See Poster in this issue for your
information.

Finally, Please ask not what your club can do for you but rather what can you do for your club!
e If you are not sailing but would be willing to make your vessel available to another please contact me so
we can start matching people to craft.
e Ifyou don't have a Solo but would like to join the training or the open or both then please contact me and
we will try to find a boat for you. (Don't worry about not being a member of the Class Assoc. it just means
that your first place position can't be counted, shame!)
e We need some helpers on the hard to man handle and marshal trolleys etc. and assist the O.0.D. with
looking after any retirees etc. during the day.

I look forward to seeing you, please support if you can as we are trying hard to make this year’s event a memorable
one. If you want any further information please get in touch and I will try to help.

Best Regards and best of luck on the day.
Ian Rawley (Solo Fleet Captain)

WIN A WILDWIND SAILING HOLIDAY IN ECPR SUPER RAFFLE.

Enclosed with this issue of Navigans are two books of tickets for an exciting new, enlarged ECPR Raffle. First
Prize is a holiday for two with Wildwind at their Mediterranean base. Second Prize winner will enjoy a two night
Getaway Break in a Best Western hotel of their choice and the Third Prize winner can stay at home and view their
brand new DVD player. There will be the usual extensive list of further quality prizes available ranging from
designer label clothing to supermarket label wine; all prizes have been donated by sponsors (listed in the
programme), whose support we gratefully acknowledge.

All proceeds will go to the charity supported by East Coast Piers Race — the Cirdan Trust. Cirdan provides sailing
adventure breaks and holidays for disadvantaged young people aboard their small fleet of traditional sailing craft —
Xylonite, Queen Galadriel, Duet and Hartlepool Renaissance. Last year’s ECPR donation of £6500 provided
bursaries for 101 young people in 8 separate groups. Watch out for the display in the clubhouse of reports and
letters of thanks from the participants.

Tickets are £1 each - £5 per book. Two books are enclosed and tickets can be sold to members or non-members.

Caister Lifeboat Appeal

Caister Lifeboat Station in Norfolk, which has run as an independent rescue service since the RNLI closed it in
1969, is appealing for funds to replace their old boat. Overhauling their existing boat could cost up to £200,000 so
they are aiming instead to buy a Dutch Valentihn class vessel which uses steer able water jets instead of propellers
and rudders. The design is ideal for use amongst the sandbanks. More details on their Website if you Search for
Caister Lifeboat, and donations can be sent to: Treasurer, Caister Lifeboat Appeal, The Lifeboat Station, Tan Lane

Caister on Sea, Norfolk, NR30 5DJ.

Tail-Piece

The racing season has started with some beautiful sailing days of sunshine and moderate breezes. Just the thing for
easing ourselves back into the sailing activity, without it becoming too much of a shock to the system. It has been
very encouraging to see that most fleet turn-outs have been good, and no doubt this will improve further as we get
into the warmer weather.

The cruiser moorings teams have been doing their usual efficient job, and most are now laid, so from now on there
will be many cruiser launches to manage and the Club will soon be back in its summer operating mode. Remember
to give launching operations as much room as possible and keep clear unless you are directly involved, in order to
make these operations as safe as possible for everyone.

Our first Open Meeting of the season has already been successfully completed — the 2 day Dart 15 Open which
drew about 15 competitors. Excellent sailing conditions made this an enjoyable event, and thanks are due to the
many that supported it by efficiently performing various duties. Unfortunately the home club did not provide the
winner — but perhaps next year ... ..!

One of the support boats used extensively during the Open, was the Orkney, which is a very useful general purpose
craft, also used frequently by the windsurfing community. I still need someone to take over the job of bosun for this
boat from Tim Sweet, and this is now a matter of some urgency, so please consider again whether you could
contribute to the Club’s well-being in this way, and let me know if you can. The job does not require specialist
knowledge or skills beyond those of a general handyman.

You will have been reading about the turmoil and uncertainties surrounding the future of the Club elsewhere in this
issue, and with all that going on it has been difficult to even think about sailing related matters. However, I have
been most impressed by the energy and determination with which your Executive Team and its co-opted “Lifeboat
Committee” experts has gone about the difficult task of attempting to protect the future of our Club, and hope that
in the next few weeks a successful outcome can be reported.

John Salmon
Rear Commodore

Club Notes

Commodore

By now, you will have received the letter from Nik Beavins asking you to apply to join Thirslet Sailing Club.
Please send these into him as soon as possible so that we do not have any delay in purchasing the site.
Before we hold the AGM in November we still have to complete the purchase of the site, the writing of the bye
laws and define the sub committee structure; and these are just some of the more important tasks.

Looking towards the future, acquiring the site and creating the company, will have an effect on the way that we
operate. Whilst we will no longer have to seek MASC approval for our spending plans, we will need to plan much
further into the future. I would suggest that in the area of capital spend such as expansion of the clubhouse,
replacement of boats, tractors and other major items, we will need to create and update a rolling twenty year plan.
We will need this both to ensure that the Treasurer can have the money available and that we do not build
something one day only to need to knock it down a couple of years later. Our new freedom may also mean that we
will qualify more easily for grants to assist us with major projects.

Two areas where the Committee would like help in this new era are people with the skills or contacts who can help
publicise the Club and locate grant money.
Obviously it is essential that the Committee concentrates on getting the new structures and the basic planning in
place so that we can continue the development of the Club into the future.
In my opinion it is essential that we continue to develop the Club and the site. This can only be successful with the
backing of all the members and by evolution not revolution.

Neil Pembleton
