Bilge Water Alarm

Many Cruisers do not have automatic bilge water pumps fitted. Why not fit an automatic bilge water alarm, using
an inexpensive home smoke detector.

Use a “DICON” (Wickes) smoke alarm with internal metal sensor enclosure, solder a 2 core flexible cord to the test
arm/contact and sensor enclosure with a T.V. co-axial plug at the bilge water end. The alarm sounds when the bilge
water bridges the plug contacts.

Sometime a “wet” boat can upset the electronics after a seasons use. Simply remove and put the detector in the
airing cupboard for a couple of days.

This same smoke detector can also be used for a simple intruder alarm using a two part magnetic reed contact
fixed to the hatch cover with a concealed “Off” switch/latching relay in series.

"Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Seven - Marquesas to the Tuamotus continued....
“

The Tuamotus. Arriving at the anchorage on the far side of the lagoon we were sheltered by the reef and a beautiful little
desert island. We were reunited with several boats that we had met on the way, including "Maritime Express' with Laura on
board. In accounts that I'd read of round-the-world rallies I'd always been amused by the idea of a floating village moving on
from one place to another. Even through we were travelling independently, the same thing seemed to be happening to us.
Every place we arrived at we seemed to know large proportion of the boats there. As new boats arrived they would
invariably be ones we already knew. It shouldn't have been surprising really. On a trade wind route, nearly everyone was
heading west within a seasonal time frame and there were only so many route options to choose from. This was certainly a
lovely place to stop. We had impromptu barbecues and sing-songs under the palm trees of the tiny island or moth. After a few
days of peace and tranquility we moved back across the lagoon to the village by the pass. At least we did once we had got our
anchor up. Nearly every boat that left the anchorage had had a fouled anchor and we were no exception. Richard from 'Fair
Hippolyta' came over and, with the snorkel, directed us around the coral heads that we were neatly wrapped around. This was
to prove to be a feature of the Tuamotus. Although we experienced some beautiful anchorages, none of them was free of coral
and some were almost entirely coral.

The village of Pouheva was a strange mixture of impressive buildings like a town hall, two churches, several shops and a
collection of simple houses. One of the shops was staffed by three transvestites, who were obviously very proud of their dress
sense. One was doing a passable impression of Tina Turner while the other posed over the freezer cabinet. When the third
particularly masculine one appeared, complete with cigarette hanging out of mouth, sweeping up, it was like something out of
an old 'Queen' video. We had already noticed in French Polynesia a particularly liberal attitude towards sexual diversity. The
local papers regularly featured mahu or raerae (transvestite)-of-the-year competitions. From Pouheva we motored in company
with 'Aldebaran' and 'Cap d'Or' along the lagoon. The lagoon was generally at least 20 metres deep but was dotted with near
vertical coral heads that stopped either just below or just above the surface. Depending on the light conditions, they were not
always easy to spot and it could get quite tiring hanging over the bow peering at the water, or so Helen kept telling me. By
going as a group we were able to take turns as lead boat which made the whole operation a lot pleasanter. We headed towards
an idyllic, almost coral-free, anchorage half way up the atoll. Sheltered from the prevailing winds by a heavily wooded moth
we were just off a deserted white sandy beach. Traversing the narrow moth to the ocean side proved to be an adventure in
itself so thick was the vegetation. The contrast between the ocean and lagoon side was amazing. It was hard to believe they
were only a few hundred yards apart. The lee shore proved to be a treasure trove. Between us we found anchor buoys, a
snorkel, one fin, and a wetsuit in excellent condition that later proved to fit Laura perfectly.

Moving on to Passe Tapuhiria, the western pass of Makemo, we anchored off the abandoned village. This was another place
where avoiding coral was virtually impossible. Our anchor ended up lodged over the edge of a coral bank. It held, but made
for an anxious night when the wind blew up. At least Helen told me it made for an anxious night, I managed to sleep through
it as I often did. In the morning the wind had come round, making the anchorage a rather uncomfortable lee shore. The lagoon
was So wide that quite a sizeable sea could build up within it. Our anchor came up alright but 'Aldebaran' had quite a struggle
with theirs. Once clear of the pass we hoisted sail and had quite a pleasant run until the evening when the wind went very light
and fickle. It eventually picked up overnight and we had a good sail, arriving off the eastern pass at Fakerava in the morning.
Anchoring just inside the pass once again, we met up with several boats that we knew, including Jim and Jo the Australian
couple on 'Atlas', a Nordhaven 65 Trawler Yacht, who had been so helpful in getting the water pump for the engine. They
hosted a party that night for everyone in the anchorage. Before that we went ashore to a small Pension run for the past 18
years by a Tahitian called Manahee. Basically a collection of straw huts that he had built himself on what was little more than
a sand bank, it was in idyllic situation. Under the guidance of his partner Tilla, we had a go at weaving palm leaves. A couple
of days later we returned and Pat and I helped Manahee roof one of his new huts.

The main island next to the pass had been inhabited until the early 20th century when the entire population had left. In the last
few years a hotel consisting of huts right on the water's edge has developed and a few people have moved back into the village.
It was fascinating walking round the remains of the old school. We did a drift snorkel with Pat and Olivia through the pass on
the incoming tide. It was an incredible experience floating by the almost sheer side to the pass. As we drifted we saw sharks
and an amazing creature that turned out to be a Napoleon fish. As we passed the hotel we gained speed and literally shot by
the fish traps that lay to the side of the channel. We took the dinghy across the entrance where there were a whole series of
uninhabited motus. On one of these we discovered a collection of human skulls. We met a young Italian couple that had been
dropped off on one of the motus for the morning as part of the 'Desert Island' experience. By now we were getting to the time
when we needed to get to Tahiti to renew our 3-month visas. This had to be done a month before their expiry. The problem
was that we had had several days with little or no wind. We decided to do the short trip across to the smaller atoll of Faaite.
After extricating our anchor with some difficulty we motored the 12 miles across to Passe Teporiaha in Faaite.

We entered on the ebb and had quite a struggle overcoming the current in the narrow channel. Eventually we managed it, but
finding the anchorage behind the pass proved difficult. 'Aldebaran', who was ahead of us, ran firmly aground on the coral,.
Luckily it was calm but Pat had to launch his dinghy to push 'Aldebaran' off. With no boats in the anchorage and no locals to
ask, we finally gave up and headed back out of the pass to start the 250 mile trip to Tahiti. Stopping outside long enough to get
our dinghies on deck and after Pat passed over some Tuna that a charter skipper had given us the night before, we motored off
long enough to get clear of the island. Determined not to motor all night we waited until there was just enough wind to fill the
sails and turned the engine off. Pat elected to motor on in the hope of keeping the trip down to two nights. We sailed on at a

stately one knot, which increased slowly overnight. By morning the wind had increased to 9 or 10 knots giving us 4 knots in
the calm sea. Later that day we were talking to 'Aldebaran' on the radio when it transpired that 'Cap d'Or' and 'Green Ghost' a
Canadian boat we had also got to know, had both left Fakarava that morning. 'Fair Hippolyta' left Tahanea that evening and
we had another informal net again with 3 of the 4 boats we had left the Los Island with.

The next day the winds were even lighter but with the spinoa up we managed to make reasonable progress. That evening just
after we'd taken the spinoa down the wind got up. Progress was good until just after midnight when the wind died away
completely. We resorted to the engine. Unfortunately at about the same time the autohelm played up. We carried two rams
but the other one had already given up on the way to the Marquesas so we were now committed to hand steering under engine.
By the morning what little wind there was died away completely and we decided to keep motoring rather than spend yet
another night at sea. At least it was a flat calm.

From dawn we could see the twin islands of Tahiti. It was hard to believe that we were actually there. This was an island that
we had been aware of for as long as we could remember. Beyond it we could already see the dramatic outline of Moorea.
After an overcast, wet night and morning, the skies cleared and we arrived in Tahiti in blazing sunshine. Arriving at the pass
off Papeete we called up Harbour Control who answered immediately and gave us clearance to enter. Having passed inside the
reef we turned away from the main harbour and followed the channel for several miles inside the reef, to the extensive
anchorage off Maeve Beach where we anchored near ‘Maritime Express' and 'Aldebaran’.

‘Muna's' Travels Part Thirty Eight - Tahiti and the Society Islands.

We had heard so many reports about Tahiti being over-touristy, expensive, etc. that we had not allowed our expectations to
ride too high. Consequently, perhaps, we were pleasantly surprised. The anchorage, though extremely busy was very pleasant
and well protected by the outlying reef. Remember the Anthony Hopkins-Mel Gibson version of Mutiny on the Bounty , I did
feel that there was a distinct shortage of bare-breasted females paddling their canoes out to meet us. There were two dinghy
docks to choose from, one at the Sofitel Hotel and one at the marina. The main culture shock in going ashore was the amount
of traffic in evidence. We hadn't really experienced more than one car at a time since leaving Panama. Our first task in the
morning was to get into Papeete to check in. Nearly every place we had visited so far had had its own unique transport system
and Tahiti was no exception. Here it was Le Truck. These as the name implies were lorry chassis with wooden structures built
on the back. Some of these looked as if they had been a weekend project in someone's back garden, but they offered a regular
if erratic and cheap service. Their long term future was apparently in some doubt as a Government Minister had decided that
they didn't fit in with the sophisticated image he thought the island should be portraying.

Checking in was a fairly lengthy but painless experience. Once again horror stories of just a couple of years ago proved
thankfully to be incorrect. There seems to have been a definite softening of official attitudes towards yachts. Papeete is a real
cosmopolitan city, where prices although not cheap, it is not nearly as expensive as we had been led to believe. Provisions in
the well-stocked supermarkets were generally at a level with English prices. During our stay we witnessed the start and finish
of the Round Moorea six-man canoe race that we had seen the Ua Pou team practising for back in the Marquesas. It was an
impressive sight. The top teams came from Shell and Mobil, and were extremely professional. They didn't even allow
themselves much self-congratulation when they finished. It was quite a relief to see the third team in clearly overjoyed with
their performance. We also saw the opening night of the Polynesian Dance Festival. It was quite spectacular seeing 40 pairs
of hips wiggling in complete synchronisation. The knee wobbling performed by the male dancers looked distinctly painful A
few nights later we went to the Friday night entertainment at the Beachcomber Hotel. For the price of a beer we saw a really
lively display with fire eaters, one of whom was spotlit, jumping from a rocky outcrop into the landscaped swimming pool.
Papeete was the first place since Panama to have a chandler's and we were able to get one or two things we had been short of.
I even found water filters that I hadn't managed to find since we'd left England. I was unable to find spares for the autohelm
rams but was able to get one of them working again. Richard and Joy from ‘Fair Hippolyta' came over and Richard fitted a
spare sender for my temperature gauge on the engine. A Belgian called Luke who had lived on his boat in Tahiti for the last
year, working as a tour guide, arranged a special cut-price tour for yachties. It was a really good day, and gave us a chance to
see more of the Island. We saw where Captain Cook first landed.

After nearly two weeks in Tahiti we were ready to move on and had a short sail across to Moorea with Laura back on board.
The short sail was not without incident as the gear part of the single lever control suddenly refused to engage. I had no choice
but to climb down through the cockpit locker to the rear of the engine to disconnect the cable and change gear by hand. In this
fashion we entered the pass into Cook's Bay and anchored behind the reef with help from Pete from ‘La Boatique' from whom
we had bought our dinghy in Panama. Having helped us anchor, Pete came on board to look at the engine controls, but even he
had no joy. He did help me set it up so that we could operate the gear change with a pair of mole grips in the cockpit. We had
a comfortable night but in the morning the wind got up and we started dragging, a rare event for us. Our anchor had been on
the edge of a ledge and had pulled over the edge into deeper water. We got the chain in and motored into the bay where we
anchored just off the small settlement. We were now able to appreciate the grandeur of our surroundings. Moorea has an
impressive and unmistakable skyline. I was able to catch the fast ferry back to Papeete where I bought a new single lever
control and the next day I had it fitted. The failed one had been fitted in the Canaries and was only 18 months old. On the day
I went back to Papeete, Helen and Laura did a long walk up to a Belvedere where they had a superb view. That evening one of
the residents of the time-share apartments nearby organised a yachtie's barbecue for which he provided chicken, beer and rum.
It turned out to be a really good night and was much appreciated. Cook's Bay proved to be a very convenient anchorage.

Ne, There was a water supply on bank where you could take the dinghy to fill up with water, have a shower, or do your washing.
A jetty was conveniently sited near a supermarket that was well stocked and much more to our liking than the huge affairs in
Tahiti. Moorea was an extremely lush island. I was amazed to see fields of pineapples. I don't think I had ever realised that
they grew straight out of the ground.

From Moorea we had an overnight sail to Huahine. It was a trip of about 85 miles which is a difficult distance to plan for.
However it worked out all right leaving as we did just before sunset. The main problem is that you don't have time to settle
down into anything of a routine before it gets dark. There was quite a sea running which made things a bit uncomfortable at
first. However there was a good wind and progress was good. We left at the same time as a cruise ship and several other
yachts and I was amazed at how many lights I could see around us. I just wasn't used to this. We had a good overnight sail
and arrived off Huahine soon after dawn. Sailing round the northern end of the island we entered the reef by the main town of
Fare and negotiated the 7-mile-long channel inside the reef to a lovely secure anchorage in the south of the island. It was a
fascinating introduction to a new island. That afternoon we went ashore and walked along one of the loveliest beaches that we
had seen in the Pacific. We spent several days in this anchorage and it quickly became one of our favourite spots. The island

of Huahine is really two islands joined by a road bridge encased within the common reef. Helen and I spent a day doing a
walking/hitching tour of the island. In the absence of any form of public transport, hitching is one of the few options for seeing
the island and we reckoned our success rate was about 50%. Over one 2-hour period, making our way down the east side of
the island we got two lifts from the only two vehicles that passed us. In the north of the island we saw a marae, or sacred site.
Unlike the ones we had seen in the Marquesas, this one was built out over the water. A number of boats that we had been
seeing on the way gathered in the anchorage and regular happy hours developed on the beach near a small bar. Laura did some
snorkelling and diving with martin from 'Rover'. All in all it was a particularly relaxed time. When we finally decided to
move back along the island we unfortunately chose a day when a slow-moving front was starting to make conditions rather
unsettled. Motoring inside the reef in light rain that I had predicted would soon clear up, but instead developed into a torrential
downpour, we were reduced to peering into the haze searching out the marks. Helen hadn't wanted to move, and stayed down
below out of the rain. 'Aldebaran' had moved the previous afternoon to the anchorage off the town of Fare and had had an
uncomfortable night, so we eventually anchored in the deep but narrow Baie Haavai where, in spite of strong gusts from the
west blowing straight in, we had a reasonable night.

We woke in the morning to more driving rain, all undecided as to whether to move on or not. In the end both 'Aldebaran' and
ourselves decided to take a chance and tackle the 20 mile trip to the next island of Raiatea. We were rewarded with a
brightening sky and a fresh northwesterly which gave us a good sail. Then, about half way across, our cockpit GPS started
giving out strange information. Just minutes later the nav station GPS also reported 'no fix'. Both GPSs are Furuno and
neither had previously given us any problems whatsoever. The real mystery was that both systems are completely independent
of each other apart from having the same battery source. This sudden loss of information quickly reduced me to a gibbering
wreck and made me realise how dependent I had become these electronics. The confusion was added to by the fact that we
had had three passes through the reef to choose from. We had originally been headed for the southernmost of the passes but
Pat had heard that the middle pass was easier. I had replied that the southern pass looked OK. We had both taken up each
other's suggestions with Pat heading for the southern pass while we headed for the middle one. These passes are very difficult
to identify so when... sorry reader - some text missing from here!) position we were able to push
while Helen put the engine into reverse and we slid off. Fortunately there didn't appear to be any real harm done apart from
scrapes on the side of the keel. We were very lucky that there was no wind or swell. Meanwhile Pat and Olivia had no luck in
extricating their anchor. We rafted alongside them and Pat got out his diving gear so that he and Laura could dive down.
Having got it clear, we motored round to Baie Faaroa. By the time we got there it was well after five and less than an hour
before dark. We discovered that there was a Stardust Charter Base with a number of moorings. Calling up on the VHF they
told us that we were more than welcome to pick up a mooring which was a great relief. We all had a much needed sundowner.
That night the rain started again and carried on pretty much unabated for the next day. It didn't take us long to top up our tanks
and fill every available receptacle. By the afternoon the wind got up and we were getting gusts of well over 30 knots.
Visibility throughout the day was minimal and we were very glad to be where we were. All sorts of debris started to come
down from the mountains, and we got advance warning of the worst of it from Harold on 'Zephyrus' who was anchored further
in to the bay. The next day the weather cleared and we ventured ashore for a pleasant walk ashore. Later in the day Pat, Laura
and I took his dinghy for an interesting trip up the river.

From Faaroa we managed to sail slowly up the coast inside the reef to the town of Uturoa where we managed to get fresh fruit
and veg. In the morning we indulged in cafe society, watching the world go by. We then motored north, still inside the reef, to
the neighbouring island of Ta Had. We met up with 'Cap d'Or' and ‘Fair Hippolyta' when we picked up a buoy to investigate an
entertainment scheduled for that evening. While we were securing to the buoy, Martin from 'Rover' came by and took Laura
off snorkelling. The hotel owner was very friendly but the price put us off so we headed back out to the reef where we
anchored on sand in about 6 metres of crystal clear water, just behind a moth. John and Sail brought Laura back to us in their
fast RIB from 'Rover' and in the morning we went snorkelling in the pass.

It was here that we had a long overdue reunion with Martin on 'Ragtime' whom we had spent a lot of time with in Tobago and
who was due to fly back to the Channel Islands for a cataract operation. We had a tremendous barbecue on the moth with a
number of boats.. We sailed right round the north end of Ta Had, inside the reef before enjoying a lively 20-mile sail across to

Bora Bora. As we rounded the outer reef we hardened up on the wind and 'Muna' revelled in it. The lagoon surrounding Bora t
Bora is nothing less than spectacular. We spent the first couple of nights in a lovely shallow anchorage behind a small island i
just to the south of the pass. We then went north around Bora Bora. At times we had just inches under our keel. Then we
would be negotiating tortuous gaps in the coral. It was pretty exciting to say the least, but the anchorages were almost perfect.
For the next few days we moved from one anchorage to another, each one giving us a different perspective on the infamous
skyline. On a couple of occasions we snorkelled with giant manta rays, some having a span of 10-15".

We had been following on the radio the fortunes of two boats who, within two days of each other, had lost their rudders while
on passage to Suvorov, the atoll made famous by Tom Neale who lived alone there for many years. The first boat was an
Italian 30 footer,'Amour', that we had first met in the Canaries, and had seen several times since. 'Amour' was a very light boat
with a skegless rudder. They lost their rudder in fairly heavy seas and had great difficulty establishing any control. They
eventually reached Suvorov where they were towed in to await the arrival of spare parts on another boat. The second boat with
a lost rudder was a Grand Soleil 43, also with a skegless rudder. They managed to fabricate some sort of temporary rudder and
carried on sailing to Samoa where they hoped to effect repairs. While we were on the east side of Bora Bora we tackled some
sail repairs on the yankee where the stitching had worn through. On a blustery Sunday we sailed back round to the west of the
island. We had the engine on, out of gear, to charge the batteries and ready in case we needed it as we negotiated the, at times,
tortuous course between the reefs. As we passed the Bora Bora Yacht Club, Helen noticed that there were several free buoys.
Heading in we suddenly smelt burning. Opening the starboard cockpit locker which leads to the engine, we were confronted
with dense acrid smoke. Helen steered for the nearest available buoy which Laura secured us to, while I attempted to remove
lines and other items from the locker. With the engine off we cleared the locker and the smoke slowly dispersed. Back in the
Tuamotus I had discovered that some of the lagging of the dry section of the exhaust had started to disintegrate. To protect
items in the locker I had wedged a piece of wood outside the pipe. This had completely burnt through and was the cause of the
acrid smoke. I tried to get some new lagging on shore but without success. Then I discovered that Barry on 'Cherokee' had
some fibreglass lagging that he kindly let me have. Meanwhile I had run the engine with the bad section of lagging removed
and detected leakage. I had some exhaust pipe repair paste on board which I liberally applied. This seemed to work. I then
covered this section of pipe with Barry's tape.

We were now ready to move on. We were facing a passage of some 1400 miles to Tonga with the widely dispersed Cook
Islands in between. We had heard very favourable reports of these islands. Their main problem is a lack of protected
anchorages. Every time we selected a possible route we would read up on the anchorages and be instantly put off. Raratonga
in the south is the main island but has a small, generally overcrowded, harbour. Penryn has a good lagoon anchorage but is a
long way to the north. Suvorov, where Tom Neale lived for many years, sounded really nice but was also fairly far north. In
the end we opted for a direct route to Tonga which would take us fairly near to Aitutaki and Palmerston where we could stop if
conditions allowed, but which would not be too much off the direct route if we carried on.

By the time we were ready to move, several boats had been waiting for more settled conditions. On the morning of
Wednesday 15th August, while I was still working on the exhaust pipe, 'Orplid', ‘Cherokee’, 'La Boatique' and 'Maritime
Express' all set off in the direction of Aitutaki, some 480 miles away. 'Aldebaran' set off just before noon and we followed mid
afternoon. As we motored out of the pass, there still seemed to be fumes in the engine room. We considered turning back but
decided to press on and were soon sailing.

to be continued, Malcolm Shaft

Club Notes

Commodore

Once again we need to say "Thank You" to Fenella for organising such a splendid Fun Day. I would like to know
her secret of predicting many months ahead when the sun will shine, a warm wind will blow and the evening
although chilly is dry. In addition to my thanks to Fenella, I would like to thank all the others who supported her to
make it such an enjoyable day. The stalwarts from the Cruiser Fleet who have cooked at the barbecue for many
years congratulate the members of the Handicap Fleet on the work and sympathise with the streaming eyes and
smoke filled clothes. Very many thanks to you all.

As many of you will know, on Sunday 8" June the wind increased quite violently which caused many problems in
the river. These were not confined to the dinghy fleet but included incidents with cruisers, particularly those racing
and members coming ashore from cruisers. Our support boats and crews did an excellent job that day and as afar as
I am aware no one was injured. The situation that afternoon acts as a timely reminder to us all that forecasts are not
always accurate and that each of us MUST be responsible for ourselves when sailing. I know of at least one cruiser
who left Brightlingsea, decided that it looked ominous and went back in, to return to the Club on the Monday. Even
if you are racing, it is YOUR decision whether to continue, not the Race Officer's.

Over recent weeks there have been a number of cruisers which have suffered damage whilst on the moorings.
Although the damage may seem superficial, a mark down the side, a gentle bump to a tender, even these are time
consuming to the owner to fix. In some cases damage can be much more substantial and costly. I. along with all the
other cruiser owners, am well aware that such damage may not have been caused by other club members as many
other amateur and professional sailors use the river. Indeed I doubt whether there is one of us who has never had a
similar accident. However I do ask that anyone who thinks they may have touched a cruiser to have the courtesy to
contact the owner; it saves accusations being made and ill will generated.

I am pleased to say that the response to the loan note scheme is very encouraging. Although we have a little way to
go to meet our target to fund the difference between the purchase cost and the bank loan, we appear to be on target
to complete the purchase late June or early July. Please note that we are not banking the cheques until the sale /
purchase contracts have been exchanged. Elsewhere in this issue the form for existing Marconi Sailing Club
members to apply to join Thirslet and the form to apply for Members Loans are reprinted.

By the time that this issue lands on your doorstep, we will have held the East Coast Piers Race on 6" July and I
would like thank all those mother boat crews, shore side helpers and backroom people who support Chris Davies
and the East Coast Piers Race Committee both throughout the year and on the day. Without you all, the Cirdan
Trust would not be able to help the same number of people who are not so fortunate as ourselves.

Neil Pembleton

Cruiser Fleet

We have now had our cruises to Burnham and Brightlingsea. We had 16 boats to Burnham with 44 sitting down
for a meal and 13 boats to Brightlingsea and although there was no meal planned, we had 28 for a carvery in the
Colne Yacht Club. Both cruises went very well with favourable winds on both trips although those who were late
back from Brightlingsea had rather more wind than was comfortable.

Looking ahead, we have the Piers Race on the 6" July which may or may not have passed by the time that you
receive this and the trip to Heybridge Basin, known as the Watercress Run, on the 12" and 13" July. The plan is to
lock in to Heybridge at approximately 11am on Saturday (high water 1200 hours) taking our tenders with us, then
during the afternoon have a trip up the river to Beeleigh in the tenders, returning for a barbeque in the evening. To
this end I have booked the barbeques on the lock side. You can either bring your own food or buy it at Tescos on
the way back from Beeleigh. There is a list on the Club notice board so if you could add your name to it, I can
inform the lock keeper of the numbers to expect.

The other forthcoming trips are St. Katharines on the week beginning 2" August and Shotley the week beginning
23" August.

BLACKWATER & COLNE SAILING PROTECTION ASSOCIATION

On 20th March this year I attended the BACSPA meeting held at the Maldon Little Ship Club and as on previous occasions I am reporting on the matters which I feel may be of interest to you.

WINDFARMS - The key issues resulting from the Environmental Impact
Statement for the GUNFLEET remain i.e. marking/lighting, rotor tip clearance and exclusion zones.
The rotor tip clearance issue has deteriorated further in that the tower height has been reduced to 80 mtrs above LET giving clearances of less than 20 mtrs in. all but good conditions. Furthermore an application for an order under the Transport and works Act seeks to be able to reduce the clearance
to as little as 14 mtrs above MHWS. - A yacht of 10.5 mtrs LOA with normal
rig would have an air height of some 16 mtrs to include the VHF aerial. The RYA/BACSPA are waiting a response from the Developer's in which they say they will offer some mitigation to this problem.
The Chairman of BACSPA had a useful meeting with the Navigation Manager at Trinity House on the issue of marking and lighting of wind-farms, with particular reference to the Gunfleet Project. A plot of the farm aray on the chart shows the SE corner to intrude on the direct line between the GUNFLEET SPIT and SWIN SPITWAY buoys which mark the extent of the Gunfleet sands by the East Swin/Kings' Channel. The Chairman received a letter from Trinity House accepting this point and they will be asking the Developer to install & maintain an additional starboard hand buoy some 600 mtrs SW of the mid point of the southern boundary of the array. Trinity House will also move the SWIN SPITWAY buoy some 330 meters SE of its present position. These changes will shift the East Swin clear route away from the farm array.

HAMFORD WATER - Hutchison Ports (UK) Ltd on their scoping report on the
proposed managed realignment in Hamford Water, which is intended to provide compensatory habitat for the Bathside Bay port development. The principal concern is the possible silting of the already shallowing PYE CHANNEL which could seriously restrict access to the WALTON BACKWATERS.

WEYMARKS - The proposed managed realignment of the sea wall between
Bradwell Nuclear Power Station & the Roman fort on the north coast of the Dengie Peninsula should have no measurable impact on the navigable area in the Blackwater Estuary.

"Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Thirty Nine - To Palmerston in the Cook Islands.

Setting off from Bora Bora the winds were light but favourable. progress was slow but conditions were pleasant and it was
good to be on the move again. When the winds were below 14 knots or so the difference between our performance and that of
the boats that we were with was at its most marked, and it was no surprise when they all pulled even further ahead. By the
Sunday, 4 days out, boats were beginning to arrive at Aitutaki. There is a very narrow, shallow, pass through the reef to a
small but sheltered anchorage, but there was continuing debate as to how deep the pass was. 'Stella' had got in scraping the
bottom and she drew 5'6". 'Capers' had been in for some time. In fact they had almost taken up residence. The only
alternative was an anchorage outside the pass that was deep with a lot of coral and which was prone to a heavy swell
depending on current conditions. 'Cherokee' decided to keep on going and head for Beveridge Reef. 'Orplid' anchored but
decided only to stay one night. 'La Boatique' arrived and were talking of leaving quite soon. Pat and Olivia on 'Aldebaran'
didn't even anchor. they took one look and decided to keep going for Palmerston. ‘Maritime Express' anchored and seemed
reasonably happy. We were undecided as to what to do. We were set to arrive at around midnight and would therefore have to
heave-to to wait until morning. In the end we kept going. The wind gradually increased and, after another couple of days, we
were charging towards Palmerston at 7 knots. Having been concerned that we would be arriving at night and once again
having to decide between standing off or not stopping, the strengthening wind ensured that we got in with just over an hour to
spare.

As we came round the island, one of the locals came out in his small aluminium runabout to guide us into the anchorage.
Palmerston is an atoll much like those we had seen in the Tuamotus, with a large lagoon surrounded by a reef on which were
situated a number of small islands or motus. The largest of these was Palmerston Island itself. There are a number of passes
into the lagoon but none is deeper than 4'. The pass nearest the anchorage is incredibly narrow and twisting, with very strong
cross currents. It would be extremely dangerous to attempt it in a dinghy, but the locals whizzed in and out in their aluminium
runabouts day and night. When a yacht arrives at the island, it is a matter of honour for each family to claim it as theirs.
Simon, who had guided us in, turned out to be the head of his particular family. Having shown us in he asked whether we
were happy to be checked in in the morning. When we told him that we were, he said he would be back first thing with the
appropriate officials. These turned out to be the Agricultural Officer and the Medical Officer. After a sociable checking in, in
the cockpit, conducted over a beer, Simon asked whether we were ready to go ashore. Soon we were having our first
experience of racing through the pass with coral heads and surging water all around. Once ashore Simon led us to his family
home in a pleasant clearing in the heavily wooded island. Over coffee and cakes we started to learn the history of the island.

Palmerston was settled in the mid-19th century by an Englishman, William Masters, who had run away from his native
Lancashire. Having deserted his ship he acquired two Polynesian wives from Penryn, another of the Cook Islands. Having
taken them to Palmerston along with a boatload of coconut seedlings, he then gained a third Polynesian wife from another
Englishman who, having previously settled on Palmerston, refused to help pay for the coconut seedlings. After some level of
disagreement he was then seen off. William Masters divided the island and the smaller surrounding motus between the three
families. These three families are still in residence today. The whole setup is fascinating. As a rule, everything is shared. it is
a bit like one of those social experiments that were popular a few years ago, except this one has survived for 150 years. When
we had finished our coffee, Simon asked us if we would like a tour of the island. It will take an hour or so he said, then we
will come back here for lunch. This turned out to be a regular feature of the week we were to spend on the island. Every day
we were ashore on the island, it was taken as read that we would stay for lunch. The hospitality was staggering. Everywhere
we went on the island, one of the 50 inhabitants would offer us coffee and biscuits or one of the ever-present coconuts. I had
never previously realised how much of the coconut could be eaten. A delicacy that was completely new to us was the inside of
a coconut that had started sprouting, where the milk had turned into a delicious substance reminiscent of marshmallow.

'Aldebaran' had arrived on the day before us and a couple of days after us 'Arganauta' and 'Maritime Express' arrived. They
had both come from Aitutaki. As this was another of the Cook Islands they had been able to bring fresh fruit and veg which
were very much appreciated by the islanders. Henry on 'Maritime Express' was also able to repair Simon's refrigeration unit.
On the Saturday night a show was staged for the benefit of the visitors. It was a memorable experience sitting on a wooden
bench in a clearing right on the edge of the beach, watching a display of Polynesian dancing accompanied by local musicians
on a variety of instruments. The whole performance was lit by a single light bulb strung between two coconut trees. The
dancing was excellent, but one of the highlights for me was when two-year-old John, who was clearly a musician/dancer in the
making, followed his mum out onto the stage and copied her entire routine, taking the whole thing extremely seriously. John
was very wary of me the whole time that we were there. He only started talking to me when it was time to say goodbye when
he repeated ‘bye bye' several times with great gusto and obvious relief! The evening finished with the yachties being invited to
join in the dancing. According to Helen, my version of Polynesian dancing was more akin to a Marquesan war dance, and
could have started in international incident. Luckily it seemed to cause great amusement, but little offence.
Sundays are a very special day on the island. No work is done and Sunday lunch is a very special event. It is the only day of
the week when the staple diet is not fish and we were treated to a veritable feast of chicken, lamb and basin birds that had been
collected the day before. The supply ship had arrived early that Sunday but, in spite of wanting many of the supplies urgently,
they would not start unloading the ship until sundown. Even that was a special concession to allow the ship to get away that
night. The week that we spent on Palmerston was a very special experience that we won't forget in a hurry. We had become
used to friendly islanders but these were exceptional. Everyone from the children up to the oldest inhabitants all seemed
genuinely thrilled to have someone new to talk to.

‘Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Forty - Beveridge Reef and Niue.

Our stay in Palmerston had fortunately coincided with sustained easterlies. The wind at this time of year and in this area is
prone to coming round to the west every few days. Such an occurrence would make the anchorage at Palmerston untenable.
When we left Palmerston the winds were light but fairly steady and from the east. It took us 2 days and 2 nights to reach
Beveridge Reef some 290 miles away. As we approached the reef at dawn, the wind slowly headed us and settled into the
west. It was good timing as the reef gives good protection from all directions. Until the advent of GPS Beveridge Reef was
considered simply as a deadly hazard lying on the route between Bora Bora and Tonga. Its position as marked on charts was
inaccurate and yachts would give it a wide berth. Now with accurate waypoints available, thanks to one or two pioneering
yachts, it is fast becoming a rather special destination. Its fascination lies in the fact that none of the reef surrounding the 3
mile long lagoon is ever above sea level. Once through the single pass, the lagoon anywhere else in the Pacific would be
considered a superb anchorage. Ten metres deep with only the occasional coral head to worry about, as an anchorage it is only
surpassed by the fact that all round the lagoon there is a 100 metre wide band of pure sand just 4 metres deep. We joined
‘Aldebaran' and 'Stella' who had arrived the day before and our anchor bit deep into the sand. The water was so clear that you
could see the chain disappear into the sand. The only landmarks as we looked around us were the different colours of the
water and a solitary wrecked fishing boat lying on the reef. It was an amazing feeling knowing you were in the middle of the
Pacific with no land for hundreds of miles in any direction. Several other boats arrived in the reef and in this desolate and
isolated spot we actually had a very sociable time. In this location we were able to converse freely on Channel 16. At times
we felt like of lot of naughty schoolboys. I kept expecting a stern reprimand from Thames Coastguard. On the last passage,
Laura had kept herself amused by compiling a list of words that end in -ship. This became an interboat contest. Our list
reached well over two hundred.

After a few days the wind showed signs of returning to the east, and in spite of very light winds we struck out on the 130 mile
trip to Niue. The light airs gradually developed into a steady breeze and we made reasonable progress overnight. By the
morning the wind was steadily increasing and we had a fast run into the island with an enjoyable beat round the back of the
island in calm seas. We picked up a buoy a couple of hours before sunset. neue is one of the smallest independent states in the
world but is the largest coral island. Anchoring of Niue can easily result in your anchor being permanently lost in a deep
chasm in the coral. We hired a car for the day with Pat and Olivia. Travelling around the island is very different from other
islands we had visited in that, being flat and very heavily wooded, there are virtually no views. However, Mary and Walley,
two friendly New Zealanders, who run the car hire as well as the Niue Yacht Club which is responsible for maintaining the 14
mooring buoys, had told us the best places to visit. With this information we did a number of short walks to some amazing
sights. Being an island made almost entirely from coral, the caves were cathedral-like and spectacular in the extreme. While
we were in Niue we realised how lucky we had been with the weather we had had since Bora Bora. We had generally had
lightish winds but enough to keep sailing. We had been aware at the time of other boats, not that far away, having to motor for
days on end. Now boats were coming into Niue, just a day or two behind us, with tales of horrendous weather. One had been
rolled by a wave, causing mayhem below decks. After we had been there a few days we became aware of a developing
situation on the Australian steel yacht 'Bifrost', on passage from Bora Bora to Tonga. We had first met Greg and Leonie and
their two sons Ben and Jessie aged 4 and 6, at Christmas on the Dutch island of Curacao. On this passage Greg had been taken
ill and, on advice over the radio from a New Zealand doctor, had taken medication for suspected malaria. It appears now that
Greg may have had Dengie Fever. He is also diabetic. In any event he reacted badly to the medication and became seriously
incapacitated. Leonie didn't know at the time what was wrong and had the boat to handle on her own, two young boys to look
after and Greg to both look after and worry about. The weather was also deteriorating. Leonie was coming up on the daily net
and after the situation had been developing from some time, Pat on 'Aldebaran' asked if she would like assistance. When she
said that she would, he considered setting off back from Niue to meet them. At this stage 'Bifrost' was some 400 miles from
Niue. Pat then realised that there were boats in Beveridge Reef who could intercept 'Bifrost' without heading back into the
prevailing winds. 'Beacon' and 'Four Winds' immediately offered to go and Pat with the aid of his chart plotter worked out
courses whereby they could meet up with 'Bifrost' without 'Bifrost' having to change course or slow down. 'Bifrost' by this
time was heading for Niue as the nearest place where Greg could be given medical attention. ‘Beacon' reached 'Bifrost' in the
middle of the night and, by means of some skilful manoeuvring, David was able to transfer some additional medication to
‘Bifrost’. Because of the conditions, it was decided not to attempt to transfer Alex from 'Beacon' which had been one of the
options. 'Four Winds' joined the group and the 3 boats continued to Niue. Leonie said that it was a great relief having the
other boats there. Pat continued to monitor the situation. It became clear that the boats would arrive in Niue sometime on
Friday night. Pat co-ordinated plans for their arrival. There were 14 buoys at Nuie and at this stage there were just 3 left. Pat
arranged for these to be reserved. When the boats arrived everyone did what they could to assist. I took Laura, and Ian from
‘Arganauta' to intercept 'Bifrost' on their way into the Bay. It was the furthest I had taken the dinghy offshore and had visions
of making and early departure for Tonga. Once on board we could relieve Leonie from the helm. It was the first time that she
had been able to talk to Greg for several hours as they have no autohelm and under power they have to handsteer. Other
dinghies guided the boats on to their respective buoys and Julius from 'Arganauta', who is a pharmacist and who had been
giving advice on medication, brought the doctor out to 'Bifrost' even before she had tied to the buoy. After he had given Greg
an initial check, the local dive boat came out with a stretcher to take Greg ashore and up to the hospital. Thanks to excellent
co-ordination the whole operation had gone extremely well. After a few days Greg felt well enough to carry on to Tonga.
Laura joined them for the trip as Greg was still not strong enough to do anything physical. In the event we sailed with them in
the company of 'Arganauta' and after 2 nights arrived in Vavau, the northern island group of Tonga. We had a bit of
excitement on the way as, during a squall, several of our sail slides disintegrated due to ultra violet deterioration. After some
difficulty, we got the main down and set the downwind rig which gave us an easy ride in quite breezy condition for the rest of

the way. In Vavau, Greg flew on to Australia for a full medical. Fortunately there appeared to be no lasting damage, just a bad
reaction to the medication taken for suspected malaria. He was soon able to return to Tonga and continue their voyage home to
Brisbane via Fiji.

'Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Forty One - Tonga

Until we were well out into the Pacific I had always thought of Tonga as one island and was quite surprised to discover that it
was in fact a widely-spaced island group. Although the most southerly island of Tongatapu is the main island and home of the
King, the Vavau Group, about 150 miles to the north, is the more popular cruising ground and it was here that we made
landfall. The group consists of one largish island of Vavau on which the main town of Niafu is situated and a number of much
smaller islands, all in quite close proximity to each other and all protected from the prevailing winds by an extensive system of
reefs to the east. The result is a sheltered cruising ground that has been taken full advantage of by the likes of Moorings and
Sunsail. There are countless anchorages within easy reach of each other. Because of the complexity of the local names,
Moorings have numbered the anchorages and this rather sterile system has even been taken over by the locals. As we arrived
on a Sunday and checking-in is limited to weekdays, we made our way to anchorage No. 7 or Port Meurelle, historically
believed to be the first anchorage for a European ship. A beautiful if rather crowded anchorage, we were immediately invited
on board 'Beacon', who had arrived just before us, for a breakfast very tasty pancakes. After a quick doze back on board we
were invited onboard 'Aldebaran' for lunch. They had a mooring in Niafu but had come down for the afternoon! In the
evening we had a Happy Hour on the beach with the crews of 'Beacon' and 'Arganauta’.

In the morning we reluctantly upped anchor so as to head up to Naifu and check in. Even in these sheltered waters we were
registering winds up to 30 knots. Pat came out in his dinghy and helped us tie up to the wharf to await customs. They have
quite strict rules here as to the importation of foodstuffs but the implementation of these rules appears to be somewhat
arbitrary. Our coconuts we had been given in Niue were confiscated but the official decided that we could keep our tomatoes
as they were a bit bruised. Nick on 'Force Eight', a South African boat, was asked what a particular vegetable was. When Nick
told him it was an aubergine, the official said, "I like them, I'd better confiscate it!" Having checked in we moved to a buoy
that Pat had managed to procure for us. We were quickly introduced to the rather strange mixture of cultures that is in
evidence here. On the one hand the foreshore is a yachtie culture with Sunsail and Moorings bases and a number of waterside
bars with dinghy docks and Happy Hours. Up the steps of the low cliff and you step into traditional Tonga with the men
wearing skirts adorned with woven mats. We saw local girls swimming, dressed from head to foot in black. Just outside the
town we came across some very basic homes with pigs running free everywhere you looked. We had a number of jobs to
attend to on the boat and we ended up staying on the buoy for 3 weeks. There was a cruiser race every Friday and Helen and I
crewed on 'Aldebaran' the first week. With Pat's dinghy racing expertise, we made a superb, if to me nerve racking start but
were gradually overhauled. The next week
I crewed on 'Arganauta'. For both weeks Laura crewed on 'Fair Hippolyta'. Helen
had a number of fascinating treks around the island. Laura took advantage of low prices and excellent facilities to do a Rescue
Diver's course on top of her advanced certificate. One night we went with Pat and Olivia to a Tongan feast on the other side of
the island. It was organised by the inhabitants of a small village and was held in a very basic straw hut on the shore. The
evening started with local dancing followed by the feast which was a fascinating mixture of local foods. We then sat cross-
legged on the floor of the hut drinking karva while local musicians entertained us. Karva is made from the root of Karva, a
local plant, and drinking it is steeped in tradition. Very much a male preserve, taking part in the ceremony is quite an
experience. The liquid, served in a huge communal wooden bowl, looks like dirty washing-up water, tastes much the same,
but has a calming effect. Some people hated it but I found it strangely compulsive. The musicians played on into the night.
Outside, the wind howled and inside the Karva flowed. Pat managed to fall asleep sitting up and I felt at peace with the world.
A truly memorable evening.

We then spent an enjoyable couple of weeks sailing round the islands experiencing a number of magical anchorages. Going
ashore on the tiny but thickly wooded island of Lappa we initially assumed it to be uninhabited, only to discover that there
were in fact 20 people living there. We came across one family collecting coconuts. They were very friendly. The mother
turned out to be the Headteacher of the local school. She invited us to supper which was served on the floor. The next
morning we visited the school which had 4 pupils. We were amazed at how isolated the inhabitants of these small islands
were. To our way of thinking the islands were so close together that communication between should have been fairly
straightforward. In fact the few local boats there were were generally outboard powered and therefore expensive to run. I was
surprised that there was no evidence of any local sailing craft. The Headteacher and her family hardly ever saw their relations
on the main island. It was interesting to hear how, in spite of the fact that they had been so welcoming, they are in fact at times
quite concerned about who might be coming ashore from the yachts. They had heard about some yachtsmen being armed.
They had also heard about the September 11th attacks on the United States and when they saw a cruise ship stop off the island
and start disgorging its passengers into zodiacs were seriously concerned that it might be an Afghan Troop Ship.

There were 2 caves only accessible from the water that we managed to visit. The first, Swallows Cave, involved hovering off
the entrance in Muna and going in in the dinghy. Once inside we landed and went through to an inner cave where once
Tongan Kings had enjoyed feasts, lowered down through a hole in the roof. The other cave, Mariners Cave, also involved
hovering off. This time several of us went in 'Aldebaran'. Here it was a case of snorkelling through an underwater pass into
the cave. We had read that it should be possible if you could snorkel under the keel of your boat from about 10' either side. I
had practised just that, that very morning and in the event had no problem. Laura of course was in an out like a mermaid. On

my way in I was swimming just below to the rock face at the very top of the entrance, feeling very pleased with myself, when I
looked down and there she was way below me, effortlessly gliding through the water. Once in, it was fascinating to be in this
dome-like cavern, only lit by the light coming up through the water. As the water outside surged the pressure inside the cave
built up and a greenish mist would form and you would have to unblock your ears.

While we were in Vavau we had been pondering our next moves. We had had extremely positive reports of the Happi Group
of islands but the charts indicated that the area had large areas of reefs. The distance to the nearest islands of the group were
an awkward 70 miles or so. In the end we went overnight, with 'Aldebaran' and 'Arganauta' leaving a little while after us. it
proved to be a really good sail. The fresh south easterly just allowed us to hold our course. As dawn broke, 'Arganauta’ and
‘Aldebaran' were just coming up behind us. Just ahead we could see the island of Haano, the most northerly of the Happi
Group. We followed 'Arganauta' through off-lying reefs into a large shallow bay. Later in the day we took the dinghy ashore
and had an interesting walk with Pat and Olivia through the village, where once again the locals were eager to talk. Helen,
Olivia and Laura spent some time exploring the beach down to the low water mark for shells. The next day we had a short
genoa run to Foa Island where, having sailed through a pass in the reef, we anchored in shallow water over a sandy bottom off
the town of Lotofoa where we checked in with a very friendly official who was very interested in our travels. We had an
interesting walk across the island to the windward side where we saw a cemetery with elaborately decorated graves. Some
even had large embroidered sheets suspended over them.

The next day was Olivia's birthday and we sailed further along the island chain to the smaller island of Voleva. Like most of
the islands in this group, Voleva is low and heavily wooded with long wide sandy beaches. This was the third time ina row
that we had been with Pat and Olivia on Olivia's birthday. We all went ashore for a walk and Olivia found a tiny locally-run
resort, catering for no more than 10 people at a time, who said that we could eat there that night. After a Happy Hour on
'Aldebaran' with 'Arganauta' and 'Cap d'Or’, the four of us went back to the resort for a meal and a wonderful evening around a
log fire on the beach. The next day we went ashore again. Helen and Olivia walked across to a beach on the other side of the
island while Pat, Laura and I were shown the sight of ancient ceremonial pigeon traps, where pigeons were caught for the
edification of Tongan Kings. We then set off towards the far beach and ended up doing a route march round the entire island.
By the time we met up with Helen and Olivia, Pat and I were exhausted. We then set off for the island of Ha'Afeva. The
wind was on the nose and it was a slow sail that turned into a motor. Pat and Olivia decided to press on a bit further to the
island of Oua. Julius and Sally on 'Arganauta' followed us into the beautiful lagoon at Ha'Afeva only to have engine failure
just before they got there. They managed to sail into the lagoon. It turned out to be a fuel problem. (Julius had unwittingly run
one of his tanks dry) and was soon resolved. We explored the island with Julius and Sally and were once again treated to the
most amazing hospitality. A young mother called Star took us into her home where her father fed us on a shark dish. They
then gave us bananas and took us into the forest where they picked fresh coconuts for us.

Heading for the island of Nomuka to the south we had to weave between all kinds of hazards. We had thought that places like
the Tuamotus were treacherous, but in fact the coral there was quite well behaved., most of it confined to the lagoons at the
centre of the atolls, and between the atolls it was generally clear of dangers. Here the coral spread haphazardly across
otherwise open water. Arriving at Nomuka Iki Island we were reunited briefly with 'Aldebaran' who, having arrived just
before us, had decided to press on that night to Nuku Alofa. We went ashore and walked right across the beautiful deserted
island that had once housed a tiny prison. The next evening we set off overnight for Nuku Alofa in company with 'Keyta' an
American 30 footer that we had got to know. We had a good beam reach and actually made better progress than we had
intended, arriving off the entrance channel to Juku Alofa well before dawn. In the meantime we had almost lost the blade to
our self steering when the pivot pin came loose. Arriving in the port of Nukalofa we anchored off the wall with our stern tied
to the shore. We spent nearly a week there and found it to be far nicer than we had been led to believe it would be. We
managed to repair the self steering and the autohelm and get stocked up for the passage to New Zealand. We witnessed the
ceremonies marking the opening of Parliament and had a brief glimpse of the King of Tonga. After we had checked out we
moved out to an outlying island for the night where we met up with 'Arganauta'. We had a very pleasant evening together at
the small island resort. The next afternoon we set off together for New Zealand.

What’s in a Name?

When you read this in early September there is good reason to hope that Thirslet Sailing Club Ltd. will own the
Sailing Club Site. You will recall that the name Thirslet Sailing Club was chosen in haste when it was important to
act quickly to react to the rapidly deteriorating situation with our parent the MASC. We can now allow ourselves
time to reflect on the name that we wish to be known by for the next 50 years.

I ask you all to think about this matter and when you have formed your views, please contact me on
[redacted].co.uk or [redacted]. I will correlate all the suggestions and produce a short list for further
consultation. No decision will be taken until the AGM but we must have a short list for consideration at that
meeting, so please contact me with your suggestions by early October.

I now wish to give you my views on our future name and ask you to take these into consideration when forming
your opinions.

Many of you will have a loyalty to the name “Marconi”. There is no doubt that we have a good reputation within
the sailing circles using that name, and, if you are like me, part of you says “Why not keep to the old name?” If that
is your view then I need to give you the downside of such a decision.

Although many members stay for many years, others do not, and we need to attract new members every year.
Indeed our Business Plan requires that we increase membership. My experience is that “Marconi” causes
difficulties with prospective members. They automatically think that they have to be a Company employee to join.
Recently, the name Marconi has been associated with a failing telecoms Company and that leads people to wonder
if the Club will sink with the Company. Also we may get some trouble from Marconi about the use of their name.
Lastly, if we continue to be associated with Marconi, even if that association is only in name, it may affect our
chances of a loan from the Sports Council when we come to improve our facilities.

In conversations I have with members, they talk of Stansgate Sailing Club giving the letters SSC — the same as our
near neighbour Stone Sailing Club. If members favour use of Stansgate, I would advocate the name Stansgate
Abbey SC giving SASC as our shorthand. Not too bad you may think, the SAS are a legendary Regiment of the
British Army, but is it right for our new Club?

You may wish to consider a name without a geographical reference — there is a Club called “Castaways” that has
been around for years, although I have no idea where they are based. After thought you may think that Thirslet SC
is not such a bad name after all.

In the title I asked the question, ““What’s in a name?” My answer is “Quite a lot actually”

Please let me have your ideas. Let’s get a dialogue going.

Please think hard.
Clive Shenton

Solo Fleet

SOLOS AT MARCONI: 157 June 2003.

26 Solos took to the water at Marconi Sailing Club on the River Blackwater on 1° June. The event was part of the
Solo Eastern Area Championships and also a Sea Series event. Fifteen visitors complemented the eleven club
members. Following a superb training day on the Saturday with bright sunshine and force 3 — 4 wind the weather
on Sunday was disappointing with thundery clouds, no wind initially and a light breeze which never picked up
above a 2.

Nevertheless the Race Officer John Weedon set a course and the first race started in a light Southerly wind on a
course using the full width of the river. Andy Davis from Bartley set an early lead which was never challenged and
it was left for others to scrap for the places. Steve Ede was second, Jerry Garner third followed by Dave Nixson
and John Salmon.

Race 2 followed very much the same pattern although the beats were more interesting in the strong tide which
changed during the race. Andy Davis first followed by Jerry Garner and Steve Ede.

With the tide now ebbing, the fleet was being swept across the line at the start of race 3 resulting in a general recall.
At the restart, Andy Davis was over the line and had to return round the end but made impressive speed to overtake
all but three of the fleet by the end of the rather long race. Steve Ede won this race with Steve Denison second and
Jerry Garner third.

In response to “What’s in a name”

Clive Shenton’s article “What’s in a name” printed in this month’s Navigans and already received by members with an email address, has prompted a lot of response. I reprint below some of the discussion to date.

“I will be sad to see the name changed as all the east coast clubs do know our club very well (even in Calais marina I am proud to be a member of such a professional organisation called 'The Marconi Sailing Club' please lets keep the name as it is..”

“Whilst I like the Stansgate Abbey SC there is a small problem in that it does not exist. The farmer's barn next door used to be the Clunic Priory of St Mary Magdeline which was a cell of Cluni Abbey in Burgandy. To be pedantic we should call it Stansgate Priory SC. Alternatively we could perhaps adopt the name "Stansgate SC" and distinguish ourselves from Stone SC by using the short form St. SC”

“I think I would go along with Stansgate Abbey Sailing Club. I don't think the SAS connection is likely to be a serious threat to our existence and at least you can find it on a map!”

“What about a twist to retain the initials 'MSC' and thus the cogitations of Marconi past (& indeed our lovely seagull logo) but use a word that reflects the club moving forward. Thus, 'My Sailing Club’.

The club does belong to 'us' now, we are all individual owners, pulling together to make the club work, without the big landlord hanging over us.

MSC reaching Olympian heights??

Will a former Marconi SC member make it to the Olympic Games? Do you remember Mark Bulkeley? He might make it to the 2004 Olympics.

Mark (as crew) partners Leigh McMillan (helm) in the Olympic-class Tornado catamaran and their campaign for Olympic selection has certainly met with some success this year. The Hyeres Pre-Olympic Regatta earlier this year attracted the best contestants, particularly those with Olympic aspirations as the event is often used as a ‘selection indicator' by some nations. The team of Mark and Leigh achieved a very good 8th place in the Tornado class ahead of the UK's leading team of Hugh Styles and Adam May who finished an unexpectedly lowly 18th. Mark and Leigh achieved even greater success at the Spa Olympic Regatta, coming Ist ahead of a very good field (including internationally acclaimed cat sailor Mitch Booth) with Styles and May in 8th
place.

Unfortunately for Mark and Leigh, the Tornado Europeans in Sardinia proved a bit of a disappointment. After a good start to the event in which they headed the Styles/May team, Mark and Leigh eventually finished 16th whilst Styles/May achieved a very good Sth place overall.

Thus it seems, the UK's selection for. the (single) spot in the Tornado class for the 2004 Olympics is still very much an open question.

Commodore

When the Executive, with the agreement of the members, formed Thirslet Sailing Club as a Company Limited by
Guarantee, we were legally obliged to provide to Companies House two documents known as the "Memorandum of
Association" and the "Articles of Association". The first defines in general terms the objectives of the Club and the
second provides the general framework for the management and running of the Club.
Of necessity these documents had to exist to allow the company to be registered to negotiate the purchase of the
site and to allow members to transfer into it. The content of these documents is drawn in part from the "Marconi
Sailing Section Rules and Constitution" and in part from the legal requirements of being a company.
As with the "Marconi Sailing Section Rules and Constitution", these two documents can only be amended by
a vote of the members in an Annual or Special General Meeting.

There is then a third document which is the By Laws.
In exactly the same way as in the "Marconi Sailing Section", these are issued by the Management
Committee and the members can rescind any specific By Law(s) by a motion being put at an Annual or
Special General Meeting.

The Executive and Management Committees in writing the By Laws are taking the opportunity to restructure them
into more defined sections, to better define the classes of membership taking account of views which have been
expressed by a number of members and to revise the sub committees to better reflect the activity of the Club today.
This is taking longer than the Executive visualised providing a problem as we approach the Annual General
Meeting in that we will not be able to complete the exercise, but we need them in place to hold the AGM.
The Management Committee has therefore concentrated on those sections essential to the AGM which are Section
One, the membership classes - Section Two, Annual Subscriptions etc. - and Section Eight, The Executive,
Management and Subcommittees. It should be noted that whilst we believe that we have identified the appropriate
Sub Committees, we still have considerable work to do to define their Terms of Reference and therefore the exact
composition of each one.

We are publishing the complete By Laws in the form that we have currently agreed so that we can elect the
Executive and Management Committees and conduct the other essential business at the AGM.
You will also find the "Memorandum of Association" and the "Articles of Association" as deposited at Companies
House in this issue.

You will see that a great deal of hard work has already been done but understand that we need your support whilst
the all-important fine tuning is undertaken.

Having referred earlier to the Annual General Meeting, you will find the preliminary notice in this issue which
includes the nomination form for the positions to be elected at the meeting.

Neil Pembleton

ECPR 2003 - ANOTHER FINE TEAM EFFORT

Others will talk about the wind — or lack of it . Yet others will report tales of how they lost three places rounding
Colne Point .... and regained them in the bar later. One of the great things about events like ECPR is that it gives
everyone, no matter how small or remote their involvement, plenty to talk about.

I will give thanks. Not just the thanks of the ‘ ..... and a list too numerous to mention’ variety but a more detailed
celebration of all of those many people who contributed to another outstanding event on the international racing
calendar. At a time of significant change within the Club I am given an opportunity to celebrate who we are and
what we do — in an alphabetical listing of all that is ECPR:

Considerations of readability lead me to the view that what follows will work best if I ask my readers to accept now
to my grateful thanks for anything at all they have done to assist the event.

BAR operations is always something of a challenge for an event of this scale. Kevin Kirby pulled together a willing
team of servers. Derek and Doreen Kirby and John and Mavis Weedon provided effective but benign management
of another efficient operation.
BRADWELL OUTDOOR CENTRE and TENDRING DO provide support craft and crews that add strength to
our safety patrols in the Mersea and Jaywick sectors.
CATERING has always been good at ECPR but we have long felt the need to provide a service that was more
versatile and homely. Belinda and her excellent, smiling team achieved this ambition for us handsomely and the
spontaneous applause for my remarks at the Awards Ceremony about them showed that our visitors appreciated the
change too.
_CHARLES ANDERSON may not have been seen or heard over the weekend but no one should doubt his
involvement in setting up and breaking down — not to mention his usual demanding role in pulling together all the
Safety cover. This year this included the creation of a formal Disaster Plan — a huge task.
CLEANING was undertaken efficiently and quietly by Jan and her helpers. A marvellous job done under extreme
pressure.

‘CLEAN UP- quick’ expresses our aims for the day after the event — the need is to remove all traces of ECPR
activity and return the site to normal without delay. An almost invisible army of club members picked litter, cleared
the bars, packed away the marks, removed signage and did all that was necessary to achieve that aim.
COMMITTEE BOAT Duet, owned and crewed by Founder Member Mike Sissons, provided a decorative and
comfortable base for the RO team.
ECPR COMMITTEE is involved year —round in the preparation for and management of such a large event. Here
is a flavour of what they undertake:
e Clive Shenton — trophies, toilets and tape (red)

NEIL, our Commodore, provides a welcome and reassuring presence throughout the weekend — giving a grunt here
and a nod there to help ensure the smooth running of the event but providing valuable back up that can be called on
in times of need.
PRIVATE CHANNEL RADIOS were provided once again by Brentwood Communications and transported by
Jenny Ball
RACE OFFICER Mike Turner brings a wealth of experience to the role and had excellent support from assistants
John Salmon and Graham Borgonon. Nick Miller and Anthony Monks gave valuable support as spotters during the
finish sequence.
RACE RECEPTION is a key area for an event like this. Competitors need to be dealt with efficiently and in a
friendly manner; care needs to be taken to handle the finances correctly; handicap issues and a myriad other
enquiries need to be dealt with and, last but not least, we need to sell Raffle Tickets and Clothing in support of the
charity. Kate Williams led a team that included Alex Shenton , Marion X, Claire Davies, Sarah Davies, Jane
Townsend and Dave Williams in the provision of a first-class service.
RADIO OPERATOR John Pine comes back year after year and looks slimmer, fitter and more dapper every time.
More importantly for us, he does a great job.
RAFFLE management was provided by Christina Hutt and she was supported by Fennella Thomas and small army
of other helpers.
REFUELLING is important in a long distance series. Dave Bladon ensures that essential supplies are in place.
RESULTS processing was again handled in the most efficient manner imaginable by Kate Williams and Jane
Townsend.
RNLI bring a stand, manned by Ron and Mary Greygoose that adds to the ambience.
RUNNER- essential legs (and occasional eyes and ears too) for the OOD were provided by Sarah Davies on the
big day and by Tim Dowley during the build up.
SPECIAL SEASIDE SPOTTERS Tony and Jack Ferguson were deployed at Walton Pier at very short notice to
deal with a potentially serious communications problem. They aided in the provision of essential information. That
info led to the decision to shorten course and so they were able to go home again — without seeing a single
catamaran!
SPONSORS are not always easy to find but their contribution is essential.
TERRITORIAL ARMY involvement was always under threat in 2003. In the event, the support given by Mark
Mackenzie - Bell and his team was as good as we have come to expect and this despite the fact that the team were
new to the event and using equipment that was completely foreign to them
TRACKING TEAM TRIO Mike and Maggie Boreham and Barbara Davies have, for more years than any of
them care to recount, provided an effective and efficient system of recording and reporting competitor positions
along the course. Nice to have for reporting progress but absolutely essential in terms of safety. Quiet, too.
TROPHY TECHNICIAN Mike Richardson gave his usual valuable support.
TROT BOAT services and local support afloat were provided by Lucy Boreham, Joe Ashley, James tovey, Sarah
Davies (yes, the same one — again), Claire Davies and Tim Dowley.
TROLLEYS could be a nightmare but over the years an excellent system has been developed by Phil Davis.
Thankfully, Phil did not see fit to protect his intellectual rights and so Steve Ash and his team adopted the system
and took on the Trolley Parking and scrutineering role this year for the first time. They carried it out with great
efficiency and good humour, making a major contribution to the smooth handling of a large number of craft to and
from the water.
WELCOME BBQ on Friday evening poses a challenge insofar as it is very difficult to predict the numbers on site.
This year the numbers were high and so was demand. Barbara and Sarah Davies (do these people sleep?) had
prepared a range of salads and served them with locally produced hamburgers and sausages. Their efforts paid off —
for the first time in living memory this operation produced a profit and the customers, too, were well satisfied.

Cat Fleet

By the time you read this the Piers Race will be a distant memory and for most of us sailing that day, that will not
be a bad thing. The weather was glorious but the all important ingredient (wind) was at times fickle to say the least.
But let’s not forget the reason for the race; to help children who are less fortunate than us. I would like to give
thanks to many people, too many to mention, for their hard work and commitment. Our donation this year to the
Cirdan Trust will be in the region of £9,000.

Club racing has been very competitive this year, the chute systems on the F18’s seem to aid our speed going around
the cans when working properly, even to the point that Steve Glynn (having had a few days at the F18 Worlds with
son Mitchell) has added a 3TM sail to his Tornado. The latest news however is that Steve has now swapped his
Tornado with son Mitchell’s F18 as he likes the kite so much! Congratulations to Steve and Mitchell who took the
Nacra F18 to Belgium for the F18 World Championships; one of only 7 UK teams at the event, finishing a healthy
mid-table in the silver fleet.

Other fast cat events in the calendar this year included the F18 Nationals in Pwllheli, North Wales over the bank-
holiday weekend. Two F18’s and 1 Spitfire attended from the club. Steve and Debbie Glynn, Christina Hutt and
myself were the only “parents” in addition to the 10 young adults that came along with us, which at times felt like a
2TM! Cadet Week! The weather was generally good although the wind was again hard to find, to the point that only
one race had been completed by Monday after a Saturday arrival. We certainly got our moneys worth on Monday
when we raced 5 races back-to-back, which left us tired to say the least! Pwllheli Sailing Club certainly hosted a
very professional National and is well worth a visit if your class is competing there.

We are now into the Autumn series, so good luck to all competing which if the final results of the Summer Series
were anything to go by (1* place to 3TM place split by 3 points) it certainly should be fun.

The Knoll Trophy Race for Cruisers was run this year for the first time as a Single-handed event. Eleven yachts
came to the MSC Club line and were started by Race Officer Ron Greygoose, on a course down river to the Nass
Beacon and back with a stiff beat to start.

Early leaders were ‘Woody’ in his Hustler ‘Lucy 2’, Roger Brown in Super Seal ‘Out of Focus’ and Nick Hilman
in Memory 19 ‘Lettie May’. “Ocean Slipper’ caught up, and at The Nass it was ‘Out of Focus’ followed by ‘Ocean
