Letters & Articles

2003 Winner of the Mamgu Trophy

“Three men and a Boat — the tale of a yacht delivery”

It all started last summer. Paul a long suffering friend had a garden party to celebrate his sons 21* birthday, and as is the
practice, good food, sun and plenty of alcoholic lubrication lulled one into a sense of self satisfaction and total happiness with
the world. Paul is a bit smart and obviously spotted this and in a moment when my guard was down approached me with a
proposition. | have known Paul for more years than | care to remember so | have become accustomed to some strange
requests, but that might be another story. On this occasion Paul asked if | would be able to help him deliver a yacht he was
buying. Details were sparse, or perhaps| just forgot them in the alcoholic haze but it seemed like a truly excellent idea, a few
weeks in the Mediterranean delivering a sailing boat to Turkey, you would be mad to say no! | checked with my social and
domestic manager (Wendy) who gave it the thumbs up, and the deal was signed with another kebab and a bottle of Becks.

That was that for a few months while Paul went off and organised the purchase a decision that | am sure required something
stronger than Becks when the time came to sign the cheque. Around January this year we started to make plans, routes were
planned; holiday booked the usual sort of thing one does when delivering a yacht from France to Turkey as we all know!
Regular weekly updates then started as the due date drew nearer, we see sawed between France and Croatia as our start
point, as the manufacturer seemed unsure as to where they were in Europe they were going to deliver the yacht. Paul seemed
not to worry about such minor details, perhaps still smarting from the cheque being cashed.

In the end we left Luton airport on sunny March day enroute for the French Riviera, in order to take delivery of “JASSPER’ so
named after Jenna, Alix, Sue, Sam Paul, Early Retirement! The plan being to be ready to sail on the 1°‘ of April, somehow the
significance of this date passed both Paul and myself by. From Nice airport a taxi took us to Antibes marina, where we met
Chris the owner of “Top Yacht’, who would be taking Paul’s boat on for charter use. Chris seemed happy as he told us that
“we” had a small problem, which was that the mast could not be stepped due to a problem with the forestay, so poor Paul's first
sight of his yacht was of one without a mast. No problem said Chris, if we can’t source the part locally one of his guys would be
fly out from the UK Tuesday with the new piece. Nothing could be done so we sent Chris off to buy supper, and we eventually
tucked in to a pizza with some other intrepid charterers.

So, our start date looked already to be in serious jeopardy. Undaunted we booked into a small French hotel and made
acquaintance with Brian who was to be our skipper/navigator for the two week journey, hoping to leave on the Wednesday.
Brian was an experienced Ocean sailor, having sailed the BT Global challenge Southern Ocean leg, surely a skill not needed in
the med! Read on. Trying to put a positive slant on things we decided to use the time to plot our course, provision the boat and
get a sun tan, not necessarily in that order. This meant lots of sitting around drinking coffee, Ok and the odd beer, carefully
scrutinising charts, and making a shopping list. The chart piece was easy when compared to 3 men planning to shop for food for
a 2 week trip is not the sort of exercise that one should expect to go with out it’s problems.

The first of the shopping problems was simply where to go, and it was then that Frank (pronounce this in a heavy French accent
as Fraank for best effect) came into the story. Fraank was a taxi driver with a difference, you could not book Fraank but you
could make an appointment, which Fraank would then negotiate with you as he “may be a /leetie late, or he may not”. Frank also
had an aversion to coins and liked to round up his fare, which was OK as he did have a Mercedes people carrier with TV and
DVD, and he needed to pay for those sharp suits. He also needed to pay for his fuel as Frannk was keen to take short cuts,
which included a trip to his parents apartment on one occasion, (they were not in but on holiday in Dakar we were informed),
and on another occasion to pass by Fraanks own apartment, of which he was particularly proud. Fraank also had an interesting
driving technique which involved often stopping just to talk to people, some he knew some he thought he knew but didn’t, and of
course the meter was always running, “Gentlemen, (long pause for thought) shall | round this up to 25 Euros’?” became a
familiar phrase of Fraanks. You will by now have established that we spent a lot of time with Fraank, and not much sailing.

The shooing trip itself was an adventure; we had our list, carefully prepared by Brian, who sensibly had decided to stay with
JASSPER to check charts (Brian did a lot of chart checking). So Paul and | picked up our two trolleys and set off. It took us
many hours to shop and got some strange looks when we got to the checkout as the mix of produce was heavily in favour of
drink. We both agreed if the bill was too much the bottled water had to go, in preference to the wine, beer and spirits.

The new part needed to allow us to step the mast did actually have to come from the UK and arrived on Tuesday, so we booked
a slot to have the mast stepped on the Wednesday and started to get excited at the prospect that we may soon have a complete
yacht. So Wednesday came and after lots of activity in the boat yard, the mast was put up, but that then meant that the yacht
needed significant work to the electrics and other bits, and all of a sudden she was engulfed with riggers and Paul, Brian and
myself were surplus, indeed seemed to be in the way!

So nothing for it, we needed another taxi trip to the Carrefore for essential provisions, while Brian finalised his chart work ready
for the big off. This time the essentials entailed electric drills, boat shoes (they were such a bargain lets have 2 pairs!), a few
pairs of trousers, yes another bargain, and assorted other bits of hardware to allow Paul to fit another piece of electronics, he
had acquired. On this trip, Fraank decided to just stop and have a little chat with a little old lady and her dog, someone he
thought he knew but actually did not! Never mind the traffic jam he caused finding this out. Paul had a doze as we flew through
the back streets on a detour, “to save time”. Stopping off on F Fraanks parents house again to check the plants were OK. More
on Pauls’ interesting ability to doze almost instantly and anywhere later in the story!

8
In the end the boat was finally ready late Wednesday evening, but by then the weather had changed and sailing was not an
option our skipper told us with some authority, after listening attentively to weather info on channel 68 and studying the synoptic
chart from the Capitainaire, Paul and | nodded with agreement. We did manage two brief shake down sails on the Thursday and
Friday and decided to “go for it” early Saturday morning, the real adventure was about to begin. So it was that at 05:50 on
Saturday the 5" of April, JASSPER with her three intrepid crew left Antibes on route for Turkey.

Our plan was to sail down the eastern coast of Corsica, through the La Magdalena straits and then on to the heel of Italy, then
Athens and finally Bodrum in Turkey. This was ambitious in the time left but fair winds and 24 hour watches might just make it
possible, we convinced ourselves, but contingency was made to stop at Athens and let another crew take over. We soon learnt
that having a contingency plan was an extremely sensible idea.

All went well, for day one we had good breeze as we watched the French Alps disappear slowly from view and then we
were alone in the Tyrannian Sea, with just the dolphins for company.

We decided to eat around 6 that evening, ready for the watch roster and sat down on deck to enjoy hearty servings of
Hot Spaghetti Bolognese, not from a tin or a packet, Oh No! All fresh. Brian our skipper describes this as “Good
Scoff’, Paul and I had shopped well at Carrefore and we felt smug!
We had set ourselves a 3 hour on 6 off watch pattern, and my first night watch went OK, | was on from 21:00 to 00:00
hours and enjoyed a wonderful sunset and a starlight night under a new moon. With great excitement| watched the
odd freighter or cruise liner pass in the distance. The dolphins were still with us and one could see them leave a
phosphorescent trail as they sped through the water only inches from JASSPERs hull.

The next day saw sunshine and the good winds holding for us, as we headed for Bonafacio, at the southern end of
Corsica, we had been told that this was an impressive sight and as the cliffs slowly came into view it was confirmed.
The cliff tops were crowned by a magnificent fortress which just seemed to be hanging on the edge, really impressive.
The sight was so delightful that we decided to stop over for a brief break and get over the slight bout of Mal de Mere
from which | was suffering, | can thoroughly recommend Stuggeron tablets and | don’t know why but regular nibbles of
Ginger Nut biscuits, also helped as a remedy. We stayed just long enough to have lunch, refill with fresh water and
discover that the fuel station was closed, as were most of the shops, it was a Sunday but we had by now lost track of
the days.

So refreshed, off we went with the next planned stop to be Reggio in Southern Italy some 4 or 5 days solid sailing was ahead of
us. The wind had freshened but was steady and the sun stayed with us as we left Bonafacio. We really started to sail the yacht
now, as we had quite a swell and could surf down the waves, good old dinghy tactics. After a little play Brain set our compass
bearing and we and headed for the La Magdalena straits between Corsica and Sardinia. Careful chart work was needed here as
we picked our way through the many impressive but dangerous looking rocks, Brian pawed over his paper charts while Paul
checked his electronic versions on the array of kit that had been fitted and was constantly being added to by Paul as a new bit
of wizardry came out of no where! After a few hours we started out into open water saying good-bye to France and Sardinia, this
was to be our last sight of land for quite a while.

That evening we again dined on deck, | can’t remember the exact meal but seem to recall it had a high pasta content, and again
was “good scoff’ according to Brian, just the stuff to keep your energy up, looking back perhaps Brian was psychic, because we
certainly needed our energy in the next 36 hours. The wind died a little and we decided to use the motor to keep our speed over
ground up to the desired level if we were to make the passage on time. It was around 20:00 hours that the wind picked enough
for us to hoist the main, unfurl the jib, then turned off the motor to enjoy another spectacular sunset over Sardinia, as she
disappeared from view. All was well in the world and as the winds got up slightly Paul started to really sail his boat and was like
a dog with two tails when he saw the boat speed hit 10.44 knots as he surfed us down the waves, great fun. Both Paul and
Brian went below to get some sleep and | took watch at 21:00. It was at about 22:00 that the wind came round to right on our
stern and JASSPER was on a dead run, not comfortable but OK provided concentration was kept up. At around 23:00 hours the
wind was veering and in order to avoid constant Gybes and waking the two down below, it was necessary to bear away from our
true course, the boat speed was averaging about 8 knots as the wind started to freshen even further. Then at precisely 23:30
hours, yes | remember this time exactly, the Depth alarm started to scream at me, we had (it said) only 2.4 metres of water
below us! With a 2 metre keel | was as you might expect just a little concerned. Logic said it was a fault, especially as a similar
incident had affected Paul’s watch the night before. We were at least 40 miles from any land, and nothing was shown on the
chart, but the alarm kept on screaming. But what has logic got to do with decision making! Brian was woken by a couple of
crash gybes and came on deck, to see what was occurring, we tried to reset the electronics but without any success. No
alternative but to get Paul up, as he was in charge of all things technical simply because he had read the manuals, and he liked
to play with these things anyway. After much fiddling, checking of manuals, lots of cursing from Brian, it was decided that the
depth gauge had had it. Paul went back to sleep, we had already learnt that Paul could wake up instantly and fall asleep just as
quickly, it was an art that Brian and | both had not mastered. Anyway, we settled down and Brian took over his watch, and |
decided to stay on deck and have a nap, it was a warm evening and this seemed sensible rather than go below and feel seasick
again! Just as well that | did because at around 01:00 hours the winds started to really pick up to over 20 knots and Brian
thought it would be wise to put a reef in the main, which we did. | was wide awake by now so stayed on deck and in just 30
minutes we had second reef in as the winds had built even further and the boat was beginning to become over powered. The
depth gauge may have given up but the anemometer was working as we had 30 knots of wind showing and a very “confused
sea” to contend with, or as the Italians described it “Molto Mosso”. Two reefs did not help we were screaming along so we had
no alternative but to drop the main. So in rising seas | went below, struggled into my oilskins and was then soon battling on the
foredeck tidying the main while Brian struggled with the helm. Paul slept soundly below! As | put the last of the sail ties around
the main | knew what it must feel like to be in a washing machine, which was not set to the delicate programme, while riding a
roller coaster. So here we were running just under headsail, averaging something like 10 knots, and still the wind built.

The sensible thing now would have been to put up the storm jib. | am sure this is entirely possible but perhaps not sensible as
the boat was now in 18ft seas and | am no mountain goat. So instead we furled the headsail to give us just enough steerage

9
and control, well everything is relative! It needs to be said that at this stage Brian had been at the helm for some 5 hours and
that despite all this activity Paul was sleeping soundly in the sea berth below, which must be a record of some sort. During all
this | tried to maintain the hourly log which at 04:00 hours showed us as having F9 winds, | gave up at 05:00 hours and simply
put in that the log was not completed due to extreme weather conditions, an understatement as just then the squall came the
stars disappeared and we recorded a gust of 42 knots! Suddenly | wished we did not have such a comprehensive set of
instruments on deck! By now Brian and | were both pretty tired, the winds had died back to 25 — 30 knots as Paul emerged from
below asking if we wanted tea! Paul duly took the helm and Brian got some well earned sleep.

As | mentioned earlier, Brian had done the Southern Ocean leg of the BT Global Challenge and he remarked on the similarity of
conditions, albeit the Med was just a little bit warmer when the waves broke over your head! | was feeling much worse for wear
now, having been up for more hours than | can remember | went below feeling decidedly sick! As Paul and Brian soldiered on,
not sure of what else to do, but in the end they decided we were not going to out run this storm, which we later found out was
officially recorded a strong gale, so they turned JASSPER round and headed for a safe haven. After 12 more hours we finally
out JASSPER into Punta Santaldia on the North West coast of Sardinia, for a well earned rest and hot shower, much relieved to
have survived. Cruising in the Med is not meant to be like this! Our schedule had been severely jeopardised, and was not going
to improve until the weather did. We ended up spending 3 days in Punta Santaldia, which would have been nice, if it wasn’t the
off-season, everything was closed, and only the Brits cruise the med in April it seems!

Anyway we amused ourselves by tidying the boat and getting to know the Capo and his staff in the harbour masters office. The
weather did not improve and in order to stop ourselves going crazy we hired a car, mainly as a distraction and means of seeing
the island, which it has to be said was very beautiful if a little rugged, real bandit country. However with a means of travel, Paul
decided we must have a NavTech so we can get some real weather information, much better than relying on the VHF forecasts,
so off we set in search of one.

Two towns and 3 chandlers later no luck but we had some nice Pizza in one of the restaurants we found!
Here is a snap of the motley crew, from left to right Brian, the skipper, Paul the owner, and myself, crew.
After three days we had a window in the weather, the harbourmaster told us, that with a “Capo like Brian” we would be OK.
Brian and the harbourmaster had built up a mutual respect for each others seamanship, even though the Capo as he was
affectionately known to his staff seemed more at home in his sports car. We decide to go that very afternoon. So we waved
good-bye to Sicily and set a course for Reggio in Italy, some 3 days sailing.

The winds held and we made good progress for a day, but we needed to make good headway, as the plan now was to leave
JASSPER in Reggio and let a replacement crew take her on to Turkey. A reluctant decision but the three of us had run out of
holiday and really wanted to get back to the UK for Easter. Whilst in Punta Santaldia Paul had contacted the charter company
and they were sourcing a crew, and his other contacts, namely his daughter Jenna who was organising transport for us back to
the UK. Out of contact we just had to hope the jig saw fitted together.
The first land we sighted was the volcanic group of islands dominated by Mount Stromboli, and we could clearly see the smoke
rising from its peak as we passed less than a mile from it’s shores. Amazingly the side of the mountain was speckled with
houses and other dwellings, clearly the possibility of an eruption held no fear for some!

It was as we passed Stromboli that we encountered a British warship, which we happily hailed on the VHF to check the weather
and also to ask for an update on the Iraqi conflict. The weather info was readily forthcoming but the response on the war was
just a little guarded, but we gathered that Baghdad had fallen, but not much more.

As the winds died we had to start the engine and power sailed our way to Italy, as the med changed from a maelstrom into mill
pond, it seems we had had any wind owing us, and got it all at once! The sea was dead calm as we entered the straits between
Italy and Sicily as the sun started to set. We needed to stay alert as the chart warned of whirlpools and sure enough we saw
these spiralling off our port side, quite strange

We finally made it to Reggio about 21:00 hours on day 13, and picked our way into the little harbour, finally mooring amongst an
assortment of cruising and racing yachts. The final evening meal on board was prepared by my good self and contained pretty
much everything, Brian again described this as good scoff and made an entry in the log to show that my cooking had at last
improved!

Early the next day caught a taxi to the railway station, we planned to travel to Naples and fly back to Stanstead only to be told
that the railways were on strike! Luckily the Italians seem to be very selective when striking, they either didn’t know about it or
they decided not to strike on the Eurostar. So it was with a heavy heart that we said our goodbyes to JASSPER, and Brian, who
was staying on an extra day to greet the new crew, and Paul and | headed off to Naples for our flight home. The adventure
ended at midnight as we touched down in the UK, and already | was missing the experience, how quickly one forgets the misery
of sea sickness, the feeling of being totally saturated, and the experience of not being able to stand up. | arrived home at 1.00
a.m. and am sure | had a grin on my face for at least a week as | recalled the journey and the things we had gone through, do it
again, yes without a doubt.

For those who need to know the yacht we sailed was a Bavaria 36 (but measures nearly 38 ft!) and, she is fitted out with 6
berths and has very spacious accommodation, which includes a good kitchen and head, with shower. Well appointed with all
navigation electronics and CD player etc. She is available for charter and Paul has selected Top Yacht to manage all
arrangements. If interested visit the web site on www.top-yacht.com or call them on 01243 520 950.

| can testify she is a good boat, she, and Brian’s exceptional seamanship, saw us through one hell of a storm

Les Hurrell-Smith

sails in the water on the Pico sailed by Rob Mead. | took the workboat over with Roy Hardwick and Grant Strong as a jumper if
needed. By the time we got to the incident the boys had recovered the rig, made it secure and had the disabled Pico in tow with
the other one sailed by Nick. This all achieved under sail; each boat single handed and with no damage or loss of gear. They

comprehensive cruising and racing programme, to include, following the success in 2003, the Jackpot, and a proposed pursuit
race back from Brightlingsea. | can't wait to see the start out of the harbour for that race! Watch out in Navigans for details of
smaller boat cruising events which we hope to introduce this season.

Commodore’s Comments

What better way to work off the excesses of Christmas than by watching other people exercise? Combine that aim with water,
barges and Morris men and you inevitably find yourself drawn towards Maldon Quay for the post-Christmas Rowing Race run by
Maldon Little Ship Club in support of RNLI. The weather was not so good for the latest running of this excellent event but the
usual large crowd turned out to support the hardy souls who actually go on the water and row or paddle the whole 3.5km
course.

Just by way of scene-setting: the thrill of skating down the paths from the car park is replaced with feelings of wonder at the
decorations around the swimming lake, followed by amusement at the Christmas Trees atop the barge masts and then a variety
of more individual emotions as you finally encounter both bag-piper and aforesaid Morris men as you press against the breeze
on to the crowded quay.

Once again MSC was represented in the race by Claire Davies (Rear Commodore), Jenny Ball (past Rear Commodore) and
David Ball (son of Vice Commodore). Now, two thoughts cross my mind; the first is that you do not need to have a connection
with the Executive in order to compete and, secondly, this trio (assisted by Lucy and Sarah on many occasions) have been the
sole MSC representative team for some years. They've done a great job — they have even won prizes for their fancy dress — but
they might welcome a bit of club support on the water. So how about a few more MSC entries next year — a Cat Fleet Team, a
Cadet Instructors team, a gender-specific team, a Caterers team ... and so on? | will put up a suitable trophy for the winning
MSC boat judged on speed over the course, style (rowing), style (sartorial) and nerve.

This outing provides a good opportunity to meet up with MSC friends, many of whom, as ex-rowers in this event, are keen to
pass on last-minute tips to the present crop of competitors. They do not seem at all perturbed by the fact that they are totally
ignored. So we just revert to the inevitable chat about how many sat down to Christmas Lunch, how much alcohol was
consumed and how long the visitors plan to stay, whilst admiring the inevitable crop of new hats, jackets, scarves and gloves.
Ray, Maureen, Ron and Mary rattled the RNLI collecting buckets and added to the £8000 or so raised for the lifeboats by the
event.

Of course the sadder ones amongst us managed to conduct some Club business along the way. Neil updated me on
some correspondence, Malcolm gave me some useful ideas for the Homepride project and Clive and I inspected the
surface of the car park in pursuit of some ideas we have for the Stansgate site. My close-up photography of the
roadway seemed to earn Barbara a few sympathetic smiles from the more caring members of the Maldon community.

Then back home for Turkey sandwiches — as all good things must come to an end. Happy New Year.

Chris Davies

Safety Co-ordinator

At sea or on the river, we all rely on good seamanship, experience and our mettle to get us through the tasks ahead. The
ultimate goal is to reach our destination safely.

Mother Nature is a fickle thing and she can throw up all sorts of challenges before us. As Sailors we are all too aware that we
have absolutely no control over the elements whilst in the course of sailing. Naturally this can add to the enjoyment of being out
on the water.

Fortunately where we can control safety issues is back on land at the club ground. By their very nature boat yards are extremely
hazardous places but with good husbandry from us all, we can significantly reduce hazards resulting in consigning risks and
unsafe practice to a thing of the past.

We all have a duty to ensure that operational equipment is in good serviceable order. Ladders are a prime example we should
all be mindful that an incomplete/structure-fatigued ladder is a hazard and has the potential to cause harm. Badly positioned
(untidy) chain, buoys, metal poles, ropes, hard core etc. can easily be made safe just by inspection and resiting.

We can all exercise good practice; there were a few near misses last year due to various reasons. We need to work to a 100%
safety factor and should members have any safety concerns please contact me via the spoken word, letter or email.

Safety should concern us all. Here’s to a trouble free year.

Christopher Pitak

COMMODORES REPORT TO THE ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING, 23 NOVEMBER 2003

Two years ago when | was elected to succeed Clive Shenton as Commodore, | did not expect to be involved in buying the site
however remote that possibility was. We all owe a great debt of gratitude to Clive and the team he assembled, which included
Pat Black, Frank Bennett, Dave Thomas, John Bird and others, who produced "The Lifeboat Plan". All that we have achieved
this year stems from that forward thinking and early basic ground work.
During the latter part of last year as the crisis within the MASC unfolded, | was extremely fortunate to have the skills of the
Executive Committee of Pat Black, John Bird, Dave Payne and John Salmon to help map out the way through the tangled mess.
We in turn owe a great vote of thanks to Dave Thomas who was on the MASC Main Committee and ensured that the Sailing
Sections interests were not overlooked.
Once it was apparent that we would need to buy the site, we were able to find a wealth of talent and expertise within the Club to
assist. Amongst many people who helped the Executive were Simon Dawkins, Simon Elwell, Chris Davies, Julian Royle and
Nick and Jan Bevins (I dare not think of the lost hours of sleep that | caused Nick and Jan by asking them to send out letters to
you all). In addition there were two anonymous people who both offered to provide immediate short term funding to buy the site
if necessary.
We all owe a great debt of thanks to Julian Royle who dealt with all the legal matters and John Bird who handled all the financial
negotiations with the bank.. In addition | would like to thank both their wives who not only put up with my incessant chasing but
did not complain (to me anyway) during the last frantic week or two when they were on holiday.
Finally the most important element in our success was you, the ordinary members. The support that you gave us at the Special
General Meeting not only boosted our confidence but also sent a clear signal to the MASC and the bank that you were
determined to succeed. This support was turned into tangible evidence by the response to the Members Loan Scheme.
|, and | am sure that | speak for all the Executive, thank you for this whole hearted support. Any criticism that we heard always
came as positive suggestions with no negative thinking at all.

As a result of the activity this year, | have not been able to pay as much attention to other aspects of the Club as | would have
liked.
Dave Payne and Clive Shenton masterminded the new electricity supply to the Clubhouse and the subsequent rewiring of the
cruiser park. In doing this they were delayed by our inability to place an order with the contractor until the site purchase was
complete. In turn the contractor was then asked to come on site with very little notice. Again many thanks to the cruiser owners
for their co-operation and to the rest of the club for tolerating the disruption at this time of year. Over this winter it is intended to
finish the rewiring required in the Clubhouse (mainly the Dell Bar) and then we will be issued with the certificate showing that we
have a Safe and legal installation.
Murray Bates and his team have so far managed to keep all our equipment running. Of special note must be the strip down,
repair and rebuild of the hydraulic pump engine in the last couple of weeks. | would like to thank all those who work under the
taskmaster. In addition Howard Griffiths and Robin Lovett have replaced the PA system. | understand that they still have some
work to carry out over the winter but it is a great improvement.
Pete Clayton, in addition to master minding the moorings, continues to fire up the team which trains our cadets. In conjunction
with Les Hurrell-Smith and Chris Davies yet another successful cadet week/camping fortnight took place. Many thanks on behalf
of all who attended to everyone who helped them.
Dave Williams and the Sailing sub committee mater minded the excellent sailing programme and co-ordinated all the necessary
support duties. They even managed to get the weather in on the act; its many years since | have enjoyed such a succession of
dry and warm sailing weekends.
Chris Davies and the East Coast Piers team again put their impressive organisational skills to good use and achieved a record
donation to the Cirdan Sailing Trust.
Fenella Thomas and her team continue to expand an already highly successful social programme and | know she is already
working on ideas for next year.

Solo Sailors Sail Together

Solo sailors are always fiercely competing against each other during the season. However, this autumn, over the weekend of
25/26 Oct, all rivalry was put aside as six of us sailed together. (Roger Smith, John Salmon, Malcolm Stuart, Steve Ash, Martin
Hall and Dennis Dear).

Roger had chartered a Sigma 36 "British Beagle"(complete with skipper, well he might come in handy), from Portway Yacht
Charters at Shotley Marina. We met there at 18.00 Friday evening and after collecting our oilskins we stowed all our gear
aboard. After a good meal, some fine ale, enthusiastic chat in the nearby restaurant, we all bunked down on board for the night.

Next morning saw us all up at 07.00 washed, shaved, breakfasted and casting off by 08.00. Once through the marina lock, sails
up, we had the ocean before us. Well, we sailed into the Orwell, passed the Parkstone quay dock area and into the North Sea.
Already the skipper was dispensed with, (or was he guiding us on the course and sailing technique) as solo sailors took the
helm with Malcolm giving us some cheer as he displayed the use of his satellite navigation direction finder.

The plan was to sail into the Deben, which needed to be entered with a good flowing tide, as there is a massive sand bar across
the mouth. Charts were consulted often and a very strict channel was followed which was very circuitous. We all enjoyed calling
out the ever decreasing depth of water below us until the words "ready about —ho " were hollered. With excellent navigation by
the skipper and good helmsmanship, we were into the river and heading up passed the Felixstowe-Bawdsey ferry.

We were now, we thought, free to sail in the Deben, but this is a narrow river. With John at the helm, the channel followed, he
neatly steered us through the many moored boats. We were very lucky with the weather and under a blue sky the river is a very
interesting and attractive one.

We stopped for lunch not far from Waldringfield (good practise here for the helm and crew members to perfect the art of catching
a mooring and tying off). Although the pheasant and port had been left behind, we filled ourselves with food from the many
boxes which Roger had supplied (a great favourite were the "Kit Kats").

We were soon Sailing again, new helm, Steve | think. After some time we expertly picked up a mooring off "The Ramsholt Arms"
where we moored until the next morning. The inflatable dinghy was pumped up and two intrepid explorers rowed ashore to see
if the natives were friendly. There were cheers of delight when they returned, declaring that we had all been booked in for a
meal that evening.

The only difficulty was that there were seven of us and the dinghy only held three. However at the appointed time, three trips
were made, those rowing doing sterling work and soon all were ashore with the inflatable stored.

After some excellent meals, good ale and more banter the clock told us it was time for those three journeys back to the boat.
After more excellent night time rowing we could safely retire to our bunks. As cruiser sailors are well aware the size and shape
of berths vary enormously. Whereas Roger had a "cabin" all to himself (well he did organise it) John volunteered to take the
"letter-box (conjure up your own image of the size of that) and the rest of the crew had something mid-way in luxury.

The Sunday morning started with a hearty breakfast of either grilled kippers or egg, bacon, fried bread and toms. Only kidding, it
was cereal, toast and a piping mug of tea, which filled us up plenty. Turns were taken with the "provisions" duties (which
included the dreaded wiping up). Soon the sails were set and we were retracing our course to re-cross the bar.

As we approached the mouth there were dozens upon dozens of Lazers sailing out to sea for what must have been a very large
open meeting (there could have been a hundred boats) As they formed up for the start they looked a very fine sight.

We were once again in the unrestricted sailing area of the sea and Martin took the helm and put the boat through some parallel
coast sailing. Our heading was northwards, towards the mouth of the Alde, with a fair breeze. After a while, having seen
Bawdsey manor, the clouds started to gather and the wind strength rose. At this juncture John said he would make us all "a nice
cup of tea" and disappeared down to the warm below. He obliviously anticipated the torrential rain and even stronger wind,
which lasted for some twenty minutes. Most sat (racing cruiser style) with their legs dangling over the side as the boat roared
along at tremendous speed while on her side. After the rain stopped and the wind slackened up popped John saying "the teas
nearly ready”.

Later, after surviving a hailstorm, viewed the desolate row of houses at Shingle Street it was time for mugs of soup (and of
course kit kats) .We had sighted the mouth of the Alde and it was now time to turn south and head towards the marina.

Although the wind was reasonable it was noticeable after some time that we were not actually making headway. Engines were
switched on and an uneventful journey was made back to Shotley, except for once incident. Not far from the marina we tried to
pull another cruiser into deeper water as we assumed she had gone aground. We could not move her and had to leave. When
we arrived back in the marina we were informed that she had snagged a submerged buoy. They had to get the big boys out to
free her (at a hefty charge for Sunday afternoon | suspect). Mooring up in the boat's berth, it was a case of all mucking in to
clean throughout the boat.

Roger who organised the trip and shopped for the provisions, which kept us well provided for during the weekend.

‘Muna's' Travels (Edited) Part Forty Two - Tonga to New Zealand.

We motored through the off lying reefs surrounding Tongatapu on the afternoon of Saturday 3rd November 2001, closely followed by
‘Arganauta’ with the prospect ahead of a 1200-mile passage to New Zealand. A fairly modest distance but what had been occupying our
thoughts for some time was that this was a notoriously difficult trip. As we headed south we were coming out of the trade wind belt and heading
into an area of relatively unpredictable changeable weather, similar in many ways to the situation you're in when setting out across Biscay. As
you approach New Zealand you run the gauntlet of a series of fronts crossing the Tasman Sea from Australia. The perceived wisdom seemed
to be to hang back while a front passes through, then go like the clappers, motoring if necessary, to get there before the next one gets you. As
we were comparatively slow and didn't like motoring, | reckoned we would just have to take our chances. | had made my first contact with Des
on Russell Radio the night before and he had indicated that it was a reasonable time to head at least as far as Minerva Reef, 250 miles away.
Minerva Reef, like Beveridge Reef on the way to Tonga, is a reef-lined lagoon with no land. the only difference is that, unlike Bereridge,
Minerva is partially uncovered at low tide. There are in fact two reefs, North and South Minerva, both of which provide relatively secure
anchorages and an ideal place to await a weather window. Our plan was to head for Minerva and then decide where to stop. Having cleared
the pass we set sail and were soon romping along in a fresh north easterly In the early part of the night the wind went to dead astern and we
were in constant danger of gybing, so we dropped the main and set the downwind rig of yankee and genny, poled out on either side. Our
repaired Monitor self steering got back to work without any fuss. Our 'repaired' autohelm had fallen apart again as soon as we had set it up so
we were relying on our wind vane. The next 2 days were very straightforward with steady winds from the north east and by Monday afternoon
we were fast approaching North Minerva Reef. 'Arganauta' had arrived there earlier that day and we reckoned we could get in by nightfall. It
was tempting to stop, especially as the New Zealand-based weather guru Bob McDavitt was advising people already in Minerva not to leave
before Thursday morning at the earliest to avoid a low currently passing below Minerva. My concern was that if we waited until then, the next
window would not be big enough for us and we would be caught out. | therefore reasoned that we might as well keep going and get a head
start, and gamble with this current low.

So we kept going. We passed quite close to South Minerva in the dark. By morning the rain started as we hit the front and it didn't really stop
for at least two days. By the evening the wind had backed to the north west and we had to dismantle the downwind rig. | was on watch at the
time and had gone below briefly. When | came back on deck, something just didn't feel right and then | realised we were heading in the wrong
direction! Early on Wednesday morning we crossed the 180 degree meridian and we were back in the eastern quadrant for the first time since
before we had left England. Now there really was no doubt that we had come half way round the world. By that evening the wind was up to 35
knots and we were down to reefed yankee, staysail and trysail. With the wind just aft of the beam we were sailing really comfortably at 6 to 7
knots. With the increase in wind, the rain had also become torrential. By this time the boat was beginning to fill up with wet clothes. Another
problem was that, moving into higher latitudes after all that time in the Tropics, we were really feeling the cold, especially when we were wet.
Soon after midnight on the Wednesday the wind suddenly dropped and went into the south west. We managed to keep sailing. By the morning
the wind was just east of south. We put the main back up and were sailing in calm seas and brilliant sunshine, only slightly off course, at up to 4
knots. The wind dropped further overnight but we kept on sailing - just! By Friday the seas were still calm, the sky still blue, but the wind was
up to a south easterly 10-15 knots. We had a superb day's sail until about 10.30 that night when the wind dropped completely and we resorted
to our first spell of motoring. By the morning the wind had got up just enough to get us sailing again and give us yet another glorious day. Once
again at night the breeze died but we persevered until it had deserted us completely. At one point our GPS showed us making 3.1 knots in 5.8
apparent wind. That's pretty good for us! On the Sunday the wind did not get up as expected so we had our first day of motoring. The sea
really was like a millpond. That evening, Des on Russell Radio, told us about an intense low developing in the Tasman Sea that was expected
to give winds further down of 40 or 50 knots plus. He was advising boats in our area to go back above the 30 degree south line. It seemed silly
to take unnecessary chances so we drifted all night and when conditions allowed in the morning, started sailing slowly northwards. Pat and
Olivia on 'Aldebaran' had left Tonga 3 days before us and had stopped at Minerva Reef, coming on a couple of days after we had passed.
When Des advised us to stop, they were about 100 miles behind so we gradually got quite close, though we never actually saw each other. We
did get a couple of sightings of other boats as we all jilled about. It was actually quite pleasant as the sea was almost totally calm and the
weather warm and sunny. We spent the time cleaning up and making sure everything was well tied down and in good order. With no wind it
was like being at anchor. During this time 'Arganauta’, 'Stella' and ‘Maritime Express' that had left Minerba Reef a couple of days after
‘Aldebaran' were gradually catching up. After a couple of days the front had moved through but had not been anything like as bad as had been
expected. Winds had got up to about 30 knots from the North West which would have suited us fine. As it was, when given the all-clear we
headed south only to run into 36 hours of 30 knots from the south west, right on the nose! Desperate not to lose too much ground we held up
as close to the wind as we could. The seas were decidedly lumpy and, with the wind, the rain returned and we were back to soggy sailing.

After a couple of days the wind dropped and for a while we enjoyed some good sailing again. Then on the Friday the wind had gone completely
and we had little choice but to motor. By the afternoon the breeze filled in enough for us to have a very pleasant sail. This kept up until the
early hours of the morning when it headed us and died. In truth the whole trip was characterised by this stop-start, all or nothing, type of sailing.
We started the engine and motored towards the Bay of Islands, getting our first sighting of New Zealand at about 6 in the morning on Saturday
17th November 2001. We were getting all sorts of ominous forecasts as we motored in a flat calm across the Bay. As the Bay opened up it
kept reminding us of the Fal that had been our last sight of England 2 % years earlier. We started seeing other yachts and then we were
approaching the Customs Dock, almost exactly 2 weeks after leaving Tonga. Not one of our fastest passages, but certainly one of the most
varied. We couldn't believe how often and quickly we had seen the ocean change from flat calm to highly confused and back again. We almost
had a nasty incident as we came alongside the Customs Dock when the throttle cable on the engine chose that moment to disengage itself from
the engine. We drifted into the dock without a problem however, and were greeted by the very efficient but friendly officials. They confiscated
some foodstuffs, but not nearly as much as we had been led to believe they would. “They” proved to be surprisingly relaxed about the whole
process. They were training a sniffer dog that previously only worked at the airport, so we were treated to the fascinating spectacle of this dog
enthusiastically examining every locker on the boat!

Within an hour or so we were secure in the marina, our first marina berth for well over a year. We had our first walk that evening on New
Zealand soil. We had arrived.

Muna's Travels. Part Forty Three - North Island, New Zealand - Bay of Islands

After our arrival on 17th November 2001 in the Bay of Islands, and the reality that we had actually arrived had begun to sink in, we began to
settle down to life in New Zealand. First of all we had to survive the arrival celebrations! For the last few days of the passage, Terry on 'Stella’,
who was just behind us and gaining fast, had been threatening a rum-drinking session on arrival. They arrived just a few hours after us so there
was no escape! A number of boats that we had got to know across the Pacific arrived either just before or just after us, so all in all there was
much merriment and conviviality. The focal point for most of this activity was the Opua Cruising Club situated next door to the marina. It proved
to be a really friendly club complete with bar and good food. In spite of having a reputation for being the most expensive marina in New
Zealand, we found Opua Marina to be extremely good value, particularly by English standards. We soon discovered that if we paid for three
weeks we could stay for a calendar month. The total cost was the equivalent of what we had paid for a week in a marina in Poole just before we
had left England. Being in a marina for the first time for over a year gave us the opportunity of having a really good clean up and for tackling
some of the jobs that urgently needed attention. Not least of these was the exhaust system on the engine, which had caused a fire in Bora Bora

and could have been extremely nasty. Although | had repaired the system as best | could, | had been extremely concerned about it. Luckily,
even before we had arrived in Opua, Richard on 'Fair Hippolyta' had given me the name of a diesel mechanic who not only knew all about
Perkins Primas but also actually liked them! | quickly made contact with Brian who gave the engine a good going over and fabricated a new wet
exhaust system as a replacement for the one that had given us problems. We took out the flexible water tanks from the bilge. Water from these
tanks had tasted a bit nasty for some time. Taking them out allowed us to give the bilges a really good clean. All in all it was good to have the
opportunity to give everything a good going over.

A slight complication was that two weeks after our arrival in New Zealand our youngest daughter Jenny and her boyfriend Rob flew in to New
Zealand for a three month stay. This had been arranged some time before and we were looking forward to seeing them. However, while on the
one hand we still had plenty to do on the boat after a busy year, on the other hand, it would have been strange not to meet up straight away,
knowing they were in the same country as us. In the event it all worked out well, but it just meant that they had two weeks in the marina at a
time when they were understandably keen to get moving. They did manage to see quite a lot of the immediate area in spite of a spell of
unsettled weather, which gave us rather a lot of rain. During this time we also had an overnight visit from Derek Hall from Marconi Sailing Club
with his nephew, which gave us a chance to catch up with news from the club and prove that we could sleep 6 on the boat. | was slightly miffed
that the club had found it necessary to send someone down to verify the fact that we had actually arrived in New Zealand!

By the time our month in the marina had passed, we had had a pretty good sort-out and were looking forward to seeing more of the superb
cruising ground that we were in the middle of. A number of locals commented on the fact that many long distance cruisers either went into the
marina and stayed there, or set off down the coast, without really exploring the immediate area which has a reputation for being one of the best
cruising areas, if not the best, in New Zealand. One advantage of Jenny and Rob arriving when they did was that it motivated us into leaving
the marina comparatively quickly when we could have easily found a number of excuses for staying put. Almost as soon as we got out into the
islands, the weather responded by brightening up and becoming warm and settled. We landed on Moturua and Urupukapuka. These islands
were once home to numerous Maori tribes. They have been more recently farmed by European settlers. Now owned by the Department for
Conservation, it is possible to take advantage of the many secluded anchorages and landing places. Whichever way the wind is blowing, there
are always sheltered anchorages to choose from. We had a wonderful time basking in the warm sun, which at times felt as hot as in the tropics,
and cooling off in the bracing clear water. Rob proved adept at collecting fresh mussels and oysters off the rocks which put him in Helen's good
books very quickly. While in the marina Rob had done a repair job on Little Mu, our seahopper sailing dinghy, which we had carried halfway
round the world without using as much as we thought we would. This was now the ideal time to make up for that.

We sailed out to Cape Brett, the southern extremity of the Bay of Islands and, hovering off Piercy Island which features the infamous ‘Hole in the
Rock’, prepared to traverse the hole on our RIB. Jenny wasn't too keen at first, so Helen went through with Rob at high speed. | looked on
enviously. While we were in the marina we had got the local Yamaha agent to service the Yamaha 8 that we had bought second-hand in
Panama. He had also fitted fins. The result was that our RIB would now plane with two on board (out of Helen, Rob or Jenny). If | wanted to
plane, it was a solitary activity! Later on we polished the underside of the RIB with the result that Helen and | could plane in calm water. When
Helen and Rob had been through and circuited the island, returning through a narrow pass between Piercy Island and a smaller rock, it was
Jenny's and my turn. Travelling at a more sedate speed we experienced quite a swell while in the Hole. All in all an exhilarating experience that
has become an important feature of the area. Several fast boats operate out of the resort of Pahia with the express purpose of taking people
through the Hole.

It was now fast approaching Christmas (2001) and the crew decided unanimously that we should have a get together with Laura who, almost
since our arrival, had been working on a fruit and veg farm near Kerikeri. She had Christmas and Boxing Day off and so we picked her up on
Christmas Eve and made our way to the Tua Puna Inlet just behind Kerikeri. We had a beautiful sheltered bay almost to ourselves and spent a
warm sunny and lazy Christmas, swimming off the boat, sailing the dinghy and exploring the shore. Later in the day we had oysters (courtesy of
Rob) and champagne (courtesy of Derek Hall) on the aft deck, before enjoying a superb Christmas dinner (courtesy of Helen). To cap it all, it
was the first Christmas that Helen and | had spent with both Laura and Jenny for about 5 years. On Boxing Day we had a leisurely sail through
the islands back up to Opua where we anchored in the bay opposite the marina. The next day Terry and Aerial from ‘Stella’ kindly lent us their
car to take Laura back to the farm. The weather had broken and we returned to the boat to find Jenny and Rob becoming a little restless.
Luckily the next day the weather improved and we set off for the outer anchorages once more.

When we had first arrived in New Zealand | had contacted my cousin Ginny who | hadn't seen for more than 50 years and who had moved to
New Zealand with her husband and 3 sons in the 70s. She reminded me on the phone that the last time she saw me; | was a chubby toddler
with short legs. On hearing this Laura commented that in that case Ginny wouldn't have any trouble recognising me! | phoned Andrew, Ginny's
eldest son, and he told me that his family always camped over Christmas and New Year at Matai Bay further up the coast from the Bay of
Islands. | looked up Matai Bay on the chart, thought it looked interesting and decided that it would be the place to aim for in the New Year.
Sailing out of the Bay of Islands for the first time we headed up the coast and negotiated a course through the Cavali Islands. it was a bit
shallow in places but there were no real problems. By this time, with the wind heading us, we were motor-sailing. We skirted Flat Island and
bore away for the narrow entrance to Whangaroa. This entrance is very difficult to spot from any distance off. The wind suddenly got up to 25-
30 knots and Rob caught a fish. In the midst of the confusion we located the entrance and steamed in. It was like entering a fjord. The narrow
entrance with towering cliffs either side opened up into a long sheltered lagoon. Sufficiently shallow to anchor almost anywhere you wanted to,
the water was deep enough for most yachts right up to the sides. A perfect anchorage.

The next day we set off early with little wind, heading still further north. As we motored across the wide expanse of Doubtless Bay in brilliant
sunshine, the wind gradually increased right on the nose. We tried sailing for a while but progress was so slow that we reverted to motor sailing.
As we closed the headland on the far side of Doubtless Bay, with Matai Bay just around the corner, there were some isolated rocks to negotiate,
and then we were in the bay. The bay is divided into two by a mini headland and we chose the southernmost of the two bays, as it appeared to
be the most sheltered in the northerly wind that we were experiencing. Since speaking to Andrew a few weeks before, | had lost his mobile
phone number. Consequently we had no idea exactly where to find them. From the boat, the camp looked fairly extensive. Having launched
the dinghy we made our way ashore. After wandering around for some time we found the camp warden who took us straight to Andrew and his
family. Andrew and his partner Shiree and their children Kiri and James, camp there every year with Shiree's three sisters and their families and
their father George. It was quite a group and we had a great reunion. The next day was New Year's Eve. Andrew and Shiree and some of the
others came out to the boat. George in particular kept marvelling at the way in which we had all come together. That night we had a superb
party ashore, culminating in seeing the New Year in from the top of the Headland, illuminated by a full moon. A magical night.

After a couple more days we bid our farewells and made our way south across Doubtless Bay in a flat calm. Although the sky was completely
clear, in the distance we could see a fog bank obscuring the coast to the south of Doubtless Bay. As we neared it, the line became even
sharper and we could see boats disappearing into the bank. We carried on with some trepidation, but just before we hit the fog bank it lifted just
enough for us to pass below it. We went through the narrow entrance to Whangaroa and anchored alongside 'Stella' who had come up from
Opua a couple of days earlier. A little later, ‘Theresa Two’, another Canadian boat, came up from Opua and a party was soon in full swing! We
ended up staying in Whangaroa for two weeks. After a couple of days Jenny and Rob caught the coach south to Auckland to stay with Andrew
and Shiree, before hiring a car to start exploring the rest of New Zealand. Helen and I had a pleasant week in the company of ‘Stella’ and for a
little while ‘Theresa Two’. We climbed up to a rocky outcrop known as the Duke's nose, did some fishing, walked on the beach, found a
waterfall and a spot of socialising! Then we had a lovely sail in company with ‘Stella’ back to the Bay. Sailing up to Opua was beginning to feel

11

Cruiser owners, please remove your tenders from the rack prior to the February working party. 12 j|
like coming home. After a few days at anchor we moved back into the marina and set about tackling more jobs that hadn't been done for quite a
q
while, like replacing all the toilet piping and cleaning out the holding tank. This had been necessitated by a complete blockage which occurred, %
fortunately, when we were on our own. As it was, the business of replacing the old system made me persona non grata for a couple of days.
People would approach along the pontoon and then rapidly back away!

Some time before, we had arranged a trip with Malcolm and Margaret from Marconi Sailing Club. They were visiting their son and his family in
Australia and Margaret had arranged the sailing diversion with us in the Bay as a surprise for Malcolm's birthday. When she heard about this,
Laura asked if it was meant to be a pleasant surprise! It all worked out extremely well. They only had about 5 days with us but we all had a
really good time in spite of the fact that it rained on a couple of days and Malcolm has a serious aversion to rain! One rainy day was spent
hiking round the island of Urupukapuka, quite a distance, and on another we visited the township of Russell. In the days of the whaling ships,
Russell had a reputation as the hellhole of the Pacific, full of brothels and alehouses. Malcolm was disappointed to find that it is now a rather
twee little place. In between the rain we basked in the sunshine in some lovely anchorages, while Malcolm got quite serious about his fishing
and Margaret soaked up the atmosphere.

After they had gone Helen and | went back into the Bay for a few days. We then made the momentous decision of doing a bit of exploring away
from the boat! Leaving Muna well secured in the marina we caught the coach to Auckland where we stayed with Andrew and Shiree in their
beautiful house. We made good use of their swimming pool and sauna and finally met up with my cousin Ginny. We had a really good time
getting to know each other. We hired a car in Auckland for eleven days and set off on a tour of the Coramandel Peninsula and the central
thermal area of the North Island. The scenery was breathtaking and the geothermal activity startling. We basked in thermal mineral pools,
walked across heath land with bubbling mud pools and towering geysers. We got back to Muna just in time to welcome Helen's cousin Michael
and his wife Susan whom| had first met when we had stayed with them in Toronto during our Canadian excursion. My introduction to Michael
had been, in fact, being whisked across Canada in his tiny Cherokee Piper, initially flying low over hills to the east of Montreal under a building
storm and then following the St Lawrence down to Toronto. During our stay in Toronto Susan had done a wonderful job of taking us round all
the sights. She had been fascinated by our ‘Muna’ trip but confessed to a deep fear of the sea and boats. It was therefore with some
trepidation that we approached their visit! The challenge was to provide enough excitement for Michael and a minimum of frights for Susan.
Initially we weren't helped by an uncharacteristically swelly sea in the Bay. Susan was stoical however and we reached a sheltered anchorage
without too much alarm, even when a squall temporarily reduced visibility to a minimum. We had several peaceful days in the islands with the
weather co-operating for the most part.

Towards the end of their time with us there was one last chance to visit the infamous Hole in the Rock. Michael was predictably keen, | got the
distinct impression Susan preferred the option of moving to another quiet sheltered bay. In the end we decided to head out towards the Hole in
the Rock and see what conditions were like. Unfortunately a swell had built up again. It's a fair way out to Cape Brett, off which Piercy Rock
with its Hole lies, and with Muna's ever dirtier bottom, progress was decidedly slow. As we approached the Hole | was alarmed to see white
water breaking in the entrance. We decided to go round the rock to what was today the leeward side to see what conditions were like there. It
was still very swelly and | had a real skipper's dilemma. If things went wrong | would be responsible for a very nasty situation, if| backed down
would | be able to live it down? | decided to take a closer look. Michael and | donned lifejackets and got into the dinghy. | approached the hole
with caution and then decided to go in. The swell was quite bad so | accelerated and was through. As | looked back the water was breaking
behind us so we rejoined 'Muna' by motoring round the rock.

From Internet:
The Hole in the Rock, off Cape Brett, has been etched by wind and wave in the Bay of Islands north of Auckland,
New Zealand. Boat cruises in the Bay of Islands may attempt to sail through the Hole in the Rock, more like the
eye of a needle, when the tide is ‘right. As well, there are jetboat rides that bring you through the Hole in the Rock in
a heart-stopping rush. Most cruises depart from Paihia.

Soon after Michael and Susan left us it was time to lift 'Muna' out of the water, which we did at Ashby's yard just upstream from Opua Marina.
We knew the bottom was bad but it was still a shock to see oyster shells and barnacles four inches deep on the keel. We then started refitting
in earnest, particularly in the galley area. After 3 weeks we closed up shop and headed down to Auckland to fly back to England for our first visit
since leaving nearly 3 years before.

Malcolm Shaft

Commodore’s Comments

| know that many of you will be beavering away at home with a variety of decoration, repair and improvement jobs that you fully
intend (honest) to get out of the way before the sailing season starts. It is certainly like that at Chez Davies.

Down the road at Stansgate, similar things are going on or are about to happen. The committees and those who work
on them have been busy over the last few months deciding on the priority issues and working out how to deal with
them. Work is about to start in a number of areas and
| want to share the good news with you.

The Ladies changing area is to be given a face lift with the installation of new vanity units (smart bowls in a counter top) and re-
tiling of the shower cubicles. Steve Glynn will lead a volunteer gang in installing these items, which are paid for out of our
normal maintenance fund.

We have responsibility for maintenance of the access road to the site (with a small contribution due from the farmer) and have
instructed a contractor to undertake repairs to the badly deformed section of road close to the Eagle gates. This will be done
during early March and is to be paid for out of our normal reserves. It is important that this work is done before this section
deteriorates any further.

We have been concerned that our tractor fleet — essential to the general maintenance of the site, handling club boats and
moving member's boats — should not be compromised by the failure of the big four wheel drive tractor. It hasn’t happened yet
but, if it did, spares are almost impossible to source. Paradoxically, that tractor has a fair value (to those who value vintage farm
machinery) so long as it is running. So the decision has been made; using reserves built up for the purpose, we have bought a
replacement machine and sold the old one to a good home. Many thanks to Peter, Derek and Murray for their efforts in
identifying and tracking down a suitably ‘low-tech’ machine to suit our purpose and our pocket.

Another concern has been the appearance and condition of the road and ground around the east side of the clubhouse. It has
deteriorated slowly over the recent past and has been seriously affected by the general wear and tear caused by the electricity
work. Simple making good was not the whole answer. Drainage has been so poor that some wag has posted a sign announcing
the Windsurfer Training Lake at the bottom of the road.... and we have lived for years with a terrible hump in the entrance to the
Cat field.

Improving this area will be a significant step towards addressing some of the issues that underlie our Homepride initiative —
protecting our investment, improving our environment and making ourselves more attractive to visitors and potential new
members. Accordingly, we have issued invitations to tender and awarded work to renew section of the road, install new
drainage, remove the Cat field hump and install Grasscrete (load bearing concrete with grass inserts) to wide flanks on either
side of the new piece of road. You might need to see it to understand exactly what | mean but you will understand, | feel sure,
that the overall appearance and usability of the area will be improved. This work will be funded from excess monies generated
through the Members’ Loan scheme and should be completed by mid March.

Thanks to everyone for all the thought and effort that is going in to these important projects... and to the rest of you for all you
will do at the Working Party at the end of February.

Now, back fo that tiling.....

Chris Davies

in brief are as follows:

Starting Procedure — All seemed happy with current procedure.
Flags vs. Boards — This was debated at length since many times during racing, the flags are not clearly visible, so perhaps a
drop down board system would be an advantage.
Air Horns — These are being looked into.
Racing Programme

This year’s programme is already complete but discussions were held for the 2005 season. Should there be more...

Pursuit Races — Response: Yes
Long Distance Races — Response: Yes
All in Races — Response: Yes
Cat Cruising Event — Response: No because generally people thought that Camping Fortnight offered ample time for this.
Spring/Summer/Autumn Points — Are there too many races in each series, since there is only 4 or 5 boats (or less in each
class) which can put in enough starts to stand a chance of winning anything — hence the feeling it would be worth shortening the
series and slotting in more races as suggested in Points 1, 2 and 3.

Proposed New Wind Generator Arrays

On the 10 February | attended a special meeting of BACSPA held at the Tollesbury Sailing Club. Not only regular
representatives from the Blackwater clubs attended but representatives from other associations including the PLA as
well as the RYA were there.

The DTI are in the process of formulating their plans for phase 2 of wind generation of electricity in the Thames Estuary. There
will be an extension to the Gunfleet site and generators will be placed on the Inner Gabbard and Galloper banks. The most
controversial new site is the proposed London Array. They plan to have wind generators extending from the Long Sand across
the Knock Deep to the Kentish Knock. The site also butts up against the navigable channel in Fishermans Gat, which is now
used by commercial shipping. It will result in the loss of Foulgers Gat. This is a narrow gutway used only by small craft and is
part of one of the safest routes across the Thames Estuary. It keeps commercial shipping and small craft apart. The cables
carrying the electricity generated may well be brought ashore between Jaywick and Walton with inevitable areas of prohibited
anchoring in the Wallet. This could have implications for the mother craft in the ECPR. The DTI will have the power of the
Electricity Act, which will enable them to deny the right of navigation in any channel they consider necessary.

At this stage the DTI plans appear ill informed of nautical considerations for all types of marine traffic and not just sailing boats.
It is essential the RYA receive our support in representing our interests. To achieve this they need to know the strength of
feeling in the member clubs. If you have ambitions to sail round to Ramsgate or Dover or if you are likely to cross the North Sea
to Ostend or Flushing write to the RYA and let them know your feelings about the proposal. If you take part in or support the
ECPR write to the RYA to make them aware of the effects that areas of prohibited anchoring could have in the conduct of the

8
race. Let us ensure that arrays of wind generators are installed and located where they will not be a hazard to small craft under
sail. Note that the cut off date for comments to the RYA is 1Mar.’04.
Dave Steward

View from the Rear

At this time of the year, you would think that the Sailing Sub Committee would have nothing to talk about. The programme is in
place, support boat rotas are published and getting a little fine-tuning, and the race officer rota is complete (you will have seen it
elsewhere in this Navigans — time to get those diaries out again).

And yet we have plenty to talk about. The ‘Foresail’ initiative that | mentioned last month has gripped the Sailing Sub’s
imagination, and a recent brainstorming session has left us with a huge list of ideas to try and make some sense of. We are
actively looking for more ideas: if you have a view on our current sailing activities, their strengths and areas of opportunity, your
fleet captain wants to hear from you! We will, | am sure, be working on ideas in a fairly abstract way for the next couple of
months, with the aim of presenting a set of proposals to you later in the season. So far we have looked at racing, cruising,
interaction between the fleets, exposure to the wider sailing community, and class and sailor development. There are sure to be
other areas to look at that we haven't got to yet. If you have one in mind, let your fleet captain know.

On a less idealistic note, the club will again be funding a number of members in achieving their RYA level 2 Powerboating for
support boat purposes. If you are interested in doing this course at Bradwell, please let me, or your fleet captain, know.

The more competitive sailors amongst you will know that the Marconi Challenge Cup, a remnant of BJRC dinghy series of yore,
has been one of the less popular events in our programme. It has always been run as an open event, although we haven’t had
any visitors for several years, and it’s Saturday timing doesn’t really draw in the punters. In 2004, the Marconi Challenge Cup
will run as a club trophy event on Sunday, 6" June, to a new format. But what format? The Sailing Sub are trying to devise an
event that will be out of the ordinary for our sailors, and one that is truly a challenge. We have a few ideas, but if you would like
to add to them, we’d love to hear from you.

So that’s the big vision, initiative stuff out of the way — now it’s back to getting the boat ready for next season!

Club Notes

Commodore’s Comments

Maintaining membership levels is an important part of our plan for survival as an independent club. Improving membership
levels will enhance our security and, in the longer term, allow us to improve our facilities. Open Day on Saturday June 5" will
therefore be an important event for the new club; important as an opportunity to showcase our facilities and activities to potential
new members and important as a vehicle for publicity for the club in a range of media. So, even if it snows on the day, we will
maximise the attention we can get for the club just through publicising the event far and wide.

If Open Day is going to work it will have to be a whole Club event — with everyone possible involved in some way or other. Our
visitors will need to be met at the gate, greeted at Reception, showed round the facilities, briefed on safety, taken afloat, fed and
watered, entertained and signed up. The site will need to look the best we can make it and there will need to be a lot of activity
both on and off the water.

We don’t know how many people our advertising and PR activity might attract but there is something that almost every one of us
can do to swell the numbers: bring a friend! Most of us will know someone — a neighbour, friend or colleague who is a potential
club sailor. Don’t worry about whether they will join now, in the near future or whether they will necessarily join at all — if they are
interested, will enjoy an active, fun day out and above all will talk to their friends and colleagues about MSC and what a good
Club it is, they are the people we need to target. Please give all the support you can to this important event. Don’t wait to be
contacted — if you have an idea speak to Fenella Thomas(Social); Claire Davies(Fleets); Ray Ball (Premises) or Simon Elwell
(Publicity) — their contact details are in the year book.

Recent attendance at an RYA Regional Forum (a perk of this job!) was an interesting and worthwhile experience. It prompted a
couple of thoughts about our own situation. The presence of our late twenties Rear Commodore gave some balance to an event
where the average age, including Claire, was mid-sixties. It underlined the value for me of the small steps we have taken in
recent years to balance the age profile in our own committees. We need to do more.

Mark Bulkely our very own Olympic hopeful names Marconi SC as his home club on a website at www.gbrtornadogold.com.
Keep an eye on this as the preparation programme progresses. We have been in contact with Mark to tell him of the interest
and support we have in and for his efforts.

A surprise for me this month was the news that Patrick Black intends to stand down as Club Secretary - once we have found
and bedded in a replacement for him. My personal disappointment at losing the services of someone who has served with

WASTE NOT WANT NOT (OR, PUT ANOTHER WAY, YOUR WASTE IS NOT WANTED)

A concerted effort has been made recently at the working party and other ‘events’ to remove waste from the site. This is
expensive both in financial terms and for the amount of members’ time and physical effort involved.

It is accepted that certain large items present their own problems of disposal, but please assist as far as possible by taking your
waste away with you.

For example | have recently taken someone’s old battery to the recycling centre and another has now appeared by the skip. If
you bring a new battery down for your boat, please take the old one away. (Your recycling centre will take it.)

Similarly, at the last count, | found six old sailboards on the site. If you have finished with your old sailboard, dinghy or what-
have-you please dispose of it yourself (off site).

Other than domestic waste for which we use the Waste-eater we don’t have a waste collection service at the site. If we did, or if
legislation forces us to in the future, it would have to be paid for out of subscriptions.

If you feel that you have finished with something which could be a real asset to the club please approach a committee member
before bringing it down or leaving it at the site. This is to ensure that what you have to offer is likely to be useful without adding
another maintenance task to somebody's list of duties; or cluttering up the place for years before it gets used. Even a seemingly
generous gift can have maintenance and safety implications.

GROUNDWORKS

The groundwork to improve the site near the clubhouse is progressing well. The area has been fenced off to ensure safety and
to prevent disturbance of the newly laid concrete. The fencing will remain in place for some time after the contractors have left
site to ensure the concrete has fully hardened before we (or worse, the various delivery lorries that visit the site) drive over it.

Please do not move any of this fencing even if it looks as though the work has all been finished. The experts tell me that a

A big "Thank You" from The Cirdan Sailing Trust

The Cirdan Sailing Trust have written to thank the members of Marconi Sailing Club for the large donation
received following the 2003 East Coast Piers Race.

Enclosed with their letter were copies of letters received from many of the young people who were able to
take part in sailing with the help of a bursary received from The Cirdan Sailing Trust - the bursaries made
possible by fund raising events like the ECPR.

Here are some extracts:

Thank you, Marconi Sailing Club, for your kind assistance in helping the Children’s Care Campaign to take a group of children
sailing in September 2003. The children that we provide activities for would not get the chance of experiencing life on a sailing
barge if it were not for people like your-selves. The children we work with are all social worker referred and come to us for a
number of different reasons; this may be from a simple lack of money in the household to children who live in difficult situations.

From our diary:

Time to set sail. We could not have wished for better weather, plenty of sun and enough wind to make it interesting
for the kids. Once they got the hang of what to do on the Barge they even started to work as a team. On Sunday
morning all of the kids, and some of the adults, had the chance to climb the rigging which we all enjoyed.

aware of all our needs! The week really made me think about sailing as a possible career and I would love to be able
