Bass Strait News (or Rays Ramblings)

Well we have been away for 6 months now and we are glad to read in Navigans that you are all busy back home with working
parties and fitting out so we thought it was time to send news from Down Under.

September
We arrived to a drought and water restrictions which was somewhat odd as it did not stop raining for days. So after checking
that Cats Chorus was still alright, as we had left her for 7 months, we opted for a quick ski trip and a long weekend walking in
the Grampians. | think we needed a bit of a holiday after the last few hectic months in the UK.

October
Still raining and cold but work commenced on the boat, having two hulls to rub down and antifoul instead of one made for a very
grumpy Jackie. Funny how Ray always seems to disappear and have urgent technical jobs to do at the onset of any nasty,
manual work! One gentleman in the boatyard was so concerned that he lent Jackie his mask.

We hit a slight problem when Ray inspected the fuel tanks and discovered that they were afloat in 150 litres of water! It seems
that the angle the boat had been left sitting on the trailer, the inspection hatches, sealant and unusually high rainfall associated
with the drought had given us our first problem. That took the rest of October!

November
Finally all the underwater jobs were completed and we were ready to launch, a very familiar experience involving a tractor,
trailer and winch. Unfortunately we did not float off with the afternoon tide even with some pushing and shoving as it was inches
away from leaving the trailer. This meant that when we did float off it was at 4am in the morning, what do you do when it is pitch
black, misty and you are in a mangrove creek? Ray decided that it would be a good idea to attach your prop to the anchor
chain of a nearby mooring, which was very effective! So in to the not so warm, muddy, crab infested creek he went to sort out
the mess.

By Thursday 13" we had moved to live onboard at last and were extremely happy to be in Hastings marina, Western Port, our
home for the next 3 months.
Work commenced on installing the new hydraulic steering system which seemed to involve a lot of crawling around and getting
in to tight spaces in order to fit 50 metres of copper tubing around the boat. We also fitted an emergency steering system.

The marina is on the Mornington Peninsula so we had a few trips out to the local vineyards or wineries as they call them to
commence the task of provisioning. This involved several visits and much sampling in order to stock up the wine locker, which
sadly is already nearly empty and we have had to resort to Chateaux Cardboard.

December
Our first visitors arrived and as we still had no steering it was sad that we could not take them out sailing. So we had to
improvise and do tours of the peninsula and undertake further provisioning.

On 19" we bled the hydraulics, yet again, and set off for our first test sail of the new steering, which involved a short 80 nm hop
around to Port Philip and Sandringham Yacht Club. We spent Christmas with Ray’s family and on Christmas morning with Cats
Chorus decked out in tinsel we had 12 on board for breakfast, swimming and a short sail. In 25 degrees with blue sky and
perfect weather everyone had a magical time but it did feel a bit odd and not really like Christmas. For New Years Eve we
decided to go in to Melbourne to watch the fireworks, us and 350,000 others, all of who it seemed were trying to get on the
same train home, it was not a good idea!

At Sandringham we were moored for several days in front of another British yacht called English Rose so Ray chatted to the
skipper and 3 months later we have just realised who he was. It was John Ridgway, the sailor and adventurer who rowed across
the Atlantic with Chay Blyth.

January

9
January in Melbourne is race month so we entered our first regatta at Western Port, SOMHR, Southern Ocean Multihull
Regatta, little did we realise that we would be the only cruiser and most of the other boats were out and out racing cats and tri’s.
Race 1 — We missed it due to sailing back from Melbourne
Race 2 — We were the only boat out there in 40 knots of wind as race control had cancelled the heat after we has already
departed.
Race 3 — We had our best race, on some tacks we were alongside other boats and did not come last.
Race 4—We had a great start and were oddly in the lead with the fleet behind us, we were just savouring the moment and
taking photo’s when we heard over the VHF that we had to do a restart or be disqualified because we were over the line at the
start! After much protesting from Ray we learnt that Aussie rules involve a 1 minute gun so back we went.
Race 5 — Things went from bad to worse, we were rammed and nearly holed by a tri as we both tacked for the start with 20
seconds to go. Then the rig of the boat in front of us collapsed so we retired and became a rescue boat!

It was a fun week and we made many new friends, it was very windy and hit over 35 knots most race days, but we did learn a lot
about handling our new boat and we did hit our top speed to date which was 16 knots so it was not all bad. At the Regatta
dinner we were embarrassed to be called up and given the trophy for winning the cruiser class, as we had been the only cruiser
racing but it was a good evening and very amusing as the skipper & crew from each boat had to do a turn, after enough alcohol
of course.

February/March
On Friday 13" February we finally unplugged from the electrics, handed back the marina key had a long shower and set off to
go cruising! We had decided that Tasmania would be a good place to start so we said farewell to all our new friends from the
live aboard pontoon, and as they waved us off and wished us well we were so excited to be departing at last.

There is so much to say about our first month cruising Tasmania that | do not know where to begin, it had been a truly wonderful
experience and we have been overwhelmed by people’s friendliness, generosity and hospitality everywhere we have been.

Highlights have included:

e Covering over 120 nm on our first day sail from Hastings to King Island
Doing over 14 knots as we surfed across the Bass Strait in huge seas and swell, at times we are both scared and
exhilarated at the same time, the boat just seems to want to go faster and faster but we keep reefing down at the
moment to control our nerves!
Exploring Tasmania by boat and visiting; Smithton, Stanley, Devonport, Launceston and the Tamar River.
Crossing from King Island to Tasmania Ray was muttering that he could not get the jib to set and | replied "We are
doing 12 knots to windward, in 35knots of wind with a choppy sea” that seemed to stop him complaining!

Lowlights have been few apart from one incident in the Flinders Islands where we managed to anchor to a rock and it did not
want to let go! Ray had to snorkel to 10 meters in 20 knots of wind to attach a trip line but we did escape.

We have now crossed back to the mainland and are planning to head north for the winter.

Best wishes to all our friends at Marconi, have a great summer sailing.
Love Jackie and Ray

P.S. As you can see we keep a very strict log!

Commodore’s Comments

We're off! Its official, the season is under way: dinghy racing has started; a successful Open Meeting has been held; on site
camping has been endured; Trumpeter, Cariad and Boogey are on their moorings — and all is right with the world!

Well almost....... we do need to ensure that the contractor finally and satisfactorily finishes the concrete works; we need to
finally clear Skip Central to a more appropriate off site location ... and so on.

Once the concrete is finished we will need to continue the tidy up in that area. So watch out for re-imposition of parking
restrictions, note that there is to be No Entry for any vehicles (tractors or cars) either way through the Race Reception entrance
to the Cat Field and expect the skip to be re-located to an equally convenient but less prominent location. New smart signage
will appear on and around the Club just as soon as we have finally agreed typefaces and colours. There are no plans to fiddle
with the logo.

We emerge from our winter hibernation with the need to acknowledge the special efforts of a number of people who have driven
and executed a number of projects aimed at maintaining and improving our lot. Thanks to everyone who has done any thing at
all and special mention for:

e Peter Clayton and Pat Black for their concrete block moulding and installation works — making the slipway a safer place
to be.
Tim Dowley for his scrubbing work — making the slipway a less slippy place to be.
Tim Dowley for his excellent efforts to keep the Orkney in service after its breakdown
Steve Glynn, Tim Dowley and Kevin Dowley for the retiling of the Ladies’ showers and installation of vanity units.
Maureen and Ray Ball for clubhouse cleaning during the absence of cleaning staff.
Gerry and the Pacemakers for all their hard work in the major installation job on the winch hydraulics.

New members get together
For the purposes of this exercise a new member is anyone who has joined the Club since last New Members’ evening. The
intention is to give you an opportunity to meet and chat with members of the Main Committee and Executive who should be able
to answer all those questions you have been meaning to ask if only you could find someone with a few answers. It is most
definitely not an occasion for us to trawl for new committee members — so come along with a light heart!

| have written individually to (hopefully all) new members to explain that this year’s even will be an informal meeting at the end
of Open Day on June 5"" _ not the date originally published in the Year Book. If anyone else would like to be involved and hasn’t
heard from me please give me a call on [redacted] — | will confirm the arrangements and you will be very welcome.

No Entry
Please note that it has been decided that no vehicles (cars or tractors) may be driven either way through the Cat Field entrance
adjacent to the flagpole and Race Reception. Please respect this rule at all times which is intended to address safety concerns
and reduce wear and tear on the turf.

Car Parking
Designated Car Parking Areas are in the Cat Field to the right of the entrance gate and in the field to the left of the entrance
gate. Windsurfers may park in their designated rigging area.

During Camping Fortnight, East Coast Piers Race and other events other areas may be made available; signs and notices will
direct members as appropriate.

Cruiser owners may park cars alongside their parked boats but must not leave these unattended (in case access to other boats
and trailers is impeded).

Cars may not be parked in the vicinity of the clubhouse other than for loading and unloading by caterers, bar managers,
cleaning staff and so on. Cars must be removed as soon as loading or unloading is complete. This rule will ensure that essential
access for boats, pedestrians, tractors and emergency vehicles is maintained.

Provided that sensible precautions are observed, cars are allowed on to the hard for loading and unloading only. The must not
be left unattended.

Do not allow guests to park their cars outside the Club entrance. Bring them through the gate and remember to include their
vehicle details when completing the signing-in book

Please pay attention to these basic rules and be prepared to comply with any necessary changes of arrangement that occur
from time to time — watch out for notices and respond positively to polite requests!

| am planning to give our new boat Fandango a taste of the water this weekend. Give me a sympathetic wave as you sail
serenely past and snigger at my attempts to cope with new and unfamiliar rigging systems — but, above all, enjoy your sailing.

Chris Davies

VICE COMMODORE’S NOTES - CLUBHOUSE & PRECINCTS os

PROGRESS ON THE GROUNDWORKS
At the time of writing there is still some work to do to complete the groundwork. The soil and seed in the grasscrete has settled
and needs ‘topping up’ and the areas surrounding the new concrete need levelling off with roadstone. The contractor is due
back to do this work and by the time you read this it should be done.

However we are already seeing benefits from the work. The more observant of you will have noticed that the recent heavy rain
drained away, as it has been designed to do, without leaving a lake - sorry kids!

Also the cat sailors are appreciating not leaving their wheels behind as they used to when pulling their boats over the hump.
This should get even better when the grass becomes established in the grasscrete.

NO SPEED HUMP - NO CARS OR TRACTORS PLEASE .
Having removed what one observer called the speed hump into the cat field at the clubhouse (north) entrance | have now
noticed that cars and tractors are attracted to this way in. This is turning the grass abutting the new grasscrete into mud which
is rather spoiling the effect of the new work.

This has been discussed in committee and it has been decided that this entrance should be for cats, dinghies and tenders only.
There is no need to use this entrance as a short cut for cars and tractors.

Please use the top (club gate) entrance to the cat field for vehicles or, if you are going to work on your cruiser, the cat field
entrance at the east end of the cruiser road.

Similarly it has become common practice to drive cars onto the cat parking area either to work on boats or to park near the
cadet hut or race cabin. Again this is turning some areas into mud or leaving deep grooves in the soft ground. There will be
times when this is necessary, but please avoid it as far as possible just as we try not to have cars in the dinghy park area.

SKIPS RUS
Sorry for the rather prolonged presence of the two large skips on the hard. Hopefully they will have been removed by the time
this issue of Navigans hits the streets. Some people have found that they provided useful shelter from winds from the south
when watching the sailing. Perhaps we should have kept them!

DOGS MESS IN THE CLUBHOUSE
Sorry folks but, except for using the formal clinical term, there is no nice way to put this.

On arriving for one of their morning cleaning sessions our cleaners were met with dogs mess in the clubhouse; and it had not
been trodden in if you follow me. Although removing doggy-dos is most certainly not in their job description they were good
enough to clear it up.

This was a nasty thing to happen at any time but happening so soon after they started working at the club our new cleaners
must have wondered what they had taken on!

| think it very unlikely that the culprit was a member's dog. It was more likely one of the stray animals that seem to like roaming
around our site. It may even have got itself accidentally locked into the clubhouse overnight. Maureen had to evict a stray dog
from the clubhouse recently.

There is little that we can do about other peoples’ dogs coming onto the site but | would ask all members to do the following:

If you bring your dog to the club please observe the club rule and do not allow your dog to go anywhere in the clubhouse. If
there are no doggy smells maybe the strays will be less interested in the building.

If you see a dog in the clubhouse firmly shoo it out.

you are shutting up the clubhouse please have a quick look around (including upstairs) to make sure that you are not locking
in any unwelcome guests.

Happy Sailing.
Ray Ball

Solo Fleet's Russian Evening

Saturday evening (20th March) saw many solo sailors and their wives dressed as Russians descend on the club house. There
was a Striking array of colour and a multitude of furry hats. All things that night were Russian, starting with a picture quiz_hung
around the walls. While we were in the warm, Malcolm and Steve were outside cooking the meal. What a sumptuous dinner was
served up. We started with Borsch (beetroot soup for the uninitiated), followed by Beef Stroganoff with a desert of Varenyky
(sweet dumplings) .A tremendous amount of hard work was carried out by Malcolm in deciding the menu, co-coordinating the
pre-cooking at home by solo members and overseeing the whole meal on the night.

After the meal and the answers to the quiz were heard, everyone was divided into three teams.
Russian titled games were then played (" Lenin's lying in state" and "Off to Siberia" being two).
The evening ended with each team acting out a sketch entitled "From Russia with love" which included some excellent Cossack
dancing by all the teams members.
This was a really good evening and thanks go out to all who helped. Next year will be another theme but don't wait till then, buy
a solo now and join in the fun.

Handicap Fleet News

Dinghy Park: My thanks to Barry who has done an excellent job laying out the dinghy park. The majority of boats so far have
been parked correctly, but a small number of large dinghies (in the ‘A’ spaces) are not aligned with the marked bays, and
therefore taking up more space than they should. This means that members bringing their boats to the club later in the spring
could have nowhere to park. Please check your boat is correctly placed. If you are asked by Barry, myself or another club
official to realign your boat please don’t take offence — we're just trying to make most efficient use of the limited space available.

Winter-stored Dinghies: The deadline for moving dinghies from their winter storage positions along the hedgerows back into the
dinghy park was Easter. Starting with the Dart 15 Open (April 17th/18"") there are numerous camping weekends throughout
April, May, June and July, not to mention camping fortnight in August. Dinghies which remain in the winter storage areas are
potentially a big problem. Please make every effort to relocate your boat as soon as possible, if you have not done so already.
All monohull dinghies should be stored in the dinghy park, not the cat field.

OK. That's the business side dealt with, now for the boating stuff........

Racing Update: As | write this in mid-April the start of the season has seen mixed fortunes. Excessive winds have scuppered
two out of three Spring Series racing days, whilst an almost total lack of wind made for frustrating sailing over the Easter
weekend. All the same it’s been good to see people down at the club, even if not always able to venture, out on the water. Dave
Williams currently leads the Spring Series with two 1° places. Richard Dixonis close behind with two go places. Check out the
club website or results notice board in the clubhouse for the latest positions.

the club.

Dart 15 Open Event (17/18 April)

The first 2004 Dart 15 TT event was held at Marconi Sailing Club in Essex with a fleet of nineteen boats. We were particularly
pleased to have 10 entries from Marconi itself which included some welcome newcomers to the racing fleet - we hope to see
you on the water during the course of the season as well!

The Saturday brought unusually mild and pleasant weather with a light breeze. The first race saw Bob Carter and Peter
Richardson hard on the heels of George Carter who was sailing sprint mode. Bob kept close enough to George to take 1st place
by only a few seconds on handicap, with Peter Richardson a close 3rd and Phillip Howden in 4th.

The breeze had strengthened for the second race and brought some interesting gusts / lulls as it came offshore — particularly
when the fleet sailed inshore to escape the strong Blackwater tide. George Carter, Bob Carter, Gordon Goldstone, Nick
Dewhirst and Philip Howden led the fleet hotly pursued by Peter Richardson and Andy Chidwick. Unfortunately, Bob Carter was
caught by one of the unexpected gusts and capsized, although he still managed to pull back to a respectable 8th place. The
winds also caught out Bob Rowntree, Nick Pavitt and Patrick Ellum who also capsized during the course of the race.

On Saturday evening - the club laid on a general knowledge quiz for our guest and club members which proved very popular.
The quiz was one by a team of visitors - the "50 plus" team with a Marconi team "the Bar team" (Andrew Dowley, Common
Browne, Tania Monks, Sophie and Clara Hurrell-Smith) coming second!

Belinda Dowley and Glynis Monks provided an excellent evening meal and Andrew Dowley kindly ran the bar and provided
music entertainment.

Sunday morning brought entirely different weather conditions with force 6 — 8 winds. A reduced fleet of 9 boats set off on the
traditional and popular figure of eight race around Osea and Northey Islands. Early starts meant four boats had to go back over
the start line, but the fleet had pulled closer together again as it shot past the end of Osea Island in the strong breeze. The race
was Closely fought all the way round with Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine finally taking 1st place, followed by Bob Carter, George
Carter, Andy Chidwick and Nick Dewhirst.

The strong winds held for the afternoon race - an exhilarating round the cans with an interesting downwind leg which claimed
Common Browne as a pitchpole victim and a few close shaves for some of the other competitors! Andy Chidwick also capsized
on the last lap which regrettably cost him 4th place. George Carter took 1st place followed by Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine, Nick
Dewhirst, Bob Carter and Gordon Goldstone.

The varied wind conditions made for some great sailing and some very interesting final results — but the clear overall winner of
the event was George Carter.

| would like to extend my thanks to the raft of people that helped make the event such a success which includes: Kate
Williams, Dave Williams, Fenella Thomas, Tim Dowley, Andrew Dowley, Belinda and Kevin Dowley, Glynis Monks, Tim Wallace,
Tina Hutt, Paul Metcalfe, Claire Davies, Sophie Hurrell-Smith, Kevin Kirby, John Nisbet, Jenny Miller, Nick Miller, Clara Hurrell-
Smith, Andy Williams, Peter Ward, David Ball and Dave Russell.

Topper Byte Open 18-04-2004

The first of the Byte open series was held at Milton Keynes S. C. on Sunday 18-04-04. The weather was good with a steady force 3 S/W wind. All Eight competitors from clubs around the country were keen to get racing on this tactically demanding lake. The weather at end of day consisted of wind and rain.

Race1: All boats crossed the start line after some hard challenging for the best position, which was the top end of the start line. Ray Smith won this first battle. Ray led the fleet around the course for the first 2 laps with the rest of the fleet hot on his heels, with many places changing on each leg. On the third and final lap the wind dropped to a force 1 and the fleet began to split. Ray began to drop back into the fleet. Nick Miller took up the lead until the last leg. Nick rounded the windward mark 50 metres in the lead and headed to the right of the lake and lost the wind. The rest of the fleet went left after rounding the mark. With very little wind every puff was vital.
The fleet was slowly closing up on the leader. At the finish line Maggie Futcher was first, 2nd Eddie Pope and 3rd Nick Miller. There were only 2 boat lengths between 1st and 3rd place. A very close and thrilling race.

Race2: Very little wind at the start, so very important to get a good start. Adrian Stell was the victor this time. Adrian led for the fist two legs of a three-leg race. At end of the first lap, 1st Eddie Pope, 2nd Adrian Stell and 3rd Maggie Futcher. The wind picked up during the second lap, at the end of which the wind had built to force 4. At the end of lap two the placing was 1st Eddie, 2nd Maggie and 3rd Nick Miller. Maggie was caught out at the next mark by the wind and capsized. For the rest of the race places were changing throughout the fleet. Coming up to the finish line the first three places were being closely contested by Eddie, Adrian and Nick. Nick Miller was 1st over the line closely followed by Eddie 2nd and Adrian 3rd, only 3 boat lengths between 1st and 3rd; a very challenging race.

Race 3: At the start the wind had changed again to North, force 3. Adrian stell capsized on the start line, only recovering 8 seconds before the start. At the first mark, 1st Adrian Stell, 2nd Nick Miller, 3rd Ray Smith. End of the first lap, 1st Adrian, 2nd Nick, 3rd Ray, with the rest of the fleet in hot pursuit. On the third lap Ami Goodyear had cut through the fleet to take up 2nd place. A very hard race at the front with 2nd and 3rd places changing nearly every leg. Nick had to finish no less than 2nd to win the open. Adrian had to win with Nick in 3rd or lower. Crossing the line in 1st place Adrian Stell, 2nd Nick Miller, 3rd Ami Goodyear. The rest of the fleet was hot on the heels of the leaders. Very good and close racing by all competitors.

BACSPA

These are brief notes of the BACSPA meeting held on 1st April at the MLSC. The chairman is also vice-chairman of the
Eastern region of the RYA so the meetings are a source of information on many matters beyond the Blackwater and Colne
estuaries.
The full minutes will be published at the end of April. Please contact me if you wish to see a copy. If there are any issues that
you would like raised with BACSPA please let me know.

RYA News

e The EU proposal that the red ensign and other national European ensigns be defaced with the EU symbol has now
been abandoned.

e The RYA is trying to maintain the availability of red diesel beyond 2006. There is currently a EU proposal to restrict red
diesel to commercial activities.

e The Rya is trying to promote more voluntary work within the clubs and the RYA. Current feeling is that the RYA
proposals may be well intentioned but are unrealistic.

10

11

e The way the RYA functions at the moment talented youngsters who do well in competitions are extracted from their
clubs for national training under the auspices of the RYA. This robs clubs of the sort of talent that is needed to train the
newer intake of dinghy sailors. | would imagine that sailing is not alone with this complaint.

Local News

e Construction of an array of wind generators on the Gunfleet sands has been postponed for one year. The RYA
has submitted its objections to the phase 2 for wind generators in the Thames Estuary.

e Further expansion of the container facilities at Felixstowe will take place over the next few years. The plans
involve widening the main channel into Harwich Harbour. If small craft are to avoid the commercial channel they
will be need to cross the shallow waters of the Harwich Shelf.

e Redevelopment of the derelict site at the entrance to Brightlingsea Harbour will now take place in a revisedform.

e Colchester Borough Council has published their development plans for the next ten years. These will be examined
closely for any impact on the recreational use of the Colne. It is likely that Tendring District Council will also
publish their 10 year plan.

e Although TBT anti fouling has been banned for amateur craft for many years its use is now to be totally prohibited.
However do not be tempted if you are offered a 45 gallon drum of the stuff at a knock down price. Its future use
will attract heavy fines and even imprisonment

e Trinity House wish to remove the E Barrow Beacon. Apparently some commercial ships have run aground in
mistaking it for a navigation buoy.

The sailing season is finally under way! It seems as though it has all cranked up very quickly — already we have had several points series
events, in which the weather has gone from the sublime to the ridiculous, with a complete blow-out for races 1 and 2 resulting in instant
cancellation, to the millpond conditions of the Easter Bank Holiday. At least the latter gave the cruiser fleet the chance to catch up with laying
their moorings after some pretty awful weather.

Already our first open meeting has been and gone. The Dart 15 Traveller event took place on 17" and 18" April, and saw 19 competitors in the
event. It was particularly pleasing to see the high turnout from Marconi’s own Dart 15 sailors. Saturday saw the best of the weather, but with the
winds increasing during the day. Sunday morning dawned with very high winds, and some competitors thought better of it and went home. Ten
boats competed in strong and challenging winds, but George Carter from Grafham held his own to win the series.

We have several other open meetings on the horizon. The Byte fleet join us on Saturday 1 May, and the Osprey fleet on the 2” and 3” May.
Both these fleets are new first-time visitors to the Club, and | am sure that everyone will welcome them. Both should make for good spectator
sport, too, although | hope we don’t distract the attention of our members during our own Bank Holiday racing on the Sunday and Monday!
Please do come and support these events. Don’t forget too that the Solo fleet arrive for their annual Marconi Open on 15" May. =

And the fun doesn’t stop there. As you will see elsewhere, we have given the Marconi Challenge Cup a new ‘look’, transforming it from_a
Saturday open with low attendance to a day-long pursuit racing event for all of you who love to pursuit race but can’t always get to the club on
time for Wednesday evening racing. It should a great event, with something a bit different for Sunday 6" June.

Visitors to the Dinghy Show at Alexandra Palace may have encountered the ‘Top Club’ stand. ‘Top Club’ is an independent event, in which
clubs will enter a team of three boats, one slow, one medium and one fast (all monohulls, I’m afraid). The organisers are allowing 80 clubs to
enter the event in September, to be held at Grafham Water. Marconi has a team place reserved, and we propose using the late May Bank
Holiday racing to select a team. Anybody who is particularly interested in being part of the team should contact me. Further information is
available at www.topclub.org.uk.

There not much to report yet on the cruiser sailing or racing fronts, unless anyone was competing to be fi retain the water, or fastest application
of antifoul. The handicap fleet though has announced two dates for handicap fleet cruises. The first is on 19"" June
— see the noticeboard or
speak to Dave Ball for more information.

Last but not least, Mike Taylor has recently successfully completed the RYA Club Racing Coach course. This is the first step on the path
towards one of our ‘Foresail’ ambitions, toimprove training for the over-18’s at Marconi. Mike will be offering race training to monohull sailors on
Saturday 22TM May. Anybody interested should contact Mike directly (details elsewherein this Navigans). Format will depend upon whole
interested and what their needs are. At this time, we can’t offer the service to the catamaran fleet — if any cat sailor would like to volunteer to do
the course so that we can expand the training programme, please get in touch.

See you on the water — | hope there is enough going on to interest everybody!

Commodore’s Comments

| write this at the end of the first decent weekend for some time. After a pleasant couple of days on our own boat it was great to
come back to the Club and see so much activity going on. The Solo Open was the main attraction on the water and the car
park (drying out well now) was nicely full both of vehicles of those involved in that event or others doing their own thing. There
was enough wind to make things enjoyable and a good time was had by all. Our visitors once again reported favourably on a
friendly and warm reception — so well done to everyone who put in effort to make the weekend a success.

Speaking of successes — Open Day on June 5" deserves to be a success since a lot has gone into the planning. Of the three
main ingredients for a good outcome, two are difficult to predict or control: the weather and the number of visitors who turn up.
The third aspect is your involvement and that is easier to influence — if you are willing to be influenced. Please do turn up to
support the event and do please bring a friend or acquaintance to see what we offer.

East Coast Piers Race, as most of you know, is an event close to my heart and | know that many of you share my enthusiasm
for the support we are able to give to Cirdan Sailing Trust. | was fortunate to be invited to join them for their Patron’s Day aboard
Xylonite and Duet sailing on the Orwell and to accept on your behalf their thanks for all we do for them. Somewhat
unexpectedly, the highlight of the day for me was to get to talk at length to some of the crews who tutor the disadvantaged and
often troubled young charges who are their guests in a normal working week. Hearing the sort of issues that they are involved
with and their stories of the impact they can make in difficult circumstances was a rewarding experience.

A couple of recent occurrences lead me to make just a couple of comments about personal safety. At this time of year more
than perhaps any other there is a lot to be done, a temptation to take short cuts and sufficient time has passed since last season
for us to have forgotten some of the safety lessons we suffered previously. So a simple plea — please be careful around your
boats and around the site; use the proper equipment (if you don’t have it you can be fairly sure that the Club or another member
has) and don’t take chances. We all do it from time to time and luckily for the most part we get away with it — but often our
mistakes are cause by oversight rather than foolhardiness. So, might | make so bold as to suggest that where any of us sees
someone apparently needing help or advice we tactfully give it — rather than suffering regrets later. After all, self-help is what we
are about; it is probably better that we give that help sooner rather than later.

| look forward to more weekends of the sort we have just enjoyed and to seeing you and your families on the water.

Chris Davies

Solo Open Event

The sun shone, the wind blew — what better recipe for a successful Solo Open meeting at Marconi S. C. on the River Blackwater
in Essex on 16" May? 22 boats including 13 visitors enjoyed the sunshine and estuary sailing at its finest in the fourth meeting
of the Solo Eastern Travellers series sponsored by Rooster Sailing. The preceding day had been taken up with a training
session from Solo Class stalwart and boat builder Tony Thresher resulting in some aching limbs come the Sunday reveille!

In a light Easterly the first race started on the flood tide and getting a good start and minimizing the effects of the tide was
paramount. Jerry Garner led at the first mark and Godfrey Clark got away to a good start only to misjudge the tide at the
windward mark and let three other boats through in the process. Jerry Garner led at the leeward mark and consequently led
through to the finish, followed by Steve Ede and Godfrey Clark. The tide had just turned by the start of the second race calling
for different tactics to be deployed. Nevertheless Jerry Garner got a useful lead again with Godfrey Clark again in the chase.
Godfrey very nearly triumphed by better judging the angle of the finish line but Garner got the verdict of the “photo-finish” to give

2

3
him an unassailable winner’s position in the event. Steve Ede came third. Race 3 started with the wind strengthened by the
sea breeze now a force 3. This time Steve Ede led all the way round pursued by Garner and Clark with regular visitor David
Walford claiming the 4" spot and local boat Michael Taylor coming in 5". Jerry Garner has changed his home club to
Papercourt which has clearly honed his tidal sailing ability to win at Marconi after several years of visiting.

Race Officer John Weedon set some interesting courses and at the prize giving Commodore Chris Davies welcomed the visitors
and thanked them for their support as well as thanking all the Marconi Club people who had made the day a success. Jerry
Garner also thanked the club for putting on a good meeting, especially the Race Officer, rescue crews, the help with the
launching trolleys and the galley. Thanks are specially due to Frank Burgess and son Mark for use of Ocean Slipper as the
committee boat once again.

Marconi Sailing Club also claimed the 8"" spot John Salmon and 11" Ron Greygoose, 12" John Burgoyne, 13" David Ball in a

Cruiser Moorings

There has been some recent concern expressed by club members about unoccupied Cruiser moorings that sink just below the
surface at high tide springs. In response | reproduce below Peter Claytons comments which | hope will go some way to explain
the problems we have and what we can do to sort out the few moorings where this problem occurs in the first weeks of the
sailing year before the cruisers are launched.

“The moorings at Stansgate are laid on a matrix determined by minimum chain lengths for the mooring to be secure, this then fixes the centre
distance and the between row distance to ensure that the moored boats do not come into contact with each other. All the deep water moorings
which are now laid were checked for correct chain lengths and condition this year immediately prior to laying. The problem of sinking buoys
could be solved by longer chain but as ever its not as simple as that. Increasing the chain length also increases the swinging circle and thus
the danger of adjacent boats hitting each other. You could increase the buoy size to overcome the problem but this has its own problems due
to the relatively exposed conditions at Stansgate. Too large a buoy for the size of boat means that in rough conditions the spring effect is
taken out of the mooring and very high snatch loads can occur between the buoy and the moored vessel which can and has caused the vessel
to break-away.
The actual problem at this time of year is exacerbated by high spring tides and the fact that a lot of the moorings have had no boat on them.
Once the mooring has been used the slack in the ground chain is pulled to the middle allowing the buoy to float. Later in the year and even
now an accumulation of weed or debris round the mooring can cause it to be pulled under. It can be a problem identifying the moorings
which are giving problems. We leave the mooring barge in the water usually until Whitsun to address this and any other problems we may
have with moorings. It is a problem we are aware of, take seriously and attempt to solve. If moorings can be identified with a specific
problem let me know and we will fix it.”

Club Notes

Commodore’s Comments

Open Day was notable for a number of reasons: support from members was superb; against the odds, we managed to make
the site presentable and the weather was fantastic. Our publicity strategy worked and the overall result was that over a hundred
families turned up and signed in on the day. (One or two more turned up on the following day — and the publicity will bring in still
others as the weeks go by). As | write this almost 20 have signed up for membership and quite a few more are expected to
return forms shortly. So, a success by almost any standard — as an example of members’ collaboration; as an enjoyable social
event; as a general publicity vehicle and as a recruitment device. Congratulations to all of you who contributed in any way.

There was one member who misconstrued my earlier requests for high levels of help — he appeared, right in the middle of our
busiest time, on the roof of the clubhouse. Oh, well.....

The new members will surely take advantage of a number of planned events that are sure to show the Club at its very best. The
first that comes to mind is Fun Day when all members from all fleets can come together for some light-hearted activity and
serious socialising. In a rather more serious and intense vein we can look forward to the 17""” running of East Coast Piers
Race. If you are not a competitor there is a lot you can do to contribute to the smooth running of this large, complex event. |
would urge Cruiser owners to contact Charles Anderson now with offers of Mother Boat support. | know that Charles or Clive
Shenton will also be pleased to receive any other offers of support from members to help with a wide variety of tasks, many of
which can be broken down into short time slots. You don’t need to commit for the whole weekend and any help you can give will
be greatly appreciated. All our efforts will, once again, be focussed on the important support Marconi SC provides through
ECPR to Cirdan Sailing Trust.

We are slowly catching up on issues affecting the appearance of the site after a long period of disruption and change. Routine
maintenance of grass on lawns and parks, strimming the margins, dealing with growth on the sea wall and sweeping the hard
are carried out by a large team of members operating on a rota basis and we should be grateful to all of them for all they do.
Nevertheless, there are times when gaps appear in the rota. Nature does not recognise such disruptions and growth continues
apace — leaving us with a bigger job when the work does get done. The work is actually quite rewarding and usually machine —
assisted — so if you feel able to get involved please do volunteer (by speaking to Dave Steward in the first instance). Looking
after your own patch and the surrounding area is important too — as is the correct disposal of rubbish. Please do your bit to keep
the site presentable.

A beacon in all of the above is the maintenance of the garden area of the Commodore’s Lawn by Elsie and Bob Anderson. Their
week-in, week-out attention to this task provides pleasure for us all.

There is sad news this month about the untimely deaths of one member and one ex-member — lan Airies and Brenda Robinson.
| have written on behalf of the Club to Angela Airies and to George Robinson to offer our condolences to them and their families.

Chris Davies

Vice Commodore

Progress on the groundworks
Thanks to Clive (and others) the grasscreted area is beginning to look good and will improve as time goes on. Thanks Clive for
all the (considerable) time that has been dedicated to this task.

Please remember that vehicles and tractors are not to use the grasscreted entrance to the cat field. It is hope eventually to get
some grass growing on the bare areas adjacent the grasscrete and this won’t happen if subjected to vehicles.

Skips - where we put them
The “Wasteater” skip has been moved so as to be less of an eyesore. As | write it is parked behind the hedge near the race
cabin. This is still far from ideal and the matter is under discussion. Who knows, it might have moved again by the time you
that read this!

We are also actively considering alternative methods of disposing of domestic waste on the site.

Skips — what you put in them
Please note that our contract with the waste company is for the collection and removal of domestic type waste only. This is
mostly from the rubbish bins in the clubhouse but can also be from boats or campers. Occasionally optimists will place bulky
items near the skip in the hope that the driver will take them. He won't. The Wasteater lorry compacts the waste so he is
unable to collect scrap metal, old furniture, etc.

Clubhouse cleaners
Unfortunately June and John Rogers were unable to continue to clean the clubhouse. They were good enough to stay on until
the beginning of June to ensure that the clubhouse was presentable for Open Day.

| am pleased to announce that Julia Whyte has agreed to take on the work and by the time you read this some of you may have
met her. Please make Julia welcome at the club.

Please also make Julia’s job as easy as possible by considerate use of the club.

Clubhouse cleaning, your help please
Elsewhere in this edition of Navigans you will see an impassioned plea from Maureen about the state of the clubhouse and the
problems involved in keeping it clean. Please take note of what she says.

The nature of our sport means that a certain amount of water, grit and mud will get trodden into the clubhouse. This is
inevitable and the clubhouse was designed to accommodate this. Cleaning is still hard work but it can be done.

| have been speaking to previous cleaners and what really ‘cheeses them off’ is not a bit of water and grit on the floors but the
avoidable work. For example, the state of the toilets after some members have used them frankly leaves something to be
desired. | cleaned the gents last Saturday and | know what they are talking about. We all expect to have decent clean facilities
but we also have a responsibility to leave facilities as we expect to find them. We do it at home, why not at the club?

Clubhouse cleaning, thanks
| don’t know the names of those involved but | am aware that some members have set to and given the changing rooms a clean
- particularly after Open Day. Thanks folks. The results show and your time and effort is appreciated.

New members
Whilst at the club recently | have had the pleasure of talking to several new members who have bought dinghies and are
planning to bring them to the club. ‘Welcome folks’, | hope that Maureen and | were able to offer some useful advice and
information.

Happy Sailing —
ay Ba

Well at last we seem to of been blessed with hot weather, we can all put those dry suits away and start using our "shorties." All
the results for the spring points series are now published, the winners are as follows. In the Solo Class John Salmon; Handicap,
Dave and Kate William's, Medium Cat, Jenny Ball; Fast Cat Tim Wallace and in the cadet series Anthony Monks. Well done!

The prize giving will be at the club after racing on Sunday 20th June. There are still several races left in the Bank Holiday
Series, following the last race John Nisbett has moved to the top of the table in his Solo.

Don't forget the summer points will be published as an am/pm series. The weekend of the 5th and 6th of June proved to be a
very busy with both the open day and the Challenge Cup. The challenge Cup was a very different format this year, 32 entrants, |
hope all enjoyed the unusual format of the two pursuit races. This was to the best of my knowledge a first so any feedback
would be appreciated. Well done to Brian Spencer for the demanding role of organizing this event, congratulations must also go
to Rory Ash for spending so long afloat and managing to hold off much faster vessels for so long. | certainly found it an
entertaining day which proved that the difference between cats and monohulls is more than the number of hulls! Well done to
Tim Wallace for such a resounding win.
Dave Hewes

Cruiser Fleet

We have had a busy month starting with the shakedown cruise to Burnham with 21 boats going round and 50 people sitting
down for a meal at the Swallowtail. We had a good sailing wind for the race on the Saturday and a pleasant sail back into the
Blackwater on the Monday. Some of us touched bottom on occasion but one, who shall be nameless, missed the Crouch
completely and only realised that he was off course when he spotted a container ship.

The Club open day exceeded all expectations with, | believe, over 300 visitors. It certainly seemed like it on the hard throughout
the day. | would like to thank Simon and Suzanne Elwell, John Walker, Frank Burgess, Nick Hillman and Hillary and Derek
Gardiner for taking visitors out for a sail throughout the day, not to mention those that | press ganged on the day for crew. Ata
rough guess | would think that around 70 visitors went out on cruisers during the day.

As | write this, we have just returned from the watercress run with 15 boats locking into Heybridge and 45 people for the evening
barbeque. Fortunately the rain held off until we were about to enter the lock on the return journey when the heavens opened.
Why is it that an outboard will run for over an hour on a tideless river but gives up the next day when you have to row against
the tide from your mooring?

Moving on to forthcoming cruises, we have a trip to Brightlingsea on the weekend of the 3% and 4" July and a week’s cruise to
Ramsgate, Dover and Chatham on the week commencing 31*' July. Lists will be appearing on the noticeboard shortly.

The ECPR is on 24"/25" July and the Club is in need of more cruisers to supply safety cover. If you can help, please contact
either Charles Anderson or myself or put your name on the list on the Club noticeboard.

Long stay car parking for those off cruising is to the east of the waste oil tank, please don’t park in the cat or dinghy fields as
these are used for camping pitches on the ECPR weekend and camping fortnight.

We still seem to have a pile of unclaimed tenders. These are by the waste oil tank and if they are not claimed within the next six
weeks they will be disposed of. Some of these tenders have been kicking about the site unused for about three years to my
knowledge. There is also a large tender by the name of “Polly” which appeared in the tender rack recently and was taking up
three spaces. If the owner would like to contact me we can sort out somewhere to store it. As a reminder, your mooring
number is your rack space number i.e. if your mooring is C10 then your rack space is C10.

Brenda Robinson

Very sadly, Brenda Robinson died on the 2" June 2004.

George and Brenda Robinson were Marconi SC members for many years and are probably best known for their boat called
"Freya" They left the Marconi club in 1996 and moved to the comfort of a marina berth in Tollesbury before going out to
Australia for five years.

Brenda contracted cancer whilst out there and successfully recovered from it. Only two months ago she was diagnosed to have
secondary cancer and was bravely undergoing treatment for it. She appeared to be making fair progress with her fight against
the cancer but unfortunately she lost her battle and unexpectedly but peacefully passed away.

Brenda will be remembered for always having a cheerful and carefree disposition and will be greatly missed by George and her
two sons Andrew and David.

Club Cleaning

Having tried it, | can vouch for the fact that cleaning the clubhouse is serious physical exercise and the Government is
absolutely right - you don’t need to spend money at a gym, just get down to some serious cleaning! Our cleaners basically have
the task of cleaning all floors, sinks and WCs, wiping down windowsills, and other odds and ends, as well as topping up soap
and paper in changing rooms. This work fills their allotted time, especially as wet and sandy floors are inevitable in a sailing
club like ours and they take time to deal with. Having experienced what work is involved | thought it fair to remind members how
they can help as we approach the club’s busiest time.

After using a lounge table, please use the bins to avoid leaving any litter on tables and floor, and wipe your table down before
you leave so it is clean for the next user. Aim to leave the changing rooms as clean and tidy as possible, taking your property
home with you and using bins for any litter - it takes time to pick up bits of damp paper from a wet floor.

Members who use the tea bar, please take a couple of minutes to wash up properly, dry and put away all crockery and cutlery
you have used, at the time of writing this, the draining board is nearly full!
This task won’t be added to the cleaner’s workload
as it is expected that the users or any occasional volunteer will between them keep the tea bar in a reasonable condition. We
are still very much a self-help club, run by the members for the members in order to keep costs down, and we can all make the
environment a pleasant one for ourselves and others by all making just a small effort.

Maureen Ball

J.E.Pateman CBE.

Jack Pateman, who died on the 28th August, was managing Director of Marconi Avionics. He was President of the Marconi Sailing Club for several years. His sloop, "Oenanthe", regularly cruised in France, Holland and our East Coast. He led the annual visit to our club to support dinghy races between his Rochester team and our club. He liked to recount how, after leaving a Laying-Up supper at the Lion & Lamb, he was fined for driving the wrong way down Duke Street!

Proposed by the Management Committee.
Questions.

boxes? Mr N Pembleton explained that charges would not be attracted towards trailers associated with a boat enjoying a paid
up Boat Permit Fee.
Mr R Mander noted that his fees for 2004 had uplifted by twenty nine percent and asked if this was likely to be the normal
increase in future years, Mr Bird replied that this would not be the case.

our membership recruitment.

Commodore’s Report for the Club AGM 2004
The first thing to say is that this report does not set out to name names. I do not intend to use this report to record all the thanks
that are due to the many people who take special responsibility for the operation of the club. The need to give those thanks is
great but it will happen elsewhere. My task here is to provide some information that is required by statute (under the
Companies Act) and to give members a summary of our management activities during the past year alongside an indication of
our intentions for the coming year.

I am required to confirm that our principle activity during the past year has continued to be the provision of sailing facilities to
our membership. Our management structure as a limited company is not dissimilar to that which applied previously. The Board
or Executive now, of course, assumes ultimate responsibility for the club operation – rather than MASC as was previously the
case– and was strengthened to allow for the additional workload. The board comprised six directors:
 Ray Ball
 John Bird (Finance)
 Peter Clayton
 Chris Davies (Managing)
 Claire Davies
 Clive Shenton

All of whom have specific operational responsibilities as Flag Officers of the Club.
The board appoints an Honorary Secretary and during the past year that post was held by Patrick Black.

The board met formally each month since the last AGM and has conducted such other meetings of sub-groups as have been
appropriate from time to time. The Management Committee, which also meets monthly, continues to provide a forum in which
representatives of all aspects of the club can share and discuss matters relating to the day to day operation of the site and
activities. Then there is a network of sub-committees that deal with specific areas of activity, who report their activities and
recommendations through the Management Committee. These various committees provide the formal focus for all our
discussions but a lot of work is done informally either face-to-face or by electronic means.

I am required to mention here any political or charitable donations made during the year. I am proud of our ongoing work in
support of the Cirdan Sailing Trust and can confirm that, through ECPR, we were able to donate £9400 to that charity. We also
donated £450 to RNLI and £50 to St Johns. However, all these sums were raised during events and were not paid from club
income

Our focus during 2004 had three elements – to better understand our operations and how we manage them, to tidy up our
presentation of the site and to focus on sailing activity. It has been and was intended to be a cautious approach both in
practical and financial terms. We were concerned to understand fully the implications of our change of status for the way we
managed ourselves and clear that consolidation of and confidence in what we have now is an essential pre-requisite to any
decisions about future development.

We have achieved a great deal – but, I suppose inevitably, live with the frustration of things not achieved or not completed.
Dealing with the positives in no particular order:
 We have maintained and developed a strong Social Calendar. We have had some excellent events, all of which were well
supported.
 We have had a full and varied sailing calendar with some innovation.
 Introduced a devolved system of budgetary responsibility and control.
 Maintained and extended the range of Open events held here.
 Our sailors have been active on the circuits on a worldwide basis.
 We have created one of the most modern websites in the sailing club world.
 We have increased our level of membership. Open day was a great success, cadet numbers are at a record level, and we
have a greatly increased number of windsurfers.
 We have continued to improve equipment in cause of safety, efficiency, convenience and cost control.
 We have made some cautious but significant improvements to the site. We removed the lake and the hump, undertook
repairs to the hard, greatly improved the Dell Bar, re-tiled the Womens’ showers and provided new wash basins there also.

We will continue during 2005 to develop on these achievements and to tackle new opportunities to ensure that the club
functions smoothly within the limits of our financial and physical resources.

It has not always been straightforward and one significant issue we have had to deal with is that of succession in the numerous
voluntary posts that are part and parcel of life in a club like this one. Turnover can be healthy but, at the same time continuity is
desirable. We have to acknowledge and respect the need for some (perhaps most) people to be able to commit themselves for
a limited time and then bow out – but we also have to build mechanisms to enable us to cope with and benefit from those
changes – rather than be penalised by them. We will continue to work on ways of making our succession planning more
effective and less stressful.

This leads me neatly into the slightly wider issue of duties and self-help. Issues that at times cause us some confusion and
even heartache. Dealing with the question of duties first of all – this Club is no different from 1000 others in that it can only
function with the direct support and co-operation of its membership. Sharing responsibility for Support Boat duties, Race Officer
Duties, OOD duties and basic housekeeping is a feature of life for the majority of sailing clubs in the land – only the well
heeled, highly expensive and therefore exclusive clubs can lay on sufficient paid support to enable members to avoid these
responsibilities completely. Of course, we employ a cleaner and we may find in the fullness of time that we can employ other
people to undertake some of the routine maintenance and administration of the club – but we will not be able to escape the

Page 8
need for member’s involvement in all the key operational areas. Members must recognise this and be prepared to do their bit.
We will manage the rotas but we rely on individual support and will take a dim view (on behalf of all members) when that
support is deliberately withheld.

The self-help ethos is a strong feature of our make up and a feature of which many of us are proud. It is an approach that
reflects the history of the club and is driven by two key elements:
 It attracts a certain type of member and is therefore self-perpetuating.
 The nature of our exposed cruiser moorings lends itself best to an owner-driven approach to provision and maintenance
and attracts owners who tend to be self-sufficient, practical and financially cautious. These owners comprise a significant
proportion of the Club membership.

Self-help can be a great strength and has often enabled us to do more than we might otherwise have been able to achieve. But
there are two problems that it can cause:

 From time to time there is a risk of division caused by a failure to acknowledge that not everybody has the ability or
inclination to be involved in every aspect or every instance of self-help activity. This can be managed so long as we are
aware of it and so long as we understand the difference between self-help projects and routine housekeeping.
 Too great a reliance on self-help can cause delays and compromise that work against our best interests. Maintenance and
major works often require speed of action and quality assurance. It is sometimes best to use tradesmen and contractors –
although there is then a corresponding need for management activity to be undertaken by members.

We will continue to manage this situation to achieve the best possible results.

In summary we have adopted a cautious approach to our first year of financial independence and this is reflected in the figures
already circulated to you. That cautious approach will continue into next year. We will continue to test and enhance our
financial controls; we will continue to test and refine our operational structure and systems; and we will continue with our
programme of protecting our investment of our facilities. There will be greater emphasis, however, on looking forward to what
we want to achieve for ourselves in the years ahead and in laying the groundwork for future decisions about how we might
improve our facilities and our operation.

I would like to close by thanking the whole membership for their support of the Board during the last year and inviting anybody
with any comments on what we do or what we hope to do to contact me or any board member now or at any time.

Chris Davies

Minutes of The Cruiser Fleet AGM 2004
Held on 20th November 2004 at 17.30

1. Apologies. Apologies were received from Mark Whitley, Frank Bennet, Robin Lovett and Alan and Carol Clark.

2. Review of 2004. 2004 was a successful season despite the weather and included the following events:-

A bowling evening was held on 20th February.
The Fitting out supper was held on 8th May. Sixty one people attended which is the maximum the clubhouse can
hold for a sit down meal.
On the May Bank Holiday twenty one boats took part in the shakedown cruise to Burnham and a meal was held at
the Swallowtail on the Sunday evening.
On 1st June the club held its open day which was hugely successful with about seventy visitors having tasters on
cruisers. The day translated to twenty eight new members.
The Heybridge trip took place on 19th/20th June with fifteen boats locking in and forty five people attending the
evening barbeque.
The Brightlingsea cruise was held on 23rd July. The forecast was poor so several people drove round whilst only
Killara and Serapin actually made the journey by sea.
At the Piers Race which was held on 25th July there was a full complement of cruisers along the race course.
The week beginning 31st July saw the Ramsgate cruise calling in at Dover, Chatham and Brightlingsea with ten
boats taking part.
The Shotley trip took place as usual on the August Bank Holiday. Unfortunatley, however, the forecast was again
bad which resulted in only ten boats taking part.

3. Review of Racing and Prize Giving. Frank Burgess reported that, despite the poor weather, a full programme of races
had been run this year.

Clive Shenton reporting on the ECPR stated that it was on track for a record year with £9,800 being donated to the
Cirdan Trust which was £500 more than last year. He thanked everyone who helped, especially the cruiser owners for
manning the course. Next year’s race will be held on 17th July.

4. Election of Fleet Captain, Vice Fleet Captain and Race Officers. Roger Camp, fleet captain, John Walker vice captain
and Frank Burgess, race officer all declared their willingness to stand again and were duly re-elected.

Page 10

seventy on trailers which indicates a gradual trend towards the use of the travel hoist. Ray Ball discussed the coming
working party.

6. Tractors and Winches - Murray Bates. Murray stated that the haul out is now complete and had been problem free.
He reported that many boats had come out on weekdays which was helpful but reminded people that they must
maintain their trailers and cradles prior to haul out in order for it to run smoothly. He also reminded members that it is
incumbent on people booking tractor drivers to turn up on the day despite the weather. The club is hoping to have a
second hydraulic winch for next season.

7. Moorings and Haul Out - Peter Clayton. This year four moorings are being left in over the winter as a trial to monitor
their state in the spring. However some anchors that had already been retrieved had been found to have dragged
together. If this problem has then to be sorted in spring it will not actually save work. Other mooring systems are also
being investigated. Peter stated that people must contact drivers prior to haul out and launching during the preceding
week to state that they are absolutely ready which means that their trailer is ready to be moved immediately. He urged
people to be more considerate towards tractor drivers who freely give up their time to help others.

8. Chain - Don Holdsworth. Don stated that there are now two sizes, 14mm and 19 mm. The price of steel has rocketed
so chain will be dearer, possibly by 8%, however shackle prices should not change. Chain will be sold in metres and
money should be paid when taking delivery.

made in time and so it was decided that emails will be sent to people for whom addresses are known in order to alert
them to the club web site to order paint.

There will be another bowling evening on Thursday 10th February.
The fitting out supper will be held on Saturday 7th May and will be limited to a maximum of sixty people.
Brightlingsea Brian is retiring in January so a function will be organised on behalf of the cruiser fleet.
In respect of the May Bank Holiday shakedown cruise to Burnham there was some discussion of alternative
venues for the future but, at the present time, Burnham was felt to be the best venue.
A cruise to Brightlingsea will be held on 18th/19th June.
The Heybridge trip will be held on 2nd/3rd July.
The ECPR will take place over the weekend of the 16th/17th July.
A trip to Lowestoft/Norfolk Broads was suggested for the week beginning 30th July.
The Shotley trip will take place over the Bank Holiday weekend of 27th August.

The Medusa race will link with the Brightlingsea weekend and the Jackpot race with dinghies will be repeated. The
club will continue to join in with BJRC with Derek Gardner to co-ordinate. A new idea being mooted for this year will be
a longer race for bigger boats to tie in with Medusa.

There followed prize giving presented by Chris Davies.

Minutes
rd
of The Handicap Fleet AGM 2004
3 December 2004 at 20:00

1. Apologies. Martin Brooks, Jon Kidd, Angela Aries, Fenella Thomas, Clive Shenton

2. Racing Review 2004

• Kate Williams presented a brief analysis of race turnouts for the 2004 season.
• The extraction of separate morning and afternoon results to generate am and pm series results was not felt to be a
success. The aim had been to support and encourage racers who generally could only make one race on a given
Sunday by giving them a fighting chance of a good series result. In the event, most sailors made all or none of the
races on a given day. Morning and afternoon results were generally identical to those for the overall series. It was
felt that the additional work for the results secretary was not justified.

3. Racing Programme for 2005

• The am/pm series will not be repeated in 2005, but a number of new features to the 2005 racing programme were
discussed:
o The Summer Points series will now be split in two, giving an Early Summer and a Late Summer series.
This should lessen the number of people forced to count one or more DNC (Did Not Compete) scores in
their series result due to summer holiday absences.
o The first racing Sunday of the year will be a designated shakedown, with rigging time in the morning, and
single race in the afternoon.
o The last racing Sunday of the year will be a designated final fling, with a single race in the morning, and
de-rigging, de-masting and trailer loading time in the afternoon.
• Various ideas were discussed to build on racing turnout. These included:
o Plan and advertise in the year book one ot two “Racing for beginners” days. These should be held on
normal points racing Sundays. One or more fleet representatives would be designated to meet, greet and
show the ropes to members who would like to try racing, but need some pointers to get started.
o Lunchtime reps could be designated, especially in the high summer to talk with less frequent/experienced
club racers between races, to discuss courses, conditions, weather, boats or anything else helpful.
o Make special efforts to publicise one-off races.
o Use all available methods of communication to engage fleet members (website, Navigans, email,
noticeboards, etc).
ACTION – Fleet Captain to put ideas into practice in 2005!

4. Cruising
• Two cruising events were held in 2004. The first, an up-river cruise to Maldon, was organised by Dave Williams
and well supported. The latter down-river cruise was less well supported, and curtailed by an absence of wind.
• In an endeavour to build on the partial success of 2004, two cruising events were also agreed for 2005:
th
o 28 May 2005 - Down River Cruise (e.g. Mersea or Bradwell) – High Tide 17:02
th
o 20 August – Up River Cruise (e.g. Maldon, Mayland or Heybridge) – High Tide 13:58
• It was agreed that, subject to club management approval and levy of a small fee, more cruising classes should be
invited and encouraged to visit MSC. This would help to raise the club profile within classes, and put more club
members get more involved with their class associations.
ACTION - All to Consider contacting cruising sections of our own class associations with a view to setting dates in
2006.
• The idea of self-organised “class days” was muted. Some types of boat (GP14, Wanderer, Laser, etc) are well
supported within the handicap fleet. Cruising, racing or social events organised by owners of specific classes
could encourage more people to sail and build new friendships.
ACTION – Fleet Captain to assist organisers of these events to contact boat owners via the membership list.

5. Dinghy Park
The layout and general use of the dinghy park was discussed. Suggestions for 2005 included:
• Consider removing the gangway which runs through the dinghy park toward the club house door and utilise this
space to park dinghies. All boats could use the club roadway to access the hard as the large handicap fleet boats
already do.
• Use the actual count of boats in each size taken in 2004 as the basis of the dinghy park layout in 2005, rather than
the membership boat list, which is not complete at the time the dinghy park layout is set. Spaces for larger boats
were in especially short supply in 2004.
• Police the positioning of ‘large’ and ‘medium’ handicap boats, to ensure they park in the right areas, and within the
marked bays.
• Number spaces in each row consecutively (A1,A2,A3,A4,A5…), rather than having odd numbering/even
numbering for alternate rows.
• Make more noticeboard space provision in the club house to enable dinghy park plans and instructions to be fully
displayed and more easily maintained.
• The club could consider supplying suitable ground anchors (at a cost) for dinghy owners who do not have the
means to secure their boats.
ACTION – Fleet Captain to liase with the dinghy park coordinator.

6. Report from the Rear Commodore

Page 11
Claire Davies updated the AGM on a number issues and initiatives:
th th
• On the 11 and 12 of June, the Byte class nationals are coming to MSC. This is a popular class amongst our
younger sailors, and we can expect a good turnout from members and visitors. This will coincide with camping and
the club Summer Ball social.
• Claire is continuing to investigate ways in which the club might be able to offer and fund club boats for use by all
members. Options include leasing or fleet purchase & buy back agreements with major dinghy manufacturers. Its
early days yet and the case for more club boats has yet to be proved.
• The sailing sub committee would like to introduce at least one additional fixed race mark for 2005. This would give
Race Officers more flexibility in setting courses. Claire is in discussion with the river bailiff regarding acceptable
sites.

7. Election of Fleet Captain
David Ball was unanimously re-elected as fleet captain.

8. AOB
• It was noted that the hard had been especially slippery at times this year. Claire confirmed that scrubbing had
taken place. It was felt that is more dinghy sailors were qualified to drive club tractors, scrubbing could be
undertaken more frequently. New concrete chocolate blocks are now being manufactured to improve grip at
smooth concrete sections.
• It was noted that the Jack B did not always appear to have a pair of binoculars on board. Claire Davies confirmed
that equipment would be checked as part of the planned review of support boat code-of-practice documents this
winter.
• The level of support boat cover at certain events was discussed. The club’s own guidelines in general require a
ratio of 1 support boat to 20 competing dinghies or catamarans.

The need to call out the coastguard or lifeboat is something

arises, we will only ever feel some guilt for the fact that our
lack of forethought or preparation has caused others to put
themselves at risk. I think and hope that this is a view
widely shared – but recent events make me feel the need
to mention it now.

We all see the BJRC events in the MSC year book and
notices around the club, but quite often cruiser owners are
not too sure what it is all about. Well here is your chance

The Blackwater Joint Racing Committee was formed
around thirty years ago and is open to members of any
RYA affiliated Sailing Club on the river Blackwater. Its
aims are to promote friendly racing between the members
of the clubs by holding eight events annually, with each
event being sponsored by one of the participating clubs.

A View From The Rear
Well, here we are at the beginning of another sailing
season. You will have received your yearbooks by now and
seen the programme, but we are ringing the changes right
at the start of the season. Nothing radical, just tweaks, I
promise! The first race of the season will be a one-off
event, the early season equivalent of the final fling. It will be
a single, all-in handicap race, with a late start after a spot of
communal boat-moving and -rigging and some warming
brunch from the galley. Our early Easter this year was an
opportunity to look at the Bank Holiday series, which
always has plenty of entries but not many real contenders
as so many of us go away for the Bank Holidays. So we
have removed one from the equation, racing instead for
Easter Eggs over the second weekend of racing. A few
more 'tweaks' to come as the season progresses, which we
hope you will agree improves rather than detracts from the
quality of our Sunday Sailing programme.

Not all our dinghy sailors race: some don't like to, some
can't make Sundays, some have never raced. For that last
group of sailors, the handicap fleet will be laying on a
couple of 'racing for beginners' events during the season.
These will be an informal opportunity to join some
seasoned racers observing the activities and learning the
basics from the shore before trying it on the water.

Please can I remind all of you who volunteered on your
renewals to support club sailing in support boats or in the
race box to check the rotas. They are all here in this
Navigans, and will shortly be on the website too, as is the
programme. Please make sure that you put the date in your
diaries as soon as possible. Without your valuable support
we cannot put on the varied programme to which we
aspire.

Finally, on a more personal note, I should let you know
that, due to a change of job, I will be moving away from the
area and will have to stand down as Rear Commodore. I
am very grateful to Clive Shenton for agreeing to a change
of 'portfolio' mid-term to take back the sailing agenda he
thought he had left behind. I am not disappearing
immediately, and will continue the duties until I have to give
up. I will be around regularly for the early season, and you
can't get rid of me that easily anyway!

Happy sailing - I look forward to seeing you on the water.

Claire Davies
Rear Commodore (Sailing)
